design_detail: Population-based nested case–control study in Ontario, Canada, 1 August 1997 to 31 December 2013, within the cohort of people eligible for the Ontario Public Drug Programs who were dispensed opioid analgesics (2,914,971 people). Cases: accidental opioid-related deaths confirmed by the Office of the Chief Coroner (autopsy, toxicology), suicides and homicides excluded; 1,256 of 1,391 eligible cases matched to 4,619 controls by incidence density sampling (up to 4 per case) on a disease risk index, age, sex, index year and chronic kidney disease. Exposure: at least one gabapentin prescription in the 120 days before the index date; secondary analyses by daily dose; prespecified negative-control exposure (NSAIDs). Conditional logistic regression adjusted for opioid dose and other covariates. Read in full as PMC HTML (PMC5626029): text, Table 1, Fig 2 (forest plot; its counts and odds ratios read on a screenshot of the image) and the competing-interest statement (author notes). Fig 1 (flow diagram, image) not read in detail. Supplements (RECORD checklist, S1 Table with the disease risk index components, S1 Text analytical plan) are Word downloads and were not opened.
can_establish: Whether, among Ontario public-drug-plan recipients of opioid analgesics, people who died an accidental opioid-related death were more often recently dispensed gabapentin than matched living controls, after adjustment for opioid dose and other recorded medicines and conditions, and whether this held at different prescribed gabapentin doses.
cannot_establish: That gabapentin causes the excess deaths rather than marking why it was prescribed or unrecorded drug use; the absolute risk of death with and without gabapentin (case–control data give no rates); anything about pregabalin, which was too rarely prescribed in this period.

sample.recruitment: Registry/records: Ontario Drug Benefit claims, physician billing (OHIP), hospital and emergency-department abstracts (CIHI), Registered Persons Database, cancer and diabetes registries, and coroner's records of opioid-related deaths, linked at ICES (Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Eligible for public drug coverage (people aged 65 or over, unemployed, receiving disability benefits, with high drug costs relative to income, receiving home care, or in long-term care); aged 15–105; at least one opioid prescription (oral morphine, codeine, oxycodone, meperidine, hydromorphone, or transdermal fentanyl; methadone and rarely used, parenteral or intranasal opioids excluded) overlapping the index date; at least 6 months of continuous eligibility; excluded invalid identifiers, prior cancer and palliative care in the previous 6 months (Methods › Setting; Identification of patients and outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: 94.5% of cases and 94.2% of controls were under 65; mean age 47.5 and 47.8 years; men 57.0% and 56.7%; lowest income quintile 42.1% and 43.8%; anxiety or sleep disorder diagnoses 81.8% in both; history of alcohol use disorder 26.0% and 23.3% (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records-based). 135 of 1,391 potential cases (9.7%, editors' calculation) could not be matched to any control and were excluded; their characteristics are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A low-income, mostly working-age population on social assistance or disability benefits, eligible for public drug coverage; the authors caution that results may not generalize to all people prescribed opioids (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Prescriptions paid privately, in cash or bought illicitly are not seen.

exposure.measurement: Ontario Drug Benefit dispensing records: at least one gabapentin prescription in the 120 days before the index date; post hoc, a prescription whose days' supply overlapped the index date. Adherence and non-prescribed supply unknown (Methods › Exposure definition; Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: prescribed daily gabapentin dose grouped as low (<900 mg), moderate (900–1,799 mg) and high (≥1,800 mg), following the product monograph's effective range; post hoc very high (≥2,500 mg). Opioid dose at the index date in morphine milligram equivalents (<20, 20–49, 50–99, 100–199, ≥200 MME) as a covariate (Methods › Exposure definition; Patient characteristics, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Recent benzodiazepines, SSRIs, other antidepressants, other psychotropic drugs or CNS depressants, pregabalin and methadone or buprenorphine (each in the prior 120 days) were adjusted for, as were alcohol use disorder and the numbers of opioid prescribers and pharmacies; 24 cases (1.9%) had heroin on toxicology, fewer than 6 of them with gabapentin; other illicit drug use not measured (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Up to 4 living opioid recipients per case from the same cohort, sampled by incidence density at the case's index date.
comparison.matching: Disease risk index (predicted probability of opioid-related death from demographic, medical and psychiatric characteristics; within 0.2 SD), age (within 5 years), sex, year of index date (within 1 year) and chronic kidney disease in the prior 5 years (Methods › Identification of patients and outcomes, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The indication for gabapentin (pain type and severity, anxiety, other uses) is unknown, as the authors state; non-prescribed drug use and opioid use disorder are captured only through proxies (methadone or buprenorphine, numbers of prescribers and pharmacies); the components of the disease risk index are in an unread supplement.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls were also opioid recipients; after matching, cases had more benzodiazepines (77.3% against 56.4%), antidepressants and high opioid doses (Table 1), all adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Coroner-confirmed opioid-related death (all sudden or unexpected deaths in Ontario are investigated, with interviews, autopsy and post-mortem toxicology), including deaths from opioids combined with other drugs or alcohol; suicides and homicides excluded (Methods › Data sources; Identification of patients and outcomes, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors call the coroner's data regularly used for opioid deaths in Ontario and cite a validation of administrative mortality data; not validated in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Accidental death to which opioids contributed, alone or with other substances; all cases had prescription opioids on toxicology.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; one outcome, one primary exposure, a dose analysis, two post hoc and one prespecified negative-control analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: coroners investigated independently of the study, though they could know the person's medicines.

analysis.effect_sizes: Recent gabapentin: 155 of 1,256 cases (12.3%) against 313 of 4,619 controls (6.8%); conditional OR 1.99 (95% CI 1.61–2.47); adjusted OR 1.49 (1.18–1.88). Days' supply overlapping the index date: aOR 1.46 (1.12–1.89). Dose: low 1.32 (0.89–1.97 in Fig 2; 0.89–1.96 in text), moderate 1.56 (1.06–2.28), high 1.58 (1.09–2.27); post hoc ≥2,500 mg 1.83 (1.04–3.22). Negative control, NSAIDs: aOR 1.14 (0.98–1.32). Case–control odds ratios from incidence density sampling estimate rate ratios; no absolute rates.
analysis.covariates: Opioid dose; age; prior-120-day pregabalin, SSRIs, other antidepressants, benzodiazepines, other psychotropic drugs or CNS depressants, methadone or buprenorphine; number of drugs in 6 months; long-acting opioid; alcohol use disorder (3 years); Charlson index; chronic lung disease; diabetes; numbers of opioid prescribers and pharmacies in 6 months. The NSAID model also adjusts for gabapentin.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A study protocol and an analytical plan (S1 Text) were approved by the Sunnybrook research ethics board; the plan was not read; two analyses are labelled post hoc and the NSAID analysis prespecified.
analysis.selective_reporting: Counts behind the post hoc very-high-dose estimate are not given; the reference category for the dose analysis is no gabapentin, and no test for trend is reported.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the dose-specific intervals are wide (about 40–60 exposed cases per dose group).

interpretation_gap.results_show: After matching and adjustment, recent gabapentin dispensing was associated with about 1.5 times the odds of accidental opioid-related death among opioid recipients (aOR 1.49, 1.18–1.88), similar when the gabapentin supply overlapped the death date (1.46). By dose, the adjusted odds ratios were 1.32 (not significant), 1.56 and 1.58, with widely overlapping intervals; the post hoc very-high-dose estimate was 1.83 (1.04–3.22). The negative-control NSAID estimate was 1.14 (0.98–1.32).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that gabapentin was associated with a substantial increase in risk; the discussion says the findings “support the existence of a life-threatening drug–drug interaction” (Discussion, 1st paragraph) and explains it by additive respiratory depression and a pharmacokinetic effect drawn from other studies; the conclusion adds particularly at higher doses, although the authors themselves say the dose–response suggestion should be interpreted with caution. The NSAID result is read as no association, though its interval allows up to a 32% increase, and as evidence against confounding by indication, which it addresses for pain severity but not for gabapentin misuse or unmeasured drug use. Clinical recommendations follow.

timeline.event: Gomes et al. (Ann Intern Med), pregabalin and opioid-related death in Ontario, a nested case–control study by the same group; described by Macleod et al. (2019) as also finding increased risk; not read (DOI list item 16).

Macleod et al. (PLOS Med), UK people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment: gabapentinoid prescription not clearly associated with drug-poisoning death (hazard ratio 1.54, 0.60–3.98; 5 deaths) but associated with deaths from other causes (1.83)

replication.where_it_stands: The only study read that estimates gabapentin with opioid analgesics; the UK treatment cohort is a different population, too small for drug-poisoning deaths, and its excess in non-poisoning deaths points to confounding by health. No independent replication in people prescribed opioid analgesics has been read.

funding.funder: Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care (MOHLTC; grant 06673; TG, DNJ, MMM); the funders had no role in design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript (Funding Statement). The acknowledgments state that no endorsement by ICES or the Ministry is intended and that parts of the data come from CIHI.
funding.declared_conflicts: TA: CIHR New Investigator Award. DNJ: expert opinion on medicolegal matters, some involving opioids, never paid work for or against opioid manufacturers; such income tithed to the Sunnybrook Department of Medicine. MMM: advisory boards and honoraria from Bristol-Myers Squibb, Eli Lilly, GlaxoSmithKline, Hoffmann-La Roche, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, Pfizer and AstraZeneca, outside the submitted work. WvdB: honoraria from Lundbeck, Indivior, Mundipharma, Novartis, Bioproject, Eli Lilly and Pfizer. Others none (author notes).
funding.affiliations_note: Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute and Department of Medicine, St Michael's Hospital; ICES; University of Toronto (health policy, pharmacy, medicine, family and community medicine); Sunnybrook Research Institute; McMaster University; Department of Psychiatry, Academic Medical Center, University of Amsterdam.

what_would_settle_it: An active-comparator cohort of people on stable opioid therapy who newly start gabapentin against people who newly start a non-sedating adjuvant for neuropathic pain, with measured substance use disorders, coroner-confirmed outcomes and gabapentin dose trajectories; or a self-controlled case series comparing each person's periods on and off gabapentin, which removes stable confounders.

domains.note: Matched on a disease risk index, age, sex, year and kidney disease, and adjusted for opioid dose, benzodiazepines, antidepressants, other CNS depressants, alcohol use disorder and proxies for misuse (numbers of prescribers and pharmacies, methadone or buprenorphine); the NSAID negative control (1.14, 0.98–1.32) argues against large confounding by pain severity. Remaining: the indication for gabapentin, gabapentin misuse and unmeasured drug use, which the negative control does not address.
Any dispensing in 120 days, public-plan retail prescriptions only; adherence and non-prescribed supply unknown; the overlap-with-index analysis gave a similar estimate (1.46).
Public drug plan population; 9.7% of eligible cases unmatched and excluded without description; controls by incidence density sampling from the same cohort (appropriate).
Not a concern for a 120-day exposure window before death.
Records-based; missing income (0.6%) and residence (0.2%) handled as separate categories.
Coroner-confirmed with toxicology, a strength; attribution of a death to opioids could be more likely when another sedating medicine is found or known, which would bias towards an association.
A protocol and analytical plan exist but were not read; two post hoc analyses (very high dose, overlap) are reported alongside the prespecified ones; no trend test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No domain is judged high: the design (coroner-confirmed accidental deaths, controls from the same cohort, matching on a disease risk index, adjustment for opioid dose and other sedating medicines, a negative-control exposure) addresses the main threats better than the other prescription studies read in this batch. Concerns remain in five domains, chiefly unmeasured indication and drug use, which could make the true association smaller but are not judged likely to remove it. The study may be cited for the adjusted association between recent gabapentin dispensing and accidental opioid-related death among public-drug-plan opioid recipients in Ontario, and for the weak and imprecise dose pattern; not for a causal interaction, a dose–response relation, pregabalin, or absolute risk.

key_findings.finding: Nested case–control study among Ontario Public Drug Programs recipients of opioid analgesics, 1 August 1997 to 31 December 2013; public drug coverage covers people aged 65 or over and people who are unemployed, on disability benefits, with high drug costs relative to income, in home care or in long-term care. Opioids included oral morphine, codeine, oxycodone, meperidine and hydromorphone and transdermal fentanyl; methadone excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Setting, 1st paragraph; Identification of patients and outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cases: opioid-related deaths confirmed by the coroner (interviews, autopsy, post-mortem toxicology), suicides and homicides excluded; index date the date of death; controls given random index dates following the cases' distribution; cancer and recent palliative care excluded; all participants had an opioid prescription overlapping the index date and at least 6 months of eligibility. Matching by incidence density sampling, up to 4 controls per case, on disease risk index (within 0.2 SD), age (within 5 years), sex, index year (within 1 year) and chronic kidney disease.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph; Identification of patients and outcomes, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Exposure: at least one gabapentin prescription in the 120 days before the index date; daily dose low (<900 mg), moderate (900–1,799 mg) or high (≥1,800 mg); post hoc very high (≥2,500 mg) and days' supply overlapping the index date; prespecified negative control: NSAIDs in the prior 120 days.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Exposure definition, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conditional logistic regression adjusted for opioid dose, age, prior-120-day pregabalin, SSRIs, other antidepressants, benzodiazepines, other psychotropic drugs or CNS depressants and methadone or buprenorphine, number of drugs in 6 months, long-acting opioid, alcohol use disorder in 3 years, Charlson index, chronic lung disease, diabetes, and numbers of opioid prescribers and pharmacies in 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 2,914,971 eligible opioid recipients, 1,391 potential cases met the criteria and 1,256 (90.3%) were matched to at least one control, giving 4,619 controls. All cases had prescription opioids on post-mortem toxicology; 24 (1.9%) also had heroin, fewer than 6 of them with recent gabapentin.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cases against controls (Table 1): under 65 years 94.5% and 94.2%; lowest income quintile 42.1% and 43.8%; opioid dose ≥200 MME daily 39.5% and 20.5% (standardized difference 0.42); long-acting opioid 62.4% and 39.6% (0.47); benzodiazepines in the prior 120 days 971 (77.3%) and 2,604 (56.4%) (0.46); SSRIs 45.1% and 36.6%; other antidepressants 49.5% and 37.6%; other psychotropic drugs or CNS depressants 35.7% and 25.8%; methadone or buprenorphine 6.2% and 4.6%; alcohol use disorder 26.0% and 23.3%; anxiety or sleep disorders 81.8% in both.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: These are descriptive comparisons after matching; no adjusted estimate for benzodiazepines is reported.

key_findings.finding: Gabapentin in the prior 120 days: 155 of 1,256 cases (12.3%) and 313 of 4,619 controls (6.8%); unadjusted OR 1.99 (95% CI 1.61–2.47); adjusted OR 1.49 (1.18–1.88), p < 0.001. With days' supply overlapping the index date: 121 (9.6%) and 240 (5.2%); OR 1.98 (1.56–2.50); aOR 1.46 (1.12–1.89), p = 0.005.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig 2 (forest plot, read on screenshot)

key_findings.finding: By prescribed daily gabapentin dose, against no gabapentin: low 41 cases (3.3%) and 101 controls (2.2%), OR 1.70 (1.17–2.48), aOR 1.32 (0.89–1.97); moderate 57 (4.5%) and 111 (2.4%), OR 2.05 (1.46–2.87), aOR 1.56 (1.06–2.28), p = 0.024; high 57 (4.5%) and 101 (2.2%), OR 2.20 (1.58–3.08), aOR 1.58 (1.09–2.27), p = 0.015. Post hoc, very high dose (≥2,500 mg daily): aOR 1.83 (1.04–3.22), p = 0.036.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Fig 2 (forest plot, read on screenshot)
key_findings.note: The text gives the low-dose interval as 0.89 to 1.96, the figure 0.89 to 1.97. The authors say the intervals overlap considerably and the dose–response suggestion should be read with caution (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Negative-control exposure: NSAIDs in the prior 120 days, 480 cases (38.2%) and 1,647 controls (35.7%); OR 1.11 (0.98–1.27); aOR 1.14 (0.98–1.32), p = 0.083.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Results, 5th paragraph; Fig 2

key_findings.finding: Of 98,288 people dispensed gabapentin in Ontario's public drug plan in 2013, 45,173 (46.0%) received at least one concomitant opioid prescription.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph; Results, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: public drug plan population, mostly under 65 and of low income; only government-reimbursed retail prescriptions; adherence, cash or illicit purchases and use as prescribed unknown; overlapping dose intervals; indication for gabapentin unknown; cases and controls differed on several measured covariates; confounding by indication possible, which the authors argue against on four grounds (risk-index matching, opioid-dose adjustment, adjustment for severity markers and exclusions, the NSAID result).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The prevalence of gabapentin co-prescription among opioid recipients is given as approximately 8% (Results, 6th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph) and as almost 10% (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); both come from the matched cases and controls (468 of 5,875 is 8.0%, editors' calculation), a sample that over-represents people who died.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither figure estimates how many opioid recipients in Ontario were co-prescribed gabapentin; only the 2013 figure (46.0% of people dispensed gabapentin had an opioid) is a population description.

reporting_issues.issue: The low-dose adjusted interval is 0.89 to 1.96 in the text and 0.89 to 1.97 in Fig 2; the abstract and author summary call the moderate and high doses a nearly 60% increase and the conclusion says particularly at higher doses, while the post hoc very-high-dose result (1.83) has no counts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the dose pattern should be cited as weak and imprecise, not as a dose–response relation.

reporting_issues.issue: 135 of 1,391 eligible cases (9.7%) were not matched and were excluded; how they differed from matched cases is not reported in the text (the flow diagram is an image).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor possibility of selection bias if unmatched cases (likely those with extreme risk indices) differed in gabapentin exposure.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5626029 (PMC HTML, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, author summary, all sections, Table 1, Fig 2 forest plot (counts and odds ratios read on a screenshot of the image), figure legends, funding, data availability, acknowledgments, reference list; the competing-interest statement and affiliations were read from the collapsed author notes with javascript_tool. Supplements (Word files) were not opened.

design_detail: Records-based cohort from the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD; 674 general practices), 1 January 1998 to 31 July 2014, of 12,118 people aged 15–64 prescribed methadone or buprenorphine as opioid agonist treatment (OAT) in primary care, with linkage to Office for National Statistics (ONS) death registrations for a subset in England (about 7,100 people). Follow-up was split into episodes on OAT and off OAT (up to 1 year after a prescription ended; a gap of more than 28 days started a new episode), and into periods on and off prescribed benzodiazepines, z-drugs and gabapentinoids (14-day gap rule). Linear regression related concurrent prescription to OAT episode duration; Cox models related co-prescription (during OAT or up to 12 months after) and concurrent prescription (during OAT) to all-cause mortality, drug-related poisoning (DRP) deaths and other deaths, adjusted for sex, age, year, a chronic-illness comorbidity index, region, OAT type and OAT period. The authors call it an observational study based on administrative data; the records were collected prospectively and analysed retrospectively. Read in full as PMC HTML (PMC6879111), including Tables 1–6 and the author notes (competing interests); supplements (protocol, patient flowchart, S1–S6 Tables, Stata appendix) are Word files and were not opened; the full NIHR report with prespecified analyses is cited but was not read.
can_establish: Whether, among people prescribed methadone or buprenorphine in UK general practice, periods with a prescribed benzodiazepine, z-drug or gabapentinoid carry higher adjusted death rates (overall, from drug poisoning, and from other causes), whether the association with drug poisoning rises with prescribed benzodiazepine dose, and whether OAT episodes with these prescriptions last longer.
cannot_establish: That the prescribed sedatives cause the excess drug-poisoning deaths rather than marking the people who receive them (heavier illicit benzodiazepine or alcohol use, mental illness), which were not measured; anything about prescriptions from specialist services, prisons or non-prescribed sources.

sample.recruitment: Registry/records: CPRD primary-care records (about 7% of the UK population, described by the authors as broadly representative of England) with ONS death registrations for a subset of English practices (Methods › OAT patients; Deaths).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methadone or buprenorphine prescriptions in primary care; excluded people prescribed them for pain (by diagnosis and formulation), people whose daily doses were below the minimum the authors expected for OAT (study condition: 20 mg methadone or 4 mg buprenorphine), and people aged under 15 or over 64 at the start, leaving 667,288 prescriptions for 12,118 patients: 65% methadone only, 22% buprenorphine only, 13% both (Methods › OAT patients, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Two-thirds men (67.3%); mean age at exit 38.8 years (SD 10.4); median follow-up 2.07 years (IQR 1.03–4.79); 31.4% with a recorded chronic comorbidity at exit; ever prescribed a benzodiazepine 46.8%, a z-drug 24.0%, a gabapentinoid 8.8%. People who died of drug poisoning: 87.6% men, mean age 37.0; people who died of other causes: 61.4% men, mean age 51.9 (Results › Study participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Records-based; follow-up ended at the earliest of study end, last CPRD collection, leaving the practice, death, or 1 year after the end of the last OAT episode. First observed episodes may be left-censored (Methods › OAT episodes, 2nd paragraph). Cause of death was available only for the ONS-linked subset.
sample.selection_effects: People whose OAT is prescribed in general practice (shared care); OAT and sedatives prescribed by specialist services or in prison are not in CPRD. Cause-specific analyses rest on the ONS-linked English subset. Exclusion of low-dose prescriptions may exclude some people in treatment.

exposure.measurement: Primary-care prescription records of 10 benzodiazepines (365,582 prescriptions), 3 z-drugs (zaleplon, zolpidem, zopiclone; 75,926) and 2 gabapentinoids (23,451), turned into treatment episodes; co-prescription counts any period on the sedative during OAT or within 12 months after an OAT episode; concurrent prescription counts only periods during OAT (Methods › Additionally prescribed medications; Introduction, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: benzodiazepine and z-drug doses classed as normal or high, high meaning a daily dose above the maximum recommended in the British National Formulary (S2 Table, not read); gabapentinoids on or off only (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit opioid, benzodiazepine and other drug use and alcohol use were not measured; the authors note that non-prescribed sedatives could not be measured and argue that this would dilute any association (Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph). Each sedative class was adjusted for the others.

comparison.controls: Periods in the same cohort without a prescription of the sedative class (on and off OAT), within the same Cox models.
comparison.matching: None; adjustment for sex, age, year of treatment, comorbidity index (17 chronic illnesses weighted 1–6, time-varying), UK region, OAT type, OAT period and the other sedative exposures (Methods › Confounding factors).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental-health diagnoses (anxiety, depression, psychosis), alcohol dependence, illicit drug use (including non-prescribed benzodiazepines), injecting, homelessness, deprivation and recent prison release, all plausible reasons both for being prescribed sedatives and for drug-poisoning death. The authors say propensity scores added little in their earlier work and that no suitable instrument was found.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Everyone was in or recently in OAT; other drug use in either group unknown.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality from CPRD records; drug-related poisoning and other causes from ONS primary and secondary causes of death, with ICD-9/ICD-10 codes based on ONS definitions extended for possible under-reporting under non-specific or unknown causes (S1 Table, not read) (Methods › Deaths).
outcomes.validity_norms: National death registration; the extended code list is not shown in the article.
outcomes.operationalization: Death from drug-related poisoning (any drug), from other causes, or from any cause.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: three mortality outcomes plus treatment duration, three drug classes, co-prescription and concurrent-prescription analyses, dose and interaction analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: death registration independent of the study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Benzodiazepine co-prescription and DRP: 39 deaths in 3,679 person-years (1.06 per 100 person-years) on against 74 in 16,270 (0.45) off; unadjusted HR 2.35 (1.59–3.47), adjusted 2.96 (1.97–4.43); normal dose 2.51 (1.57–4.01), high dose 4.57 (2.46–8.47); linear trend 2.22 (1.69–2.92). All-cause 1.17 (0.97–1.42); other causes 0.91 (0.66–1.25). Z-drugs DRP 2.75 (1.57–4.83), all-cause 1.26 (0.94–1.69), other 0.79 (0.49–1.28). Gabapentinoids DRP 1.54 (0.60–3.98), all-cause 1.71 (1.33–2.20), other 1.83 (1.28–2.62). Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription (Table 6): DRP 3.34 (2.14–5.20), all-cause 1.87 (1.55–2.25), other 1.73 (1.28–2.33). OAT episode duration with concurrent benzodiazepine 416 against 244 days (adjusted means).
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching; the footnotes to Tables 4–6 list sex, year, comorbidity, region, OAT type and OAT period and the other sedatives, without age.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The protocol was reviewed by the CPRD Independent Scientific Advisory Committee (protocol 14_073R2) and the full NIHR report with prespecified analyses is published; neither was read, so deviations cannot be checked (Methods › Study protocol and pre-specified analyses).
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity analyses (Poisson regression, excluding first episodes, competing risks) are only in unread supplements, described as similar. Gabapentinoid results are omitted from Table 6 because they showed no effect on treatment duration.
analysis.power: The authors call the gabapentinoid DRP analyses underpowered (5 exposed deaths); z-drug dose estimates rest on 10 and 5 deaths, high-dose benzodiazepine on 14.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this primary-care OAT cohort, periods with a prescribed benzodiazepine had about three times the adjusted rate of drug-poisoning death (2.96), higher above the formulary's maximum dose (4.57 against 2.51), similar during and in the year after OAT, with no clear excess in all-cause mortality in the same model (1.17) and none in other deaths (0.91). Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription was associated with longer OAT episodes and, in a separate model, with higher drug-poisoning (3.34), all-cause (1.87) and other-cause (1.73) mortality. Z-drugs were associated with drug-poisoning death (2.75) without a dose gradient; gabapentinoids with other deaths (1.83) but not clearly with drug poisoning.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that benzodiazepine co-prescription was specifically associated with drug-poisoning death, and the discussion says benzodiazepines increased drug-poisoning mortality about threefold and that the paper provides the strongest evidence available that benzodiazepine co-prescription “is of itself a cause of increased risk of death from DRP” (Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 1st paragraph). The specificity argument rests on Table 4 (other deaths 0.91), but Table 6 shows an excess in other deaths with concurrent prescription (1.73); the statement that adjustment did not reduce the estimates holds for a covariate set without mental-health, alcohol or illicit-drug measures. The author summary is more cautious (may cause; people prescribed benzodiazepines may differ in unmeasured ways).

timeline.event: Park et al. (BMJ), US veterans prescribed opioid analgesics, not people in OAT: benzodiazepine prescription associated with overdose death (adjusted hazard ratio 3.86); cited among North American studies (refs 20–21)
Sun et al. (BMJ), privately insured US adults: overlapping benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions associated with hospital-treated opioid overdose

Gomes et al. (PLOS Med), Ontario: gabapentin with opioid analgesics associated with accidental opioid-related death (adjusted odds ratio 1.49); one of two Canadian case–control studies cited (refs 23–24)

Earlier studies described in this paper and not read: a Scottish study of people prescribed methadone (ref. 10) with no clear excess in all-cause mortality but an excess in drug-related poisoning (HR 4.35, 1.32–14.30) with co-prescribed benzodiazepines; a Swedish register study (ref. 22) linking benzodiazepines, z-drugs and pregabalin with mortality in OAT, more strongly for all-cause than drug-poisoning deaths.

replication.where_it_stands: In people in OAT, the excess in drug-poisoning deaths with prescribed benzodiazepines agrees in direction with the Scottish study the authors describe; the specificity to poisoning deaths differs between this paper's own tables and from the Swedish study. All are records-based without measures of illicit drug or alcohol use.

what_would_settle_it: A linked cohort of people in OAT (primary care, specialist services and prisons) with recorded mental-health diagnoses, alcohol use and urine toxicology for non-prescribed benzodiazepines, comparing people who start a prescribed benzodiazepine with similar people who do not (target-trial emulation), or a randomized trial of benzodiazepine maintenance against tapering in people in OAT who use benzodiazepines, with drug-poisoning deaths and retention as outcomes.

domains.note: Adjustment was limited to sex, age, year, a comorbidity index of 17 chronic illnesses (components not listed in the article), region and treatment variables; mental-health diagnoses, alcohol, illicit drug use (including non-prescribed benzodiazepines), deprivation, homelessness and prison release, which plausibly lead both to sedative prescribing and to poisoning death, were not measured. Adjustment moved estimates away from the null (DRP 2.35 to 2.96; concurrent all-cause 1.22 to 1.87), which the measured covariates cannot explain as removal of confounding.

Primary-care prescriptions, not use; sedatives from specialist services, prisons or illicit sources unrecorded; co-prescription includes up to 12 months after OAT; high dose defined by the formulary maximum.
People in primary-care OAT only; low-dose OAT and ages over 64 excluded; first episodes left-censored; cause-of-death analyses limited to the ONS-linked English subset.

Treatment duration is affected by the exposure (longer episodes with benzodiazepines) and affects mortality; the concurrent-prescription analysis addresses this in part; changes in OAT dose and supervision are not considered.
Cause of death known for the linked subset only (7,106 of 12,118; the abstract says 7,016); linked and unlinked people are compared only descriptively in Table 1.
National death registration with a published code list extended for non-specific causes; misclassification between poisoning and other deaths is possible but unlikely to depend on prescriptions.

A reviewed protocol and prespecified analyses exist but were not read; inconsistencies between Tables 4 and 6 and misattached p-values (see reporting issues) leave doubt about which results represent the primary analysis.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because the confounders most likely to explain the association (illicit benzodiazepine and alcohol use, mental illness) were not measured, and adjustment for the measured ones increased rather than reduced the estimates. The study may be cited for the adjusted association between prescribed benzodiazepines (and z-drugs) and drug-poisoning death in people in primary-care OAT, its absolute rates, the prescribed-dose gradient for benzodiazepines, the longer OAT episodes, and the imprecise gabapentinoid results; not for a causal effect or for the claim that the excess is specific to poisoning deaths.

key_findings.finding: From 49,279 CPRD patients prescribed methadone or buprenorphine between 1 January 1998 and 31 July 2014, the authors excluded 26,324 prescribed them for pain and 9,950 whose doses were below the minimum expected for OAT (at least 20 mg methadone or 4 mg buprenorphine per day), and people aged under 15 or over 64, leaving 667,288 prescriptions for 12,118 patients (65% methadone only, 22% buprenorphine only, 13% both).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods and findings); Methods › OAT patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Follow-up was divided into OAT episodes (a gap of more than 28 days started a new one) and off-treatment periods up to 1 year after a prescription ended; sedative treatment episodes used a 14-day gap; there were 365,582 benzodiazepine, 75,926 z-drug and 23,451 gabapentinoid prescriptions. Adjustment: sex, age, year, a time-varying comorbidity index of 17 chronic illnesses, UK region, OAT type, OAT period and the other sedative exposures.
key_findings.locator: Methods › OAT episodes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Additionally prescribed medications; Confounding factors

key_findings.finding: Deaths from all causes came from CPRD; causes from ONS for a subset in England, with drug-related poisoning defined from ONS codes extended for non-specific causes, and other deaths analysed separately.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Deaths, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 29,540 OAT episodes (17,391 methadone, median 0.30 years; 9,180 buprenorphine, median 0.11 years; 2,969 with more than one drug); 36,126 person-years; 657 deaths. In the ONS-linked subset (7,106 patients), 113 drug-related poisoning deaths (87.6% men, mean age 37.0) and 285 other deaths (61.4% men, mean age 51.9). Concurrent benzodiazepine prescription with OAT: 42.2% of all patients, 61.9% of those who died of drug poisoning and 47.0% of those who died of other causes; concurrent gabapentinoid prescription: 7.6% of all patients and 31.6% of those who died of other causes.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Data characteristics, 1st paragraph; Study participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine co-prescription among patients on OAT fell from 43% (95% CI 40%–46%) in 1998 to 28% (26%–29%) in 2014; z-drug co-prescription stayed at 13% (11%–15%); gabapentinoid co-prescription rose from 0.5% (0.1%–1.1%) to 12% (11%–14%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence of co-prescription over time, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adjusted mean OAT episode duration: no concurrent prescription 244 days (236–252); concurrent benzodiazepine 416 (404–429); z-drug 441 (421–461); gabapentinoid 189 (159–219). For methadone: 286 (275–297) without and 466 (450–483) with a benzodiazepine. Adjusted log-duration coefficients: benzodiazepine 0.48 (0.42 to 0.54), z-drug 0.77 (0.69 to 0.85), gabapentinoid 0.23 (0.10 to 0.36).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Association of concurrent prescription of benzodiazepines, z-drugs, and gabapentinoids with duration of OAT episodes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Drug-related poisoning deaths by benzodiazepine co-prescription: off 74 deaths in 16,270 person-years (0.45 per 100), on 39 in 3,679 (1.06); unadjusted HR 2.35 (1.59–3.47), adjusted HR 2.96 (1.97–4.43), p < 0.001. Normal dose 25 deaths in 2,889 person-years (0.87), adjusted HR 2.51 (1.57–4.01); high dose 14 in 790 (1.77), adjusted HR 4.57 (2.46–8.47); linear effect of dose adjusted HR 2.22 (1.69–2.92).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Associations of co-prescription with mortality › Benzodiazepines, 1st paragraph; Table 4, DRP rows

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality by benzodiazepine co-prescription: 144 deaths in 7,361 person-years (1.96 per 100) on against 513 in 28,766 (1.78) off; adjusted HR 1.17 (0.97–1.42). Other (non-DRP) deaths: 50 in 3,757 (1.33) against 235 in 16,628 (1.41); adjusted HR 0.91 (0.66–1.25).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Table 4, all-cause and non-DRP rows

key_findings.finding: Z-drug co-prescription: DRP 15 deaths in 1,110 person-years (1.35 per 100) against 98 in 18,838 (0.52), adjusted HR 2.75 (1.57–4.83); normal dose 10 deaths, adjusted HR 3.66 (1.86–7.19); high dose 5 deaths, 1.55 (0.59–4.06); all-cause 1.26 (0.94–1.69); other deaths 0.79 (0.49–1.28).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Z-drugs and gabapentinoids, 1st paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Gabapentinoid co-prescription: DRP 5 deaths in 538 person-years (0.93 per 100) against 108 in 19,410 (0.56), adjusted HR 1.54 (0.60–3.98), p = 0.373; all-cause 83 deaths in 998 person-years (8.32 per 100) against 574 in 35,129 (1.63), unadjusted HR 2.79 (2.20–3.54), adjusted 1.71 (1.33–2.20); other deaths 46 in 571 (8.06 per 100) against 239 in 19,815 (1.21), adjusted HR 1.83 (1.28–2.62); no dose analysis possible.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Z-drugs and gabapentinoids, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: In the PMC HTML rendering of Table 4, the non-DRP rows for z-drugs and gabapentinoids carry labels shifted by one row; the values above follow the pattern of the other blocks and the text.

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine co-prescription and DRP by OAT period: on OAT, 20 deaths in 2,914 person-years (0.69 per 100) against 24 in 10,091 (0.24), adjusted HR 2.92 (1.60–5.33); off OAT (up to a year after), 19 in 764 (2.49) against 50 in 6,179 (0.81), adjusted HR 2.92 (1.70–5.02); no interaction with treatment period.
key_findings.locator: Results › Interactions between benzodiazepine co-prescription and OAT period, 1st paragraph; Table 5

key_findings.finding: Concurrent prescription during OAT against none (Table 6), unadjusted and adjusted HRs: DRP benzodiazepine 1.98 (1.35–2.90) and 3.34 (2.14–5.20), z-drug 1.24 (0.81–1.89) and 1.64 (1.02–2.64); all-cause benzodiazepine 1.22 (1.04–1.42) and 1.87 (1.55–2.25), z-drug 0.97 (0.79–1.19) and 1.37 (1.09–1.72); other deaths benzodiazepine 1.10 (0.86–1.40) and 1.73 (1.28–2.33), z-drug 1.11 (0.82–1.50) and 1.37 (0.95–1.96). The authors found no sign that longer treatment with concurrent prescription led to lower mortality.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Overall association of concurrent prescription with mortality risk, 1st paragraph; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Poisson regression, exclusion of first episodes and competing-risk analysis were reported as giving similar results (S4–S6 Tables, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge confounding by indication, that propensity scores had added little in their earlier work, that no instrument was available, and that non-prescribed sedatives were not measured (which they expect to dilute associations); they nonetheless describe their study as the strongest evidence that benzodiazepine co-prescription is itself a cause of drug-poisoning death, with weaker evidence for z-drugs and gabapentinoids.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 7,016 patients with ONS cause-of-death data; Table 1 gives 7,106.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one figure is a transposition.

reporting_issues.issue: Co-prescription shares are reported on different bases: the abstract says 42% of OAT episodes involved benzodiazepine co-prescription and 29% concurrent prescription; the results text says 42% of individuals were co-prescribed benzodiazepines; Table 1 gives 46.8% of patients ever prescribed and 42.2% concurrently; the data paragraph says benzodiazepines were prescribed during 10,022 OAT episodes (33.9% of 29,540) in 7,059 patients (58.3% of 12,118; editors' calculations). Mean follow-up is given as 3.4 years per patient, while 36,126 person-years over 12,118 patients is 2.98 years (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Shares should be cited with their denominator (Table 1 for patients; Table 2 gives 7,961 of 27,598 episodes, 29%, with concurrent benzodiazepines); the patient count of 7,059 contradicts Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: p-values are attached to estimates they do not belong to: the z-drug high-dose DRP estimate, 1.55 (0.59–4.06), is given p = 0.001, and concurrent z-drug DRP, 1.64 (1.02–2.64), p < 0.001; both are the joint tests for the variable shown in Tables 4 and 6. The text also says all concurrent prescription was associated with increased risk of all mortality classes, although Table 6 gives 1.37 (0.95–1.96) for z-drugs and other deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: The z-drug results are weaker than the text implies; only the interval estimates should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Specificity is reported inconsistently: Table 4 gives an adjusted HR of 0.91 (0.66–1.25) for other deaths with benzodiazepine co-prescription, the basis of the abstract's and discussion's statement that the excess was specific to drug-poisoning deaths, but Table 6 gives 1.73 (1.28–2.33) for other deaths with concurrent benzodiazepine prescription, and its adjustment moves every estimate away from the null.
reporting_issues.consequence: The specificity argument the authors use for causation is not supported by the paper as a whole; a claim must report both results.

reporting_issues.issue: For gabapentinoids, Table 2 gives a shorter adjusted mean OAT duration with concurrent prescription (189 against 244 days), while Table 3 gives a positive adjusted log-duration coefficient (0.23, 0.10 to 0.36), i.e., longer episodes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the gabapentinoid–retention association is unclear; it should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: In the PMC HTML rendering of Table 4, the non-DRP block's labels for z-drugs and gabapentinoids are shifted by one row (for example the row labelled Off carries the exposed z-drug data, 20 deaths in 1,134 person-years); the person-years of the DRP analyses (19,948–19,949) and of the non-DRP analyses (20,385–20,386) differ within the same linked subset without explanation (editors' sums); the methods list age as a covariate but the footnotes to Tables 4–6 do not.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; values must be read by pattern, and the small person-time difference and the covariate list should be checked against the NIHR report.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6879111 (PMC HTML, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, author summary, all sections, Tables 1–6, funding statement, disclaimer, acknowledgments; the competing-interest statement and affiliations were read from the collapsed author notes with javascript_tool. Supplements (Word files) and the NIHR report were not read.

design_detail: Case-cohort study within the US Veterans Health Administration (VHA), financial years 2004–2009: all 2,400 veterans who died of a drug overdose while receiving outpatient opioid analgesics (cases) and a subcohort of 420,386 veterans drawn as 5% annual random samples of VHA patients receiving outpatient opioid analgesics; 422,786 analysed. Every person-day on an opioid prescription was classified by benzodiazepine prescription history (current, former, none) from pharmacy fill dates and days' supply; Cox models with a risk-set approach and robust variance gave hazard ratios for death from overdose (any drug, any intent; National Death Index), adjusted for demographics, area poverty, psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, comorbidity, other psychotropic drug classes and time-varying opioid dose (Model 1); Model 2 examined benzodiazepine dose, type and schedule within periods of current receipt. Rates were scaled to the whole source population by the inverse sampling fraction. The paper calls the design similar to a nested case–control study; it is filed here as a records-based cohort because the subcohort is a random sample of the source population and the analysis estimates hazard ratios and population rates. Read in full as PMC HTML (PMC4462713), including Tables 1–4; the figure (rates by opioid dose and benzodiazepine history) is an image whose values were not extracted. No supplement is listed.
can_establish: Whether, among veterans filling opioid analgesic prescriptions, person-time with a filled benzodiazepine prescription carries a higher rate of overdose death than person-time without one, after adjustment for recorded diagnoses, other prescriptions and opioid dose, and whether that rate rises with the prescribed benzodiazepine dose.
cannot_establish: That benzodiazepines cause the excess deaths rather than marking the conditions they are prescribed for (anxiety and other psychiatric disorders, substance use, and their severity) or unrecorded use of other drugs; how much medicine was actually taken; or whether risk differs from that of benzodiazepines taken without opioids, because everyone studied was receiving opioids.

sample.recruitment: Registry/records: VHA electronic medical records (National Patient Care Database), VHA Pharmacy Benefits Management fill records and National Death Index cause of death, for veterans who received VHA medical services and outpatient opioid analgesics in financial years 2004–2009 (Methods › Study design and population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data sources).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Veterans receiving outpatient opioid analgesics (codeine, morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, oxymorphone, hydromorphone, fentanyl, propoxyphene, and methadone for pain only; buprenorphine not included). Excluded: 221 veterans prescribed methadone for maintenance and 5,816 with palliative-care consultation or hospice indicators. Observation began at the first filled opioid prescription after the first medical visit of the year, to avoid immortal time; only days of current opioid receipt were analysed (Methods › Study design and population, 2nd paragraph; Drug prescribing patterns, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Mostly men (94% of those without and 91% of those with benzodiazepines); 27% filled at least one benzodiazepine prescription. Those with benzodiazepines were more often women (33% of women against 26% of men), aged 40–59, white and from wealthier areas, and had more recent mental-health or substance-use admissions (4% against 1%), post-traumatic stress disorder (22% against 9%), other anxiety disorders (20% against 5%), depression (38% against 19%), bipolar or psychotic disorders (11% against 4%), substance use disorders (13% against 10%), and more antidepressant (58% against 31%), antiepileptic (38% against 23%) and antipsychotic (25% against 11%) prescriptions (Results › Sample, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable in the usual sense: records-based follow-up to death from any cause or the end of financial year 2009. More than 99% of deaths had a full social security number match to the National Death Index; zip-code poverty data were missing for 4.3% and singly imputed (Methods › Data sources; Covariates).
sample.selection_effects: US veterans in VHA care, mostly men; the authors note that veteran status and male sex are both associated with accidental poisoning mortality, which may limit generalization (Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of study). People prescribed methadone for maintenance, buprenorphine and people in palliative care were excluded, so the sample is people treated with opioids for pain. Prescriptions from outside the VHA are not seen. Prevalent opioid recipients were included (observation began at the first fill of each year), so people who had tolerated opioids for years are mixed with new starters.

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy records of filled outpatient oral benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions (fill date, days' supply, schedule). Each person-day was classified as current benzodiazepine receipt (from a fill to the end of its days' supply), former receipt (after a prescription ended, until another fill) or none (before the first fill, or never). Doses were computed 'as prescribed': all milligram equivalents in a prescription divided by days' supply, assuming the maximum amount prescribed was taken, including for as-needed prescriptions (Methods › Drug prescribing patterns, 1st–3rd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: benzodiazepine dose as diazepam-equivalent mg per day as prescribed, in categories 0, >0–10, >10–20, >20–30, >30–40 and >40 mg/day; opioid dose as morphine-equivalent mg per day, >0–<20, 20–<50, 50–<100 and ≥100 mg/day, time-varying; oral route; benzodiazepine schedule regular, as needed or both; types alprazolam, chlordiazepoxide, clonazepam, diazepam, lorazepam, temazepam and five less used ones (Methods › Drug prescribing patterns; Tables 2–4).
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug and alcohol use were not measured; substance use disorder diagnoses in the year before observation were a covariate. Receipt of antidepressants, antiepileptic and anti-parkinsonism drugs, and antipsychotic and neuroleptic drugs in the year before observation was adjusted for (Methods › Covariates). The authors note that people with more severe addiction may take more than prescribed and use illicit drugs (Discussion › Findings in context, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Person-time of the same source population on opioid prescriptions with no benzodiazepine prescription history (and, separately, person-time after a benzodiazepine prescription had ended).
comparison.matching: None: the subcohort was a random sample, and confounding was handled by adjustment (Model 1 covariates: sex, age, race, ethnicity, area poverty, time-varying daily opioid dose, recent hospital admission related to substance use disorder, Charlson comorbidity index, diagnoses of substance use disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, other anxiety disorder, depression, bipolar or psychotic disorder and cancer, and use of other drugs; Table 3 note).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity of the anxiety, other psychiatric disorders or substance use for which benzodiazepines were prescribed (indications are not linked to VHA pharmacy data); alcohol and illicit drug use; suicidality; diagnoses were fixed at the year before observation rather than updated. The authors use the former-receipt category to address unmeasured confounding and still find a raised risk in it (Discussion › Findings in context, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Both groups were receiving opioid analgesics by design; other drug classes were adjusted for as prior-year receipt; non-VHA and illicit drugs unknown.

outcomes.instruments: National Death Index cause of death, ICD-10 codes X40–X45 (unintentional), X60–X65 (intentional) and Y10–Y15 (undetermined intent) for poisoning by any drug, with no T-code (specific drug) required; sensitivity analyses excluded intentional deaths or kept only deaths coded to opioids or benzodiazepines (Methods › Deaths from drug overdose; Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death certificate coding; the authors chose a broad definition because intent is often unclear and many certificates do not name the drugs. Not validated in this sample.
outcomes.operationalization: Death from overdose of any drug and any intent while receiving opioid analgesics; this includes suicides and deaths in which neither opioids nor benzodiazepines were named.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; one outcome with several exposure contrasts (history, dose, type, schedule) and four sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: death certification was independent of the study; certifiers could know of prescriptions found at the death scene.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unadjusted overdose death rates per 100,000 person-years (scaled to the source population): none 71 (95% CI 66–76), former 187 (170–205), current 316 (298–334). Adjusted hazard ratios (Model 1): former 2.33 (2.05–2.64), current 3.86 (3.49–4.26) against none. Model 2, current receipt only, against >0–10 mg/day: >10–20 mg 1.69 (1.42–2.01), >20–30 mg 2.34 (1.91–2.86), >30–40 mg 2.65 (2.10–3.33), >40 mg 3.06 (2.38–3.92); temazepam against clonazepam 0.63 (0.48–0.82); schedule not associated. Editors' calculation: the unadjusted rate difference between current and no receipt is 245 per 100,000 person-years (about 3.2 against 0.7 deaths per 1,000 person-years); the current-to-former hazard ratio ratio is 1.66.
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching; diagnoses and other drug receipt measured in the year before observation; opioid dose time-varying.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is cited; the transparency declaration says any discrepancies from the study as planned have been explained.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity analyses (excluding intentional deaths, restricting to opioid- or benzodiazepine-coded deaths, excluding people with cancer, extending current periods by 10% of days' supply) are reported only as giving minor differences, without estimates (Results › Sensitivity analyses). The figure's stratified rates are shown only as an image.
analysis.power: Not addressed formally; 2,400 deaths give precise estimates for the main contrasts (intervals within about ±10% of the hazard ratios).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among veterans receiving opioid analgesics, overdose death rates were 316 per 100,000 person-years during current benzodiazepine prescription, 187 after it ended and 71 with none; adjusted hazard ratios were 3.86 and 2.33. Within current receipt, adjusted hazards rose with prescribed benzodiazepine dose (1.69 to 3.06 against the lowest category). About half of all overdose deaths (1,185 of 2,400) occurred during current benzodiazepine prescription. The relative association did not differ detectably by opioid dose (interaction P = 0.60), and opioid dose gradients were similar in all three benzodiazepine strata (Table 4).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the boxed summary state the results as associations and add that the association was dose-dependent. The discussion is cautious: it says the design cannot show that benzodiazepines cause the deaths, that the association may partly reflect the conditions benzodiazepines are prescribed for, and that benzodiazepines “might be better conceptualized as a marker of risk” (Discussion › Findings in context, 2nd paragraph). The results describe the non-significant interaction as relations “neither greater nor less than additive” (Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph), which misreads a product term in a multiplicative (Cox) model (see reporting issues). The clinical advice (caution in prescribing; include this group in naloxone efforts) is framed as following from the raised risk whatever its cause.

timeline.event: Dunn et al. (Ann Intern Med; cited as ref. 13) reported an association between sedative-hypnotic receipt and combined fatal and non-fatal overdose in people prescribed opioids for chronic pain, which the authors describe as hypothesis-generating (Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Findings in context, 1st paragraph); not read.

Bohnert et al. (JAMA; cited as ref. 12) in the same VHA population linked higher opioid doses with overdose death; this paper shows that gradient within each benzodiazepine stratum (Table 4); not read.

Sun et al. (BMJ), privately insured US adults: overlapping benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions associated with emergency visits or admissions for opioid overdose (adjusted odds ratio 2.14), a different outcome and population, without adjustment for opioid dose

Gomes et al. (PLOS Med), Ontario: 77.3% of people who died an accidental opioid-related death had a benzodiazepine dispensed in the prior 120 days, against 56.4% of matched controls (Table 1; no adjusted estimate for benzodiazepines)
Macleod et al. (PLOS Med), UK people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment: benzodiazepine co-prescription associated with drug-poisoning death (adjusted hazard ratio 2.96), with a dose gradient

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the association is consistent across a veteran cohort (deaths), a privately insured cohort (non-fatal hospital events) and a UK treatment cohort (drug-poisoning deaths), all records-based and all unable to separate the medicine from the reasons it was prescribed. No study read so far uses an active comparator or measures actual use.

funding.funder: Veterans Affairs Health Services Research and Development Service Career Development Award (CDA-09-204; ASBB) and National Institutes of Health (R03 AG042899); the sponsors had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation or the decision to submit (Funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: Financial support as above; RS has received consultant and annual travel fees from The BMJ as editor of the journal Evidence Based Medicine; no other relationships declared (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University (Departments of Medicine and of Psychiatry and Human Behavior; first author); Boston University School of Public Health (Saitz); Department of Veterans Affairs HSR&D, Ann Arbor, and University of Michigan Department of Psychiatry (Ganoczy, Ilgen, Bohnert), the group whose earlier VHA study of opioid dose and overdose (Bohnert et al., 2011) the paper builds on (author information block). Ethical approval: Ann Arbor VA human studies committee, consent waived.

what_would_settle_it: An active-comparator cohort of people on stable opioid therapy who newly start a benzodiazepine against people who newly start a non-sedating treatment for the same indication (for example an SSRI for anxiety), with measured psychiatric and substance-use severity, toxicology-confirmed cause of death, and dispensing linked across all prescribers; or a randomized trial of benzodiazepine tapering against continuation in people co-prescribed both, with overdose as an outcome.

domains.note: Adjusted for many recorded diagnoses, comorbidity, prior-year psychotropic receipt and time-varying opioid dose, but not for the severity of the indication, alcohol or illicit drug use, or suicidality, all of which plausibly drive both benzodiazepine prescribing and overdose death. The raised hazard after benzodiazepine prescriptions ended (2.33, against 3.86 during them) shows that a large part of the association may not be due to the current medicine; the authors themselves call benzodiazepines possibly a marker of risk.

Fills, not consumption; doses assume the maximum prescribed was taken; VHA prescriptions only, so benzodiazepines from other prescribers or illicit sources are missed (misclassifying some 'none' and 'former' time). Extending current periods by 10% changed little (no numbers given).

Prevalent opioid recipients entered at their first fill each year; people on methadone maintenance, buprenorphine or palliative care excluded; how cases sampled into the subcohort were handled is not stated.
No intervention after exposure is likely to have been driven by benzodiazepine receipt in a way that biases the comparison; opioid dose was modelled as time-varying.
Records-based with near-complete death linkage (over 99% full match); 4.3% missing zip-code poverty data singly imputed.

Death certificate coding of any-drug, any-intent poisoning; certifiers may more readily call a death an overdose when prescription sedatives are found, and the broad outcome includes suicides, which benzodiazepine indications also predict; the restricted outcomes were said to give similar results without numbers.
No protocol cited; sensitivity results not quantified; several exposure contrasts (dose, type, schedule) without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because confounding by indication is not controlled and the study's own former-receipt contrast shows it may be large; the other concerns (prescription as a proxy for use, a broad outcome) are moderate. The study may be cited for the association between current benzodiazepine prescription and overdose death in veterans prescribed opioid analgesics, its absolute rates, the prescribed-dose gradient and the absence of detectable modification by opioid dose on the relative scale; not for a causal effect, for people using illicit opioids, or for an additive interaction.

key_findings.finding: Case-cohort design: all 2,400 veterans who died of a drug overdose while receiving opioid analgesics and 420,386 controls drawn as 5% annual random samples of VHA patients receiving outpatient opioid analgesics in financial years 2004–2009; 221 veterans on methadone maintenance and 5,816 with palliative or hospice care excluded; final sample 422,786; observation from the first opioid fill after the first visit of each year; controls followed to death or end of financial year 2009.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Participants); Methods › Study design and population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Outcome: National Death Index cause of death, any unintentional (X40–X45), intentional (X60–X65) or undetermined (Y10–Y15) poisoning by any drug, with no specific drug code required; deaths matched by social security number, sex and date of birth (over 99% full social security number match).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 1st paragraph; Deaths from drug overdose, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure: outpatient fills of oral benzodiazepines and opioids; each person-day classified as current, former or no benzodiazepine receipt by days' supply; only days of current opioid receipt analysed; doses computed as prescribed (maximum daily amount, diazepam or morphine equivalents), time-varying; methadone counted only when prescribed for pain; buprenorphine not included.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Drug prescribing patterns, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Of 422,786 veterans, 112,069 (27%) filled at least one benzodiazepine prescription. Compared with those without, they were more often women (33% of women against 26% of men received benzodiazepines) and had more post-traumatic stress disorder (22% against 9%), other anxiety disorders (20% against 5%), depression (38% against 19%), bipolar or psychotic disorders (11% against 4%), substance use disorders (13% against 10%), recent mental-health or substance-use admissions (4% against 1%) and antidepressant receipt (58% against 31%); all comparisons P < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sample, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Of the 2,400 overdose deaths, 1,185 (49%) occurred during current benzodiazepine prescription, 421 during former receipt and 794 with no receipt. Unadjusted overdose death rates per 100,000 person-years (scaled to the source population): none 71 (95% CI 66–76; 1,116,346 person-years), former 187 (170–205; 225,171), current 316 (298–334; 375,332).
key_findings.locator: Results › Unadjusted rates of death from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; Table 2, benzodiazepine prescription history rows
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: rate difference current against none 245 per 100,000 person-years, about 3.2 against 0.7 deaths per 1,000 person-years; unadjusted rate ratio 4.45.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted rates by prescribed daily benzodiazepine dose (diazepam equivalents) per 100,000 person-years: >0–10 mg 152 (133–172), >10–20 mg 301 (271–333), >20–30 mg 518 (454–586), >30–40 mg 600 (513–694), >40 mg 805 (689–930); by type: clonazepam 379, diazepam 381, alprazolam 288, lorazepam 170, temazepam 154, other 309, multiple 625; by schedule: regular only 265, as needed only 334, both 658.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, daily dose, type and schedule rows
key_findings.note: The >0 mg dose rows sum to the current-receipt totals (1,185 deaths, 375,332 person-years; editors' arithmetic). The 0 mg/day row is inconsistent: see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted hazard ratios for overdose death (Model 1), against no benzodiazepine receipt: former receipt 2.33 (95% CI 2.05–2.64); current receipt 3.86 (3.49–4.26).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 3, Model 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the current hazard ratio is 1.66 times the former.

key_findings.finding: Model 2, periods of current benzodiazepine receipt only, adjusted as Model 1: against >0–10 mg/day, >10–20 mg 1.69 (1.42–2.01), >20–30 mg 2.34 (1.91–2.86), >30–40 mg 2.65 (2.10–3.33), >40 mg 3.06 (2.38–3.92). Against clonazepam: alprazolam 0.93 (0.75–1.14), diazepam 0.93 (0.77–1.13), lorazepam 0.79 (0.62–1.00), temazepam 0.63 (0.48–0.82), other 1.09 (0.67–1.77), multiple 1.05 (0.83–1.33). As-needed only 0.98 (0.86–1.13) and both schedules 1.07 (0.80–1.43) against regular.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 3, Model 2

key_findings.finding: The interaction between benzodiazepine history and opioid dose was not significant (P = 0.60). Adjusted hazard ratios by daily opioid dose (morphine equivalents) against >0–<20 mg, within each stratum: no benzodiazepine 1.57 (1.28–1.91), 2.81 (2.26–3.50) and 3.30 (2.62–4.16) for 20–<50, 50–<100 and ≥100 mg; former receipt 1.17 (0.86–1.60), 2.33 (1.69–3.21) and 3.00 (2.19–4.11); current receipt 1.54 (1.24–1.90), 2.95 (2.37–3.66) and 3.92 (3.17–4.85).
key_findings.locator: Results › Adjusted analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: In unadjusted rates stratified by opioid dose (figure), the difference between current and former benzodiazepine receipt was not significant in the lowest opioid dose category but was significant at higher categories.
key_findings.locator: Results › Unadjusted rates of death from drug overdose, 1st paragraph; figure (image, values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses excluding intentional overdose deaths, keeping only deaths coded to opioids or benzodiazepines, excluding people with cancer, or extending current benzodiazepine periods by 10% of days' supply gave only minor differences in the association and no change in inferences; no estimates are shown.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph; Results › Sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that benzodiazepines were more often prescribed to people with substance misuse and psychiatric disorders, that residual confounding by the severity of those conditions could remain, that half of the overdose deaths occurred without a benzodiazepine prescription, that the raised risk during former receipt could reflect the underlying conditions or continued use of illicit, non-VHA or leftover benzodiazepines, and that benzodiazepines might be better seen as a marker of risk with unknown causal links.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Findings in context, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: veterans, mostly men (both linked to accidental poisoning mortality); non-VHA prescriptions and encounters not captured; doses assume drugs were taken as prescribed, and retained or additional supplies would inflate estimates if linked to benzodiazepine receipt; indications not available.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of study, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The non-significant interaction between benzodiazepine history and opioid dose (P = 0.60) is read as showing relations “neither greater nor less than additive”. In a Cox model the product term tests departure from multiplicative hazards: no detectable interaction means the hazard ratios combine by multiplication, which on the absolute scale implies larger excess death rates at higher opioid doses, not additivity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot be cited for an additive (or a 'no more than additive') joint effect; it can be cited for no detectable modification of the relative benzodiazepine association by opioid dose. Additive interaction was not estimated.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2, the 0 mg/day benzodiazepine dose row gives 421 deaths, 376,645 person-years and a rate of 112 per 100,000; the 421 deaths equal the former-receipt deaths, but the former-receipt person-years are 225,171 (rate 187). The >0 mg rows sum exactly to the current-receipt totals (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 0 mg/day row is mislabelled or its person-years misprinted; it should not be cited. The dose rows above 0 mg are internally consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity analyses that matter most for the outcome definition (excluding intentional deaths; restricting to opioid- or benzodiazepine-coded deaths) are described only as giving minor differences, without hazard ratios.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the association holds for unintentional opioid-involved deaths specifically cannot be checked from the article; claims should state that the outcome includes suicides and deaths from any drug.

reporting_issues.issue: The text describes identifying 2,400 cases and 420,386 controls and then excluding 221 methadone-maintenance and 5,816 palliative-care veterans, yet the final sample (422,786) equals 2,400 + 420,386; how cases falling into the random subcohort were counted is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the order of exclusions and the handling of overlap between cases and subcohort are unclear; no effect on the main estimates is apparent.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4462713 (PMC HTML, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, all sections, Tables 1–4, figure legend (figure values not extracted), funding, competing interests, contributors, transparency and data-sharing statements, reference list.

design_detail: Retrospective analysis of US private-insurance claims (Truven MarketScan), 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2013. Closed cohort of 315,428 people aged 18–64 continuously enrolled with medical and pharmacy benefits for all 13 years, without cancer, who filled at least one opioid prescription; the unit of analysis is the person-year with an opioid fill. Exposure: concurrent benzodiazepine use, defined as at least one day of overlap between the days' supply of an opioid and a benzodiazepine prescription in the calendar year. Outcome: an emergency-room visit or inpatient admission for opioid overdose during an opioid prescription interval or within 7 days after it. Logistic regression with standard errors clustered by person, adjusted for age, sex, year, comorbidities and prior health spending; results also given separately for intermittent and chronic opioid prescriptions, with a population attributable fraction and a residual-confounding analysis. Read in full as PMC HTML (PMC5421443): text, Table 1 and figure legends; Figs 1–3 are images whose values were not extracted beyond those in the text. The appendix (sample flow, drug code lists, sensitivity results) is a PDF and was not opened.
can_establish: Whether, among privately insured working-age adults filling opioid prescriptions, person-years with any overlapping benzodiazepine prescription carry a higher adjusted share with a hospital-treated opioid overdose than person-years without, and how the share of opioid prescription recipients co-prescribed benzodiazepines changed from 2001 to 2013.
cannot_establish: That benzodiazepines cause the excess (the analysis does not adjust for opioid dose or the reasons benzodiazepines were prescribed, and does not order the overdose and the overlap within the year); anything about overdose deaths, overdoses not treated in hospital, illicit drugs, or people outside private insurance.

sample.recruitment: Registry/records: employer-sponsored private health insurance claims (MarketScan); compared with the US population, more women, more people from the South and fewer from the West (Methods › Data, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Continuous enrolment with medical and pharmacy benefits for the whole 13-year period; aged 18–64 at entry; no cancer; at least one outpatient opioid prescription during the period, excluding hydrocodone cough and cold products (Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Variables, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Described only for 2001 (Table 1): mean age 42.4 years without and 44.5 with benzodiazepines; men 43% and 35%; depression 4.4% and 17%; diagnoses coded as alcohol abuse 0.30% and 1.1% and as drug abuse 0.22% and 1.2% (ICD-9 categories as studied); every listed comorbidity except chronic kidney disease more common with benzodiazepines (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: None by design (closed cohort). The authors note that requiring 13 years of continuous enrolment excludes people who died or lost employment-based insurance, possibly after opioid-related events, and test a broader sample of 3,810,747 people enrolled for at least 2 years (Methods › Sensitivity analyses, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Privately insured, employed or employer-linked, working-age people who stayed insured and alive for 13 years: a healthier and more stable population than people treated in public systems or people who use illicit opioids. The authors call it broadly representative of the privately insured US population.

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy claims: fill date, quantity and days' supply; generic name and dose via Red Book linkage. Each opioid and benzodiazepine prescription defines an interval from the fill date for the days' supply; concurrent use in the main analysis is any overlap of at least one day between an opioid and a benzodiazepine interval in a calendar year; a stricter definition (at least 25% of opioid days overlapping) was used in a sensitivity analysis (Methods › Data, 2nd paragraph; Variables, 1st paragraph; Sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No dose analysis: opioid and benzodiazepine doses were not used as exposures or covariates. Opioid prescriptions were classed as chronic (more than 10 prescriptions or more than 120 days' supply in a year) or intermittent (all others) (Methods › Analyses, 1st paragraph). Study conditions only.
exposure.polysubstance: Diagnoses coded as alcohol abuse and drug abuse were covariates (Table 1); heroin and prescription drugs bought illegally are not captured, as the authors state (Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Person-years with an opioid prescription and no overlapping benzodiazepine prescription.
comparison.matching: None; multivariable adjustment for age, sex, year, the comorbidities in Table 1 (congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, myocardial infarction, liver disease, alcohol abuse, drug abuse, psychosis, depression) and mean daily health spending before the first opioid fill of the year (Methods › Variables, 2nd paragraph; Analyses, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Opioid dose, anxiety diagnoses (in the veteran study, anxiety disorders other than PTSD were recorded in 20% of people with and 5% without benzodiazepines), pain conditions, and the severity of substance use are not among the covariates. A residual-confounding analysis assumed an unmeasured binary confounder present in 75% of person-years with and 0% without concurrent use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Both groups filled opioid prescriptions; illicit drug use unknown in both.
