outcomes.instruments: Claims ICD-9 diagnosis codes for an emergency-room visit or inpatient admission, following the method of Dunn et al.: codes for opioid poisoning or a potential opioid adverse event such as respiratory depression together with a code for opioid overdose; counted only if within an opioid prescription interval or 7 days after it; alternative windows (within 30 days; exactly within the interval) in sensitivity analyses (Methods › Outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The algorithm is not validated in this database in the paper. Only hospital-treated events in people who survived are counted (Discussion › Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: At least one hospital-treated opioid overdose event in the person-year (binary).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; one outcome, three population groupings (all, intermittent, chronic) and several sensitivity analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: routinely coded claims.

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted annual incidence of a hospital-treated opioid overdose: all, 1.16% (95% CI 1.13–1.18) without against 2.42% (2.32–2.51) with concurrent benzodiazepines, odds ratio 2.14 (2.05–2.24); intermittent opioid prescriptions 1.02% (0.996–1.04) against 1.45% (1.36–1.51), OR 1.42 (1.33–1.51); chronic 3.13% (2.94–3.31) against 5.36% (5.12–5.61), OR 1.81 (1.67–1.96); all P < 0.001. Population attributable fraction 0.15 (0.14–0.16) overall, 0.043 intermittent, 0.27 chronic. Editors' calculation: the adjusted incidences are in ratios of 2.09, 1.42 and 1.71.
analysis.covariates: See comparison.matching. Not adjusted: opioid dose, anxiety diagnoses, pain conditions.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The sensitivity analyses with alternative exposure and outcome definitions are reported only as qualitatively similar, with results in an appendix not read; the broader-sample analysis reports relative risks only for the two subgroups, not for all people combined.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the cohort is large and intervals are narrow.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In privately insured adults filling opioid prescriptions, person-years with any overlapping benzodiazepine prescription had about twice the adjusted share with a hospital-treated opioid overdose (2.42% against 1.16%; OR 2.14), less so with intermittent (OR 1.42) than with chronic opioid prescriptions (OR 1.81). The share of opioid prescription recipients co-prescribed benzodiazepines rose from 9% in 2001 to 17% in 2013. The model did not include opioid dose, and the overlap and the overdose are not ordered in time within the year.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The objective is framed as the impact of co-prescribing trends on overdose admissions; the abstract's results attach a condition to the attributable fraction (if the association is causal), but the abstract's conclusion says concurrent use significantly contributed to the overall population risk of overdose, the results and discussion say eliminating concurrent use could reduce the population risk by 15%, and the boxed summary repeats the 15% without the condition (Abstract; Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion › Principal findings). The discussion judges an unobserved confounder strong enough to explain the result unlikely, from a residual-confounding analysis with arbitrary extreme assumptions. Clinical and policy recommendations follow.

timeline.event: Park et al. (BMJ), US veterans on opioid analgesics: current benzodiazepine prescription associated with overdose death (adjusted hazard ratio 3.86), with a prescribed-dose gradient; cited here as ref. 24

Dasgupta et al. (Pain Med; cited as ref. 26), North Carolina: described by these authors as finding a tenfold increased risk of overdose death with any benzodiazepine and opioid use in the same year, without measuring overlap; not read.
Macleod et al. (PLOS Med), UK people in opioid agonist treatment: benzodiazepine co-prescription associated with drug-poisoning death (adjusted hazard ratio 2.96)

replication.where_it_stands: The direction agrees with the veteran mortality cohort and the UK treatment cohort; this is the only study read that uses non-fatal hospital events and a privately insured population, and the only one without adjustment for opioid dose.

funding.funder: ECS: mentored research training grant from the Foundation for Anesthesia Education and Research and the Anesthesia Quality Institute; KNH: Veterans Affairs health services research and development service; sponsors not involved in design, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: Support from grants from the Foundation for Anesthesia Education and Research; no financial relationships with organizations that might have an interest in the work in the previous 3 years; no other relationships (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Stanford University School of Medicine (anesthesiology, perioperative and pain medicine; psychiatry; health research and policy), University of California San Francisco (anesthesiology), VA Palo Alto Health Care System, and the National Bureau of Economic Research (author information block). An accompanying editorial (j1224) is noted on the page; not read.

what_would_settle_it: An analysis of the same kind of claims data in people newly starting a benzodiazepine against people newly starting a non-sedating treatment for the same indication, adjusted for daily opioid dose and diagnoses of anxiety, depression and substance use, with the overdose required to follow the overlap in time and with linkage to death records so that fatal overdoses are counted.

domains.note: No adjustment for opioid dose, a strong predictor of overdose that is higher in people co-prescribed benzodiazepines, nor for anxiety disorders, pain conditions or substance-use severity; the residual-confounding analysis uses arbitrary assumptions (a confounder present in 75% against 0%) and its methods paragraph describes a surgical sample the study does not have.

A single day of overlap anywhere in the calendar year labels the whole person-year as exposed; the overdose can precede the benzodiazepine fill or fall outside any overlap, so exposure and outcome are not ordered in time; fills, not use.
Thirteen years of continuous enrolment selects people who stayed insured and alive; in the broader sample the subgroup estimates changed (intermittent 1.66 against 1.42; chronic 1.61 against 1.81).
No intervention after exposure is described that would bias the comparison.
Missing or unrecorded covariate information in claims is not discussed; the sample flow is only in the unread appendix.

An unvalidated code algorithm that includes potential opioid adverse events such as respiratory depression; about 1 in 100 person-years without benzodiazepines met it, which suggests it captures more than overdoses; deaths outside hospital are not counted.
No protocol; sensitivity results only in the appendix or described qualitatively; effect measure changes between analyses (odds ratios, then relative risks).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because of uncontrolled confounding (above all by opioid dose and indication) and an exposure definition that does not order the overlap and the overdose in time. The study may be cited for the trend in co-prescribing among privately insured adults from 2001 to 2013 and for the adjusted association between any yearly overlap and hospital-treated opioid overdose; not for deaths, a causal effect, or the 15% attributable fraction as an estimate of what removing co-prescription would achieve.

key_findings.finding: MarketScan claims, 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2013: 595,410 people continuously enrolled with medical and pharmacy benefits; after excluding 28,780 with cancer and 142,789 aged under 18 or over 64 at entry, 423,841 remained, of whom 315,428 filled at least one opioid prescription (the analysed sample). Compared with the US population, MarketScan includes more women, more people from the South and fewer from the West.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Participants); Methods › Data, 1st paragraph; Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Outcome: an emergency-room visit or inpatient admission in the calendar year with ICD-9 codes for opioid poisoning or a potential opioid adverse event (such as respiratory depression) and a code for opioid overdose, counted only during an opioid prescription interval or within 7 days after it. Only events in people who reached hospital and survived are counted.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure: at least one day of overlap between opioid and benzodiazepine prescription intervals (fill date plus days' supply) in a calendar year; covariates age, sex, year, comorbidities from ICD-9 codes (Table 1 list) and daily health spending before the first opioid fill of the year; person-year logistic regression with standard errors clustered by person. Chronic opioid prescription: more than 10 prescriptions or more than 120 days' supply in a year.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Variables, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Analyses, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In 2001, people filling opioid prescriptions with benzodiazepines (n = 5,425) against without (n = 53,389): mean age 44.5 against 42.4 years; men 35% against 43%; depression 17% against 4.4%; alcohol abuse diagnoses 1.1% against 0.30%; drug abuse diagnoses 1.2% against 0.22%; psychosis 0.55% against 0.13%; every comorbidity except chronic kidney disease (P = 0.16) more common with benzodiazepines (P < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: The share of people filling opioid prescriptions who also had overlapping benzodiazepine prescriptions rose from 9% in 2001 to 17% in 2013; for intermittent opioid prescriptions from 7% to 13%; for chronic opioid prescriptions it was 46% in 2001 and stayed fairly constant.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The counts printed beside these shares do not reproduce them consistently: see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Age-adjusted annual incidence of a hospital-treated opioid overdose without benzodiazepines: 1.08% (0.99–1.16) in 2001 and 1.35% (1.26–1.43) in 2013 (intermittent 1.05% to 1.15%; chronic 2.00% to 3.51%); with benzodiazepines 2.01% (1.64–2.39) in 2001 and 3.99% (3.58–4.21) in 2013.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig 2 (image)

key_findings.finding: Adjusted annual incidence of a hospital-treated opioid overdose, without against with concurrent benzodiazepines: all 1.16% (1.13–1.18) against 2.42% (2.32–2.51), odds ratio 2.14 (2.05–2.24); intermittent opioid prescriptions 1.02% (0.996–1.04) against 1.45% (1.36–1.51), OR 1.42 (1.33–1.51); chronic 3.13% (2.94–3.31) against 5.36% (5.12–5.61), OR 1.81 (1.67–1.96); all P < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results, 4th paragraph; Fig 3 (image)

key_findings.finding: Population attributable fraction of concurrent benzodiazepine use for hospital-treated opioid overdose: 0.15 (0.14–0.16) overall, 0.043 (0.034–0.051) intermittent, 0.27 (0.23–0.30) chronic; calculated from the logistic models, meaning a 15% lower population risk if concurrent use were removed and the association were causal.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Methods › Analyses, 3rd paragraph; Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: requiring 25% of opioid days to overlap a benzodiazepine prescription, and alternative outcome windows, gave results described as qualitatively similar (appendix, not read). In a broader sample enrolled for at least 2 years (n = 3,810,747), the adjusted relative risk was 1.66 (1.64–1.69) for intermittent and 1.61 (1.58–1.63) for chronic opioid prescriptions.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sensitivity analyses, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Residual-confounding analysis: assuming an unmeasured binary confounder with 75% prevalence among concurrent and 0% among non-concurrent person-years, it would need an odds ratio of at least 2.40 overall (1.45 intermittent, 1.89 chronic) to remove the association.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Sensitivity analyses, 3rd paragraph; Results, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: unobservable differences between people with and without benzodiazepines; selection by continuous enrolment; only hospital-treated, survived events; behaviour changes if co-prescribing fell (for example higher opioid doses); heroin and illegally bought prescription drugs not captured.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 1st–5th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The 2001 share is printed as 9% (5425/53 389), but 5,425 of 53,389 is 10.2%; 53,389 is the group without benzodiazepines in Table 1, and 5,425 of all 58,814 is 9.2% (editors' calculation). The 2001 subgroup counts (intermittent 4,122 of 55,960; chronic 1,596 of 3,457) sum to 5,718 of 59,417, not the 5,425 of 58,814 in Table 1; the 2013 intermittent share is printed as 13% for 9,292 of 65,114 (14.3%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Denominators are unclear (age adjustment may account for some differences, but the text gives raw counts); cite the shares as printed percentages, not the fractions.

reporting_issues.issue: The residual-confounding method is described as assuming a confounder with 75% prevalence among the surgical sample and 0% among non-surgical patients, although the study has no surgical sample; the results restate it for concurrent and non-concurrent use, joined by or rather than and. Other wording slips: concurrent benzodiazepine/opioid overdose for concurrent use; concurrent opioid/baseline for concurrent opioid/benzodiazepine use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sensitivity analysis is described in text apparently carried over from another study and rests on arbitrary assumptions; it cannot support the authors' judgment that confounding is unlikely to explain the result.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the standardized differences have inconsistent signs (negative for a lower share of men and for higher shares of every comorbidity, positive for higher age), and the value for sex (−0.30) does not match the printed shares (43% against 35% gives about 0.17 with a group-size-weighted pooled SD, editors' calculation, a method that reproduces the printed depression value of 0.55). The text says all differences except depression were below 0.2 SD, which the −0.30 in the table contradicts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the standardized differences are not reliable descriptors of imbalance.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Fig 2 says unadjusted incidence, while the text describes the values shown in Fig 2 as age adjusted; the 2013 interval for people with benzodiazepines, 3.99% (3.58% to 4.21%), is asymmetric around its estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the trend figures should be cited from the text with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The main estimates are odds ratios, but the broader-sample sensitivity analysis reports adjusted relative risks without saying how they were obtained; its intermittent estimate (1.66) is higher and its chronic estimate (1.61) lower than in the main sample (1.42 and 1.81), yet both are called qualitatively similar.
reporting_issues.consequence: The robustness to sample construction is weaker than described; the subgroup pattern (stronger with chronic prescriptions) is not stable.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5421443 (PMC HTML, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, all sections, Table 1, figure legends (Figs 1–3 images, values not extracted beyond the text), funding, competing interests, author information, reference list. The appendix (PDF) was not opened.

design_detail: Repeated cross-sectional analysis of all US opioid-involved poisoning deaths, 1999–2017, from the CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death files (National Vital Statistics System): annual shares of opioid overdose deaths whose death certificates also list alcohol (T51.0, T51.9) or benzodiazepines (T42.4), overall and by opioid subtype (heroin, methadone, natural and semisynthetic 'prescription' opioids, synthetic opioids such as fentanyl), with a 2015–2017 breakdown by sex and state and two ecological (state-level) Pearson correlations: with self-reported binge drinking (BRFSS, 2015–2017) and with benzodiazepine prescribing rates (IMS Health, 2012). Aggregate data only; no individual-level linkage. Read in full as PMC HTML (PMC7146101): text, Table and figure legends; Figures 1–4 are images (trend lines and state scatter plots) whose values were not extracted; the eTable supplement (state rates, PDF) was not opened.
can_establish: How often US death certificates for opioid overdose deaths also named alcohol or benzodiazepines, how those shares changed from 1999 to 2017, and how they differed by opioid type, sex and state.
cannot_establish: Whether alcohol or benzodiazepines raise the risk of dying from an opioid overdose, or by how much (there is no denominator of people using opioids with and without them); how many deaths involved both alcohol and benzodiazepines; amounts or blood levels; whether the state-level correlations hold for individuals.

sample.recruitment: Registry: all US death certificates with an underlying cause of drug poisoning (ICD-10 X40–X44, X60–X64, X85, Y10–Y14) and an opioid code among the multiple causes (T40.0, T40.1, T40.2, T40.3, T40.4, T40.6), CDC WONDER (Methods › Data Source, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All intents (unintentional, suicide, assault, undetermined) included; opioid subtypes are not mutually exclusive; deaths without a specific drug recorded cannot enter the opioid-involved set.
sample.demographics: 1999–2017: 66.0% male; 51.2% aged 35–54. 2015–2017: 67.1% men; women were 42.6% of deaths involving prescription opioids and 28.8% of those involving synthetic opioids (Results › Trends, 1st paragraph; Current co-involvement, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Complete national coverage of certified deaths, but drug identification depends on investigation and toxicology practices that vary by state and year: about 20% of drug poisoning deaths in 2011 and 12% in 2017 had no specific drug listed, and states' ability to name at least one drug ranged from 54.7% to 99.3% in 2017 (Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

exposure.measurement: Mention of alcohol (T51.0 ethanol, T51.9 alcohol unspecified) or benzodiazepines (T42.4) among the multiple causes on the death certificate (Methods › Data Source, 2nd paragraph). For the ecological analyses: state prevalence of self-reported binge drinking (BRFSS: 5 or more drinks on one occasion for men, 4 or more for women, in the past month) and state benzodiazepine prescriptions per 100 persons in 2012 (Methods › Analytical Strategy).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: no blood levels or amounts; the authors note that toxicology levels were unavailable (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Opioid subtypes overlap; cocaine and other drugs were not analysed; combinations of alcohol and benzodiazepines in the same death cannot be counted from the aggregate data.

comparison.controls: None for risk: shares are among people who died of opioid overdose. Ecological comparisons across states only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a descriptive analysis; for the ecological correlations, state differences in reporting, testing and opioid supply are uncontrolled.

outcomes.instruments: Death certificate multiple-cause coding (the paper labels the codes ICD-10-CM).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite known misclassification, incomplete drug information and state variation; alcohol is often under-reported and excluded from drug-related deaths; guidance from the National Association of Medical Examiners (first published 2013) recommends testing for benzodiazepines but does not address alcohol (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Share of opioid overdose deaths with alcohol or benzodiazepine co-involvement, by year, opioid subtype, sex and state.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable for descriptive shares; three correlation tests without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Alcohol co-involvement 12.4% (1999) to 14.7% (2017); benzodiazepines 8.7% (1999), 26.2% (2010), 21.0% (2017). 2015–2017: alcohol 18,419 of 122,940 (15.0%), benzodiazepines 26,728 (21.7%). Ecological correlations: binge drinking with alcohol co-involvement r = 0.34 (P = .02); benzodiazepine prescribing with benzodiazepine co-involvement r = 0.57 (P < .001); alcohol with benzodiazepine co-involvement across states r = 0.08 (P = .56). No intervals are given for any share.
analysis.covariates: None (descriptive shares; unadjusted correlations).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None mentioned; STROBE followed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Annual values are shown only in figures (images); the text reports selected years and ranges.
analysis.power: Not applicable for national counts; the state correlations rest on about 43–50 states.

interpretation_gap.results_show: On US death certificates, alcohol was named in about one in seven opioid overdose deaths throughout 2008–2017 (14.7% in 2017) and benzodiazepines in about one in five in 2017 (21.0%, after a peak of 26.2% in 2010). In 2015–2017, alcohol was named more often in men's deaths and benzodiazepines in women's and in deaths involving prescription opioids or methadone (about one in three). Shares varied widely between states and correlated with state binge drinking and benzodiazepine prescribing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The importance statement says that using benzodiazepines or alcohol with opioids increases overdose risk, and the discussion calls both modifiable risk factors for overdose with synergistic effects, statements drawn from other literature rather than from these data. The authors acknowledge that the state-level correlations are not causal and that the counts are likely underestimated (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph). The conclusion that alcohol is an underrecognized co-intoxicant is plausible from the under-reporting they describe but is not measured.

timeline.event: Gomes et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend; cited as ref. 5), Ontario coroner data: alcohol involved in 22.3% of opioid-related deaths, higher than in these US certificate data, as described by these authors; not read (DOI 10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2017.07.008).

Barocas et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend; ref. 33), Massachusetts toxicology-linked data: 21% benzodiazepine-only and 18% alcohol-only co-intoxication and 42% polysubstance involvement, as described by these authors; not read.

Gomes et al. (PLOS Med), Ontario public-plan opioid recipients: 77.3% of accidental opioid-related deaths had a benzodiazepine dispensed in the prior 120 days, a prescription-based rather than certificate-based measure
Park et al. (BMJ), US veterans on opioid analgesics: 49% of overdose deaths occurred during a benzodiazepine prescription, a prescription-based measure

replication.where_it_stands: Certificate-based shares are lower than toxicology- or prescription-based ones (two studies cited by the authors found benzodiazepines in 60% of deaths on toxicology), consistent with under-recording; the direction (alcohol and benzodiazepines common in opioid deaths) is consistent across sources.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement appears in the article or its notes.
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr Larochelle reported research support paid to Boston Medical Center from OptumLabs outside the submitted work; no other disclosures (Article notes).
funding.affiliations_note: Boston University School of Medicine and Boston Medical Center (Department of Medicine; Clinical Addiction Research and Education Unit and Section of General Internal Medicine) and Boston University School of Public Health (Department of Community Health Sciences).

what_would_settle_it: Individual-level, toxicology-confirmed death data with blood alcohol and drug concentrations, combined with a denominator from a cohort of people who use opioids (or a case-crossover design comparing the day of overdose with the same people's other days) to estimate how much alcohol or benzodiazepines change the risk of a fatal opioid overdose.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: All US death certificates are the right frame for the share of certified opioid overdose deaths naming alcohol or benzodiazepines.
A census of certified deaths, not a sample.
399,230 deaths; national shares are precise (sampling error negligible), although no intervals are given.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sex, age group, opioid subtype and state are reported; intent, race and other characteristics are not; state rates are only in the unread supplement.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Deaths with no specific drug listed (about 20% in 2011, 12% in 2017) cannot be identified as opioid-involved or co-involved, and coverage differs by state (54.7%–99.3% naming at least one drug in 2017).

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Death certificate mentions depend on whether toxicology was done and recorded; alcohol is known to be under-recorded; no validation of co-involvement codes is reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Testing and reporting practices changed over the period (guidance from 2013 recommends benzodiazepine but not alcohol testing; 8 more states reporting in 2007 with 481 additional alcohol-involved deaths) and differ between states.

Descriptive shares are appropriate, but trends are called nonlinear without a test, no intervals are given, and the correlations are ecological, run in Excel with one-sided tests by the methods (the printed P values look two-sided).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: No response rate applies; incomplete drug recording is covered under items 5 and 6.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of what US death certificates record, the counts are complete and probably accurate; as estimates of how often alcohol or benzodiazepines were actually present, they are floors, and trends partly reflect changing testing and reporting. The study may be cited for certificate-based shares and their pattern by opioid type, sex and state; not for the risk added by alcohol or benzodiazepines, for individual-level associations from the state correlations, or for the true prevalence of co-involvement.

key_findings.finding: Data: CDC WONDER multiple-cause-of-death files, all US deaths 1999–2017 with an underlying cause of drug poisoning (X40–X44, X60–X64, X85, Y10–Y14) and an opioid code (T40.0 opium, T40.1 heroin, T40.2 natural and semisynthetic opioids, called prescription opioids, T40.3 methadone, T40.4 synthetic opioids such as fentanyl and tramadol, excluding methadone, T40.6 other); co-involvement from T51.0 or T51.9 (alcohol) and T42.4 (benzodiazepines); subtypes not mutually exclusive.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Source, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 399,230 opioid-involved poisoning deaths in 1999–2017: 263,601 (66.0%) male, 135,629 female, 204,560 (51.2%) aged 35–54.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The female share is printed as 40.0%; 135,629 of 399,230 is 34.0% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Alcohol co-involvement in all opioid overdose deaths rose from 12.4% in 1999 to 14.7% in 2017, near 15% since 2008; benzodiazepine co-involvement rose from 8.7% in 1999 to 26.2% in 2010 and fell to 21.0% in 2017. From 1999 to 2017 death rates for opioid overdoses involving benzodiazepines rose 10.3-fold and those involving alcohol 5.5-fold, against 5.0-fold for all opioid overdose deaths.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Key Points; Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (image)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol co-involvement by opioid subtype: heroin 10.3%–20.1% over the period and 15.5% in 2017 (0.7 deaths per 100,000 persons); synthetic opioids 11.5% in 2013 to 14.9% in 2017 (1.3 per 100,000); prescription opioids 9.0%–15.4% over the period and 14.3%–15.4% in 2007–2017 (0.7 per 100,000 in 2017); methadone below 10% until 2017 (0.1 per 100,000).
key_findings.locator: Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 (image)

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine co-involvement by opioid subtype: heroin 4.0% in 1999 to 17.1% in 2017 (0.8 deaths per 100,000); synthetic opioids 15.0%–25.9% over the period (1.5 per 100,000 in 2017); methadone 15.6% in 2000 to 32.0% in 2017 (0.3 per 100,000); prescription opioids 15.6% in 2000 to 33.1% in 2017 (1.5 per 100,000).
key_findings.locator: Results › Trends in Alcohol and Benzodiazepine Co-involvement, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3 (image)

key_findings.finding: 2015–2017 (Table), 122,940 opioid overdose deaths (82,506 men, 40,434 women): alcohol 18,419 (15.0%; men 17.2%, women 10.5%); benzodiazepines 26,728 (21.7%; men 19.2%, women 26.9%). Heroin deaths 43,940: alcohol 16.5%, benzodiazepines 15.9%. Methadone 9,868: 10.0% and 32.4%. Prescription opioids 41,709: 14.2% and 33.3%. Synthetic opioids 57,459: 14.9% and 17.4%. Synthetic opioids were involved in 46.7% and prescription opioids in 33.9% of all deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Current Co-involvement in 2015-2017 by Opioid Subtype, Sex, and State, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table

key_findings.finding: State variation in 2015–2017: alcohol co-involvement from 7.4% (Mississippi) to 28.7% (District of Columbia), median 13.3%; benzodiazepines from 5.4% (Delaware) to 45.5% (Arkansas), median 22.0%; no correlation between the two across states (r = 0.08; P = .56).
key_findings.locator: Results › Current Co-involvement in 2015-2017 by Opioid Subtype, Sex, and State, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ecological correlations across states: self-reported binge drinking with alcohol co-involvement in opioid overdose deaths, 2015–2017, r = 0.34 (P = .02); benzodiazepine prescribing per 100 persons with benzodiazepine co-involvement, 2012, r = 0.57 (P < .001); seven jurisdictions lacked enough benzodiazepine-involved deaths in 2012 and South Dakota was excluded from both.
key_findings.locator: Results › Association of Co-involvement With State-Level Binge Drinking and Benzodiazepine Prescribing, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: death-certificate misclassification and state variation; about 20% (2011) and 12% (2017) of drug poisoning deaths without a specific drug, so counts are likely underestimated; changing standards likely increased recognition of co-intoxicants in recent years; 2013 medical-examiner guidance recommends benzodiazepine but not alcohol testing; alcohol under-reported; reporting changes in 2007 (8 more states; 481 additional alcohol-involved deaths in 8 others); 54.7%–99.3% of deaths with at least one drug specified by state in 2017; no individual-level data and no toxicology levels; state correlations not causal.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors contrast their shares with toxicology-based studies: alcohol in 22.3% of opioid deaths in Ontario (Gomes et al.); 21% benzodiazepine-only, 18% alcohol-only and 42% polysubstance in Massachusetts (Barocas et al.); benzodiazepines in 60% of deaths in two toxicology studies, which they call inconsistent with any of their data.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The female count is printed as 135,629 (40.0%) of 399,230 deaths beside 263,601 (66.0%) male; 135,629 of 399,230 is 34.0% (editors' calculation), and the two shares as printed exceed 100%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the counts or 34.0%.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says benzodiazepines were present in 17.1% of synthetic opioid deaths in 2017; the results give 17.1% for heroin deaths in 2017 and only a 15.0%–25.9% range for synthetic opioid deaths (the 2015–2017 Table gives 17.4%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's 2017 synthetic-opioid figure is unsupported by the text; cite the 2015–2017 Table instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table footnote says code T40.4 includes fentanyl and trazodone; the methods say fentanyl, fentanyl analogues and tramadol. In the Table, men's and women's alcohol-involved synthetic-opioid deaths (6,787 and 1,767) sum to 8,554, not the printed 8,584, and men's heroin share is printed 40.1% for 33,229 of 82,506 (40.3%) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; trazodone is a slip for tramadol; the totals differ by 30 deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods set significance at one-sided P < .05, but the printed P values (r = 0.34, P = .02; r = 0.08, P = .56) correspond to two-sided tests for about 50 states (editors' calculation: two-sided P = .016 and .58; one-sided .008 and .29).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no conclusion changes, but the stated test is not the one reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Benzodiazepine co-involvement in 2000 is given as 15.6% both for methadone deaths and for prescription-opioid deaths; the trend figure is an image and could not be checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values may be a copying error; cite the 2017 and 2015–2017 values.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7146101 (PMC HTML, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): key points, abstract, all sections, Table, figure legends (Figures 1–4 images, values not extracted), reference list; article notes (author contributions, conflict-of-interest disclosures, affiliations) read with javascript_tool. The eTable supplement (PDF) was not opened.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Mantel-Haenszel, Review Manager 5.1) of observational studies of recent cannabis use and motor vehicle collisions: case-control, culpability and historical prospective designs with a comparison group; experimental, laboratory and simulator studies excluded. Searches of 19 databases (13 August to 2 September 2010), reference lists, an unpublished-studies search and the team's own libraries, with no limit by year or language. 2,975 records led to 10 selected studies, one of which was dropped for duplicated data, leaving 9 (published 1982 to 2007) in drivers treated for serious injury or involved in a fatal crash. Recent cannabis use was a positive whole-blood test for active THC (or its active metabolite 11-hydroxy-THC) or self-report of use in the 3 hours before the crash. The pooled analysis took only drivers with THC and no alcohol or other drug detected, against drivers with none. Quality was scored with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale by two reviewers; the authors rate the overall evidence “moderate” using GRADE principles but show no GRADE table. No protocol or registration is cited.
can_establish: The pooled size and spread of the association, across nine observational studies of drivers in serious-injury or fatal crashes (published 1982 to 2007), between a positive test for active THC (or self-reported use in the preceding 3 hours), with no alcohol or other drug detected, and being in the crash group, and how that pooled odds ratio differs by design, crash severity and study quality.
cannot_establish: That cannabis causes crashes (all studies observational; the odds ratios in the forest plot are crude; the authors expect uncontrolled confounders); impairment (a positive test shows presence, not that the driver was impaired); risk when cannabis is combined with alcohol (the pooled estimate excludes it, and the review's statement about the combination gives no numbers); dose-response or any legal THC limit (the authors say their data cannot assess thresholds); risk in minor collisions (only serious injury or death); differences between occasional and regular use (one study); current risk (the newest included study was published in 2007); or the absolute risk to a person who drives after using cannabis (odds ratios only).

sample.recruitment: Database search (Cochrane Library, Medline, Embase, PsycInfo, CINAHL, SocIndex, Sociological Abstracts, Web of Science, Academic Search Premier, ProQuest, Alcohol Studies Database, Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Database, LegalTrac, TRIS Online, OSHLINE; 13 August to 2 September 2010), reference lists of included studies and related reviews, a search for unpublished studies and the team's personal libraries. The Methods say published reports were included; three of the nine sources are agency reports and one is a conference paper (reference list). Study authors were emailed for missing data (Methods › Literature search and selection; Synthesis of results).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies with a control or comparison group (cohort, case-control, culpability) of motor vehicle collisions as the World Health Organization defines them (any motor vehicle, fatal or non-fatal), in which recent cannabis use was measured by toxicology on whole blood or by self-report; participants from hospital, roadside, police-record or self-report studies. Excluded: experimental, laboratory and simulator studies; studies of inactive metabolites; studies whose urine and blood results could not be separated (three included studies also tested urine, and their data were used only where the active metabolite was confirmed in blood); one study dropped for duplicated data (Methods › first and second paragraphs; Results › Study selection, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not tabulated. The Methods say mean age, male sex and setting were extracted, but the Table of included studies gives none, and countries are described only as “different countries”. One study used only drivers aged 20 to 49. Cannabis was detected in 2% to 15% of crash-group drivers and under 1% to 7% of comparison drivers (Results › Characteristics of included studies, 1st paragraph; Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level: of 10 studies selected, one was excluded for duplicated data. Eligible studies were limited to those where a cannabis-only group could be separated from drivers with alcohol or other drugs detected.
sample.selection_effects: Only serious-injury and fatal crashes were studied, so minor collisions are not represented. Drivers with alcohol or other drugs detected were removed, which also removes the drivers in whom combined effects would appear. Blood is taken near the time of death in fatal crashes but hours after non-fatal ones, and the authors note that drivers in non-fatal crashes more often refuse drug testing (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Two comparison designs with different meanings of “control” are pooled.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used: toxicology on whole blood (gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, or radioimmunoassay confirmed by it, in several), serum or plasma in two, or self-report of use in the 3 hours before the crash (Blows 2005, self-report only; Mathijssen 2005, self-report or serum screening confirmed by GC-MS). Most studies counted any amount above zero or 1 ng/mL as positive; one used 2 ng/mL (Methods › Synthesis of results, 2nd paragraph; Results › Characteristics of included studies; Risk of bias assessment, 3rd paragraph; the Table).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not available in the pooled analysis. The Discussion says three of the nine studies gave odds ratios at different THC concentrations and each found higher risk with more THC; none is shown or pooled, and the Limitations say the studies did not have enough concentration data to examine dose-response (Discussion, 5th paragraph; Limitations, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Addressed by restriction: the pooled odds ratios use only drivers whose system contained THC with no other drug or alcohol (cases and controls). The authors say alcohol data were available but there was not enough information to account for other illicit drugs (Results › Risk of bias assessment, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: drivers were tested after a crash or at the roadside.

comparison.controls: Two kinds. Case-control (3 studies): random samples of drivers from roadside checks (Blows 2005; Mathijssen 2005) or other emergency-department attendees (Mura 2003). Culpability (6 studies): drivers in the same crashes judged not responsible (non-culpable). Drivers with no THC and no alcohol or other drug are the reference group.
comparison.matching: Not described in the review. The odds ratios in the forest plot equal the crude odds ratios recomputed from each row's printed counts (editors' recalculation of all nine), so none is adjusted. The authors say three medium-quality studies were unclear about which factors were controlled for (Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors state that other potentially important confounders were probably not controlled for in these studies (Limitations, 2nd paragraph). Age, sex, time of day, distance driven, speed, fatigue and tolerance from regular use are not examined; only one study assessed infrequent or habitual use (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison groups were limited to drivers with no alcohol or other drug detected.

outcomes.instruments: Crash involvement and severity from police, medical, coroner and administrative records (for example the Fatal Accident Reporting System database), with crash type classed as fatal or non-fatal by each source study; culpability judged by each source study's own method, which this review does not describe. Study quality by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (maximum nine stars).
outcomes.validity_norms: High quality was defined as nine stars and medium as seven or eight; four studies were high and five medium, none low (Methods › Quality assessment for individual studies; Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph). Only the category is given for each study, not the stars by domain.
outcomes.operationalization: The odds that a driver with THC detected (and no alcohol or other drug) was in the crash group (all crashed drivers, or culpable drivers), compared with the odds for drivers with none. The abstract describes the exposed drivers as driving “under the influence of cannabis” and the reference group as “unimpaired”, but no study measured impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One primary pooled estimate and six subgroup estimates (case-control, culpability, high quality, medium quality, fatal, non-fatal), presented as exploratory; the Methods state a priori that random effects would be used because the populations would be heterogeneous (Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening, data extraction and quality assessment were each done by two reviewers (screening and quality independently), with a third reviewer for disagreements in extraction; one discrepancy in quality assessment was resolved by discussion.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled odds ratio (all nine studies): 1.92 (95% CI 1.35 to 2.73), z = 3.63, P = 0.0003; heterogeneity tau-squared 0.18, chi-squared 42.74 on 8 df, I-squared 81%. By study, from the forest plot, odds ratio (95% CI), THC-positive drivers in crash group over comparison group, weight: Bedard 2007 1.39 (1.25 to 1.54), 1,106 of 19,511 against 541 of 13,032, 18.0%; Blows 2005 7.16 (2.77 to 18.52), 32 of 552 against 5 of 587, 7.9%; Drummer 2004 3.25 (1.29 to 8.21), 51 of 1,214 against 5 of 376, 8.1%; Laumon 2005 2.38 (1.89 to 2.99), 322 of 3,972 against 100 of 2,793, 17.0%; Longo 2000 0.82 (0.45 to 1.49), 21 of 1,038 against 23 of 937, 12.0%; Mathijssen 2005 1.36 (0.59 to 3.15), 6 of 108 against 148 of 3,571, 9.0%; Mura 2003 2.48 (1.45 to 4.24), 49 of 321 against 21 of 310, 12.8%; Terhune 1982 4.40 (1.40 to 13.84), 13 of 129 against 4 of 161, 6.2%; Terhune 1992 0.84 (0.37 to 1.93), 16 of 541 against 9 of 258, 9.1%. Subgroups (studies; sample; I-squared): case-control (3; 5,449; 71%) 2.79 (1.23 to 6.33); culpability (6; 43,962; 83%) 1.65 (1.11 to 2.46); high quality (4; 9,444; 60%) 2.21 (1.25 to 3.90); medium quality (5; 39,967; 79%) 1.78 (1.07 to 2.94); fatal collisions (5; 42,836; 88%) 2.10 (1.31 to 3.36); non-fatal collisions (4; 6,575; 71%) 1.74 (0.88 to 3.46). Editors' calculation from the printed tau-squared and interval (t distribution, 7 df): a 95% prediction interval for the odds ratio in a new setting of about 0.65 to 5.7.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. The pooled odds ratios come from cannabis-only against drug-free counts, not from adjusted models; adjustment in the source studies was not used.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or checklist is cited. The Methods describe an approach “similar to” the Cochrane Collaboration's and say a priori that random effects would be used. The searches date from 2010.
analysis.selective_reporting: All subgroups named in the Methods (design, quality, outcome severity) are reported. The statement that every study of cannabis with alcohol found a higher odds ratio than cannabis alone gives no estimates, and the concentration-specific odds ratios from three studies are mentioned but not shown. The only check on publication bias is a funnel plot of nine studies.
analysis.power: No formal calculation. Subgroups have 3 to 6 studies, and heterogeneity stays at 60% to 88% in every one, so the subgroup contrasts (for example case-control against culpability, whose intervals overlap) cannot be taken as explaining the heterogeneity.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In nine observational studies of drivers in serious-injury or fatal crashes, drivers with THC detected and no alcohol or other drug had about 1.9 times the odds of being in the crash group compared with drivers with none (crude odds ratio pooled 1.92, 1.35 to 2.73), with wide disagreement between studies (0.82 to 7.16; I-squared 81%; prediction interval about 0.65 to 5.7). Estimates were higher in 3 case-control studies (2.79) than in 6 culpability studies (1.65), and the interval for non-fatal crashes (1.74, 0.88 to 3.46) included 1. Whether the combination with alcohol carries more risk is not shown by any number in the paper.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says driving “under the influence of cannabis” was associated with a significantly increased risk of collision “compared with unimpaired driving”; “What this study adds” says acute cannabis consumption “nearly doubles the risk” of a serious or fatal collision; the Discussion calls the review a more definitive statement and the first to look at real-life settings, rates the evidence “moderate”, and says every study that looked at cannabis together with alcohol found a higher odds ratio, “suggesting” synergy. Gaps: (1) a positive test or self-report is read as being under the influence, with no measure of impairment; (2) odds ratios from case-control and culpability designs are described as risk (“nearly doubles”), and the culpability comparison is between crashed drivers; (3) the pooled estimates are crude and the authors themselves expect uncontrolled confounders; (4) “moderate” is given with no GRADE table although observational evidence starts low and heterogeneity is high; (5) synergy is asserted from four cited sources with no numbers and no test of interaction.

timeline.event: Laumon et al., BMJ: French population-based study of fatal crashes (culpability design), one of the nine pooled studies (odds ratio 2.38, weight 17.0%).

Li et al. (Epidemiol Rev), a second meta-analysis of crash studies (nine studies, 2001 to 2010; pooled odds ratio 2.66, as described by Rogeberg and Elvik; not read). Hartman et al. describe it and this review as each showing about doubled crash risk with cannabis.
This review (BMJ, 9 February 2012); the authors call it the first to examine cannabis use and collision risk in real-life settings.
Hartman et al., a driving-simulator study of cannabis with and without alcohol, cites this review as showing roughly doubled crash risk.

Dubois et al. (Forensic Sci Int), 150,010 US drivers blood-tested after fatal crashes (1991 to 2008): THC alone, adjusted for age, sex, alcohol, other drugs and driving history, gave an odds ratio of 1.165 (1.082 to 1.255) of a police-recorded unsafe driver action (1.28 without those adjustments); the paper cites this review's pooled 1.92. Read for this library from the accepted manuscript.

Rogeberg and Elvik (Addiction), a re-analysis of this review and of Li et al.: re-extracting the counts changed the odds ratios of four of this review's nine studies by more than 10%, all downwards (for example Blows 2005 from 7.2 to 2.6, Terhune 1982 from 4.4 to 1.7); case-control and culpability estimates are not comparable without a correction; small-sample bias and the use of unadjusted counts also raise odds ratios; and the pooled estimate for the same nine studies falls from 1.92 to roughly 1.25 to 1.6 depending on the corrections (read by eye from a plot; the original lies outside the revised intervals). Their updated meta-analysis of 28 estimates from 21 studies gives 1.36 (1.15 to 1.61) and 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36). Read for this library.
Rogeberg, Accid Anal Prev, a meta-analysis of culpability studies aimed at avoiding interpretational bias (10.1016/j.aap.2018.11.011, open access): not read.

replication.where_it_stands: Replicated in direction, not in size. A 2016 re-analysis by Rogeberg and Elvik (read for this library) found that this review's pooled 1.92 rests on some mis-extracted counts, on crude rather than adjusted odds ratios and on an estimator that overstates the odds in culpability studies, and put the corrected pooled value for the same nine studies at roughly 1.25 to 1.6; its own meta-analysis of 28 estimates, which includes the large Dubois et al. (2015) analysis, gave 1.36 (1.15 to 1.61) and 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36). The two reviews share primary studies, so they are not independent confirmations of each other. This review gives no number for cannabis with alcohol; Dubois et al. do (see their card).

funding.funder: Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the funding source had no role in design, analysis, writing or the decision to submit. The authors had financial support from Dalhousie University and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research.
funding.declared_conflicts: None: no financial relationships with organisations that might have an interest in the work in the previous 3 years, and no other relationships or activities that could appear to have influenced it.
funding.affiliations_note: The review was carried out with the assistance of two decision makers: the Nova Scotia Road Safety Advisory Committee and the Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Analysis of the same crash studies at the level of individual drivers, adjusted for age, sex, time of day and other driver and trip features; measured THC concentrations and time since use; a clear separation of cannabis alone, alcohol alone and the two together, with the interaction estimated and reported with its interval; control groups drawn from the driving population at the time and place of the crashes rather than from crashed drivers judged not at fault; inclusion of minor crashes; a registered protocol, a list of excluded studies, and a GRADE table with each domain rated.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Drivers; recent cannabis use by blood toxicology or self-report; drivers without it; motor vehicle collisions (World Health Organization definition); designs specified.
No protocol, registration or checklist is cited; the Methods say only that the approach is similar to the Cochrane Collaboration's.
The Introduction explains why observational designs were chosen over laboratory and simulator studies, and the Methods name case-control, culpability and historical prospective designs.

19 databases with the search terms given, no limit by year or language, reference lists, an unpublished-studies search and personal libraries, within about 17 months of publication; no study registries or expert consultation are described. The printed search string has an unmatched parenthesis and mixes OR and AND without grouping, so it cannot be re-run as printed.
Two reviewers screened independently at title, abstract and full-text stages and reached consensus at each.
Two reviewers extracted separately on pretested forms, with a third to settle discrepancies.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The reasons for exclusion are given in general terms (inactive metabolites; urine and blood not separable; one duplicate) and in Figure 1 (an image not read), but there is no list of excluded studies; the paper says details of excluded studies are available on request.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The Table gives design, outcome, sample, cases, controls, data setting, test procedure and quality, but no ages, sexes, countries or cut-offs by study; the Methods say age and sex were extracted.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale by two reviewers (selection, comparability and exposure), but only a high or medium category is reported per study, and selective reporting is not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel pooling chosen a priori for expected heterogeneity, with subgroup analyses by design, severity and quality. A close call: crude odds ratios from two designs with different comparison groups are pooled at I-squared 81%, and the subgroups do not explain it (60% to 88% inside each).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Pooled estimates are given separately for high-quality and medium-quality studies (2.21 and 1.78), though both are exploratory.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion and Limitations name the control group problem in culpability studies, unmeasured confounders, measurement timing and heterogeneity, though the abstract and the “What this study adds” box say cannabis “nearly doubles the risk”.
I-squared reported and discussed; differences by design and by fatal against non-fatal outcome are interpreted (Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
A funnel plot of the nine studies is shown and the authors caution that it is under-powered for fewer than 10 studies. No statistical test.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the authors' declarations are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 scores two critical items as “no” (no protocol or registration cited; no list of excluded studies), which mechanically gives critically low confidence; items 4 and 9 are met in part and items 11, 13 and 15 are met. This rates how far the pooled number can be trusted as an unbiased summary, not the value of the work: screening and extraction in duplicate, a broad search, appropriate random-effects methods, a quality score for each study and a plain list of limitations are all present. The practical consequences are that the pooled estimate is a crude summary of nine studies that disagree with each other, from two designs with different meanings of control, with no information on what each study adjusted for. The source may be cited for the size and spread of the unadjusted odds ratio in these nine studies and for the authors' own caveats; it may not be cited for risk, impairment, causation, dose, or any statement about alcohol.

key_findings.finding: Searches of 19 databases between 13 August and 2 September 2010, plus reference lists, unpublished sources and the team's libraries, found 2,975 records; 222 were taken to abstract review and 23 to full text; 16 more came from reference lists. Ten studies were selected (nine from the full-text search, one from the reference search) and one was dropped for duplicated data, leaving nine.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Literature search and selection, 1st, 2nd and 6th paragraphs; Results › Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig 1 (image; not read)

key_findings.finding: Nine studies (the Table): six culpability designs (Bedard 2007, Drummer 2004, Laumon 2005, Longo 2000, Terhune 1992, Terhune 1982) and three case-control (Blows 2005, Mathijssen 2005, Mura 2003); five of fatal collisions and four of injuries; samples of 290 to 32,543 drivers (49,411 in all, after removing drivers with alcohol or other drugs detected); four rated high quality and five medium. All tested blood or used self-report of use within 3 hours of the crash. THC was found in 2% to 15% of crash-group drivers and under 1% to 7% of comparison drivers.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of included studies, 1st paragraph; the Table; Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary analysis, all nine studies: pooled odds ratio 1.92 (95% CI 1.35 to 2.73), P = 0.0003, I-squared 81%; the Fig 2 footer gives tau-squared 0.18, chi-squared 42.74 on 8 df, z = 3.63.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results; 5th paragraph); Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 1st paragraph; Fig 2 (image, read in the viewer)

key_findings.finding: Study odds ratios in Fig 2 range from 0.82 (Longo 2000) and 0.84 (Terhune 1992), below 1, to 7.16 (Blows 2005); the two largest weights are Bedard 2007 (1.39, 18.0%) and Laumon 2005 (2.38, 17.0%). Recomputing each study's odds ratio from its printed counts reproduces the printed value, so the odds ratios are crude. The text says seven studies found increased risk and two a lower risk, and the positive range 1.36 (Mathijssen) to 7.16 (Blows).
key_findings.locator: Fig 2 (read in the image viewer; each odds ratio recomputed from its counts); Results › Risk of bias assessment, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The citation numbers in that paragraph for the two lower-risk studies do not match the figure (reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: case-control (3 studies) 2.79 (1.23 to 6.33), P = 0.01; culpability (6) 1.65 (1.11 to 2.46); high quality (4) 2.21 (1.25 to 3.90); medium quality (5) 1.78 (1.07 to 2.94); fatal collisions (5) 2.10 (1.31 to 3.36), P = 0.002; non-fatal (4) 1.74 (0.88 to 3.46), P = 0.11. I-squared inside the subgroups: 71%, 83%, 60%, 79%, 88%, 71%.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Fig 3 (image, read in the viewer)
key_findings.note: The culpability P value in the text (0.07) does not fit its interval (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Method: “cannabis only” drivers (THC in blood with no alcohol or other drug) were compared with drivers with none; the primary analysis used measures of recent use (active THC or 11-hydroxy-THC in blood). The review states that estimates in earlier studies are confounded by failing to separate alcohol and other drugs. Other illicit drugs could not be fully accounted for.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Synthesis of results, 1st paragraph; Results › Risk of bias assessment, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Alcohol: “In all studies assessing cannabis use in conjunction with alcohol”, the estimated odds ratio for the combination was higher than for cannabis alone, which the authors take to suggest synergy; they cite four sources (Mura 2003; Laumon 2005; Drummer 1995; Longo 2000, part 2) and give no estimates. Elsewhere, the Discussion says the association between cannabis and crashes is less robust than alcohol's, and cites a relative risk of 2.69 for blood alcohol at the common legal limit from two other sources.
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No numbers for the combination are in the paper; the 2.69 comes from outside the review.

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: four of nine rated high quality, five medium. Medium-quality problems named: a large difference in response rates for cases and controls with no objective confirmation of self-report; data only from drivers aged 20 to 49; three studies unclear about which factors were controlled. The main exposure bias named is alcohol and other drugs taken together with cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Quality assessment for individual studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors rate the overall quality of evidence “moderate”, say the results can be generalised to cannabis-related crashes with serious injury or death in which alcohol and other drugs are not confounding factors, and report no sign of important small-study bias on a funnel plot of nine studies that they caution is under-powered.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overall quality of evidence, 1st paragraph; Publication bias, 1st paragraph; Fig 4 (image; points not read)

key_findings.finding: Interpretation offered by the authors: the culpability comparison group (crashed drivers not at fault) is not a true control and biases effect sizes down; fatal-crash blood is taken near death and non-fatal-crash blood many hours later, so studies of fatal crashes may show higher THC; drivers in non-fatal crashes more often refuse testing. Three studies gave odds ratios at different THC concentrations and each found higher risk with more THC, but none is shown.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations named: legal thresholds differ and impairment can peak at low blood THC, so the data cannot assess legislation based on thresholds; positive results are defined differently across studies (serum, whole blood, self-report); heterogeneity I-squared 81%; hidden confounders probably remain; only serious injury and death were studied, and minor collisions may involve lower concentrations.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: Canadian Institutes of Health Research, no role in the review; authors had support from Dalhousie University; no competing interests declared; two decision-maker partners (the Nova Scotia Road Safety Advisory Committee and the Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse).
key_findings.locator: Contributors; Funding; Competing interests (end matter)

reporting_issues.issue: The culpability subgroup is printed as 1.65 (1.11 to 2.46); P = 0.07, in the abstract and the Results. An interval of 1.11 to 2.46 excludes 1; recalculated from the interval, P is about 0.014 (editors' calculation). The other five subgroup P values fit their intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two numbers is wrong. A reader taking P = 0.07 would call the culpability estimate non-significant, against its own interval; the card uses the odds ratio and interval and does not use the P value.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results cite studies 39, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46 and 47 as finding raised risk and 23 and 48 as finding lower risk. In Fig 2 the two odds ratios below 1 are Longo 2000 (0.82; reference 45) and Terhune 1992 (0.84; reference 48), and Laumon 2005 (reference 23) is 2.38.
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts (seven and two) agree with the figure but the reference numbers for Laumon and Longo are swapped; anyone checking which studies disagree must use the forest plot, not the sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The total for the crash-group column in Fig 2 is printed as 27,286 drivers, but the nine rows add up to 27,386; the text's total of 49,411 (also the sum of the Table's sample sizes) agrees with 27,386 plus the 22,025 comparison drivers.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical slip in the plot footer; the pooled estimate is not affected, but the case count in the footer should not be copied.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the legal alcohol threshold as 0.8 g/100 mL (17.36 mmol/L). That concentration in mmol/L corresponds to 0.8 g/L, which is 0.08 g/100 mL, the usual limit.
reporting_issues.consequence: A unit slip of a factor of ten; the related relative risk of 2.69 is taken from other sources and was not examined in this review.

reporting_issues.issue: “Overall quality of evidence: moderate” is stated with no table of GRADE domains. The Methods list internal validity, generalisability, heterogeneity and precision, which are not the GRADE domains, and observational evidence begins low in GRADE. Nothing in the paper shows an upgrade, while the heterogeneity (I-squared 81%) and uncontrolled confounding the authors describe point to downgrading.
reporting_issues.consequence: The rating cannot be reproduced; the library's own certainty for any claim from this review is set separately.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's fifth paragraph opens by saying simulator studies have found a dose-response effect “in which raised concentrations of tetrahydrocannabinol were associated with increased crash risk”, then cites three of the included epidemiological studies, which gave odds ratios at different concentrations that are not shown. The Limitations say there was not enough concentration data to examine dose-response.
reporting_issues.consequence: Crash risk is not measured in simulators, and the concentration-specific odds ratios are neither shown nor pooled; the review gives no usable dose-response information.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table labels Blows 2005 as a study of deaths (and it is one of five studies in the fatal-collision subgroup), but the reference list gives its title as “Marijuana use and car crash injury”.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not checked against the source study. If it includes non-fatal crashes, the fatal against non-fatal contrast that the abstract highlights is partly misclassified.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed PubMed-style search string has an unmatched closing parenthesis and combines OR and AND without grouping in its third line.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be re-run exactly from the paper; whether this is a typesetting error is not known.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3277079 (PMC HTML, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, all sections, the characteristics table, funding, contributors and competing interests, reference list. Figures 2 and 3 were read from the image viewer and the nine study odds ratios recomputed from the printed counts; Figure 4 (funnel plot) was viewed but its points were not read; Figure 1 was not viewed.

design_detail: Case-control analysis of records from the US Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), 1991 to 2008: drivers aged 20 or older of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks who were in a fatal crash and had a blood alcohol result and at least one blood drug test. Cases were drivers with at least one recorded potentially unsafe driver action (UDA; FARS driver-related factors 20 to 60, for example weaving), controls drivers with none, so the comparison is among drivers already in a fatal crash and the UDA is the authors' proxy for responsibility; it is not a comparison with drivers who did not crash. Logistic regression built in four steps (Models 1 to 4, with a step-down procedure); the final model has age (linear and quadratic), sex, blood alcohol concentration (BAC; linear and quadratic), THC (any positive test), a THC-by-BAC term, age-by-sex and age-by-BAC terms, other drug classes (depressants, narcotics, stimulants, other) and the previous three-year driving record (crashes, drink or drug driving convictions, speeding, other convictions, licence suspensions). Predicted odds and odds ratios were computed from the final model for male drivers aged 45 (Table 3). A secondary analysis used 1,004 drivers with two or three THC-positive tests (1993 to 2008). Read as the journal's accepted manuscript (not the typeset article); Appendix 1 is not in the PDF.
can_establish: How the odds that a driver in a fatal US crash had a police-recorded unsafe action differed with blood alcohol, a THC-positive blood test and both, after adjustment for age, sex, other drugs and driving record, and how the THC association changed as blood alcohol rose (negative THC-by-BAC term).
cannot_establish: Crash risk (every driver studied was in a fatal crash); impairment, timing or amount of cannabis use (THC is a yes/no blood marker); causation; non-fatal crashes; drivers who were not blood tested for both alcohol and drugs (about four in five eligible drivers); or, with a printed test, that THC adds to alcohol at BAC .05 or .08.

sample.recruitment: Registry: FARS, compiled by the National Center for Statistics and Analysis of the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration; all drivers in the 1991 to 2008 files who met the criteria; details of the source are in an earlier paper by the authors (Methods › Data Source, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: drivers of passenger cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks; age 20 or older (younger drivers left out because they would not have had enough driving history); a valid blood alcohol content from a blood test (FARS range 0 to .94 g/dL); at least one confirmed blood drug test. Left out: 47 drivers with sex not coded, 397,396 not blood tested for alcohol, 174,814 blood tested for alcohol but not for drugs, and, from the primary analyses, 1,004 drivers with two or three THC-positive tests. A comparison of the three testing groups is said to be in Appendix 1, which is not in the manuscript PDF (Methods › Inclusion Criteria; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (alcohol- and THC-free, alcohol only, THC only, THC plus alcohol): mean age 46.5 (SD 19.2), 35.7 (13.1), 32.5 (11.4), 30.7 (9.6) years; male 64.3%, 82.5%, 78.8%, 85.2%; previous drink or drug driving conviction 1.8%, 10.6%, 4.5%, 11.8%; licence suspension 9.8%, 26.0%, 26.8%, 33.0%; stimulants 5.0%, 8.9%, 21.0%, 15.5%; any other drug class 15.4%, 18.1%, 37.0%, 27.1%. Race, ethnicity, vehicle, time of day and place are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records), but only 150,010 of 722,220 eligible drivers (20.8%, editors' calculation) had both blood tests: 55.0% had no blood alcohol test and 24.2% a blood alcohol test without a drug test. The four exposure groups add to 149,006; the other 1,004 of the 150,010 were outside the primary analyses (editors' arithmetic). Previous-record variables are missing for 1.6% to 7.8% of drivers (Table 1 footnote); how missing values were handled is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Selection into testing: which drivers get blood alcohol and drug tests depends on state practice, on the driver surviving and probably on police suspicion, and testing for drugs rose from about 30% of alcohol-tested drivers in 1991 to about 70% in 2008. The authors adjust the prevalence trend for this but do not discuss selection into testing as a limit on the odds ratios. Everyone studied was in a fatal crash, so the findings concern drivers in fatal crashes in the United States, and the comparison group is crashed drivers without a recorded unsafe action, not drivers in general (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 1st and 5th paragraphs).

exposure.measurement: Blood (serum) tests recorded in FARS: alcohol as BAC in g/dL, and THC as any positive result among eight THC-containing drug codes (delta-9, hashish oil, hashish, marijuana, Marinol, tetrahydrocannabinoid, THC, cannabinoid of unknown type). Drugs were recorded by group in 1991 and 1992 and individually from 1993, with up to three serum analyses per driver. Whether a positive result means parent THC or an inactive metabolite is not stated, and no concentration is recorded (Methods › Cannabis, and other drug classification and exposure; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: FARS has no route of administration, no blood concentration at the time of the crash and no dose, so THC is a yes/no marker; the authors note THC can stay in the blood for hours or even days. Time between use and the crash is unknown (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug classes (depressants, narcotics, stimulants, other: hallucinogens, PCP, anabolic steroids, inhalants) enter the final model as separate terms. Among the 7,734 THC-positive drivers, 56% (4,347) also had alcohol, 31% (2,433) another drug and 18% (1,386) a stimulant. Alcohol is modelled by BAC with linear and quadratic terms and a THC-by-BAC term (Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: tests were taken after the crash; time since use is not available.

comparison.controls: Drivers who were themselves in a fatal crash and had no unsafe driver action recorded, a stand-in for drivers who did not contribute to the crash. For the exposure, the reference is a driver with BAC 0.00 and no THC detected.
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age (linear and quadratic), sex, other drug classes and the previous three-year driving record, with age-by-sex and age-by-BAC terms (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Risk-taking and the reasons for THC use: the previous driving record is the authors' stand-in for risk-taking. FARS does not say why THC was present, and therapeutic use or underlying conditions (for example sleep or musculoskeletal disorders) may account for part of the association (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Time of day, road, vehicle and number of vehicles are not in the final model (Table 2).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other drug classes adjusted for: depressants OR 1.55, narcotics 1.33, stimulants 1.84, other 1.15 (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: At least one FARS unsafe driver action (driver-related factors 20 to 60; police-recorded actions that may have contributed to starting the crash) as a yes/no proxy for responsibility; the manuscript gives weaving as the only example (Methods › Proxy measure of responsibility).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say UDAs are preferred to traffic violations, which can be under-recorded, and that in crash configurations where responsibility can be inferred (head-on, rear-end) the driver of the striking vehicle usually gets most UDAs, citing a 1998 report and their own 2013 research-showcase paper; not checked here. The manuscript does not say how alcohol or drug involvement itself is coded.
outcomes.operationalization: The odds that a driver in a fatal crash had a recorded unsafe action for a given BAC and THC status, against a driver with BAC 0.00 and no THC. The paper words this as culpability odds, responsibility and crash risk; it is neither crash risk nor a measure of impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated: one outcome, a step-down model-building procedure over age, sex and interaction terms, and a secondary analysis by number of THC-positive tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: administrative records. Police coded unsafe actions at the scene, before laboratory results, but could have known or suspected alcohol or drug involvement; the manuscript does not address this.

analysis.effect_sizes: Final model (Table 2; referent BAC 0.00 and no THC): THC at BAC 0.00, B 0.153 (SE 0.038), OR 1.165 (95% CI 1.082 to 1.255); BAC per 0.01 g/100 mL, B 0.109 (0.002), OR 1.115 (1.110 to 1.120); BAC squared, B -0.002 (0.000), OR 0.998 (0.998 to 0.999); THC-by-BAC, B -0.013 (0.003), OR 0.987 (0.981 to 0.994); depressants 1.553 (1.451 to 1.662), narcotics 1.334 (1.241 to 1.435), stimulants 1.837 (1.734 to 1.945), other 1.149 (1.085 to 1.216); previous crashes (one, two, three or more) 1.128, 1.268, 1.385; suspensions 1.256, 1.329, 1.329; a previous drink or drug driving conviction was not associated (0.954, 1.002, 0.939). Model 1 (THC with linear and quadratic BAC only): THC 1.28 (1.21 to 1.36); BAC from .00 to .01, 1.11 (1.110 to 1.118); the linear THC-by-BAC term was significant in Model 2 (Wald 18.16, P < .001). Male THC-negative drivers, BAC .08 against .00, at ages 20, 40, 60, 80: 1.98, 2.18, 1.99, 1.49. Table 3 (male driver aged 45; predicted odds of a recorded unsafe driver action without THC and with THC; odds ratio against no alcohol and no THC for alcohol alone, B:A, and for alcohol with THC, C:A, with 95% CI): BAC .00: 1.07 and 1.25; B:A 1.00 (not applicable); C:A 1.16 (1.08 to 1.26). BAC .01: 1.19 and 1.37; 1.11 (1.11 to 1.12); 1.28 (1.19 to 1.38). BAC .02: 1.32 and 1.50; 1.24 (1.23 to 1.25); 1.40 (1.31 to 1.50). BAC .03: 1.46 and 1.64; 1.37 (1.35 to 1.38); 1.53 (1.44 to 1.64). BAC .04: 1.61 and 1.79; 1.51 (1.49 to 1.53); 1.67 (1.57 to 1.78). BAC .05: 1.78 and 1.94; 1.66 (1.63 to 1.69); 1.81 (1.70 to 1.93). BAC .06: 1.95 and 2.10; 1.82 (1.78 to 1.86); 1.96 (1.84 to 2.09). BAC .07: 2.13 and 2.27; 1.99 (1.94 to 2.04); 2.12 (1.99 to 2.26). BAC .08: 2.32 and 2.44; 2.17 (2.11 to 2.23); 2.28 (2.13 to 2.44). Editors' calculations from the printed predicted odds (odds divided by one plus the odds): for the reference driver of Table 3 only, about 52 in 100 (51.7%) had a recorded unsafe driver action at BAC .00 with no THC, 56 (55.6%) with THC alone, 64 (64.0%) at BAC .05 and 66 (66.0%) at .05 with THC, 70 (69.9%) at .08 and 71 (70.9%) at .08 with THC. The ratio of predicted odds with THC to those without it at the same BAC is 1.17 at .00, 1.09 at .05 and 1.05 at .08, which matches 1.165 multiplied by 0.987 for each .01 of BAC. The combined odds ratio is close to the sum of the two separate excesses up to BAC .04 (for example .04: 1.51 + 0.165 = 1.68 against 1.67 printed) and a little below it above that (.05: about 1.83 against 1.81; .08: about 2.34 against 2.28), and below the product of the two odds ratios (1.93 at .05; 2.53 at .08). The constant (0.140) and the sex coefficient (-0.074) reproduce the printed 1.07 at BAC .00 only if the other covariates are at their reference values (no other drugs, no previous crashes, convictions or suspensions). Secondary analysis (1993 to 2008, all THC-positive drivers, THC coded 0, 1, 2 or more positive detections): OR 1.18 (1.09 to 1.27) for one and 1.38 (1.13 to 1.68) for two or more; linear trend P = .002, quadratic trend P = .972. Prevalence of any THC detection (Fig 1, read by eye): unadjusted about 1.4% (1991) to 7.9% (2008); adjusted to the 1993 testing rate, about 1.5% (1991) to a maximum of 4.6% (text), above 3% from 1996 and above 3.5% from 2002 (text); THC with alcohol was more common than THC alone in every year.
