analysis.covariates: Age and age squared, sex, BAC and BAC squared, THC, THC-by-BAC, age-by-sex, age squared by sex, age-by-BAC, age squared by BAC, depressants, narcotics, stimulants, other drugs, and counts (0, 1, 2, 3 or more) of previous crashes, drink or drug driving convictions, speeding convictions, other convictions and licence suspensions over three years (Table 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The Introduction states two hypotheses: alcohol detection would fall and THC detection rise from 1993 to 2008, and the combination would raise the odds of an unsafe action compared with alcohol- and THC-free drivers (a comparison with alcohol alone is not stated as a hypothesis).
analysis.selective_reporting: The hypothesised fall in alcohol detection has no reported result (Fig 1 shows THC only). The THC-by-BAC term was kept because of a significant Wald test in Model 2 and the final model was reached by a step-down procedure, so the interaction is data-driven. Appendix 1, with a worked example of the predicted odds and the comparison of tested and untested drivers, is not in the manuscript.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the sample is large (7,734 THC-positive drivers), the intervals for the THC odds ratio are narrow, and the intervals for alcohol alone and for the combination overlap at BAC .05 and .08.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among drivers of cars in fatal US crashes (1991 to 2008) who had blood tests for alcohol and drugs, a recorded unsafe driver action was more likely with higher BAC (OR 1.115 per 0.01, flattening slightly) and, at BAC 0.00, with a THC-positive test (adjusted OR 1.165, 1.082 to 1.255; 1.28 with only BAC terms in the model). For a male driver aged 45 with no other drugs or record, the printed odds ratios against no alcohol and no THC are 1.66 (1.63 to 1.69) at BAC .05 and 1.81 (1.70 to 1.93) with THC, and 2.17 (2.11 to 2.23) at .08 and 2.28 (2.13 to 2.44) with THC. The negative THC-by-BAC term (0.987 per 0.01) means the odds ratio for THC shrinks as BAC rises: about 1.17 at .00, 1.09 at .05 and 1.05 at .08 (editors' calculation). The combination is close to the sum of the two separate excesses and below their product.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title is about impact on crash risk and the Highlights speak of culpability odds. The abstract and conclusion say drivers positive for both agents had greater odds of making an error than drivers positive for either one; the Conclusion speaks of the additive effect of cannabis at low BAC, and the Discussion that public health education should consider highlighting the association between low levels of alcohol, cannabis and crash risk. Gaps: (1) the outcome is a recorded unsafe action among drivers already in a fatal crash, not crash risk; (2) THC is a yes/no blood marker of unstated analyte, so impairment and timing are not measured; (3) greater than alcohol alone rests on adjacent, overlapping intervals in Table 3 (1.81 against 1.66 at .05; 2.28 against 2.17 at .08), with no printed test of THC's added effect at those levels, which is about 9% and 5% of the odds (editors' calculation); (4) additive in the Conclusion is not what the model tests, since the product term concerns departure from multiplicative combination; (5) the stated hypothesis compares the combination with alcohol- and THC-free drivers; (6) the Abstract and Discussion give the 2008 THC prevalence as above 10%, against almost 8% in the Results and Fig 1.

timeline.event: Bédard, Dubois and Weaver (Can J Public Health): earlier analysis of FARS by the same group, THC alone 29% higher odds of an unsafe action, as the Discussion cites it; not read.
Asbridge et al. (BMJ): nine studies, pooled odds ratio 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73) for acute cannabis use and collisions, from crude counts; cited in the Introduction; read for this library.

Hartman et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend): driving simulator, 18 adults analysed; effects of THC and alcohol on lane weaving added up with no interaction detected. Different design and outcome; read for this library.

Rogeberg and Elvik (Addiction): meta-analysis of 28 estimates; this paper enters as 1.10 (1.02 to 1.18), the heaviest weight (10.68%), after conversion for the culpability design; pooled 1.36 and 1.22, and 1.11 to 1.18 where alcohol was controlled. Not independent of this paper; read for this library.

replication.where_it_stands: THC alone (adjusted 1.165) sits within the 1.1 to 1.4 range of the 2016 pooled estimates, which contain this study as the largest weight, so the two are not independent; the 2012 pooled 1.92 is higher. For the combination, a small driving-simulator study read for this library (Hartman 2015) also found effects that added up, on a different outcome; the older on-road studies the Introduction cites disagree with each other and were not read. No independent crash-data analysis of THC with low blood alcohol was read.

funding.funder: AUTO21 Network of Centres of Excellence and the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation (Acknowledgements). The manuscript says nothing about the funders' role.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated in the accepted manuscript (no declaration of interests section).
funding.affiliations_note: Research Department, St. Joseph's Care Group; Centre for Research on Safe Driving, Lakehead University; Northern Ontario School of Medicine, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Roadside or crash-site samples matched on place and time, with blood THC concentration and time since use, so that the comparison is with drivers who did not crash; police coding of the unsafe action made without knowledge of alcohol and drug results; alcohol in bands (none, below .05, .05 to .08) with THC's added odds ratio and its interval printed at each band; the interaction tested on the additive and the multiplicative scale; and a model of who gets tested.

domains.note: The model adjusts for BAC as a measured dose, age, sex, other drug classes and a three-year driving record, the main confounders named. Not in the model: time of day, road, vehicle, speed, and traits that predict both driving after cannabis and unsafe actions beyond the record; no negative-control exposure.

Laboratory blood tests, but THC is a yes/no marker of unstated analyte with no concentration or timing; misclassification of impairment is probably unrelated to the outcome and would pull estimates towards no effect, as the authors say.

Only about one in five eligible drivers had both blood tests; testing depends on state practice, survival and probably suspicion; testing rose from 30% to 70% over the period; the comparison of tested and untested drivers is in an appendix not available. Both groups are drivers in fatal crashes, which conditions on the outcome of the crash.
Not a concern for a blood test taken after a crash.
Previous-record variables are missing for 1.6% to 7.8% of drivers (valid percentages), and handling is not described.

A police-recorded unsafe action is a proxy for responsibility, validated by the authors' own cited work only (striking-vehicle drivers get more UDAs); coding at the scene could be influenced by suspected alcohol or drug involvement, and the factors counted are not listed.

No protocol is mentioned; the interaction term and final model came from a step-down procedure; a stated hypothesis on alcohol detection trends has no reported result; the key contrast of combination against alcohol alone has no printed test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and two domains are judged high: selection into blood testing (about 21% of eligible drivers, with practice changing over the period) and the outcome, a police-coded proxy for responsibility among drivers already in fatal crashes. The study is large and its handling of BAC, other drugs and driving record is careful, and the authors state the main limits of the THC marker. It may be cited for the pattern of odds of a recorded unsafe action by BAC and a THC-positive test among tested drivers in fatal US crashes, for the sub-multiplicative, close to additive pattern of the combination in Table 3 and for the small added odds ratio for THC at BAC .05 to .08 (about 1.09 and 1.05, editors' calculation); it may not be cited for crash risk, impairment, causation, a THC concentration, non-fatal crashes, or the risk to any one driver.

key_findings.finding: Aim and design: to explore the combined influence of low blood alcohol (BAC up to .08) and cannabis on crash risk. Drivers aged 20 or older tested for both drugs and alcohol after a fatal crash in the United States, 1991 to 2008, were examined in a case-control design: cases had at least one potentially unsafe driver action recorded, controls none. Two hypotheses: alcohol detection would fall and THC detection rise over time, and the combination would raise the odds of an unsafe action compared with alcohol- and THC-free drivers.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Data and inclusion: FARS records of drivers of passenger cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks, aged 20 or older, with a valid blood alcohol test and at least one confirmed blood drug test. The unsafe-driver-action proxy is preferred to traffic violations, which can be under-recorded, and is supported by the observation that the driver of the striking vehicle usually gets most UDAs.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Source; Inclusion Criteria; Proxy measure of responsibility

key_findings.finding: Exposure and covariates: eight THC-containing drug codes counted as THC; drugs recorded by group in 1991 and 1992 and individually from 1993, up to three serum analyses per driver; the primary analysis counts drivers with one THC drug positive. Other drug classes and the previous three-year driving record (crashes, drink or drug driving, speeding, other convictions, suspensions) enter the model.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cannabis, and other drug classification and exposure; Previous Driving History

key_findings.finding: Analysis: Pearson chi-square and analysis of variance for characteristics; prevalence by year, unadjusted and adjusted to the 1993 testing rate; logistic regression in four steps (Model 1 THC with linear and quadratic BAC; Model 2 THC-by-BAC; Model 3 age, sex and their interaction by a step-down procedure; Model 4 final) and predicted odds and odds ratios with 95% intervals from the final model.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical Analyses, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sample: 834,328 drivers of cars in fatal crashes, 722,267 aged 20 or older, 722,220 after dropping 47 without sex; 150,010 were blood tested for alcohol and drugs (397,396 not tested for alcohol, 174,814 tested for alcohol only). Of the 150,010: 87,280 alcohol- and THC-free, 53,992 alcohol only, 3,387 THC only, 4,347 THC with alcohol; 1,004 more had two (909) or three (95) THC-positive tests and were left out of the primary analyses. Drivers positive for alcohol, THC or both were younger, more often male and had poorer driving records; polydrug use was commonest with THC, stimulants the most frequent class.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Prevalence: unadjusted THC detection rose from less than 2% to almost 8% by 2008 (Fig 1 Panel A, about 1.4% in 1991 and 7.9% in 2008 by eye); THC was found with alcohol more often than alone in every year (the authors give an average percentage difference of about 29%, from 7% in 1997 to 44% in 1995). Drug testing of alcohol-tested drivers rose from about 30% to 70%; adjusted to the 1993 rate, detection was relatively stable, from 1.5% in 1991 to as high as 4.6%, above 3% from 1996 and above 3.5% from 2002.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Fig 1 (Panels A and B); Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Fig 1 values are read by eye from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol: from BAC .00 to .01 the odds of an unsafe action rose by 11% (Model 1 OR 1.11, 1.110 to 1.118); each later .01 step was slightly smaller (quadratic term 0.99). THC alone with BAC terms only: 28% higher odds (OR 1.28, 1.21 to 1.36); the linear THC-by-BAC interaction was significant (Wald 18.16, P < .001; Model 2).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Final model: age had a curved relation with unsafe actions (highest for the youngest and oldest drivers) and interacted with BAC (for male THC-negative drivers, BAC .08 against .00 gave odds ratios 1.98, 2.18, 1.99 and 1.49 at ages 20, 40, 60 and 80) and with sex. After adjustment, depressants, narcotics, stimulants and other drugs raised the odds of an unsafe action by 55%, 33%, 84% and 15%; one previous crash by 13% and three or more by 39%; one previous suspension by 26% and three or more by 33%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: THC and alcohol in the final model: THC at BAC 0.00, OR 1.165 (1.082 to 1.255); linear BAC OR 1.115 (1.110 to 1.120) and quadratic 0.998 per 0.01; THC-by-BAC OR 0.987 (0.981 to 0.994), which the authors read as the effect of combining the two being greatest at lower BAC.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Predicted odds and odds ratios (male, age 45): see Table 3. At BAC .05 the odds ratio against no alcohol and no THC is 1.66 for alcohol alone and 1.81 (1.70 to 1.93) with THC; at .08, 2.17 and 2.28 (2.13 to 2.44). At BAC 0.00 THC alone gives 1.16 (1.08 to 1.26). Discussion states these as 66% and 117% greater odds for alcohol at .05 and .08 and 81% and 128% with THC.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Checked on the rendered page. Table 3 is for a 45-year-old man; the other covariates are not stated (editors' check: reference values reproduce 1.07).

key_findings.finding: Fig 2 plots the log odds of an unsafe action by BAC for ages 25, 45 and 65, both sexes, with and without THC; the THC and no-THC lines move closer together as BAC rises (the negative THC-by-BAC term); the slopes with BAC are steepest in middle-aged and younger drivers and flatter at 65. The male age-45 values (log odds 0.07 and 0.22 at BAC 0, 0.84 and 0.89 at .08, by eye) match the natural logs of Table 3 (1.07, 1.25, 2.32, 2.44).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Fig 2

key_findings.finding: Secondary analysis of the 1,004 drivers with two or more THC-positive tests (1993 to 2008): log odds 1.61, 1.78 and 1.93 for 0, 1 and 2 or more detections at BAC 0; odds ratios 1.18 (1.09 to 1.27) for one and 1.38 (1.13 to 1.68) for two or more; linear trend P = .002 and no quadratic trend (P = .972).
key_findings.locator: Results, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion: prevalence figures resemble other crash studies (4% to 12%); THC alone with BAC 0.00 gave 16% higher odds of an unsafe action, lower than the 29% from the authors' earlier study, which they attribute to a wider age range and a model that accounts for alcohol and other drugs. As BAC rises the impairing effects of alcohol dominate the relationship between THC and alcohol. Among 7,734 THC-positive drivers, 56% had alcohol, 31% another drug and 18% a stimulant.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limits the authors state: FARS has no route of administration, blood concentration at the time of crash or dose, so THC is a yes/no marker; THC can stay in blood for hours or days, so some THC-positive drivers may not have been impaired, which they say would understate the culpability odds; FARS does not say why THC was present, and therapeutic use or underlying conditions may account for some of the association. Strengths named: number of fatal crashes, control for age, sex, record and other drugs, narrow intervals, exploration of the combination by age, sex and number of THC detections.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: drivers positive for both agents had greater odds of making an error than drivers positive for either alone; further research is needed on low to legal BAC levels (.05 and .08), cannabis concentration and specific driving behaviours, to support roadside screening and public health education about the additive effect of cannabis at low BAC. Funded by AUTO21 Network of Centres of Excellence and the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Conclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Acknowledgements

key_findings.finding: Background the Introduction gives: research generally suggests the effect of alcohol and cannabis together is additive or possibly synergistic, with some studies finding no additive effect; on-road studies disagree at low alcohol with small cannabis doses (no clear difference in a driving proficiency test in one, severe impairment with the combination but minor to moderate impairment with each alone in another); a 2012 meta-analysis gave a pooled odds ratio of 1.92 for acute cannabis use and collisions.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Background statements about other studies, not read for this card.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2008 prevalence of THC detection is given as above 10% in the Abstract and Discussion (1st paragraph) but as almost 8% in the Results (2nd paragraph); Fig 1 Panel A shows any THC at about 7.9% in 2008, and no bar reaches 10%. The five-fold rise matches about 1.4% in 1991 and about 7.9% in 2008. The Results also say less than two percent in 1992, while Fig 1 shows about 1.4% in 1991 and about 2.2% in 1992 (by eye).
reporting_issues.consequence: The prevalence figure should be taken from Results and Fig 1, not the Abstract; it does not affect the odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample used for analysis is given as 150,010 drivers, but the four exposure groups add to 149,006; the other 1,004 (909 with two and 95 with three THC-positive tests) were left out of the primary analyses, and the 7,734 THC-positive drivers quoted in the Discussion equal 3,387 plus 4,347.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary-analysis sample is 149,006 (editors' arithmetic); the paper's headline figure includes drivers used only in the secondary analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: Model 1 is described as run without adjustment for other factors, yet the Results label its odds ratios (1.11 for BAC, 1.28 for THC) as adjusted. They are adjusted for BAC terms only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The THC odds ratio adjusted for age, sex, other drugs and record is 1.165 (Table 2), not 1.28; the Highlights and Abstract use 16%.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion say drivers positive for both agents had greater odds than drivers positive for either alone, but no test or interval is printed for the addition of THC to alcohol at BAC .05 or .08; Table 3 intervals for alcohol alone and for the combination are adjacent (1.63 to 1.69 against 1.70 to 1.93 at .05) or overlap (2.11 to 2.23 against 2.13 to 2.44 at .08). From the printed coefficients the added odds ratio for THC is about 1.09 at .05 and 1.05 at .08 (editors' calculation, no interval).
reporting_issues.consequence: How much THC adds to alcohol at legal-limit BAC is small and its precision is not given; the statement is better read as the combination being close to the sum of the single effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion speaks of the additive effect of cannabis at low BAC, but the model does not test additivity: the product term tests departure from multiplicative combination of odds ratios, and its odds ratio below 1 (0.987) shows a smaller-than-multiplicative combination. Close to additive is shown only by the editors' arithmetic on Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Additive and interaction are used for different things in the paper; no additive-scale test is reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix 1 is cited for the comparison of tested and untested drivers and for a worked example of the predicted odds, and it is not in the manuscript PDF. Table 3's footnote gives only male drivers centered at age 45; the values of the other covariates are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selection into testing cannot be assessed from the manuscript; the other covariates are inferred (editors' check) to be at reference values.

reporting_issues.issue: The THC analyte (parent THC or a metabolite, such as the inactive carboxy-THC) and the detection limit are not stated, although the Discussion says THC can stay in the blood for hours or days. Eight FARS drug codes, including Marinol and hashish, count as THC.
reporting_issues.consequence: A THC-positive result may reflect use long before the crash; the authors attribute only underestimation to this.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give the sex difference as males having greater predicted odds than females, most pronounced in the youngest and oldest drivers. In Fig 2 (BAC 0, no THC; by eye) males are higher at age 25 (log odds about 0.56 against 0.37) but females are higher at 45 (about 0.11 against 0.07) and at 65 (about 0.41 against 0.29).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the alcohol and THC estimates; Table 3 is for male drivers aged 45, where the sexes are closest.

reporting_issues.issue: The hypothesised fall in alcohol detection from 1993 to 2008, and the Abstract's examination of the prevalence of driving under the influence of alcohol, have no reported result; Fig 1 shows THC only.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not relevant to the odds ratios; one hypothesis is left without an answer.

verification.source_read: PDF Dubois_2015_AlcoholCannabisCrashRisk.pdf (the journal's accepted manuscript, 27 pages; not the typeset article, so cited by section and paragraph, with paragraphs counted in running text), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout. Read: highlights, abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 3, Figs 1 and 2, references and acknowledgements. Tables 1 and 3 and Fig 2 were viewed on rendered pages (Table 3 numbers and the negative coefficients of Table 2 checked there; Fig 1 and Fig 2 values read by eye). Appendix 1, cited in the text, is not in the PDF and was not read.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of the Euro-DEN Plus Registry, a multicentre registry of consecutive emergency department (ED) presentations with acute recreational or illicit drug toxicity at sentinel hospitals in Europe, 1 October 2013 to 31 December 2016 (22 EDs in 14 countries took part in this analysis; 18 contributed patients). Patients with acute toxicity from GHB, GBL or 1,4-butanediol (pooled as GHB/GBL) and no other drug were split by report of ethanol co-ingestion into Group A (GHB/GBL alone, n = 183) and Group B (GHB/GBL with ethanol, n = 426). Case and ethanol status were taken from the patient or companions, the attending physician or toxicology at the physician's discretion; each centre's principal investigator adjudicated cases with no central review. Nineteen predefined clinical features, ED management and outcome were compared with chi-square or Fisher tests, t tests and unadjusted odds ratios from univariable logistic regression; no multivariable model. Read as the journal's accepted manuscript (one named author; not the typeset article).
can_establish: How reported ethanol co-ingestion went with the clinical features, treatment, disposition and hospital stay of 609 ED patients who had taken GHB/GBL and no other drug, as unadjusted comparisons across 18 European centres.
cannot_establish: That ethanol caused the differences; effects at known amounts or concentrations of either drug; risk in people who do not reach an ED; whether breathing is affected (slow breathing, oxygen saturation and intubation were not detectably different, with wide intervals and about one in five breathing rates missing); or which single difference would survive correction for the more than 30 unadjusted comparisons.

sample.recruitment: Registry: Euro-DEN Plus sentinel EDs, consecutive presentations with acute recreational or illicit drug toxicity, entered on a purpose-designed minimum dataset; the network began in 2013 with a European Commission grant and had 32 centres in 21 countries by the end of 2017; investigators meet about yearly to harmonise inclusion; case adjudication by each centre's principal investigator, with no external or central review (Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: acute toxicity related to GHB/GBL, alone or with ethanol, when the patient or companions reported GHB/GBL use, or the attending physician reported the presentation as related, or toxicology at the physician's discretion confirmed GHB/GBL and no other drug except ethanol; the same sources decided ethanol co-ingestion. Excluded: presentations with any other drug, and (Fig 1) 467 GHB/GBL presentations with no data on ethanol (Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Age 32.0 years (SD 8.4; 10 missing); women 19.0% (81% men). Group A against Group B: age 33.1 (7.9) against 31.5 (8.5), P = 0.029; women 16.4% against 20.2%, P = 0.274; arrival by ambulance 68.3% against 86.6%, P < 0.001 (Table 2). Race, ethnicity, setting, time since ingestion and medical history are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registry), but 467 of 2,349 patients with GHB/GBL involvement (19.9%, editors' calculation) had no ethanol data and were excluded. Missing values in the analysed 609: temperature 54.4%, respiratory rate 20.7%, blood pressure 18.6%, Glasgow Coma Score 9.5%, heart rate 7.7%, age 1.7% (Table 2); how missing values were handled is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Only patients who reached an ED at 18 centres: six centres provide 93% of the patients (editors' arithmetic from Table 1: two London centres 297, two Oslo centres 209, Tallinn 33, Barcelona 26), so the series reflects London and Oslo practice and patients; one Oslo centre is an accident and emergency outpatient clinic. The share with ethanol differs by centre (54% to 86% in the six large centres, editors' calculation), and the threshold for calling an ambulance, attending an ED, admitting to critical care or giving sedatives may differ by centre and by whether alcohol is known to be involved. People managed before the ED, and those who died before arrival, are not in the registry; 67.6% of GHB/GBL patients with ethanol data (1,273 of 1,882) had other drugs and are excluded, so the analysed patients are a minority of GHB/GBL presentations (Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Fig 1; Table 1).

exposure.measurement: Report by the patient or companions, report by the attending physician, or toxicology at the physician's discretion, with the same criteria for GHB/GBL and for ethanol. Toxicology was done in 38 patients (6.2%) in a minority of centres and found GHB/GBL in 28.9% of them (11 of 38, editors' arithmetic), which the author attributes to the short detection window (Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Table 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: no amount of GHB, GBL, 1,4-butanediol or ethanol, no time since ingestion, no product or route; ethanol is a yes/no report and the three GHB-related compounds are pooled.
exposure.polysubstance: Excluded by design: 1,273 presentations with other drugs (cathinones, methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine, opiates, cannabis, MDMA, ketamine, poppers; Fig 1). The author says unreported or unanalysed co-ingestion cannot be excluded and cites earlier work showing high agreement between admitted use and toxicology; the authors also say excluding other drugs may have biased the intubation estimate towards a lower rate (Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).

comparison.controls: Group A, patients with GHB/GBL toxicity and no reported ethanol (n = 183) at the same centres.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Amount and timing of each drug, regular use and tolerance, circumstances (the author names sexualised drug use, chemsex, as one that may differ by area), time between ingestion and arrival, and medical and psychiatric history are not recorded or not reported (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other drugs excluded by design; unreported co-ingestion unmeasured. No adjustment for age, sex or centre.

outcomes.instruments: Nineteen predefined clinical features recorded in routine ED care (reduced consciousness as a Glasgow Coma Score below 13; bradycardia below 60 and tachycardia above 100 beats per minute; bradypnoea below 12 and tachypnoea above 20 breaths per minute; hypothermia below 35 and hyperthermia above 39 degrees C; systolic pressure below 90 or above 180 mm Hg; vomiting, seizures, agitation and others), ED treatment, disposition, length of stay and death (Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated in this paper; features recorded by the treating team, with the time of measurement not given (the Discussion says features refer to the whole ED stay).
outcomes.operationalization: Percentage of patients with each feature among those with data; critical care admission as a share of patients hospitalised; length of stay in hours.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 33 between-group comparisons are reported in Tables 2 and 3 (21 in Table 2, 11 in Table 3, and death) and three within-group intubation comparisons; the author notes only the risk of missing real differences (beta error).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: clinicians recorded features, gave sedatives and decided on admission knowing the history, including alcohol.

analysis.effect_sizes: Group A (GHB/GBL alone, n = 183) against Group B (with ethanol, n = 426); odds ratios unadjusted, from univariable logistic regression. Decreased consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13) 49.1% against 58.9% (P = 0.034 in Results and Table 2; 0.031 in the Abstract), OR 1.490 (1.029 to 2.158), 309 of 551 patients with data. Bradycardia 23.5% against 15.7% (P = 0.027), OR 0.604 (0.386 to 0.948). Bradypnoea 11.6% against 8.2% (P = 0.246; 20.7% missing); tachypnoea 14.0% against 14.7% (P = 0.839); vomiting 10.3% against 15.0% (P = 0.129); seizures 6.9% against 7.2% (P = 0.675); agitation 34.9% against 33.1% (P = 0.679); hypotensive episode 1.5% against 2.2% (P = 1.00); arrhythmia 1.2% against 0.8% (P = 0.645). Fig 2 (unadjusted odds ratio for ethanol co-ingestion, 95% CI; read on the rendered page): headache 1.711 (0.477 to 6.141); vomiting 1.536 (0.880 to 2.683); hallucinations 1.496 (0.486 to 4.611); decreased level of consciousness 1.490 (1.029 to 2.158); hypotensive episode 1.461 (0.306 to 6.968); hypothermia 1.365 (0.657 to 2.839); chest pain 1.272 (0.254 to 6.365); anxiety 1.258 (0.723 to 2.19); seizures 1.165 (0.570 to 2.380); tachypnoea 1.071 (0.601 to 1.910); tachycardia 1.019 (0.619 to 1.676); agitation or aggressive behaviour 0.924 (0.637 to 1.341); psychotic signs and symptoms 0.735 (0.212 to 2.544); bradypnoea 0.684 (0.354 to 1.322); arrhythmias 0.663 (0.110 to 4.003); bradycardia 0.604 (0.386 to 0.948); palpitations 0.555 (0.190 to 1.624); hypertensive episode 0.498 (0.155 to 1.597). Management (Table 3): any treatment 49.2% against 60.4% (P = 0.011); sedative drugs 12.8% against 20.1% (P = 0.034); orotracheal intubation 3.9% against 5.9% (P = 0.321; 32 of 609 overall, 5.3%); naloxone 19% against 21.5% (P = 0.495); flumazenil 3.4% against 3.4% (P = 0.703). Disposition: discharge 63.4% against 64.1% and hospitalisation 36.6% against 35.7% (P = 0.842); among patients hospitalised (219), critical care 15 of 67 (22.4%) against 84 of 152 (55.3%) and medical ward 76.1% against 43.4% (P < 0.001); as shares of all patients in each group, critical care 8.2% against 19.7% (editors' calculation). Median time in hospital 2 h 18 min (IQR 1:01 to 4:11) against 3 h 11 min (1:56 to 7:13), P < 0.001; more than 6 hours 16.9% against 28.4% (P = 0.003). Deaths: 0 against 2 (0.5%), P = 1.00. Intubation by Glasgow Coma Score: 0.7% at 15, 2.1% at 8 to 14, 14.5% below 8 (P < 0.001); not related to vomiting (6.3% against 5.3%) or seizures (7.5% against 5.3%). Editors' rough calculation from the printed counts and percentages for intubation: odds ratio about 1.5 with a 95% interval of about 0.7 to 3.7. Table 1 counts by centre, editors' arithmetic: the share of patients with ethanol in the six centres with more than 25 cases runs from 54% (Oslo accident and emergency outpatient clinic, 75 of 139) and 58% (Tallinn, 19 of 33) to 76% (Guy's and St Thomas', 188 of 246), 82% (King's College, 42 of 51) and 86% (Oslo University Hospital, 60 of 70).
analysis.covariates: None: univariable comparisons only, with no adjustment for age, sex, centre, time of presentation or any other variable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A secondary analysis of a registry; no protocol or registration for this analysis is mentioned. The 19 clinical features are described as predefined in the registry's minimum dataset.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 19 features appear in Table 2 and 18 in Fig 2 (none had hyperthermia); the Abstract and Highlights feature the significant differences. Some Abstract values do not match the Results and tables (consciousness P = 0.031 against 0.034; ages labelled Group A/B as 31.5/33.1 when Table 2 gives A 33.1 and B 31.5; consciousness and sedatives listed B/A while the other pairs are A/B). No correction for about 33 comparisons.
analysis.power: Not calculated; the author states some features were too infrequent to detect differences (beta error). Intervals for the rare features (hypotension, arrhythmia, chest pain, seizures) are very wide (Fig 2).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 609 ED patients with GHB/GBL toxicity and no other drug, those reported to have taken ethanol (Group B) arrived by ambulance more often (86.6% against 68.3%), were younger (31.5 against 33.1 years) and were recorded with a Glasgow Coma Score below 13 more often (58.9% against 49.1%; OR 1.49, 1.03 to 2.16), were given any treatment (60.4% against 49.2%) and sedatives (20.1% against 12.8%) more often, and, among those hospitalised, went to critical care more often (55.3% against 22.4%); they stayed longer (median 3 h 11 min against 2 h 18 min). Bradycardia was less frequent (15.7% against 23.5%). No difference was detected in slow or fast breathing, seizures, vomiting, other features, intubation (5.9% against 3.9%), antidotes or overall disposition. Two patients died, both in Group B. All comparisons are unadjusted.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Highlights and Conclusions say co-ingestion of ethanol increases the adverse effects in patients intoxicated by GHB/GBL, leading to greater depression of consciousness, need for treatment, admission to the ICU and longer hospital stay, and the Conclusions call the results first evidence about the influence of ethanol on the clinical profile. Gaps: (1) increases states a causal effect, from unadjusted comparisons in which the groups differ in age, mode of arrival and centre mix, and exposure rests on report; (2) depth of depression of consciousness is not measured, only the share below a Glasgow Coma Score of 13 (9.5% missing); (3) the critical care percentages are shares of patients hospitalised (22.4% and 55.3%), not of all patients (8.2% and 19.7%), and the Abstract does not give the denominator; (4) about 33 uncorrected comparisons with a borderline P = 0.034 for the main clinical feature; (5) no difference in intubation or breathing features is described as no difference, with wide intervals and a possible downward bias the author names; (6) first evidence overlooks a controlled volunteer experiment of ethanol with GHB (not cited).

timeline.event: Thai et al. (J Clin Psychopharmacol): a randomized double-blind crossover study in 16 healthy volunteers; ethanol with GHB lowered oxygen saturation by a little more than either alone (about 2 points at the largest mean fall); a different design and outcome; not cited in this paper; read for this library.
Liechti et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend): clinical features of GHB and GBL toxicity and concomitant drug and alcohol use, cited here as background; not read.
Miro et al. (Toxicology Letters): same registry, pure GHB intoxication compared with that combined with other substances, cited as background; not read.
This paper: ED patients with GHB/GBL alone or with ethanol, unadjusted comparisons.

replication.where_it_stands: In direction, the two sources read for this library agree: ethanol with GHB went with more sedation or physiological effect (more reduced consciousness and critical care use in patients; a small extra fall in oxygen saturation in volunteers). They measure different outcomes at unrecorded (patients) or fixed (volunteers) amounts, neither is large enough or adjusted enough to size the risk, and no study read measured both drugs in the blood of patients. A later independent analysis was not found among the sources read.

funding.funder: No funding statement for this analysis. The Euro-DEN network was funded by a European Commission grant (JUST/2012/DPIP/AG/3591) in 2013 to 2015 (Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 1st paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships (Declaration of interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Hospital Clinic Barcelona (corresponding author); the registry is run by the Euro-DEN Plus research group. The accepted manuscript names one author. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A registry or prospective analysis that records the amount and time of GHB/GBL and ethanol, measures both in blood, adjusts for centre, age, sex and other recorded drugs, uses fixed rules for the timing of Glasgow Coma Score, breathing rate and oxygen saturation, and defines critical care admission by criteria that do not depend on knowing about alcohol; for breathing, controlled studies in volunteers with continuous measurement at graded alcohol exposure, as far as ethics allow.

domains.note: Univariable comparisons only. The groups differ in age and mode of arrival and probably in centre mix, amounts taken, regular use, setting and time since ingestion; none is adjusted for.

Ethanol (and GHB/GBL) status rests on report by the patient, companions or the physician; toxicology in 6.2%, detecting GHB/GBL in 28.9% of those; no amounts or times. Patients with reduced consciousness may be less able to give a history, so unreported ethanol in Group A is plausible and may be related to severity.

ED attendance only, 93% from six centres and 83% from London and Oslo; 467 presentations without ethanol data excluded; 67.6% of the rest excluded for other drugs; the threshold for attendance, ambulance use and admission may differ with alcohol.
Treatment and admission are also outcomes here and depend on local practice and on knowing alcohol was involved.
Temperature missing in 54.4%, respiratory rate 20.7%, blood pressure 18.6%, Glasgow Coma Score 9.5%; complete-case percentages, handling not described.

Predefined features recorded in routine care with unstated timing; Glasgow Coma Score cut-off is a reasonable marker, but sedative use, treatment and critical care admission depend on clinicians who knew the history.
A secondary analysis with no protocol mentioned; all predefined features are shown; about 33 comparisons without correction; Abstract values differ from the tables in places.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and four domains are judged high (confounding, exposure measurement, selection and missing data). The series is large for GHB/GBL, covers several countries, excludes other drugs by design and shows all predefined features, and the direction of the main differences is plausible. It may be cited for the unadjusted differences between reported ethanol co-ingestion and no co-ingestion in ED patients (consciousness, treatment, critical care, stay), for the absence of a detected difference in breathing features and intubation with wide intervals, and for the two deaths; not for a causal increase, for any amount or concentration, for breathing risk, or for risk in people who do not attend an ED.

key_findings.finding: Aim and design: to study the clinical impact of ethanol co-ingestion in patients presenting to the ED with acute GHB/GBL toxicity. Secondary analysis of the Euro-DEN Plus Registry (14 countries, 22 EDs; 17,371 consecutive patients with acute recreational drug toxicity over 39 months, October 2013 to December 2016): lone GHB/GBL (Group A) against GHB/GBL with ethanol (Group B), without other drugs.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Objective; Method); Introduction, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Case definition: GHB/GBL toxicity was diagnosed from clinical history and/or data collected during emergency care; a case was included when the patient or companions reported GHB/GBL use, or the attending physician reported the presentation as related, or toxicology at the physician's discretion confirmed GHB/GBL and no other drug except ethanol; the same factors decided ethanol co-ingestion; presentations with other drugs were excluded. Case adjudication by each centre's principal investigator, with no external or central review.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 2nd paragraph; Study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Data and tests: demographics, 19 predefined clinical features, ED management and outcome (disposition, length of stay, death), and toxicology when done; chi-square (or Fisher) and t tests, and the association of ethanol with each feature estimated univariately as an odds ratio by logistic regression; P below 0.05 or an interval excluding 1 counted as significant.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Flow: 17,371 registry patients; 15,022 without GHB/GBL; 2,349 (13.5%) with GHB/GBL; 467 without ethanol data; 1,882 with ethanol data, of whom 183 (9.7%) were Group A, 426 (22.6%) Group B and 1,273 (67.6%) had other drugs and were not included. Four of the 22 centres included no patient; six centres with more than 25 cases each supplied 93% (565 of 609; the two London centres 297 and the two Oslo centres 209, editors' arithmetic from Table 1).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig 1; Table 1
key_findings.note: Fig 1 and Table 1 were checked on the rendered pages; the counts by centre add to 609.

key_findings.finding: Patients: mean age 32.0 years (SD 8.4), 81% men; Group B were younger (31.5 against 33.1 years, P = 0.029) and arrived by ambulance more often (86.6% against 68.3%, P < 0.001); no difference by sex.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Clinical features: the most common was reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13) in 56.1% (309; 58 missing), more frequent in Group B (58.9% against 49.1%, P = 0.034; Abstract P = 0.031); the second was agitation or aggressive behaviour (33.6%, no difference). Bradycardia was more frequent in Group A (23.5% against 15.7%, P = 0.027). The other 16 features tested did not differ (overall: vomiting 13.6%, anxiety 12.6%, bradypnoea 9.1%, seizures 7.0%, tachypnoea 14.5%, hypotensive episode 2.0%, arrhythmia 0.9%; Table 2); no patient had hyperthermia.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Percentages in Table 2 are of patients with data for each feature; missing values range from 1.7% to 54.4%.

key_findings.finding: Fig 2 gives unadjusted odds ratios for ethanol co-ingestion for 18 clinical features: only decreased level of consciousness (1.490, 1.029 to 2.158) and bradycardia (0.604, 0.386 to 0.948) exclude 1; intervals for the rarer features, such as hypotensive episode (1.461, 0.306 to 6.968), arrhythmia (0.663, 0.110 to 4.003) and chest pain (1.272, 0.254 to 6.365), are very wide.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Fig 2
key_findings.note: Both interval columns of Fig 2 are headed 95% CI (lower limit); the second column is the upper limit.

key_findings.finding: ED management: any treatment 60.4% against 49.2% (P = 0.011); sedative drugs 20.1% against 12.8% (P = 0.034); no differences in antidotes (naloxone 21.5% against 19%, flumazenil 3.4% in both) or orotracheal intubation (5.3% overall; 5.9% against 3.9%, P = 0.321). Intubation rose as the Glasgow Coma Score fell (0.7% at 15; 2.1% at 8 to 14; 14.5% below 8; P < 0.001) and was not related to vomiting or seizures.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Disposition and stay: 63.9% discharged (389; 66 against medical advice) and 35.9% hospitalised (219), with no overall difference between groups (P = 0.842); among patients hospitalised, critical care 55.3% in Group B against 22.4% in Group A and medical ward 43.4% against 76.1%; median time in hospital 3 h 11 min against 2 h 18 min (P < 0.001); stay over 6 hours 28.4% against 16.9% (P = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Deaths: two patients (0.3%), both in Group B (P = 1.00): a 35-year-old man with an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, intubated and ventilated by paramedics, who died in the ED despite resuscitation, and a 32-year-old man with an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, return of circulation after resuscitation, admission to intensive care, hypoxic ischaemic brain injury on CT, and care withdrawn 2 days later to allow organ donation. The author notes mortality may be higher, as deaths outside hospital and direct admissions to intensive care are not in the registry.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion: co-ingestion of ethanol is associated with significant differences in clinical features, generally leading to greater severity (more reduced consciousness, more treatment, more critical care admission, longer stay); agitation may reflect low doses early on or recovery; vomiting (13%) was less frequent than in earlier series (mean 23%); no difference in intubation, which the author says may be biased towards a lower rate because other drugs were excluded; level of consciousness, not seizures or vomiting, leads to intubation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limits stated: the reference populations may not represent the consumption habits of each city or country; more than 90% of presentations came from six EDs; the context (for example chemsex) was not analysed; patients managed by prehospital services and not brought to an ED are not included; toxicology in 38 patients (6.2%), only in a minority of centres, detecting GHB/GBL in 28.9%; unreported co-ingested drugs cannot be excluded; low frequencies of some features may hide differences (beta error).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the results provide first evidence of the influence of ethanol on the clinical profile of patients who used GHB/GBL, with significant differences in depth of depression of consciousness, need for treatment, admission to the ICU and length of ED stay, all higher with ethanol. No competing interests declared; the Euro-DEN network was funded by a European Commission grant in 2013 to 2015.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Declaration of interests; Methods › Euro-DEN plus Registry, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract labels the ages Group A/B 31.5/33.1, the reverse of Table 2 (A 33.1, B 31.5); gives consciousness and sedatives as B/A while the other pairs are A/B; and gives P = 0.031 for consciousness where Results and Table 2 give 0.034.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the Abstract cannot be read pair by pair without the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The critical care percentages in the Abstract (22.4% and 55.3%) are shares of patients hospitalised (15 of 67 and 84 of 152), not of all patients in each group (8.2% and 19.7%, editors' calculation); the Abstract does not give the denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read without the denominator, the figures overstate how many patients needed critical care.

reporting_issues.issue: The Highlights and Conclusions say ethanol co-ingestion increases adverse effects, but all comparisons are unadjusted; the groups differ in age, arrival by ambulance and probably centre (the share with ethanol ranges from 54% to 86% across the six large centres), and ethanol status rests on report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The differences are associations; a causal increase is the author's reading, supported by physiology but not shown by the design.

reporting_issues.issue: Depth of depression of consciousness is claimed, but only the share with a Glasgow Coma Score below 13 is compared, 58 patients (9.5%) are missing, and the timing of the score is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether consciousness was more deeply depressed (not only more often below the cut-off) is not shown.

reporting_issues.issue: About 33 between-group comparisons are reported without correction for multiplicity; the main clinical difference, reduced consciousness, has P = 0.034 and an interval whose lower limit is 1.029.
reporting_issues.consequence: One or two of the eight differences reported as significant may be chance; consciousness would not survive a Bonferroni correction (editors' note).

reporting_issues.issue: No difference in intubation (5.9% against 3.9%, P = 0.321) and in slow breathing (8.2% against 11.6%; 20.7% of breathing rates missing) is reported, and the Discussion explains the intubation result by the exclusion of other drugs; the intervals are wide (intubation odds ratio about 1.5, about 0.7 to 3.7, editors' rough calculation) and no oxygen saturation, arterial gas or airway outcome other than intubation is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not show that ethanol leaves breathing unaffected; it shows that a difference was not detected in this unadjusted, incomplete comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 and the Results give 19.9% of discharged patients as leaving against medical advice; 66 of 389 is 17.0% (editors' calculation), and 19.9% is close to Group A's 19.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A transcription error of no consequence for the ethanol comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text gives the share of admitted patients going to conventional wards as 77.6% (Group A) and 44.7% (Group B); Table 3 gives 76.1% (51 of 67) and 43.4% (66 of 152), which the printed counts reproduce.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small text-table mismatch in the complement of the critical care share; the table values are used here, and the critical care shares (22.4% and 55.3%) agree in text and table.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions say the results are the first evidence of the influence of ethanol on patients who used GHB/GBL, but the reference list includes earlier clinical series with concomitant alcohol and drug use (Liechti 2006; Miro 2017) and omits the controlled experiment of ethanol with GHB in volunteers (Thai 2006).
reporting_issues.consequence: Novelty is overstated; the earlier controlled study measured a different outcome (oxygen saturation) at fixed amounts.

verification.source_read: PDF Galicia_2019_EthanolCoingestionGHB.pdf (the journal's accepted manuscript, 16 pages; not the typeset article, so cited by section and paragraph, counted in running text), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout. Read: highlights, abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 3, Figs 1 and 2, references and declaration of interests. Tables 1 to 3 and Figs 1 and 2 were checked on rendered pages (counts by centre add to 609; Fig 1 flow adds up; Fig 2 odds ratios read from the printed column); discussion paragraphs were checked on the rendered pages.

design_detail: Within-person, placebo-controlled human laboratory study in a full-motion driving simulator (National Advanced Driving Simulator, University of Iowa). Six sessions at least 1 week apart, in randomized order: placebo, low-THC (2.9%) or high-THC (6.7%) vaporized cannabis (500 mg, inhaled ad libitum over 10 minutes), each with an oral placebo or alcohol drink aimed at an approximate peak breath alcohol of 0.065%. Each person drove a 45-minute night route 0.5 to 1.3 hours after the start of cannabis dosing. Blood THC and breath alcohol during the drive were modelled from samples taken before and after it, and lateral-control measures were analysed by event against those modelled concentrations (stepwise general linear model, SAS GLM Select, Schwarz information criterion) rather than by dose condition. 19 people drove; 18 were analysed. A registry number is cited (NCT01620177); the record was not read. Double-blinding is stated only in the Discussion and Conclusion.
can_establish: In 18 healthy people who used cannabis occasionally, in a simulator and in the conditions given, that blood THC and breath alcohol during the drive were each associated with more lane weave (SDLP), that alcohol but not THC was associated with more lane departures and lateral acceleration, and roughly how much lane weave a given blood THC level gave compared with a given breath alcohol level.
cannot_establish: Real-road driving or crash risk (the authors say SDLP is not directly validated against crashes; one simulator, one 45-minute night drive per condition); whether cannabis with alcohol is worse than the sum of the two (the stepwise model selected no interaction term, but the study gives no estimate or interval for it, and its by-condition tests were not significant for either drug); effects at alcohol levels above the target of about 0.065% (the range of during-drive concentrations analysed is not reported); effects in regular cannabis smokers, in women (5 of 18), at other ages, or with other drugs or sleep loss.

sample.recruitment: Not described. The paper says only that healthy adults gave written consent in an Institutional Review Board-approved study run with the University of Iowa Clinical Research Unit and the driving simulator (Methods › 2.1; Acknowledgments). Participants entered the clinical research unit 10 to 16 hours before drug administration, to rule out acute intoxication.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 21 to 55; cannabis use at least once in 3 months but no more than 3 days a week over the past 3 months (Cannabis Use Disorders Identification Test); light or moderate alcohol use on the Quantity-Frequency-Variability scale or, if heavy, no more than 3 to 4 servings on a typical occasion; licensed driver for at least 2 years; at least 1,300 miles driven in the past year. Excluded: clinically significant illness; a clinically significant adverse event with cannabis or alcohol, or motion sickness; blood donation in the past 2 weeks; pregnancy or nursing; interest in drug treatment in the past 60 days; medicines contraindicated with cannabis or alcohol or known to affect driving; need for non-standard driving equipment; earlier participation in a similar simulator study (Methods › 2.1).
sample.demographics: 19 entered: 13 men and 6 women, ages 21 to 37 (mean 26.1, SD 4.1), 74% White, mean body mass index 26.3. Most used cannabis at least twice a month and up to 3 days a week; last use a median of 4 days before admission (range 0.3 to 120 days); 6 to 23 years of driving (median 10). The 18 analysed: 13 men and 5 women (editors' count from Table 1), mean age 26.3 (SD 4.2).
sample.attrition: No dropouts reported. Participant 12 (a woman) was excluded from all driving analyses because her data were extreme in almost every measure and condition, including placebo with placebo, and videos showed erratic, inattentive driving in all conditions. No rule set in advance and no analysis that keeps her data are reported.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers who passed medical screening, had no serious past reaction to cannabis or alcohol, were willing to drink and inhale before driving, and were experienced drivers; only occasional cannabis smokers and light-to-moderate drinkers aged 21 to 37. The authors note that participants knew their driving was observed and might have driven more carefully, or wanted to show that cannabis does not affect driving.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered. Alcohol: 90% grain alcohol in fruit juice drunk ad libitum over 10 minutes, or placebo juice with an alcohol-swabbed rim and 1 mL alcohol on top to mimic taste and smell. Cannabis: 500 mg of vaporized cannabis supplied by NIDA (Volcano Medic vaporizer) inhaled ad libitum over 10 minutes: placebo 0.008%, low 2.9% or high 6.7% THC. Blood THC assayed by a published method (protein precipitation, solid-phase extraction; linear range 1 to 100 µg/L) at 0.17, 0.42, 1.4 and 2.3 hours after inhalation, oral fluid collected alongside; breath alcohol (Alco-Sensor IV) at the same times. Concentrations during the drive were modelled: individual power-curve regression for THC, linear interpolation for alcohol.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: placebo, low or high vaporized cannabis (500 mg containing 0.008%, 2.9% or 6.7% THC) inhaled over 10 minutes, after a placebo or alcohol drink drunk over 10 minutes (target peak breath alcohol about 0.065%); six single-dose sessions at least 1 week apart; the drive began 0.5 to 1.3 hours after the start of cannabis dosing. Because inhalation was ad libitum, achieved THC overlapped between the two active doses: 6 of 18 people had a higher peak blood THC after the low dose than after the high dose, and 4 had peaks within 20% of each other despite a two-fold dose difference (Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Figure 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were occasional cannabis smokers and light-to-moderate alcohol drinkers; people taking medicines known to affect driving were excluded; no urine or other drug screen is mentioned. Blood THC at the pre-dose baseline sample was above zero in some sessions (maximum 6.3 µg/L, Table 6), which shows residual THC or use between sessions. Not otherwise controlled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants entered the unit 10 to 16 hours before dosing to rule out acute intoxication; last cannabis use before admission a median of 4 days earlier (range 0.3 to 120 days; Table 1). Abstinence was not verified beyond the baseline blood sample.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant drove under all six conditions, including placebo cannabis with placebo alcohol. The Discussion and Conclusion call the design double-blind and placebo-controlled; the Methods describe no blinding procedure beyond the placebo preparations.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person). Condition order was randomized (method not described). Three drive scenarios with varied event order were used across the six drives to limit practice effects; how scenarios were assigned to conditions is not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Stable between-person differences are absorbed by the subject term (the drug-free predicted SDLP ranged from 24.7 to 44.8 cm across people, a spread larger than the drug effects). Not measured or not reported: sleep and time of day before each session, caffeine or tobacco, tolerance beyond self-reported use, expectancy about the drugs, and learning across the six drives.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same participants as the active conditions.

outcomes.instruments: NADS-1 simulator (a 1996 sedan in a 7.3 m dome with full motion). One 45-minute night drive with urban (25 to 45 mph), interstate (70 mph) and rural segments, other traffic and hazards. Measures: standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP, cm), standard deviation of steering-wheel angle (curvy and straight events), lane departures per minute, maximum lateral acceleration (events with and without sharp turns). Each was analysed by event with speed limit and curvature as covariates. Blood and oral fluid THC and breath alcohol were measured to model exposure.
outcomes.validity_norms: SDLP is described by the authors as a sensitive and widely used measure in drug-driving research but not directly validated against crash risk (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). They take about 2.4 cm, the SDLP increase linked to a blood alcohol of 0.05 in a report they cite (Lococo and Staplin, 2006; not read), as the lowest criterion of impairment. No norms for the simulator are given.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment is an increase in a lateral-control measure relative to the drug-free drive, expressed in centimetres and as a percentage of the drug-free median (31.4 cm at 55 mph on a straight road). The paper sets no threshold for unsafe driving; the equivalences between THC and alcohol levels are read from the model's point estimates.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Terms entered each of the six models (Table 2) by the Bayesian information criterion; there was no adjustment across models, and hundreds of other performance variables were monitored in the study but are not reported here.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Outcomes are automated simulator records. The exclusion of participant 12 followed review of the data and driving videos; whether the reviewers knew the condition is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: SDLP model (18 drivers; error df 1,916; model F 28.24): blood THC b = 0.26 cm per µg/L (SE 0.07, t = 3.6, p = 0.0004); breath alcohol b = 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (SE 0.15, t = 2.9, p = 0.0037); no THC by alcohol term and no quadratic terms selected; speed limit 0.50 (SE 0.03) and inverse curvature 464 (SE 49) significant. Editors' calculation, estimate ± 1.96 SE (normal approximation): THC 0.12 to 0.40 cm per µg/L; alcohol 0.13 to 0.71 cm per 0.01 g/210 L; probably too narrow, because many events within each drive are treated as independent (reporting issue 6). Model predictions at 55 mph on a straight road against a drug-free median of 31.4 cm (between-person range 24.7 to 44.8): THC 5, 10 and 20 µg/L: +1.3, +2.6 and +5.2 cm (4.1%, 8.2%, 16%); breath alcohol 0.05, 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L: +2.1, +3.4 and +4.2 cm (6.7%, 11%, 13%); THC 5 µg/L with 0.05 g/210 L: +3.4 cm (11%), the same as 0.08 g/210 L alone, because the additive model sums the two effects (Table 3). The paper states that about 8.2 and 13.1 µg/L THC gave lane weave like 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L, without intervals. Editors' calculation (delta method on the two slopes, covariance ignored): the THC level matching 0.05 g/210 L is about 8 µg/L with an approximate 95% interval of about 1 to 15 µg/L. Lane departures per minute: alcohol b = 0.030 (SE 0.009, p = 0.0055); maximum lateral acceleration, non-sharp events: alcohol b = 0.0023 m/s² (SE 0.0007, p = 0.0005); THC not selected in either; steering-angle variability and sharp-event acceleration: neither drug. By administered condition (Table 5; no tests or intervals), mean SDLP against 28.8 cm for placebo with placebo: alcohol alone 32.3 cm (+12%); low THC alone 31.3 (+9%); high THC alone 31.2 (+8%); low THC with alcohol 34.2 (+19%); high THC with alcohol 32.2 (+12%). Repeated-measures linear mixed model by achieved peak THC group (Table 4), SDLP: THC group p = 0.28, alcohol p = 0.067, THC by alcohol p = 0.24; the authors call it low-powered.
analysis.covariates: Speed limit, inverse road curvature and a subject term (17 df) in the SDLP model; sex, age, driving experience, usual cannabis and alcohol use, and drive scenario were not entered.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A ClinicalTrials.gov number is given (NCT01620177, Effects of Inhaled Cannabis on Driving Performance). The record was not read, so its registration date, registered outcomes and analysis plan were not compared with the paper. The paper describes its model-selection procedure as aimed at describing the data without assuming which terms would matter.
analysis.selective_reporting: Hundreds of performance variables were monitored; only the lateral-control subset is reported, as the first of a series of papers. The by-condition mixed models (Table 4) were not significant and are set aside as low-powered in favour of the concentration-based model; one participant was excluded after the data were reviewed, with no analysis that keeps her; no correction across six models.
analysis.power: No sample-size or power calculation is reported; 18 people analysed. The authors suggest that a simulator study with 80 participants (Downey et al., 2013) detected cannabis effects on lane straddling that this study did not because of higher power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 18 healthy occasional cannabis smokers in a simulator, modelled blood THC and breath alcohol during the drive were each associated with greater lane weave (0.26 cm per µg/L; 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L). Lane departures and lateral acceleration rose with alcohol but not THC. The stepwise model selected no THC by alcohol term, so its combined predictions are sums. Descriptive means by administered condition do not order by THC dose (low and high THC alone +9% and +8%; with alcohol +19% and +12%), and the by-group mixed model found no significant THC, alcohol or interaction effect on SDLP.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that cannabis and alcohol effects on SDLP were “additive rather than synergistic”, and that during-drive blood THC of 8.2 and 13.1 µg/L increased SDLP like breath alcohol of 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L, with THC at or above 8.2 µg/L described as matching notably impairing alcohol levels. The Discussion calls the design rigorous, says the observed increase may be substantial enough to count as impairment, says simulator use is not a significant limitation, and recalls that cannabis roughly doubled crash risk in two meta-analyses (Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; 4.1, 5th paragraph). The Discussion also calls the models descriptive; the abstract does not.

timeline.event: Robbe (Hum Psychopharmacol), an on-road study whose title reports cannabis impairment as moderate alone and severe with alcohol (cited by Hartman et al.; not read).

Ramaekers, Robbe and O’Hanlon (Hum Psychopharmacol), on-road: as summarised by Hartman et al., THC at 100 to 300 µg/kg raised SDLP by 1.7 to 3.5 cm, THC at 100 or 200 µg/kg with a target blood alcohol of 0.04% raised it by 5.3 and 8.5 cm, and only the combinations significantly raised time out of lane (not read).
Lenné et al. (Accid Anal Prev), simulator: independent effects of cannabis and alcohol and no interaction, like this study (as described by Hartman et al.; not read).

Ronen et al. (Accid Anal Prev), simulator: lane-position variability rose significantly only when 13 mg THC and alcohol at 0.05% were combined, although neither drug alone had a significant effect (as described by Hartman et al.; not read).

Li et al. (Epidemiol Rev) and Asbridge et al. (BMJ), two meta-analyses of crash studies that Hartman et al. describe as showing about doubled crash risk with cannabis; the second is read for this library.

Downey et al. (Accid Anal Prev), simulator, 80 participants: dose-dependent cannabis effects on straddling lane barrier or solid lines, with or without alcohol (as described by Hartman et al.; not read).
Two companion papers from the same sessions report oral fluid and blood cannabinoid kinetics (Hartman et al., 2015a and 2015b; not read; not independent of this study).

Dubois et al. (Forensic Sci Int), 150,010 US drivers blood-tested after fatal crashes (1991 to 2008): the odds of a police-recorded unsafe driver action with THC and alcohol together were above those with either alone and close to the sum of their separate excesses (at 0.05 g/100 mL: 1.81 with both, 1.66 with alcohol alone, 1.16 with THC alone, against drivers with neither), and THC's added effect shrank as alcohol rose (THC by blood alcohol interaction odds ratio 0.987 per 0.01 g/100 mL, 0.981 to 0.994). Read for this library from the accepted manuscript; a different design and outcome from this simulator study, and not a repeat of it.

Rogeberg and Elvik (Addiction): re-analysis of the meta-analyses that this paper's Discussion recalls as showing doubled crash risk. After re-extracting counts and using adjusted estimates, the pooled odds ratio for 28 estimates from 21 studies was 1.36 (1.15 to 1.61; random effects) or 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36; small-study-adjusted); estimates from studies that controlled for alcohol were lower (1.11 and 1.18) than those that did not (1.79 and 1.69). Read for this library.

replication.where_it_stands: As the paper itself describes them, the few simulator and on-road studies of the combination disagree: this study and Lenné 2010 found no interaction on lane position, while Ronen 2010 and the on-road work of Robbe and Ramaekers found effects with the combination that neither drug showed alone. This study's no-interaction finding rests on a stepwise model with no estimate for the interaction, so its combined values are sums by construction. A large real-world analysis read for this library (Dubois et al., 2015) found the combination close to the sum of the single-drug excesses, with THC adding little to alcohol at 0.05 to 0.08 g/100 mL, but that is a different outcome (a recorded unsafe driver action in fatal crashes) and design. The 'about doubled' crash risk that this paper's Discussion recalls was revised downwards in a 2016 re-analysis (Rogeberg and Elvik). No on-road study of the combination was read.

funding.funder: US Office of National Drug Control Policy; Intramural Research Program, National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (Role of Funding Source).
funding.declared_conflicts: The vaporizer and oral-fluid collection devices and supplies (Storz and Bickel; Immunalysis) were provided by their manufacturers through Materials Transfer Agreements; no commercial entity played a role in design, conduct, analysis, writing or the decision to publish; the authors declare no personal conflicts of interest (Conflicts of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The affiliation list was collapsed on the page and was not extracted. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, adequately powered randomized factorial crossover study of several THC and alcohol levels, analysed with the interaction estimated and reported with its interval (and with the person and the drive, not the single event, as the unit of analysis), in an on-road or high-fidelity simulator test that also includes regular cannabis smokers and women, with the achieved concentrations during the drive measured or tightly bracketed, and with outcomes tied to crash-relevant events such as lane departures and braking.

domains.note: Order is stated as randomized, but sequence generation, concealment and the sequences used are not described. Within-person contrasts remove between-person confounding.

Sessions at least 1 week apart, but no period effect is modelled, scenario assignment to sessions is not described, and baseline blood THC was above zero in some sessions (up to 6.3 µg/L, Table 6), consistent with use between sessions or carryover.

Double-blinding is stated only in the Discussion and Conclusion; how it was kept or checked is not described, and the effects of cannabis and of alcohol at these levels are perceptible. Inhalation was ad libitum, so achieved THC differed from assigned dose and overlapped between doses; analysis by achieved concentration is not protected by the randomization.
18 of 19 analysed and no dropouts reported; the one exclusion was made from the driving data themselves and is counted under selection of the reported result.

SDLP and the other measures are automated simulator records. During-drive THC and alcohol were modelled from samples before and after the drive, which adds uncertainty about the exposure but is not a bias in the outcome.

No sample-size calculation or analysis plan in the paper and the registry record was not read. The headline model is a data-driven stepwise selection on modelled concentrations, used after the by-condition mixed models were not significant; hundreds of variables were monitored and only the lateral-control subset is reported; one extreme participant was excluded after the data were seen; no correction across six models.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 is applied as for a crossover trial. The randomized, placebo-controlled within-person contrasts are protected against confounding, but the paper's headline estimates are regressions on achieved, partly self-titrated concentrations chosen by a stepwise procedure, with event-level standard errors that treat repeated events as independent. Four of six domains raise some concerns; none is judged high because the exposure was administered under control, the outcome is automated and the dropout is minimal. The source may be cited for the direction of the associations between during-drive THC or breath alcohol and lane weave in 18 healthy occasional cannabis smokers in a simulator, and for the lane-departure and lateral-acceleration results for alcohol. It may not be cited for synergy or for the absence of synergy, for the THC and alcohol equivalences as if they had intervals, for real-road crash risk, or for effects in regular cannabis smokers.

key_findings.finding: 19 healthy adults drove (13 men, 6 women; ages 21 to 37, mean 26.1, SD 4.1; 74% White). Participant 12, a woman, was excluded from all driving analyses because her data were extreme in almost every measure and condition, including placebo with placebo, with markedly erratic driving on video, leaving 18 analysed (13 men and 5 women by the editors' count from Table 1; mean age 26.3, SD 4.2).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (row 12 and the N = 18 summary rows)
key_findings.note: The abstract calls the 18 completers; all 19 completed the sessions.

key_findings.finding: Six conditions (placebo, 2.9% or 6.7% THC vaporized cannabis, each with placebo or alcohol) in randomized order, at least 1 week apart. Alcohol drunk over 10 minutes, aimed at an approximate peak breath alcohol of 0.065%, then 500 mg of cannabis inhaled over 10 minutes; a 45-minute night drive (urban, interstate, rural segments) began 0.5 to 1.3 hours after the start of cannabis dosing; three scenario variants limited practice effects.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.2 Study Design/Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.4 Drives, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: During-drive blood THC was modelled by individual power-curve regression from samples at 0.17, 0.42, 1.4 and 2.3 hours, and breath alcohol by linear interpolation. Driving data were analysed by event with SAS GLM Select (stepwise, Schwarz information criterion; candidate terms blood THC, breath alcohol, their product, speed limit, inverse curvature, subject; effect hierarchy not enforced). Quadratic terms for THC and alcohol were added to test for a ceiling effect and neither was selected.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.6 Data Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Achieved blood THC overlapped between the two active doses: 6 participants had a higher peak after the low than the high dose and 4 had peaks within 20% of each other despite a two-fold dose difference. The authors therefore analysed by concentration and call analysis by dose group not scientifically meaningful. They infer self-titration of inhalation and, from a companion paper (not read), say 52.6% of participants showed evidence of it.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Figure 3 (image; values not extracted); Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: SDLP model: blood THC b = 0.26 cm per µg/L (SE 0.07, t = 3.6, p = 0.0004); breath alcohol b = 0.42 cm per 0.01 g/210 L (SE 0.15, t = 2.9, p = 0.0037); no THC by alcohol term selected; speed limit 0.50 (SE 0.03) and inverse curvature 464 (SE 49); model df 21, F 28.24, error df 1,916. Increases of 0.8% per µg/L THC and 1.3% per 0.01 g/210 L breath alcohol relative to the drug-free median SDLP.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph; Table 2, SDLP block
key_findings.note: Table 2 does not state the unit of the alcohol estimate; 0.42 is per 0.01 g/210 L as given in the text and Table 3.

key_findings.finding: Model predictions at 55 mph on a straight road (Table 3): drug-free median SDLP 31.4 cm (between-person range 24.7 to 44.8). THC 1, 2, 5, 7, 10 and 20 µg/L: +0.26, +0.52, +1.3, +1.8, +2.6, +5.2 cm (0.8%, 1.6%, 4.1%, 5.8%, 8.2%, 16%). Breath alcohol 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L: +0.42, +0.84, +2.1, +3.4, +4.2 cm (1.3%, 2.7%, 6.7%, 11%, 13%). THC 2 µg/L with alcohol 0.05: +2.6 cm (8.4%); THC 5 µg/L with alcohol 0.05: +3.4 cm (11%), the same as alcohol 0.08 alone (+3.4 cm, 11%).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: The combined rows equal the sum of the single effects because the selected model has no interaction term; they are model outputs, not observed values.

key_findings.finding: Stated equivalences: breath alcohol of 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L, the most common legal limits, gave lane weave like blood THC of 8.2 and 13.1 µg/L; THC of 1 and 2 µg/L gave increases like 0.01 g/210 L; at 5 and 10 µg/L SDLP rose 4.1% and 8.2%, against 6.7% for alcohol 0.05 and 11% for alcohol 0.08.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › 3.2 Driving, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend (image; values not extracted)
key_findings.note: No intervals are given for the equivalences.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol, not THC, increased the less sensitive measures: lane departures per minute (b = 0.030, SE 0.009, t = 2.8, p = 0.0055) and maximum lateral acceleration in events without sharp turns (b = 0.0023 m/s², SE 0.0007, t = 3.5, p = 0.0005); at 0.05 g/210 L these rose 35% (0.13 per minute) and 9.5% (0.11 m/s²), at 0.08 g/210 L 55% and 15%. THC was not selected in either model; neither drug affected steering-angle variability or acceleration in sharp events.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 (lane departures, steering angle and acceleration blocks); Table 3

key_findings.finding: Mean SDLP by administered condition, 18 drivers each (Table 5, second block): placebo with placebo 28.8 cm (SD 17.8); alcohol alone 32.3 (+3.5 cm, +12%); low THC alone 31.3 (+9%); high THC alone 31.2 (+8%); low THC with alcohol 34.2 (+19%); high THC with alcohol 32.2 (+12%). Lane departures per minute: 0.52 placebo; 0.74 alcohol alone; 0.73 low THC with alcohol; 0.80 high THC with alcohol. No statistical test or interval is given for these means.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Table 5, administered dose conditions
key_findings.note: The Table 5 note says analysis of variance could not be conducted by dose condition because of unbalanced cells from self-titration, but these cells are balanced (18 each); the by-dose comparison could have been tested.

key_findings.finding: By achieved peak THC group (median split at 8.6 µg/L; Table 5, first block), mean SDLP: placebo with placebo 28.8 cm (N = 18); no alcohol, below-median THC 32.3 (N = 11, +12%) and above-median 29.8 (N = 12, +3%); with alcohol, placebo THC 32.3 (N = 18, +12%), below-median 34.6 (N = 18, +20%), above-median 32.2 (N = 16, +12%).
