Repeated-measures linear mixed model by group, SDLP: THC group p = 0.28, alcohol p = 0.067, THC by alcohol p = 0.24; lane departures per minute p = 0.45, 0.13, 0.12; acceleration p = 0.25, 0.092, 0.49. The authors say this analysis has low power and uncertain interpretation.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Driving, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Table 5, achieved concentration conditions
key_findings.note: See reporting issue 1 on duplicated SDLP values in this table.

key_findings.finding: Mean (SD) blood THC in all 19 participants, in µg/L, with 2.9% and 6.7% cannabis without alcohol and with alcohol: 0.17 hours 35.9 (16.7), 56.2 (36.4), 40.5 (18.2), 75.0 (48.1); 0.42 hours 10.0 (4.5), 16.8 (10.9), 10.4 (3.4), 19.0 (11.9); 1.4 hours 3.9 (2.3), 5.7 (3.9), 3.6 (1.4), 6.8 (4.6); 2.3 hours 2.2 (1.8), 3.2 (2.6), 1.8 (1.1), 3.2 (2.5). Pre-dose baseline median 0, up to 6.3. Between-person variability was larger for oral fluid THC than for blood at every time point (coefficients of variation 125% to 207% against 45% to 65% at the first post-dose sample; the Discussion calls it 2- to 5-fold).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Pre- and Post-drive Blood and OF THC Concentrations, 1st paragraph; Table 6; Discussion, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: Mean blood THC at the first sample was higher with alcohol than without (75.0 against 56.2 at 6.7%; 40.5 against 35.9 at 2.9%); the paper does not test this.

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: participants know driving is observed and may drive more carefully or may want to show cannabis does not affect driving; only occasional cannabis smokers were studied, and frequent smokers show tolerance to some effects; the stepwise procedure was used to describe the data without assuming which terms matter; and they do not regard use of a simulator rather than a road as a significant limitation.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.1 Strengths and limitations, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: US Office of National Drug Control Policy, NIDA Intramural Research Program and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Devices and supplies supplied by manufacturers under Materials Transfer Agreements; no personal conflicts declared. Registered as NCT01620177.
key_findings.locator: Role of Funding Source; Conflicts of Interest; Clinical Trial Registration (end matter)

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5 (first block) the row for below-median THC with placebo alcohol (N = 11) prints exactly the same SDLP values as the row for placebo THC with alcohol (N = 18): mean 32.3 cm, SD 21.7, difference 3.5 cm, 12%. The second block gives 32.3 cm with SD 19.3 for placebo THC with alcohol, so the same condition has two different SDs (21.7 and 19.3). The lane-departure and acceleration columns of the two rows differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of these SDLP entries is a transcription error. The by-group means cannot be relied on to judge whether lane weave rises with achieved THC; the claim uses them only descriptively and cites the administered-dose block.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract refers to 18 completers, but all 19 participants completed the sessions; one was excluded from every driving analysis after review of the driving data and videos. No exclusion rule set in advance and no analysis that keeps participant 12 are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: A post hoc, outcome-informed exclusion; as her data were extreme in the placebo condition too, a large effect on the drug contrasts is unlikely, but this cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that at or above 8.2 µg/L THC the study met the lowest criterion of impairment, about 2.4 cm (the SDLP increase at 0.05 blood alcohol in a cited report). By the paper's own coefficients 8.2 µg/L gives about 2.1 cm (Table 3: 7 µg/L 1.8 cm, 10 µg/L 2.6 cm), so the 2.4 cm criterion is reached at about 9 µg/L; 2.1 cm is the study's own 0.05 g/210 L equivalent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement mixes the external 2.4 cm benchmark with the study's own 2.1 cm equivalent; the difference is small but the abstract's THC thresholds are point estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The THC and alcohol equivalences (8.2 and 13.1 µg/L for 0.05 and 0.08 g/210 L) are ratios of two slopes (0.26, SE 0.07; 0.42, SE 0.15) given without intervals. Editors' calculation by the delta method, covariance ignored: about 8 µg/L with an approximate 95% interval of about 1 to 15 µg/L for the 0.05 equivalent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The equivalences are far less precise than the abstract's wording suggests; they cannot support a precise concentration limit.

reporting_issues.issue: The range of during-drive THC and breath alcohol values analysed is not reported. The alcohol dose was aimed at a peak of about 0.065%, yet Table 3 predicts lane weave at 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L, and the abstract compares THC with 0.08.
reporting_issues.consequence: The predictions at 0.08 and 0.10 g/210 L (and the 13.1 µg/L equivalence) may lie beyond the data, which would make them extrapolations; the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: Error degrees of freedom in the models are 1,916 (SDLP), 427 and 1,936 (steering angle), 840 (lane departures) and 2,026 and 304 (acceleration), for data from 18 drivers in 108 drives (18 drivers by 6 conditions). For SDLP that is about 18 events per drive treated as independent observations, with a subject term only for each person's average.
reporting_issues.consequence: Standard errors and p-values for THC and alcohol are probably too small (editors' inference; the paper does not describe correction for repeated events), so the intervals calculated from them are likely too narrow.

reporting_issues.issue: The finding of additive, not synergistic, effects is drawn from the absence of a THC by alcohol term in a stepwise model selected by an information criterion. No estimate or interval for the interaction is given. Table 3's combined rows are sums by construction.
reporting_issues.consequence: Additivity here is the model's structure, not a measured result; the paper cannot be cited as showing that the combination is no worse than the sum.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5's note says analysis of variance could not be conducted by dose condition, but the administered-dose cells are balanced (18 each) and the by-dose block was reported only as descriptive means.
reporting_issues.consequence: Contrasts by administered dose were not tested; the descriptive means show no ordering between low and high THC (+9% and +8% alone; +19% and +12% with alcohol).

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say all participants reported driving at least once a week, but participant 2 gave no response for driving frequency or years of driving (Table 1, footnote c). Table 1 also gives 120 days since last cannabis use for participant 13 (analysed), which is outside the inclusion window of use at least once in the past 3 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both are self-reports and the eligibility checks cannot be audited from the paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4536116 (PMC HTML, author manuscript, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 6, figure legends (Figures 1 to 3 are images; their values were not extracted), funding, contributors, conflicts of interest and registration statements, reference list. The three supplementary files (one docx, two pdf) were not read.

design_detail: Two linked analyses of observational studies of recent cannabis use and motor vehicle crashes. Study 1 replicates two published meta-analyses (Asbridge et al., BMJ 2012, nine studies; Li et al., Epidemiol Rev 2012, nine studies) after re-extracting counts from the primary studies (contacting study authors where counts could not be checked), correcting for the mixing of two incompatible designs (case-control and culpability), for small-sample (sparse data) bias and for the use of unadjusted counts, and re-pooling by DerSimonian-Laird random effects (metafor, R). Study 2 is an updated meta-analysis: studies before 2011 taken from three earlier reviews (Asbridge; Li; Elvik 2013, a wider overview of drugs and crashes), studies since 2011 from a structured search of Web of Science and Google Scholar (the first 500 results, 5 April 2015) and the authors' libraries. 74 estimates from 46 studies were found, and 28 estimates from 21 studies (13 countries, 1982 to 2015) fitted the criteria: a case-control or culpability design, with the best available information on cannabis use. Confounder-adjusted estimates were used where available; culpability estimates were converted with a correction based on each study's baseline culpability rate; crude counts got a Laplace correction. Pooling by random effects and by PEESE (precision-effect estimate with standard errors, a weighted least-squares meta-regression for small-study effects), with trim-and-fill, and subgroup analyses by design, quality, confounder control, quality of use data, alcohol control and crash severity. One author extracted the data for new studies and the other checked every result against the source study. No protocol or registration is cited; the supporting information (Appendix S1, study selection and data extraction) was not in the PDF.
can_establish: The size and spread of pooled odds ratios between a positive test for recent cannabis use (laboratory analysis of body fluids in all but one study) and being in a crash, or being judged responsible for one, across 28 estimates from 21 case-control and culpability studies (1982 to 2015); how those figures change with the method (raw counts against adjusted estimates, alcohol controlled or not, study quality, design); and that the 2012 pooled values (1.92 and 2.66) fall after re-extraction, adjustment and correction.
cannot_establish: That cannabis causes crashes (the authors say remaining selection effects may bias estimates in either direction); impairment (a positive test shows presence, not impairment, and the lowest-quality measures, urine tests and self-report, are in the pool); the effect of cannabis together with alcohol (alcohol is restricted or adjusted for, not studied as a combination); dose-response (tested in five studies, found in three, none pooled); a separate figure for minor crashes; risk to any one person who drives after cannabis; how much the estimates differ between studies (no heterogeneity statistic is printed); or how each study's estimate was extracted and converted (Appendix S1 not read).

sample.recruitment: Studies from before 2011 were taken from three earlier reviews (Asbridge 2012; Li 2012; Elvik 2013, which covered 42 cannabis estimates); studies since 2011 from a structured search of Web of Science and Google Scholar (search string printed in a footnote; the first 500 results assessed, 5 April 2015) and the authors' personal libraries. Where several reports used overlapping data, estimates adjusted for relevant confounders and larger samples were preferred (Study 2 › Sources; Results › Study selection). Study authors were contacted to check counts (Study 1 › Data extraction, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: case-control or culpability studies of the effect of acute cannabis intoxication on traffic crashes involving motor vehicles; the primary criterion was the quality of the information on cannabis use, in particular whether there was reason to believe cannabis had been used while driving or recently enough for effects to persist. Of 74 estimates from 46 studies, 28 from 21 were included; the 25 studies left out had worse information on use (average score 2.16 of 5, against 4.11 for those included). The reasons for each exclusion are not in the main text (Results › Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not given per study; Table 2 lists country, design, crash severity, measure of drug use and confounders controlled. Countries: United States, Australia, France, Canada, Norway, New Zealand, Netherlands, Thailand, Belgium, Denmark, Italy, Lithuania and Portugal.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Only crashes are studied, mostly injury or fatal; 17 of 28 estimates come from studies with limited or no confounder control. The authors name non-response among roadside controls (probably more common in controls affected by drugs or alcohol, which inflates the odds ratio), testing practices in register-based culpability studies (bias either way), and at least one study whose controls were not drawn from non-crash-involved drivers (Risk of bias assessment, 2nd paragraph), and selection on effect and into “driving after use” (Discussion › Alternative interpretations).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used: laboratory analysis of body fluids in all studies but one (Blows 2005, self-report). The quality score for information on use ran from 5 (blood for all subjects) through 4 (saliva), 3 (urine or mixed fluids), 2 (prescriptions) to 1 (self-report); included studies averaged 4.11 of 5 (Study 2 › Quality assessment, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not available in the pooled analysis: five studies tested a dose-response pattern and three found one (Longo 2000, Drummer 2004, Laumon 2005; Table 2); none is pooled by dose.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled by subgroup: 14 estimates control for alcohol (by restriction or adjustment) and 14 do not; the combination of cannabis with alcohol is not analysed. Pooled odds ratio with alcohol controlled 1.11 (random effects) and 1.18 (PEESE); not controlled 1.79 and 1.69 (Table 3).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: drivers were tested after the crash or at the roadside. The authors note that poor measures of use, such as urine tests for inactive metabolites, bias estimates towards no effect (Risk of bias assessment, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Two kinds: case-control (17 estimates; drivers not involved in a crash, for example roadside samples) and culpability (11 estimates; crashed drivers judged not responsible, used as a stand-in for the driving population).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Each study's own adjustment was used where available (Table 2 lists age, gender, alcohol, other drugs, driving history, time of day and others, which vary widely); for culpability studies the point estimate was rescaled with the baseline culpability rate of drivers without the drug (Study 1 › Study selection and comparability, footnote 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors say driving after cannabis is concentrated among young men and people with high-risk driving habits, including drink-driving, and that residual confounding of this kind would bias estimates upwards; selection on effect (driving when impairment is judged low) would bias them downwards (Discussion › Alternative interpretations, 2nd to 4th paragraphs).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Control for other drugs in some studies (Table 2); alcohol controlled in 14 of 28 estimates.

outcomes.instruments: Crash involvement (fatal, injury or property damage only, as each study defined it) or, in culpability studies, being judged responsible for the crash, by each source study's method; the effect measure is the odds ratio with its standard error, adjusted where available. Study quality by four criteria scored out of 20 (use measure 5, severity specification 2, confounder control 11, dose-response test 2; Table 1, taken from Elvik 2013).
outcomes.validity_norms: The cut-offs between low, medium and high quality, and between limited and high confounder control, are not stated in the main text. The authors call formal quality scoring controversial and use the scores as a screening device for subgroups (Study 2 › Quality assessment for individual studies, last paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: The odds that a driver with a positive test for cannabis was in a crash (case-control) or responsible for it (culpability), compared with drivers with a negative test. The paper words this as “acute cannabis intoxication” and “cannabis-impaired driving”; no included study measured impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One primary pooled estimate and 14 subgroup rows (Table 3), each pooled two ways and each with a publication-bias test.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Data extraction by one author, with every result then checked against the source study by the other.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary analysis, 28 estimates from 21 studies: pooled odds ratio 1.36 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.61) by DerSimonian-Laird random effects (called “mixed effects” in Table 3 and the Discussion) and 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36) by PEESE meta-regression; PEESE publication-bias test P = 0.52; trim-and-fill trimmed mean 1.23 (Abstract; Results › Publication bias; Table 3). Subgroups (estimates; random effects; PEESE meta-regression; PEESE bias test P): case-control (17) 1.60 (1.19 to 2.15), 1.32 (1.04 to 1.68), 0.55; culpability (11) 1.12 (1.05 to 1.20), 1.20 (1.08 to 1.35), 0.78; high quality (9) 1.39 (1.06 to 1.83), 1.18 (1.05 to 1.34), 0.10; medium quality (12) 1.30 (0.95 to 1.78), 1.15 (0.87 to 1.51), 0.90; low quality (7) 1.45 (0.97 to 2.17), 1.79 (1.34 to 2.39), 0.36; limited or no confounder adjustment (17) 1.52 (1.07 to 2.15), 1.70 (1.19 to 2.41), 0.62; high confounder adjustment (11) 1.17 (1.04 to 1.33), 1.18 (1.06 to 1.31), 0.49; low-quality use data (7) 1.07 (0.92 to 1.25), 1.08 (0.90 to 1.30), 0.83; medium-quality use data (9) 1.81 (1.23 to 2.66), 1.90 (1.41 to 2.55), 0.61; high-quality use data (12) 1.37 (1.05 to 1.79), 1.20 (1.04 to 1.39), 0.37; alcohol controlled (14) 1.11 (1.04 to 1.18), 1.18 (1.07 to 1.30), 0.75; alcohol not controlled (14) 1.79 (1.28 to 2.51), 1.69 (1.25 to 2.28), 0.90; fatalities involved (15) 1.32 (1.08 to 1.61), 1.24 (1.10 to 1.40), 0.92; fatalities not involved (13) 1.51 (1.02 to 2.24), 1.11 (0.82 to 1.49), 0.37. Study estimates (Fig 5; odds ratio, 95% CI, weight; read on the rendered page): Terhune 1983 (US) 1.25 (0.35 to 4.43), weight 1.54%; Williams 1985 (US) 0.63 (0.24 to 1.67), 2.35%; Terhune 1992 (US) 0.75 (0.31 to 1.81), 2.79%; Longo 2000 (Australia) 0.91 (0.50 to 1.63), 4.75%; Lowenstein 2001 (US) 0.86 (0.15 to 4.93), 0.87%; Mura 2003 (France) 2.50 (1.49 to 4.18), 5.44%; Brault 2004 (Canada) 1.60 (1.08 to 2.36), 6.92%; Drummer 2004 (Australia) 2.21 (0.84 to 5.78), 2.42%; Assum 2005 (Norway) 2.40 (0.21 to 27.78), 0.46%; Blows 2005 (New Zealand) 0.80 (0.20 to 3.25), 1.29%; Laumon 2005 (France) 1.43 (1.13 to 1.81), 8.99%; Mathijssen 2005 (Netherlands) 1.45 (0.64 to 3.29), 3.08%; Woratanarat 2009 (Thailand) 1.00 (0.37 to 2.69), 2.32%; Hels 2011 Denmark 2.17 (0.61 to 7.75), 1.53%; Hels 2011 Italy 1.88 (0.85 to 4.16), 3.21%; Hels 2011 Netherlands 0.29 (0.04 to 2.11), 0.69%; Hels 2011 Norway 3.91 (1.17 to 13.07), 1.67%; Hels 2011 Portugal 0.22 (0.03 to 1.60), 0.68%; Hels 2011 Lithuania 6.59 (0.60 to 72.86), 0.48%; Kuypers 2012 (Belgium) 13.40 (3.95 to 45.44), 1.64%; Gjerde 2013 (Norway) 1.90 (0.79 to 4.56), 2.80%; Li 2013 (US) 1.84 (1.42 to 2.39), 8.68%; Poulsen 2014 (New Zealand), three estimates: 1.31 (0.58 to 2.97), 3.08%; 0.99 (0.44 to 2.21), 3.15%; 1.45 (0.56 to 3.78), 2.43%; Romano 2014 (US) 0.92 (0.60 to 1.41), 6.49%; Compton 2015 (US) 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 9.56%; Dubois 2015 (US) 1.10 (1.02 to 1.18), 10.68%. Editors' count from Fig 5: 17 of the 28 point estimates are above 1 (7 with intervals excluding 1: Mura, Brault, Laumon, Hels Norway, Kuypers, Li, Dubois), 9 are below 1 (none with an interval excluding 1) and 2 print as 1.00; the four largest weights (Dubois, Compton, Laumon, Li) together carry about 38%. Study 1, from the text: re-extraction changed four of the nine Asbridge et al. odds ratios by more than 10%, all downwards (Blows 2005 from 7.2 to 2.6; Terhune from 4.4 to 1.7 when “partly culpable” drivers are handled as in Drummer; two others by about 20%), and total counts by more than 10% for three studies; in Li et al. only one study changed substantially (Fergusson and Horwood, 2.4 to 1.4). Study 1 pooled values appear only as plotted points (Fig 4), read by eye from a 300 dpi crop and approximate: nine Asbridge studies, reported counts 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73); corrected counts about 1.59 (1.22 to 2.08); plus Laplace correction about 1.58 (1.22 to 2.04); plus adjusted culpability estimator about 1.40 (1.13 to 1.72); adjusted estimates from the underlying studies about 1.31 (1.0 to 1.73); plus adjusted culpability estimator about 1.25 (1.0 to 1.57). Nine Li studies: reported 2.66 (about 2.07 to 3.40); corrected counts about 2.41 (1.70 to 3.43); plus Laplace about 2.43 (1.72 to 3.43); adjusted estimates about 1.55 (1.09 to 2.20).
analysis.covariates: PEESE is a weighted least-squares regression of the estimates on their standard errors squared (small-study correction); no other covariates. Subgroup analyses by category; no multivariable meta-regression.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is cited. The authors say they suspected that earlier meta-analyses handled confounders insufficiently (Introduction, 3rd paragraph); the choice of subgroup analyses is described in the Methods only. The supporting information (Appendix S1, study selection and data extraction) was not available.
analysis.selective_reporting: All subgroups named in the Methods appear in Table 3, with both pooling methods and a bias test. The Study 1 pooled values are only plotted (Fig 4), with no numbers. No heterogeneity statistic (I-squared, tau-squared or a prediction interval) is printed although the Discussion says there is heterogeneity. Fig 5 has six rows for one multi-country project (Hels 2011) and three for one New Zealand study (Poulsen 2014), nine of the 28 estimates, and the text does not say how this dependence was handled.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Subgroups have 7 to 17 estimates, and the two pooling methods can differ widely within a subgroup (low quality 1.45 against 1.79; fatalities not involved 1.51 against 1.11), so contrasts between subgroups cannot be read finely.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 28 estimates from 21 case-control and culpability studies, a positive test for recent cannabis went with a pooled odds ratio of 1.36 (1.15 to 1.61; random effects) or 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36; PEESE) for being in a crash or being judged responsible for one. When alcohol was controlled for the pooled values were 1.11 (1.04 to 1.18) and 1.18 (1.07 to 1.30); when it was not, 1.79 (1.28 to 2.51) and 1.69 (1.25 to 2.28). Individual estimates range from 0.22 to 13.40, 17 are above 1 and 9 below; the largest-weight study is Dubois 2015 (1.10, 1.02 to 1.18). Re-extraction, adjustment and the culpability correction move the nine Asbridge et al. studies from 1.92 to roughly 1.25 to 1.6, and the nine Li et al. studies from 2.66 to about 1.55 (read from a plot).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says acute cannabis intoxication is associated with a statistically significant increase in crash risk “of low to medium magnitude”, that Study 1 substantially revises earlier estimates downwards, with both original point estimates outside the revised interval, and that remaining selection effects may limit causal interpretation. The Discussion says the effect sizes represent an average risk increase for people who drive after cannabis, that under a causal reading roughly 20 to 30% of crashes involving cannabis use occur because of it, that an average effect of 1.2 to 1.4 is comparable to the crash risk at a blood alcohol of 0.04 to 0.05, and that alcohol at 0.02 to 0.05 raises fatal-crash risk by 100 to 360%. Gaps: (1) “intoxication” and “impaired driving” are read from positive tests, with urine tests and self-report in the pool and no measure of impairment; (2) odds ratios from culpability and case-control designs are read as risk, although the authors show the culpability estimator overstates it and use an approximate correction that leaves the standard errors unchanged; (3) the interval statement holds for the fully adjusted pooled values but not for the corrected-counts values, whose intervals still include 1.92 and 2.66 (Fig 4, read by eye); (4) “20 to 30%” follows from (odds ratio minus 1) divided by the odds ratio only for odds ratios of 1.25 to 1.43; for 1.22 and 1.36 it is 18% and 26% (editors' calculation); (5) the comparison with alcohol sets pooled odds ratios against a relative risk of 7.5 for fatal crashes taken from another source. The paper is explicit about the limits of a causal reading.

timeline.event: Asbridge et al. (BMJ): nine studies, pooled odds ratio 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73), from crude counts; read for this library and re-analysed in Study 1 of this paper.
Li et al. (Epidemiol Rev): nine studies, pooled odds ratio 2.66; re-analysed in Study 1 (not read).
Elvik (Accid Anal Prev), overview of drugs and crashes with 42 cannabis estimates, whose quality scoring this paper uses (not read).

Dubois et al. (Forensic Sci Int): 150,010 US drivers tested after fatal crashes; THC alone, adjusted, odds ratio 1.165 (1.082 to 1.255) of a recorded unsafe driver action; enters this paper's Fig 5 as 1.10 (1.02 to 1.18), the heaviest weight (10.68%). Read for this library.
This paper (Addiction, 111): re-analysis and update, pooled odds ratio 1.36 and 1.22.
Rogeberg, Accid Anal Prev: a meta-analysis of culpability studies aimed at avoiding interpretational bias (10.1016/j.aap.2018.11.011, open access); not read.

replication.where_it_stands: The size of the association depends on method: about 1.9 (2012 review, crude counts), 1.25 to 1.6 (the same nine studies corrected), 1.2 to 1.4 (this paper's update, adjusted where possible) and 1.1 to 1.2 where alcohol was controlled for. The 2012 review and this paper share primary studies and are not independent confirmations of each other; the direction (positive, small to moderate) is shared by most large adjusted estimates. A later paper by the first author on culpability designs was not read.

funding.funder: Norwegian Research Council grant 240235 (partial financing of the first author). The funding source had no role in the design, collection, analysis or interpretation of data, in writing, or in the decision to submit; both authors worked independently of the funder (Declaration of interests; Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The first author reports grants from the Norwegian Research Council during the study; the second author has nothing to disclose.
funding.affiliations_note: Ragnar Frisch Centre for Economic Research and Institute of Transport Economics (Norwegian Centre for Transport Research), Oslo. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A registered protocol for a pooled analysis of individual-driver data from the largest crash and roadside studies, with one definition of recent use (blood THC concentration and time since use), estimates within strata of blood alcohol (none, low, high) so that cannabis alone and the combination are separate, case-control and culpability analyses reported separately without conversion, a printed heterogeneity measure and prediction interval, a list of excluded studies with reasons, and a design that separates the effect of cannabis on driving from who chooses to drive after use (for example roadside samples matched on place and time of day).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Drivers; acute cannabis use by body-fluid test (or self-report, one study); drivers without it; crash involvement or responsibility; case-control and culpability designs. The criteria are partly implicit but all elements can be found.
No protocol or registration is cited.
The Introduction explains why observational studies are needed (laboratory studies' external validity is unclear), and Study 1 explains the two designs and why their odds ratios are not comparable.

Three earlier reviews, Web of Science and Google Scholar with the string printed, the first 500 results, the authors' libraries; no registries, no grey-literature search and no consultation of experts are described (authors were contacted for data); search 7 months before submission.
Not described; one author extracted data for the recent and added studies.

A close call: one author extracted and the other checked every result (odds ratio and standard error) against the original study and documented where each came from; Study 1 re-extracted all counts and contacted authors.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The main text gives only the numbers (74 estimates from 46 studies, 28 from 21 included) and the reason in general terms (information on use). The supporting information, Appendix S1 (study selection and data extraction), was not available, so this item cannot be judged and the overall rating is provisional.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives design, country, year, severity, measure of use, confounders and dose-response for each, but no sample sizes, ages, sexes or concentration cut-offs.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A four-part quality score (use measure, severity, confounder control, dose-response) with the authors' note that scoring is controversial; confounding, selection (non-response, testing practices, control-group choice) and exposure measurement are covered; outcome ascertainment and selective reporting are not assessed per study.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

A close call. Adjusted estimates were preferred, pooling by random effects and by PEESE with trim-and-fill, subgroups for the main sources of difference, and the authors replaced a wrongly pooled design mix with a correction. Weaknesses they or the editors note: the culpability correction leaves the standard errors unchanged (footnote 1), nine of 28 estimates come from two studies and the handling of that dependence is not described, and no heterogeneity statistic is printed.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Pooled separately by study quality, confounder control, quality of use data and alcohol control (Table 3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion and Conclusions describe confounding, selection effects in both directions and the limit on causal reading.

Heterogeneity is acknowledged and explored by subgroup (higher estimates with case-control design, low quality, limited confounder control, medium-quality use data, alcohol not controlled), though no statistic is printed.
PEESE test (P = 0.52) and trim-and-fill (weak bias; trimmed mean 1.23), within each subgroup as well.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Declared in the Declaration of interests and Acknowledgements.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 scores one critical item as no (no protocol or registration cited) and cannot judge a second (the list of excluded studies, which may sit in Appendix S1, not read), so the overall rating is provisional: low confidence now, and critically low if the supplement has no list; items 4 and 9 are met in part and items 11, 13 and 15 are met. This rates how far the pooled number can be trusted as an unbiased summary, not the value of the work: the paper's main contribution is to show, with simulation, re-extracted counts and adjusted estimates, why earlier pooled figures were too high, and it states the limits of a causal reading plainly. The practical consequence is that its pooled values (1.36 and 1.22) are best read as a range for the odds of a crash or of responsibility for one among drivers with a positive cannabis test, in a pool where most estimates come from studies with little adjustment and from two designs that mean different things. The source may be cited for that range, for how it moves with alcohol control and quality, and for the authors' reasons for revising the 2012 figures; it may not be cited for impairment, for causation, for a dose, for the combination with alcohol, or for the size of risk in any one person.

key_findings.finding: Aims and design: whether, and by how much, acute cannabis intoxication raises motor vehicle crash risk. Study 1 replicates the 2012 meta-analyses of Asbridge et al. (nine studies, five countries, 1982 to 2007) and Li et al. (nine studies, six countries, 2001 to 2010) after correcting methodological shortcomings; Study 2 updates the evidence with 28 estimates from 21 observational studies in 13 countries (1982 to 2015), pooled by random effects and meta-regression. Total counts: 50,877 (27,967 cases and 22,910 controls) for Asbridge et al. and 93,229 (4,236 cases and 88,993 controls) for Li et al.; Study 2, 222,511 in studies with adjusted estimates plus 17,228 crude counts, 239,739 in all.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Aims; Design; Setting; Participants); Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: Comparability: the nine studies in Li et al. measure different things (self-reported crashes in people who had ever used cannabis against people who had never used it, self-reported crashes with self-reported intoxicated driving, acute intoxication among crashed and other drivers), so people who use cannabis but do not drive after it are in the exposed counts of some studies and the control counts of others; its selection criteria are unclear. Asbridge et al. state theirs clearly (acute intoxication; serious injury or fatal crashes; counts from the no-alcohol subsamples) but pool two designs that give incompatible estimators.
key_findings.locator: Study 1 › Study selection and comparability, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Culpability against case-control: a case-control odds ratio compares crashed with non-crashed drivers; a culpability odds ratio compares culpable with non-culpable crashed drivers and so estimates the increased risk of a culpable crash, necessarily higher than the increase in all crashes. A simulation (100,000 studies of 500 drivers; non-intoxicated drivers 50% culpable; intoxication doubling the risk of a culpable crash) shows the culpability estimator is biased upwards. For adjusted odds ratios the authors convert a culpability estimate into the case-control-type (alternative) estimate: alternative estimate = culpability estimate times the baseline culpability rate plus one minus that rate, which pulls the value towards 1; baseline culpability in the culpability studies used by Asbridge et al. ran from 42 to 76%. Footnote 1: the correction does not reduce the standard error appropriately.
key_findings.locator: Study 1 › Study selection and comparability, 4th to 7th paragraphs and footnote 1 (p. 2); Fig 1 (p. 3)
key_findings.note: Fig 1, read by eye: with a true increase of 1.5 in the simulated example, the culpability estimator averages about 2.0 and the alternative estimator about 1.5.

key_findings.finding: Data re-extraction: of the nine studies in Asbridge et al., four odds ratios changed by more than 10%, all downwards: Blows 2005 from 7.2 to 2.6 (a published table had been misread; counts requested from the authors), Terhune from 4.4 to 1.7 (partly culpable drivers counted as culpable in Terhune but excluded in Drummer; excluding them in both), and two others (Terhune 1992, Laumon 2005) by about 20%; Drummer would be 3 rather than 3.25 if contributory cases were included. Total counts changed by more than 10% for three studies. In Li et al. only Fergusson and Horwood changed (1.4 rather than 2.4).
key_findings.locator: Study 1 › Data extraction, 1st to 4th paragraphs and footnote 2

key_findings.finding: Sparse data bias and unadjusted counts: odds ratios from small cell counts are biased upwards; a resampling analysis (10,000 draws per study) shows this affects a third of the Asbridge et al. studies and one of Li et al. (Fig 2); a Laplace correction largely removes it. Both earlier reviews used raw counts rather than adjusted estimates (Asbridge et al. restricted to no-alcohol subsamples), which the authors say raises estimates systematically and substantially (Fig 3 plots counts-based against adjusted odds ratios).
key_findings.locator: Study 1 › Sparse data bias in ORs, 1st paragraph; Known and observable confounders, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Figs 2 and 3 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Figs 2 and 3 were viewed, not read point by point.

key_findings.finding: Overall impact of the corrections (Fig 4, read by eye from a 300 dpi crop; approximate): nine Asbridge et al. studies 1.92 (reported counts), about 1.59 (corrected counts), 1.58 (plus Laplace), 1.40 (plus adjusted culpability estimator), 1.31 (adjusted estimates from the underlying studies), 1.25 (plus adjusted culpability estimator); nine Li et al. studies 2.66, about 2.41, 2.43 and 1.55. The text says the originally reported pooled values lie outside the 95% intervals of the revised ones and that the main remaining shortcoming of Li et al. is the lack of clear selection criteria.
key_findings.locator: Study 1 › Overall impact of methodological issues on pooled estimates, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Fig 4 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The text gives no numbers for these steps; footnote 3 says sparse data bias could not be corrected for in pooled estimates based on adjusted odds ratios.

key_findings.finding: Study 2 methods: studies before 2011 from Asbridge, Li and Elvik 2013; studies since 2011 from Web of Science and Google Scholar (printed string; first 500 results; 5 April 2015) and the authors' libraries; one author extracted and the other checked each result against the source study, documenting where each number came from; adjusted odds ratios and standard errors used whenever available; culpability estimates adjusted with the baseline culpability rate and crude counts given a Laplace correction; pooling by DerSimonian-Laird random effects, PEESE meta-regression and trim-and-fill.
key_findings.locator: Study 2 › Sources, 1st paragraph (pp. 3-4) and footnote 4 (p. 4); Data collection, 1st paragraph (pp. 4-5); Synthesis of results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 5-6); Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Study quality criteria (Table 1, from Elvik 2013): measure of drug use (5 blood for all subjects; 4 saliva; 3 urine; 2 prescriptions; 1 self-report), crash severity specification (0 to 2), control of nine named confounders (age, gender, distance driven, drug-use history, dose, other drugs, alcohol, health status, place of residence; 9 points, plus up to 2 more) and a dose-response test (0 to 2); relative score out of 20.
key_findings.locator: Study 2 › Quality assessment for individual studies, 1st to 7th paragraphs (p. 5); Table 1 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Selection: 74 estimates from 46 studies were found; 28 estimates from 21 studies (13 countries; 1982 to 2015) fitted the criteria. All used case-control (17 estimates) or culpability (11) designs and the odds ratio; nearly all studied injury or fatal crashes; cannabis use was measured by laboratory analysis of body fluids in all studies but one (self-report); studies differed greatly in confounders controlled; a minority tested dose-response (Table 2: five tested, three found).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Characteristics of included studies, 1st paragraph (p. 6); Table 2 (pp. 7-8)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: included studies averaged 4.11 of 5 on quality of information on use (not included, 2.16); poor measures bias towards no effect; small-sample bias is likely in several studies; non-response among roadside controls probably inflates odds ratios; register-based culpability studies may test drivers more often when they seem culpable or intoxicated, biasing either way; some studies (for example Mura 2003) draw controls from people other than non-crash-involved drivers.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias assessment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6, continued p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Primary result: pooled odds ratio 1.36 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.61) by random effects and 1.22 (1.10 to 1.36) by PEESE meta-regression across 28 estimates; PEESE shows no sign of publication bias (P = 0.52; best estimate 1.23); trim-and-fill indicates weak bias with a trimmed mean of 1.23. Fig 5 gives the 28 study estimates (0.22 to 13.40; Dubois 2015 weight 10.68%, estimate 1.10).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary and secondary analyses, 1st paragraph; Publication bias, 1st paragraph (p. 8); Fig 5 (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Subgroups (random effects; PEESE): alcohol controlled (14 estimates) 1.11 (1.04 to 1.18) and 1.18 (1.07 to 1.30); alcohol not controlled (14) 1.79 (1.28 to 2.51) and 1.69 (1.25 to 2.28); high confounder adjustment (11) 1.17 (1.04 to 1.33) and 1.18 (1.06 to 1.31); limited or no adjustment (17) 1.52 (1.07 to 2.15) and 1.70 (1.19 to 2.41); case-control (17) 1.60 (1.19 to 2.15) and 1.32 (1.04 to 1.68); culpability (11) 1.12 (1.05 to 1.20) and 1.20 (1.08 to 1.35); fatalities involved (15) 1.32 (1.08 to 1.61) and 1.24 (1.10 to 1.40); fatalities not involved (13) 1.51 (1.02 to 2.24) and 1.11 (0.82 to 1.49). Subsample values run from 1.07 to 1.81 (random effects) and 1.08 to 1.9 (PEESE).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the revised value for the Asbridge et al. studies lies between the two pooled values of Study 2 (1.36 and 1.22). Under a causal reading the authors say roughly 20 to 30% of crashes involving cannabis use would be due to cannabis, against about 85% for alcohol (relative risk 7.5 for fatal crashes, from another source). The average effect of 1.2 to 1.4 is comparable to the crash risk at a blood alcohol of 0.04 to 0.05; for a blood alcohol of 0.02 to 0.05 the risk of fatal crashes is said to rise by 100 to 360%, and no comparable rise appears in the cannabis fatal-crash subsample. The importance of confounding is most evident for alcohol: below 1.2 where alcohol is controlled, 1.79 and 1.69 where it is not.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 8-10)

key_findings.finding: Alternative interpretations: the causal reading is a moderate effect on traffic risk, but remaining selection effects may bias estimates either way. People who use cannabis tend to know they are impaired, so if they drive when they judge impairment low, estimates understate the risk of those who do not drive (selection on effect); an opposite bias comes from residual confounding by traits that predict both driving after use and higher crash risk (high speeds, close following, drink-driving). The two predict opposite patterns as more people drive after use.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Alternative interpretations of the results, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: acute intoxication is associated with a statistically significant increase in crash risk of low to moderate magnitude; the higher 2012 estimates came largely from methodological issues, chiefly counts without adjustment for known confounders; remaining selection effects may complicate causal interpretation. Policy implications: simple extrapolations from the estimates to the effect of law changes are unlikely to be robust.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Policy implications, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests: Norwegian Research Council grant 240235 partly financed the first author; the funder had no role in the work; the second author has nothing to disclose.
key_findings.locator: Declaration of interests (p. 10); Acknowledgements (p. 11)

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled values for Study 1, the paper's central re-analysis, appear only as plotted points in Fig 4; neither the text nor a table gives them. The text says only that the original pooled estimates lie outside the 95% intervals of the revised ones.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot take the revised Study 1 figures from the paper; this card gives them read by eye (approximate) from a 300 dpi crop.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that both original pooled values lie outside the revised intervals holds for the fully adjusted steps only. In Fig 4 the intervals after re-extraction and the Laplace correction alone (steps 2 and 3: about 1.22 to 2.08 and 1.22 to 2.04 for Asbridge et al.; about 1.70 to 3.43 for Li et al.) still contain the original 1.92 and 2.66.
reporting_issues.consequence: Much of the downward revision comes from switching to adjusted estimates and from the culpability correction, which are analytic choices, not only from corrected data errors.

reporting_issues.issue: No heterogeneity statistic (I-squared, tau-squared or prediction interval) is printed, although the Discussion refers to heterogeneity across studies and Fig 5 spans 0.22 to 13.40.
reporting_issues.consequence: How far a single study can be expected to differ from the pooled value cannot be read from the paper; the 2012 review's I-squared was 81%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's “roughly 20 to 30%” of cannabis-related crashes that would be due to cannabis does not match the usual attributable-fraction formula, (odds ratio minus 1) divided by odds ratio, which gives 18% for 1.22 and 26% for 1.36; the paragraph also treats odds ratios as relative risks and sets them against a relative risk of 7.5 for fatal crashes from another source.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison with alcohol (about 85%) is not like for like; the percentages are conditional on a causal reading the authors themselves question.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig 5 lists six estimates for Hels 2011 (Denmark, Italy, Netherlands, Lithuania, Norway, Portugal) and three for Poulsen 2014, while Table 2 shows four rows and one row for them; nine of the 28 estimates come from two studies. The text does not say what the three Poulsen estimates are or how estimates from one study were treated as dependent or independent.
reporting_issues.consequence: If these estimates share controls or samples, the pooled intervals may be too narrow; the effect on the pooled value cannot be judged without the supporting information.

reporting_issues.issue: The cut-offs that define low, medium and high study quality, quality of use data and confounder control (limited against high) are not given in the main text, although each defines a row of Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup contrasts cannot be reproduced from the paper alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The random-effects model of the Abstract and Methods is called “mixed effects” in the Discussion and in the heading of Table 3; the pooled estimate is the same, 1.36.
reporting_issues.consequence: Terminology only; a reader could take them for two different models.

reporting_issues.issue: Dubois et al. (2015) enter Fig 5 as 1.10 (1.02 to 1.18). That paper's adjusted odds ratio for THC alone is 1.165 (1.082 to 1.255). The conversion for each included study is not shown in the main text (the culpability rescaling of footnote 1 would lower a value like this), and the interval printed is wider than a rescaled one would be, which fits the footnote's statement that the standard error is not reduced.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which number was taken from each study, and how it was converted, can be checked only in the supporting information (not read).

verification.source_read: PDF Rogeberg_2016_CannabisCollisionRevisited.pdf (12 pages; the journal's online-first version with the article's own page numbers), text extracted once with pdftotext -layout. Read: abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 3, Fig 5, footnotes and the reference list. Fig 4 was read from a 300 dpi crop (values approximate); Fig 5 and Table 3 were checked on the rendered page against the text (no negative numbers occur); Table 2 was read on the rendered, rotated pages; Figs 1 to 3 were viewed (Fig 1 read by eye, Figs 2 and 3 not read point by point). The supporting information (Appendix S1) was not available.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, four-arm crossover study in a hospital clinical research centre (San Francisco General Hospital): placebo, ethanol, GHB and ethanol plus GHB in random order (4 by 4 Latin square), four 24-hour visits at least 2 days apart, after an overnight fast. Each person received ethanol 0.3 g/kg (vodka in juice) or placebo juice at about 8:00, then 15 minutes later GHB 50 mg/kg (sodium oxybate, Xyrem) or placebo with a second ethanol 0.3 g/kg or placebo. Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and skin temperature were recorded at intervals for 4 hours, oxygen saturation by continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours, and blood and urine sampled for 24 hours for GHB and ethanol concentrations. 22 adults enrolled and 16 completed all four visits and were analysed. Subjective effects, cognitive testing and differences by sex and race are to be reported separately and are not in this paper.
can_establish: In 16 healthy, light-drinking adults in a hospital research unit, after a single GHB dose and a single ethanol dose given alone or together: whether mean oxygen saturation, blood pressure, heart rate and skin temperature differed between the four conditions, how often vomiting and brief low blood pressure occurred, and whether ethanol changed GHB blood levels by an amount large enough to detect with 16 people (about 25%).
cannot_establish: Whether the combination causes respiratory failure, loss of consciousness or death in real-life use (mean oxygen saturation fell by about 2 percentage points at most; no event needed treatment; sedation, breathing rate and cognitive effects are not reported in this paper); effects at higher or unknown doses, with other drugs, or in people with lung disease; effects of GBL or 1,4-butanediol; whether the combined fall is greater than the sum of the single-drug falls (no interaction test is reported); and pharmacokinetic effects smaller than about 25%.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond “recruited” (the Acknowledgments thank a staff member for recruitment); potential participants were not selected by race or ethnicity (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 21 to 45 by history, physical examination and screening laboratory tests. Excluded: any significant medical history, pregnancy or obesity; people who used illicit drugs; people taking prescription drugs other than oral contraceptives; more than light alcohol use (more than 3 drinks a week) or GHB use (more than twice in the previous 6 months).
sample.demographics: 16 completers: 7 men and 9 women, aged 22 to 34; weight 47.9 to 83.0 kg (mean 66.2); height 146 to 183 cm (mean 169); 7 white (44%), 6 Asian or Pacific Islander (38%), 1 Latino (6%), 2 of multiple ethnicities (12%).
sample.attrition: 6 of 22 (27%) withdrew: 1 man after his first visit (lost interest) and 5 women (1 lost interest, 2 poor intravenous access, 2 protocol violations). The 16 completers are the minimum the power calculation required. No adverse event led to withdrawal or needed medical treatment. The completers' distribution across the four Latin-square sequences is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, light-drinking adults with almost no prior GHB use who agreed to take GHB and ethanol in a research unit, mostly women, tested supine and monitored. They are unlike people who present to emergency departments after taking GHB with alcohol, who may have taken higher or unknown amounts, other drugs, or both, in uncontrolled settings.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered. Pharmaceutical sodium oxybate (Xyrem, supplied by its manufacturer) and vodka in orange or cranberry juice, with placebo juice. Plasma GHB by a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry method (limit of quantitation 5 µg/mL, because lower values are in the range of the body's own GHB) and blood ethanol by an enzymatic assay.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral GHB dose of 50 mg/kg, which the authors describe as comparable to doses used to treat narcolepsy, with or without ethanol 0.3 g/kg by mouth before and 0.3 g/kg by mouth together with the GHB 15 minutes later (0.6 g/kg in all), after an overnight fast. Average peak blood ethanol was 70.7 mg/dL alone and 76.6 mg/dL with GHB, against about 50 mg/dL projected (Table 2).
exposure.polysubstance: People using illicit or prescription drugs were excluded; alcohol was not allowed for 3 days before each visit and caffeine, tobacco and food were withheld overnight. No drug screen is mentioned.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: No alcohol for 3 days before each study day and an overnight fast from food, caffeine and tobacco, by instruction; not verified.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each of the 16 had placebo, ethanol alone, GHB alone and both. The study is described as double-blind, but the paper does not say how the placebo for GHB was matched or whether blinding was checked.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (within-person). Order by 4 by 4 Latin square; visits at least 2 days apart.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: sleep before each visit, menstrual cycle phase, use of oral contraceptives (allowed), usual alcohol intake within the light range, and tolerance. Weight-based dosing means men and women, who differ in body water and fat, received different absolute amounts.

outcomes.instruments: Dinamap automated blood pressure; heart rate; skin temperature; respiratory rate (recorded, not reported); oxygen saturation by continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours (device and averaging not described); plasma GHB and blood ethanol for pharmacokinetics; adverse events (Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No clinical threshold is applied and no baseline oxygen saturation, lowest individual value or number of people below any threshold is reported. The authors call the 2% change modest in absolute terms.
outcomes.operationalization: Respiratory effect is the change in pulse oximetry saturation from a pre-dose baseline (the paper defines baseline for hemodynamic variables as the average of readings at 0, 15 and 30 minutes before dosing and does not say so separately for oxygen saturation), shown as the maximum mean change and the 0 to 4 hour area under the change curve. Breathing rate, carbon dioxide and sedation are not outcomes in this paper.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated: five pharmacodynamic outcomes (systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, skin temperature) compared pairwise across four conditions, and 11 pharmacokinetic parameters (7 for GHB, 4 for ethanol) compared by paired t tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind is stated in the abstract and Methods; automated measurements. Not stated whether the people reading the oximeter or analysing the data knew the condition; sedation from the drugs would be visible to staff.

analysis.effect_sizes: Oxygen saturation: all three active conditions lower than placebo; the combination gave the greatest drop, with a maximal mean change of −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points at 90 minutes, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); all active conditions stayed significantly below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring (Results › Oxygen Saturation, 1st paragraph). Read by eye from Figure 2 (approximate, mean change from baseline in percentage points): at 90 minutes, combination about −2.2, GHB alone about −1.6, ethanol alone about −0.75, placebo about −0.6; the placebo curve itself drifts down by roughly 0.4 to 0.9 over the 4 hours. No interaction contrast, confidence interval or baseline saturation is given. Blood pressure and heart rate: ethanol alone lowered systolic pressure (peak −15.7 ± 3.0 mm Hg at 105 minutes, P = 0.0006 against GHB alone) and raised heart rate (peak +13.5 ± 2.3 beats per minute at 45 minutes, P = 0.006 against placebo); GHB alone had no significant effect and the combination was not greater than ethanol alone; diastolic pressure with the combination fell by up to 16.9 ± 2.5 mm Hg (P = 0.012 against placebo). Skin temperature rose by up to 2.9 ± 0.7 °F with the combination (P < 0.001 against placebo, P = 0.028 against ethanol alone). Adverse events: vomiting on 8 study days (combination 6, GHB alone 1, ethanol alone 1) and 2 brief asymptomatic drops in systolic pressure to 71 to 73 mm Hg after the combination; no test. Pharmacokinetics of GHB (mean ± SD, alone against with ethanol; Table 1, all P > 0.05 by paired t test): peak 72.6 ± 16.2 against 84.0 ± 25.8 µg/mL (+16%); half-life 51.8 ± 21.3 against 67.0 ± 48.4 minutes (+29%); area under the curve 9,330 ± 3,390 against 11,360 ± 4,796 µg·min/mL; clearance 6.2 ± 2.7 against 5.0 ± 2.4 mL/min/kg. Editors' calculation: area under the curve +22% and clearance −19%, no intervals given. Ethanol (Table 2, all P > 0.05): peak 70.7 ± 11.6 against 76.6 ± 13.3 mg/dL; area under the curve 19,810 ± 5,342 against 18,840 ± 6,450 mg·min/dL.
analysis.covariates: A random subject effect and fixed effects for treatment and all two-way interactions in a mixed-effects regression of the area under the change curve; no adjustment for sex, weight or order.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration number or analysis plan is given. The paper states that the primary aim was the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interaction between the two drugs, and that other outcomes will be reported separately.
analysis.selective_reporting: Respiratory rate was recorded but is not reported. Subjective effects, cognitive tests and sex and race differences are held for other papers, so the outcomes closest to sedation and consciousness are not in this one. The headline oxygen saturation figure is a change from baseline, not from placebo.
analysis.power: Powered for a 25% difference in GHB clearance with ethanol (80% power, 2-sided 0.05, 16 completers). The observed clearance difference was about 19%, and the half-life, peak and area-under-the-curve differences were 29%, 16% and 22%: smaller than the study was designed to detect, so “not statistically significant” cannot be read as “no interaction”. No power calculation for oxygen saturation or adverse events.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 healthy, light-drinking adults given a single moderate GHB dose and a moderate ethanol dose in a research unit, mean oxygen saturation fell by about 2 percentage points at most when the two were taken together, more than with GHB alone (P = 0.027) or ethanol alone (P = 0.013); vomiting happened on 6 of 8 days with vomiting after the combination; two brief asymptomatic drops in systolic blood pressure occurred after it; blood pressure and heart rate changes came from ethanol. GHB blood levels were about 16% higher at peak and the half-life about 29% longer with ethanol, but 16 people could not detect differences of that size.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that GHB plus ethanol “resulted in more adverse effects” including gastrointestinal disturbance, hypotension and decreased oxygen saturation, “but only minimal pharmacokinetic interactions”. The Discussion says the combination “intensifies respiratory depression, which may explain” some of the severe toxicity and deaths seen in recreational use (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Gaps: (1) respiratory depression is inferred from a fall of about 2 percentage points in pulse oximetry with no breathing rate, carbon dioxide or ventilation data (breathing rate was recorded but not reported), and the authors themselves call the change modest; (2) “more adverse effects” rests on 6 against 1 and 1 vomiting days and 2 brief hypotension episodes in 16 people, untested; (3) “minimal” pharmacokinetic interaction rests on non-significance in a study powered for a 25% change in clearance, where every estimate moves the same way; (4) the step from a single modest dose in healthy supine volunteers to deaths in recreational use is not tested by this design; (5) whether the effect of the two together exceeds the sum of their separate effects is not examined.

timeline.event: Mattila et al.: a study of GHB with low-dose ethanol reported significantly impaired reaction time with the combination (as described by Thai et al.; not read).
Chin et al.: clinical course of GHB overdose in 88 emergency department patients, 11 intubated and 21 with raised arterial carbon dioxide (as described by Thai et al.; not read).
Van Sassenbroeck et al.: in rats, ethanol did not change GHB blood levels or area under the curve but prolonged sleeping time (as described by Thai et al.; not read).
This study: the first human pharmacokinetic and hemodynamic study of the combination, by the authors' account.

Galicia (Toxicol Lett), Euro-DEN Plus Registry (22 emergency departments in 14 European countries, 18 of which contributed cases), 609 patients with acute toxicity from GHB or GBL alone (183) or with ethanol (426) and no other drug: reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Score below 13) 58.9% with ethanol against 49.1% without (P = 0.034), more admissions to critical care among those admitted (55.3% against 22.4%), no detectable difference in slow breathing or intubation, and two deaths, both with ethanol. Read for this library from the accepted manuscript: a different design (observational, univariable), population and outcomes, and not a repeat of this crossover.

replication.where_it_stands: No repeat of this crossover design in humans was identified in the paper's reference list. The direction (more central nervous system depression with the combination) is echoed in one emergency department registry analysis read for this library (Galicia, 2019), which measured consciousness, treatment and critical care rather than oxygen saturation, did not adjust for the GHB amount taken or for centre, and found no detectable difference in slow breathing or intubation. Neither study repeats the other.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse grants (DA 14935, DA12393), a clinical pharmacology training grant and a General Clinical Research Center award from the National Institutes of Health. The GHB used (Xyrem) was provided by its manufacturer, Orphan Medical Company; the paper does not state whether the manufacturer had any role in the study.
funding.declared_conflicts: Two authors have given paid medicolegal consultation in cases involving GHB; the other two declare none.
funding.affiliations_note: The affiliation list was collapsed on the page and was not extracted; the ethics committee and the research centre are at the University of California, San Francisco and San Francisco General Hospital. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized crossover study, powered for the interaction between the two drugs on oxygen saturation and breathing (with respiratory rate, carbon dioxide and sedation reported as well), at several GHB and ethanol levels that can safely be given, reporting the interaction contrast with its interval and the lowest individual values; together with emergency department and poison-centre series that record coma, intubation and intensive-care admission with and without ethanol and adjust for the GHB amount taken, which only observational data can reach.

domains.note: Random order by a 4 by 4 Latin square, but how sequences were generated and concealed is not described, and the 16 completers' spread across sequences is not given. Within-person contrasts remove between-person confounding.
At least 2 days between visits, long after GHB (half-life about an hour) and ethanol are cleared; order balanced by the Latin square. No period effect is reported.

Described as double-blind, but the paper does not say how GHB (a salty-tasting solution) and ethanol were matched by placebo or whether blinding was checked, and both drugs cause effects participants and staff can notice. Two women withdrew for protocol violations.

6 of 22 (27%) did not complete, 5 of them women, for reasons that appear unrelated to the outcome (loss of interest, poor intravenous access) but with no analysis of enrolled participants; the 16 completers are the minimum the power calculation required.

Continuous pulse oximetry is automated, but the device, its accuracy, the averaging and the baseline values are not described, the change measured is small (about 2 points), and breathing rate was recorded but not reported.

No registration or analysis plan; respiratory rate not reported; sedation, cognitive and subjective outcomes deferred to other papers; many pairwise tests without correction; the headline saturation change is from baseline, not from placebo, and no interaction contrast is given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The randomized, placebo-controlled within-person design protects the comparisons between conditions against confounding, and the exposure was administered under control; but 5 of 6 domains raise some concerns (unreported blinding method, a 27% dropout, incomplete outcome reporting and no interaction test), none judged high because the outcome is automated and the dropouts seem unrelated to it. The source may be cited for the direction and rough size of the mean oxygen saturation change under these conditions and for the vomiting and blood pressure observations. It may not be cited for the size of the risk to breathing or consciousness in real use, for whether the combined effect exceeds the sum of the single effects, or for a lack of pharmacokinetic interaction.

key_findings.finding: 22 healthy adults aged 21 to 45 enrolled; 16 completed (7 men, 9 women, aged 22 to 34, mean weight 66.2 kg). Eligible people used alcohol lightly (no more than 3 drinks a week) and had taken GHB no more than twice in the previous 6 months; people who used illicit or prescription drugs (other than oral contraceptives) were excluded. 6 withdrew (1 man, 5 women).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results › Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Randomized, double-blind, four-arm crossover (4 by 4 Latin square) with placebo, ethanol, GHB and the combination at four 24-hour visits at least 2 days apart: ethanol 0.3 g/kg or placebo at about 8:00, then 15 minutes later GHB 50 mg/kg (Xyrem) or placebo plus a second ethanol 0.3 g/kg or placebo; supine for 3 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Monitoring: heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and skin temperature at 30 and 15 minutes before dosing, at dosing, every 15 minutes for 2 hours and every 30 minutes for the next 2 hours; oxygen saturation by continuous pulse oximetry for 4 hours; blood at 15, 30, 45, 60 and 90 minutes and 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12 and 24 hours; urine to 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Design and Procedures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Respiratory rate is listed here but no result for it appears; the blood pressure and heart rate area-under-the-curve window (0 to 6 hours) and the statement that ethanol lowered systolic pressure for 5 hours are longer than the 4-hour schedule given (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Statistics: powered to detect a 25% difference in GHB clearance caused by ethanol (16 completers, 80% power, 2-sided 0.05); pharmacokinetic parameters by paired t tests; pharmacodynamic data by mixed-effects regression with treatment, all two-way interactions and a random subject effect, with pairwise comparisons; baseline for blood pressure and heart rate was the average of readings at 0, 15 and 30 minutes before dosing; area under the change curve for oxygen saturation over 0 to 4 hours and for heart rate and blood pressure over 0 to 6 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical and Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Pharmacokinetic Analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oxygen saturation fell with all three active conditions relative to placebo. The combination gave the largest drop: maximal mean change −2.12 ± 0.34 percentage points at 90 minutes, greater than placebo (P < 0.0001), GHB alone (P = 0.027) and ethanol alone (P = 0.013); saturation stayed significantly below baseline for the 4 hours of monitoring with all three active conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamics › Oxygen Saturation, 1st paragraph; Abstract (Results)
key_findings.note: The −2.12 is the change from each person's baseline, not from placebo; Figure 2 shows the placebo curve itself below baseline.

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 (mean change in percentage points from baseline over 240 minutes, with 95% confidence intervals), read by eye and approximate: combination near −0.75 at 15 minutes, −1.6 at 30 to 45 minutes, about −2.2 at 90 minutes, −2.0 at 105 and 150 minutes, and about −1.4 to −1.6 from 180 to 240 minutes; GHB alone about −1.6 at 90 minutes and −1.5 at 150 to 240 minutes; ethanol alone between about −0.4 and −1.2; placebo between about +0.4 at 15 minutes and −0.9 at 210 minutes. The paper reports no interaction contrast; from the plot, the combined fall looks about the size of the GHB-alone fall plus a small ethanol fall.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (image, read by eye)
key_findings.note: Approximate reading; the paper gives numbers only for the combination's maximum.

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: vomiting on 8 study days (6 with the combination, 1 with GHB alone, 1 with ethanol alone) and 2 episodes of brief asymptomatic hypotension (systolic 71 to 73 mm Hg, under 15 minutes) after the combination; none needed treatment and all resolved by themselves; no event led to withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Events, 1st paragraph; Subject Characteristics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure and heart rate: ethanol lowered systolic pressure for 5 hours (peak −15.7 ± 3.0 mm Hg at 105 minutes, P = 0.0006 against GHB alone) and diastolic pressure (peak −16.9 ± 2.5 mm Hg 2 hours after the combination, P = 0.012 against placebo) and raised heart rate (peak +13.5 ± 2.3 beats per minute at 45 minutes, P = 0.006 against placebo); GHB alone had no significant effect on either, and the combination was not greater than ethanol alone. Skin temperature rose by up to 2.9 ± 0.7 °F with the combination (P < 0.001 against placebo, P = 0.028 against ethanol alone) in the first hour.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamics › Blood Pressure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Heart Rate, 1st paragraph; Skin Temperature, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pharmacokinetics (Tables 1 and 2; mean ± SD, n = 16; all differences P > 0.05): GHB peak 72.6 ± 16.2 alone against 84.0 ± 25.8 µg/mL with ethanol; half-life 51.8 ± 21.3 against 67.0 ± 48.4 minutes; area under the curve 9,330 ± 3,390 against 11,360 ± 4,796 µg·min/mL; clearance 6.2 ± 2.7 against 5.0 ± 2.4 mL/min/kg; renal clearance and the share of the dose recovered in urine (about 5%) unchanged. Ethanol peak 70.7 ± 11.6 alone against 76.6 ± 13.3 mg/dL with GHB (against about 50 mg/dL projected); rate of blood ethanol decline 0.24 ± 0.07 against 0.26 ± 0.08 mg/dL per minute.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the table means: GHB area under the curve +22%, clearance −19%.

key_findings.finding: Authors' reading: the combination “was found to have increased respiratory depressant effects”; a fall of about 2% in saturation is modest in absolute terms but could matter if a person has taken other drugs that slow breathing or has lung disease; intensified respiratory depression “may explain some of the severe toxicity and deaths reported”. They add that a small ethanol effect on GHB clearance or bioavailability could matter more at higher GHB doses such as unintentional overdoses.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Funding: US National Institute on Drug Abuse and National Institutes of Health grants; Xyrem provided by its manufacturer; two authors have been paid medicolegal consultants in GHB cases.
key_findings.locator: Acknowledgments; Conflict of Interest Statement (end matter)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says blood pressure and heart rate effects were significant “compared with baseline”, but the Results give the P values against GHB alone (systolic pressure, P = 0.0006) and against placebo (heart rate, P = 0.006; diastolic pressure, P = 0.012).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which comparison each P value belongs to differs between the abstract and the Results; the Results wording should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline oxygen saturation change (−2.1%, “P < 0.0001 vs placebo”) is the change from baseline with the combination, not a difference from placebo. In Figure 2 the placebo curve is itself below baseline for most of the 4 hours (by eye, about 0.4 to 0.9 points), and the paper gives no baseline saturation, lowest individual value or number of people under any threshold.
reporting_issues.consequence: The fall attributable to the drugs is smaller than the headline (by eye, about 1.5 points at 90 minutes for the combination against placebo), and how close any person came to a clinically relevant level cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: Respiratory rate was recorded (Methods) but no result for it is reported. Subjective effects, cognitive testing and effects by sex and race are said to be reported separately.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only breathing outcome reported is pulse oximetry, and nothing about sedation or consciousness is in this paper, though the abstract and Discussion speak of respiratory depression and sedative effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods give vital-sign recording every 15 minutes for 2 hours and every 30 minutes for the next 2 hours (4 hours), but the analysis window for heart rate and blood pressure is 0 to 6 hours and the Results say ethanol lowered systolic pressure “for 5 hours”.
reporting_issues.consequence: The monitoring schedule for blood pressure and heart rate is incompletely described; the results beyond 4 hours cannot be traced to a stated measurement schedule.

reporting_issues.issue: The study was powered to detect a 25% change in GHB clearance. The observed differences with ethanol (peak +16%, half-life +29%, area under the curve about +22% and clearance about −19% by editors' calculation) were each “not significant”, no confidence intervals are given, and the abstract concludes that only “minimal” pharmacokinetic interactions were observed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of statistical significance in 16 people is not evidence of no interaction; all four estimates point to more GHB exposure with ethanol, and an effect of 20% to 30% could not be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The mixed-effects model is described as including all two-way interactions, but no interaction estimate (whether the combined effect exceeds the sum of the single effects) is reported; the conclusions rest on pairwise comparisons only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot be cited for synergy or for additivity; “more than either alone” is shown, “more than their sum” is not tested.

reporting_issues.issue: The ethanol dose was projected to give blood levels near 50 mg/dL; the average peak was 70.7 mg/dL alone and 76.6 mg/dL with GHB (Table 2). The Methods do not discuss the difference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The average peak was roughly 40% to 55% above the projection (editors' calculation), so the study does not describe a 50 mg/dL condition.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2766839 (PMC HTML, author manuscript, read in the app's browser; text saved once with get_page_text): abstract, introduction, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion, acknowledgments, conflict statement, reference list. Figure 2 was viewed as an image and read by eye (approximate values); Figure 1 (concentration curves) was not read. The companion papers on subjective effects and cognitive testing were not read.

design_detail: Review article in the New England Journal of Medicine’s Current Concepts series (17 March 2005; nine pages, 50 references) by two medical toxicologists, one at the University of Massachusetts, Worcester, and both at Children’s Hospital, Boston. There is no methods section: no search, selection criteria or appraisal is described. It covers definition and epidemiology, clinical manifestations, mechanisms, diagnosis (a decision algorithm adapted from Dunkley and colleagues), differential diagnosis, management and prevention; the management section gives treatment doses, which this card does not record.
can_establish: How two medical toxicologists described, in 2005, what serotonin toxicity looks like, which drug classes and drug pairs the literature they chose had linked to it, and which diagnostic rule they preferred; it points to primary sources.
cannot_establish: How often any drug pair causes serotonin toxicity or how severe it is (no rate is given for any pair); whether the diagnostic rule it recommends works outside the one unit that derived it (the accuracy figures come from a single source and are not independently confirmed in the review); what happened in the individual cases behind its drug lists; or that mixes it does not list are safe, since no search was done.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review; no search described). Its epidemiology rests on a US poison-centre surveillance report for 2002, a post-marketing study of one antidepressant and one toxicology unit’s registry of 2,222 overdose admissions (Dunkley and colleagues, reference 2), which is also the source of its list of clinical findings and its diagnostic algorithm.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated: no criteria for choosing the 50 references.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The clinical findings and the diagnostic rule come from one source, a single Australian toxicology unit’s overdose registry; the drug lists rest largely on case reports and series, which report what was noticed and published, mostly in overdose or in hospital, and not what happens across all people who take these drugs.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Drug exposure is described as listed in the cited literature: Table 1 lists drug classes and seven interaction pairs or groups.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the causes. Treatment doses appear in the management section and are not recorded in this library.
exposure.polysubstance: The review lists combinations (phenelzine with meperidine; tranylcypromine with imipramine; phenelzine with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; paroxetine with buspirone; linezolid with citalopram; moclobemide with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; tramadol, venlafaxine and mirtazapine) and says that monoamine oxidase inhibitors are strongly associated with severe cases, especially with meperidine, dextromethorphan, serotonin reuptake inhibitors or MDMA. It gives no count of cases for any pair.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.
