outcomes.instruments: The review’s own description of mild, moderate and severe serotonin syndrome by examination findings and temperature (Figures 1 and 2; Manifestations), and the Hunter decision rules as its preferred diagnostic criteria (Figure 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review says the rules were compared with a gold standard, the assignment of a diagnosis by a medical toxicologist (p. 1114); the source paper says there is no gold standard and calls its approach arbitrary.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed. Severity is described by findings: afebrile with tachycardia and reflex changes in mild cases, a core temperature as high as 40 °C in moderate intoxication and more than 41.1 °C in life-threatening cases (p. 1113, no source given for the temperatures).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new analysis. Figures the review quotes from other sources: serotonin syndrome in approximately 14 to 16 percent of people who overdose on SSRIs (reference 8); 26,733 SSRI exposures with significant toxic effects in 7,349 people and 93 deaths in the 2002 US poison-centre report (these count SSRI toxicity in general, not serotonin syndrome); an incidence of 0.4 case per 1,000 patient-months among people taking nefazodone (reference 10); about 60 percent of people with serotonin syndrome presenting within six hours of starting a medicine, an overdose or a change (reference 28); the Hunter rules compared with Sternbach’s criteria, sensitivity 84 against 75 percent and specificity 97 against 96 percent (references 1 and 2).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged. The review does not carry over the Hunter rules’ authors’ own cautions: a reference diagnosis from the same unit, a test set that includes the derivation set, and the need for validation in other settings (Dunkley and colleagues, pp. 640–641); it calls the toxicologist’s diagnosis a gold standard.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative synthesis of the literature to 2004: serotonin toxicity is a spectrum from mild to life-threatening caused by excess serotonin, recognised by examination (clonus, reflexes, tremor, agitation, sweating, rigidity, temperature), linked to many drugs and drug mixes and most severely to monoamine oxidase inhibitors taken with other serotonergic drugs; no rate is given for any mix.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review states that monoamine oxidase inhibitors are strongly associated with severe cases, especially with meperidine, dextromethorphan, serotonin reuptake inhibitors or MDMA (p. 1113); that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City resulted from meperidine with phenelzine (p. 1112); that its preferred decision rules are simpler, more sensitive and more specific than the original criteria (p. 1115); and that the toxicologist’s diagnosis is a gold standard (p. 1114). Gaps: (1) strongly associated rests on case reports and reviews, with no counts or denominators; (2) the single death is stated as fact and cited to one 1988 article, and how the cause was established is not discussed; (3) the accuracy figures are one unit’s, from a reference its authors call arbitrary, and are presented without their caveats; (4) the temperatures given for moderate and life-threatening poisoning (40 °C and above 41.1 °C) carry no reference and are higher than the severity thresholds in the source the review adapts its rules from.

timeline.event: Sternbach’s criteria, derived from 38 published cases (cited as reference 1 and described in Dunkley and colleagues, p. 636; not read).
Dunkley and colleagues derive and test the Hunter decision rules in one toxicology unit’s overdose registry; the review’s source for its findings list and its algorithm.
This review restates the rules and the 84 against 75 percent and 97 against 96 percent figures without new data.

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source: its figures for the diagnostic rules and its list of clinical findings trace to one primary paper (Dunkley and colleagues, 2003), which this library has read; its drug lists trace to case reports and earlier reviews that were not read.

funding.funder: A grant from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (DA-14929, to Dr. Boyer) (p. 1119).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed in the article. The journal publishes disclosure forms separately online; they were not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Medical toxicologists at the University of Massachusetts, Worcester, and Children’s Hospital, Boston (p. 1112). Neither author appears in the 50 references. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review of the case literature for each drug pair with counts and a structured appraisal, an independent prospective validation of the decision rules in emergency departments against a reference diagnosis made blind to the rules, and population-level surveillance that counts the people exposed to each pair, so that rates can be stated.

domains.note: No methods section; no search, criteria or selection process described; the 50 references were chosen by the authors.

Some appraisal of treatment evidence (cyproheptadine’s efficacy is called not rigorously established, and some case reports of other treatments probably involved misdiagnosis), but the diagnostic study the review depends on is not appraised and its reference diagnosis is called a gold standard.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Neither author is cited among the 50 references.

Mechanism statements are hedged (several lines of evidence converge), but the temperature figures and the statement about one patient's death are given as fact with no source or discussion, and recommendations are stated as preferences without a stated evidence base.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the diagnostic rules and the listed drug mixes
domains.note: The rules are presented without their authors’ caveats or any competing criteria beyond Sternbach’s; the drug lists give no sign of how many reports stand behind each entry.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. Without a search method the review cannot show that its drug lists are complete or that the evidence for each entry is of any particular strength. It may be cited for how two toxicologists described the condition and its recognition in 2005, for the drug classes and pairs named, and for pointing to primary sources. It may not be cited for the accuracy of the decision rules beyond the source it takes them from, for the risk of any drug pair, or for the temperature thresholds it gives.

key_findings.finding: The review defines the serotonin syndrome as a potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction that can follow therapeutic use, intentional self-poisoning or an unplanned interaction between drugs; not an idiosyncratic reaction but a predictable result of excess serotonin stimulation of receptors in the central nervous system and the periphery; producing a spectrum from barely perceptible to lethal.
key_findings.locator: Opening paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review states that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City more than 20 years earlier resulted from coadministration of meperidine (pethidine, an opioid) and phenelzine (an MAOI), and calls it the most widely recognized example of this preventable condition. It cites a 1988 article in the same journal (reference 4), whose title refers to the case.
key_findings.locator: Opening paragraph (final sentence)
key_findings.note: One case stated as fact; the review does not discuss how the cause of death was established.

key_findings.finding: The serotonin syndrome is often described as a triad of mental-status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular abnormalities, but not all are present in every person; signs range from tremor and diarrhoea in mild cases to delirium, neuromuscular rigidity and hyperthermia in life-threatening cases; mild symptoms are easily overlooked.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Quoted from other sources: in 2002 the US poison-centre surveillance system reported 26,733 exposures to SSRIs that caused significant toxic effects in 7,349 people and resulted in 93 deaths (figures for SSRI toxicity generally, not serotonin syndrome); 0.4 case per 1,000 patient-months in people taking nefazodone; more than 85 percent of physicians unaware of the diagnosis; the syndrome occurs in approximately 14 to 16 percent of people who overdose on SSRIs.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review lists barriers to diagnosis: protean manifestations (tremor, diarrhoea, hypertension or anxiety may be dismissed or put down to mental state), strict use of Sternbach’s criteria that rules out mild, early or subacute cases, and clinicians’ unawareness; the syndrome has been identified at all ages.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, 3rd paragraph (continues at the top of p. 1113)

key_findings.finding: Drug classes linked to the syndrome include MAOIs, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, opiate analgesics, cough medicines, antibiotics, weight-reduction agents, antiemetics, antimigraine agents, drugs of abuse and herbal products. MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are said to be strongly associated with severe cases, especially in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA (references 4, 8, 15, 26 and 27).
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs

key_findings.finding: The same paragraph says a single therapeutic dose of an SSRI has caused the syndrome, that adding drugs that inhibit the liver enzymes CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 to an SSRI regimen has been associated with it, and that serotonergic agents given within five weeks after stopping fluoxetine have produced an interaction, presumably through a long-lasting metabolite (reference 13).
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs
key_findings.note: The five-week window is the basis for the first question in the review’s Figure 4.

key_findings.finding: Mild cases may be afebrile with tachycardia, shivering, sweating, dilated pupils, intermittent tremor or myoclonus and brisk reflexes; moderate cases have tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia (a core temperature as high as 40 °C is called common), dilated pupils, hyperactive bowel sounds, sweating, and reflex and clonus changes greater in the legs, with mild agitation; severe cases may have severe hypertension and tachycardia that abruptly deteriorate into shock, agitated delirium and muscular rigidity, with a core temperature of more than 41.1 °C in life-threatening cases. Laboratory abnormalities in severe cases include metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, raised aminotransferases and creatinine, seizures, renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, many arising from poorly treated hyperthermia.
key_findings.locator: Manifestations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: No reference is given for the temperatures; Dunkley and colleagues use above 38 °C in their rule and at or above 38.5 °C for severe toxicity.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists drugs associated with the syndrome (among them the MAOIs phenelzine, moclobemide, clorgiline and isocarboxazid; the analgesics meperidine, fentanyl, tramadol and pentazocine; dextromethorphan; and MDMA, LSD and Syrian rue among drugs of abuse) and drug interactions associated with severe serotonin syndrome: phenelzine with meperidine; tranylcypromine with imipramine; phenelzine with SSRIs; paroxetine with buspirone; linezolid with citalopram; moclobemide with SSRIs; tramadol, venlafaxine and mirtazapine.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: The review describes its main source as the clinical findings in 2,222 consecutive cases of self-poisoning with serotonergic drugs from a toxicology registry, compared with the gold standard of a medical toxicologist’s diagnosis; findings with a significant association were mainly neuromuscular (hyperreflexia, inducible, ocular and spontaneous clonus, myoclonus, peripheral hypertonicity, shivering), with tachycardia, mydriasis, sweating, bowel sounds and diarrhoea, agitation and delirium; a temperature above 38 °C was not as strongly associated but occurred in severely intoxicated people.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning To better delineate the signs and symptoms (continues at the top of the right-hand column of p. 1114)

key_findings.finding: The onset is usually rapid, with findings often within minutes of a change in medication or self-poisoning; approximately 60 percent of people present within six hours of starting a medicine, an overdose or a change in dosing (reference 28); mild cases may present subacutely or chronically and severe cases may progress rapidly to death.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning The onset of symptoms is usually rapid (top of the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: No laboratory test confirms the diagnosis; it is inferred from the history and examination. The history should cover prescription and over-the-counter drugs, illicit substances and supplements, and the evolution of symptoms; the examination should assess reflexes, clonus, muscle rigidity, pupils, mouth dryness, bowel sounds, skin colour and sweating.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors prefer the decision rules in Figure 4, described as simpler, more sensitive (84 against 75 percent) and more specific (97 against 96 percent) than the original diagnostic criteria (references 1 and 2), and call clonus (inducible, spontaneous and ocular) the most important finding.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Hyperthermia and hypertonicity occur in life-threatening cases, but muscle rigidity may mask clonus and hyperreflexia and so cloud the diagnosis.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (ends at the foot of the left-hand column of p. 1116)

key_findings.finding: Anticholinergic poisoning, malignant hyperthermia and the neuroleptic malignant syndrome are said to be readily distinguished from the serotonin syndrome on clinical grounds and the medication history: for example, normal reflexes, absent bowel sounds and dry skin in anticholinergic poisoning; slow onset over days with lead-pipe rigidity in the neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, paragraphs beginning The differential diagnosis includes, Malignant hyperthermia is, and The neuroleptic malignant syndrome is (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Figure 4, the diagnostic algorithm, begins with whether a serotonergic agent has been administered in the past five weeks; if so, the answer is serotonin syndrome when there is spontaneous clonus; tremor with hyperreflexia; inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; or muscle rigidity with a temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus. It is labelled as criteria adapted from Dunkley and colleagues.
key_findings.locator: Figure 4
key_findings.note: The five-week condition is added by the review; Dunkley and colleagues’ rules say in the presence of a serotonergic agent.

key_findings.finding: Table 2 sets severe serotonin syndrome against anticholinergic poisoning, the neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia by medication history, time to develop (under 12 hours for the serotonin syndrome), vital signs, pupils, mucosa, skin, bowel sounds, muscle tone, reflexes and mental status.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (printed sideways)

reporting_issues.issue: The review says the rules were compared with the gold standard of a toxicologist’s diagnosis. The source paper says there is no gold standard for clinically significant serotonin toxicity, that its approach was arbitrary for that reason, and that the diagnosis it used is the standard it chose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference diagnosis is given more authority than its authors claim for it, which makes the accuracy figures look firmer than they are.

reporting_issues.issue: The 84 against 75 percent sensitivity and 97 against 96 percent specificity are given without saying that they come from one unit’s records, from a test set that includes the records the rules were derived from, with no intervals and no independent test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take the figures as established accuracy; the source’s authors say the rules need validating in other settings.

reporting_issues.issue: Temperatures are given as a core temperature as high as 40 °C being common in moderate intoxication and more than 41.1 °C in life-threatening cases, with no reference, while the rule the review adopts uses above 38 °C and its source treats at or above 38.5 °C as marking severe toxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review’s moderate (40 °C) and life-threatening (above 41.1 °C) temperatures sit 1.5 and 2.6 degrees above its source’s severe threshold of 38.5 °C (editors’ calculation), and the review does not reconcile them.

reporting_issues.issue: The surveillance figures (26,733 exposures, 7,349 people with significant toxic effects, 93 deaths) are for SSRI exposures in general; the paragraph is about the serotonin syndrome and gives no count of serotonin syndrome cases from this report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The numbers are not serotonin-syndrome counts and cannot be used as the number of people who had it or died of it.

reporting_issues.issue: The death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City is stated as having resulted from meperidine with phenelzine, on the strength of one 1988 article, with no discussion of how the cause was established or of other possible contributors.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single case stated as fact is a weak basis for the strength of the MAOI and opioid interaction; the review’s other support for it is a table entry without counts.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1112–1120 (full text: opening paragraph, all sections, Tables 1 and 2, Figures 1 to 4, funding line, reference list); paragraph breaks, Table 1 and the sideways Table 2 were checked against page renders. The management section was read for context only and its doses are not recorded. The cited primary sources were not read except Dunkley and colleagues (2003).

design_detail: Practice Pointer in the BMJ (published online 19 February 2014; four pages, 20 references) by three consultant toxicologists in Sydney and Newcastle, Australia; commissioned and externally peer reviewed. There is no methods section: no search or selection is described. Question-and-answer format (What is serotonin syndrome? How does it present? How do we diagnose it? How can we treat it? How can we prevent it?), with a box of drugs, summary points, a figure of the spectrum of effects and a flowchart of the Hunter criteria. The treatment section gives doses, which this card does not record.
can_establish: How three toxicologists described in 2014 what serotonin toxicity is, how it presents and is recognised, which drug classes have been linked to it, and what they take the case literature to show about which combinations produce severe toxicity; it points to primary sources.
cannot_establish: How often any combination causes serotonin toxicity or death (no rate is given for any pair); whether the Hunter criteria have been independently validated in the sense the word implies (only the paper that derived them is cited); whether nearly all severe cases involving a monoamine oxidase inhibitor is a feature of the disorder or of what has been published; or anything about pairs the chosen literature does not cover.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review; no search described). The figures it gives come from the authors’ own group: a large case series of SSRI overdoses (moderate toxicity in 15%, no severe cases; reference 5) and a series of moclobemide overdoses (reference 15, not read for this library). The statement that nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI rests on six cited reviews of case reports, four of them by one author (references 3, 4, 9 and 10, Gillman).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated: no criteria for choosing the 20 references.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The review’s central generalisation rests on published case reports and reviews of them, which record what was noticed and published, and on one toxicology group’s overdose series; people with mild toxicity and people who took mixes that were never written up would not appear.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Drug exposure is described as listed in Box 1 and in the cited literature.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the causes. The treatment section gives doses, which are not recorded in this library.
exposure.polysubstance: The review says severe toxicity usually occurs only with a combination of two or more serotonergic drugs (even when each is at a therapeutic dose), one of which is generally an MAOI; that interactions of an SSRI with any MAOI might be lethal; that interactions with other serotonin reuptake inhibitors are likely to be minor and interactions with serotonin-releasing agents such as amphetamines might even attenuate toxicity (one cited volunteer study of citalopram with MDMA, reference 18, not read); and that moclobemide overdose alone did not produce toxicity, while with a second serotonergic drug toxicity was nearly always present and severe in about half (reference 15, not read).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Clinical diagnosis by the triad of neuromuscular, autonomic and mental-status features, and the Hunter criteria (Figure 2) to confirm moderate or severe toxicity.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review says the Hunter criteria have been validated and cites one source for this, the paper that derived them (reference 13, Dunkley and colleagues, two of whose authors are authors of this review).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed. Moderate toxicity is described as occurring in 15% of SSRI overdoses; severe toxicity as a rapidly rising temperature with rigidity.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new analysis. Figures quoted, mostly from the authors’ own group: moderate serotonin toxicity in 15% of SSRI poisonings, with no severe cases (reference 5); no toxicity in overdoses of moclobemide alone, but with a second serotonergic drug toxicity nearly always present and severe in about half (reference 15); mortality below 1% when the supportive approaches described had been applied (references 5 and 15); in the spectrum figure, multiples of 3 to 5, 5 to 10 and 10 to 100 for the rise in serotonin efflux seen in animal models, set against mild, moderate and severe toxicity.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged. The review says spurious associations and cautions have proliferated elsewhere and that product information impedes sensible decision support, and names a few interactions it regards as unsupported (carbamazepine, most tricyclic and atypical antidepressants, triptans), without listing the evidence for each.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A practice-oriented synthesis, by authors whose own units produced much of the data, of what serotonin toxicity is, how it is recognised and which drugs are implicated, concluding that severe toxicity usually needs a combination of serotonergic drugs, generally including an MAOI; no rate is given for any pair.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review says the Hunter criteria have been validated (p. 2), that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (p. 3), that an SSRI with any MAOI might be lethal (p. 3), and that interactions of an SSRI with serotonin-releasing agents such as amphetamines might even attenuate toxicity (p. 3). Gaps: (1) validated rests on the derivation paper alone, by two of this review’s three authors’ group, with no independent test cited; (2) the MAOI statement rests on reviews of case reports, four of six by one author, in a literature where an MAOI is likely to be named whenever a severe case is written up; (3) might be lethal and nearly all are statements of likelihood without counts or denominators; (4) the figures for SSRI and moclobemide overdoses are from the authors’ own earlier papers, and the attenuation statement rests on one volunteer study not read here.

timeline.event: Dunkley and colleagues derive and test the Hunter criteria; the review’s only citation for validated.
Isbister and colleagues: moclobemide overdose, toxicokinetics and occurrence of serotonin toxicity (reference 15; as described in this review; not read).
Gillman’s review of MAOIs, opioids and serotonin toxicity, cited among the reviews of case reports (reference 10).
This review restates the conclusions of those reviews for general doctors.

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source from the group that produced the Hunter criteria; its generalisation about MAOIs matches the one in Gillman’s 2005 review, which it cites, so the two are not independent. No new case data are given.

funding.funder: No funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that they have read the journal group’s policy on declaration of interests and have no relevant interests to declare (p. 3).
funding.affiliations_note: Consultant toxicologists at the NSW Poisons Information Centre, the University of Sydney, Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and the University of Newcastle (p. 1). Two of the three authors (Dawson and Isbister) are authors of Dunkley and colleagues (2003), the source of the Hunter criteria the review calls validated, and seven of the 20 references (1, 5, 7, 8, 13, 15 and 16) include one or more of the three authors. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An independent prospective validation of the Hunter criteria in emergency departments against a reference diagnosis made blind to the rules; a systematic review of the case literature for each drug pair that states its search and counts the reports; and surveillance that counts the people exposed to each pair, so that the share of severe cases involving a monoamine oxidase inhibitor can be set against how often these inhibitors are taken with other serotonergic drugs.

domains.note: No methods section; 20 references chosen by the authors; the reviews it relies on are called systematic without their methods being described.

Some appraisal (the treatment evidence is called weak, and many interaction warnings are called unsupported), but the Hunter criteria are called validated on the strength of the derivation paper, and the cited reviews of case reports are not appraised.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Seven of 20 references (1, 5, 7, 8, 13, 15, 16) include at least one of the three authors, including the sources of the Hunter criteria, the SSRI overdose figure and the moclobemide figure.

Uncertainty is marked (presumably, seem to, it is unclear, no evidence has been found, no clinical trials or other strong evidence for any treatment), and the animal-model basis of the spectrum figure is stated.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the diagnostic rules and the listed drug mixes
domains.note: The case against over-broad interaction warnings is argued well, but the evidence for the MAOI generalisation is one group’s data and reviews, and the attenuation statement for serotonin-releasing agents rests on a single volunteer study.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. There is no search method, and a third of the references are the authors’ own. It may be cited for how three toxicologists described the condition and its recognition in 2014 and for the drug classes they list; it may not be cited for the Hunter criteria being independently validated, for the share of severe cases that involve an MAOI as an established figure, or for any risk of a pair of drugs.

key_findings.finding: The review defines serotonin syndrome as a drug-induced cluster of dose-related adverse effects caused by raised serotonin in the central nervous system; it is also called serotonin toxicity because it covers a spectrum from mild to severe, depending, presumably, on how far serotonin is raised. It is described as potentially fatal and largely avoidable.
key_findings.locator: Standfirst; What is serotonin syndrome?, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug induced syndrome

key_findings.finding: Severe toxicity usually occurs only with a combination of two or more serotonergic drugs (even when each is at a therapeutic dose), one of which is generally an MAOI; moderate toxicity has been reported with an overdose of a single drug and occasionally from increasing therapeutic doses; in large case series of overdoses, moderate toxicity occurred in 15% of SSRI poisonings.
key_findings.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, same paragraph

key_findings.finding: Severe or life-threatening effects (rigidity and hyperthermia) are said to result only from stimulation of 5-HT2 receptors, and the drug classes implicated are largely serotonin precursors, agonists, releasers, reuptake inhibitors and MAOIs; a few interactions are clearly linked to classic cases although the mechanism is unclear.
key_findings.locator: What is serotonin syndrome?, paragraph beginning Severe or life threatening effects (continues in the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Serotonin toxicity starts within hours of taking the drug or drugs; the classic triad is neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, rigidity), autonomic excitation (hyperthermia, tachycardia) and altered mental state (agitation, confusion); the acute onset of these features should prompt a search for a toxic explanation, alongside withdrawal, non-convulsive seizures and encephalitis.
key_findings.locator: How does it present?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the authors’ group’s case series, moderate toxicity occurred in 15% of SSRI overdoses with no severe cases; toxicity did not occur in overdoses of moclobemide alone, but if a second serotonergic drug was taken toxicity was nearly always present and was severe in about half of these cases.
key_findings.locator: How does it present?, 2nd paragraph (references 5 and 15)
key_findings.note: The moclobemide series (reference 15) was not read for this library.

key_findings.finding: Box 1 lists drugs associated with moderate to severe serotonin toxicity. Under the heading monoamine oxidase inhibitors: phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid, isocarboxazid, moclobemide (a reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A), linezolid and methylene blue. Under the heading serotonin releasing agents: fenfluramine, sibutramine, amphetamine, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, phentermine, ecstasy and cathinones, and, listed beneath it, serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, venlafaxine and related drugs, clomipramine and imipramine), the opioid analgesics pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan, and St John’s wort. Under miscellaneous: lithium, tryptophan and buspirone. The footnote says severe toxicity generally involves a combination of agents from different drug classes.
key_findings.locator: Box 1 and its footnote

key_findings.finding: The diagnosis is clinical and plausible only after starting or increasing the dose (or overdose) of a potent serotonergic drug, or shortly after a second is added. Contributing drugs can be hard to identify because some have persistent activity (irreversible MAOIs) or long half-lives (fluoxetine) and may have been stopped weeks earlier; drugs not marketed as serotonergic, such as tramadol, fentanyl, linezolid and methylene blue, are described as a trap.
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) is the classic feature, forming the key components of the Hunter criteria, which the review says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited is Dunkley and colleagues (reference 13).
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning Some pathognomonic features)

key_findings.finding: Severe toxicity is characterised by a rapidly rising temperature and rigidity and is diagnosed on clinical grounds; investigations are of no diagnostic value except to diagnose complications; neuroleptic malignant syndrome is distinguished by slow onset over days, extrapyramidal features and rigidity, and no clonus.
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 4th paragraph (beginning Severe serotonin toxicity is characterised; it continues in the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Mild serotonin toxicity is difficult to tell from many medical conditions or other drug effects; people taking therapeutic SSRIs commonly have lower-limb hyperreflexia or a few beats of ankle clonus without toxicity; a diagnosis of mild serotonin syndrome may be tempting for any febrile, tachycardic, agitated or confused person on psychiatric drugs, and many reports quote the non-specific Sternbach criteria without the classic Hunter features.
key_findings.locator: How do we diagnose it?, 5th paragraph (beginning A different problem relates to mild serotonin toxicity, right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: The treatment section states that there are no clinical trials or other strong evidence supporting any of the treatment approaches it describes, but that recovery is usual and mortality low (under 1%) when such approaches have been applied (references 5 and 15).
key_findings.locator: How can we treat it?, paragraph beginning Serotonin antagonists and in particular 5HT2A receptor antagonists (the sentence beginning There are no clinical trials, at the foot of the left-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Prevention section: spurious associations and cautions have proliferated, and product information impedes sensible decision support; interactions of an SSRI with any MAOI might be lethal; interactions with other serotonin reuptake inhibitors are likely to be minor (additive); interactions with serotonin-releasing agents such as amphetamines might even attenuate toxicity (one volunteer study, reference 18); many listed interactions have little or no evidence that serotonergic effects increase.
key_findings.locator: How can we prevent it?, 1st paragraph (beginning Several systematic reviews clarify)
key_findings.note: The statement on serotonin-releasing agents concerns an SSRI taken with a releasing drug, which is the subject of another reader’s claim on MDMA and antidepressants.

key_findings.finding: It is apparent from systematic reviews of case reports (references 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11) that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and the relatively small number of these can easily be committed to memory.
key_findings.locator: How can we prevent it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning An awareness of drugs with potent serotonergic effects)
key_findings.note: Four of the six cited reviews are by one author (Gillman); the one read for this library (Gillman 2005) gives only a one-sentence description of its search (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, p. 437).

key_findings.finding: Susceptibility differs between people but strong consistent pharmacogenetic associations have not been found; no evidence supports theories that dietary MAOI compounds cause serotonin toxicity in highly susceptible people.
key_findings.locator: How can we prevent it?, 3rd paragraph (beginning Some individuals seem to be more susceptible, right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Provenance and declarations: commissioned and externally peer reviewed; the authors have no relevant interests to declare; no funding statement.
key_findings.locator: Contributors, Competing interests and Provenance statements

key_findings.finding: Summary points: serotonin syndrome is the clinical manifestation of excess serotonin in the central nervous system, from therapeutic use or overdose of serotonergic drugs; the most severe cases involve drug interactions, particularly between MAOIs and serotonin reuptake inhibitors or serotonin-releasing drugs; the diagnosis is clinical, suspected on the triad, with confirmation based largely on the neuromuscular features in the Hunter criteria; the spectrum runs from mild to life-threatening.
key_findings.locator: Summary points box

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 sets severe toxicity (an MAOI plus SSRI combination as the typical cause: rigidity, respiratory failure, coma, severe hyperthermia), moderate toxicity (SSRI overdose; sustained clonus, agitation, mydriasis, sweating and a low fever below 38.5 °C), mild toxicity (ecstasy use; inducible clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertension, tachycardia) and the least (SSRI in therapeutic use; brisk reflexes) against approximate multiples of serotonin efflux from animal models. Figure 2 is a flowchart of the Hunter criteria that gives yes at spontaneous clonus; inducible or ocular clonus with agitation, sweating or (hypertonia and temperature above 38 °C); or tremor with hyperreflexia.
key_findings.locator: Figures 1 and 2
key_findings.note: The multiples in Figure 1 are approximate figures from animal models; the typical-cause labels are the authors’ and carry no counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says the Hunter criteria have been validated, with a single citation, the paper that derived them; no independent test is cited. The derivation paper itself says the rules need validating in other settings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Validated is stronger than the evidence cited; two of the review’s three authors are authors of the derivation paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The review calls references 3, 4, 6, 9, 10 and 11 systematic reviews; four are by one author, and the one read for this library (reference 10, Gillman 2005) gives only a one-sentence description of its search (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, p. 437).
reporting_issues.consequence: Nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI is a conclusion from narrative reviews of published case reports, so it may reflect which cases were written up; it is not a rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The moclobemide statement (no toxicity with moclobemide alone; with a second serotonergic drug nearly always present and severe in about half) comes from the authors’ own earlier paper, reference 15, and gives no number of cases in this review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The numbers behind about half cannot be checked here; the source was not read for this library.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 is headed as a spectrum with approximate multiples of serotonin efflux from animal models, and names ecstasy use as the typical cause of mild toxicity and an MAOI plus SSRI combination as the typical cause of severe toxicity, without a reference for the pairing of cause and severity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels read as findings but carry no counts or source for the pairings; they cannot be used to rank the danger of MDMA against other causes.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1–4 (full text: standfirst, all five sections, Box 1, summary points, Figures 1 and 2, declarations, reference list); the figures were checked against a page render. The treatment doses were read for context only and are not recorded. The cited primary sources were not read except Dunkley and colleagues (2003) and Gillman (2005).

design_detail: Retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected clinical toxicology database (Hunter Area Toxicology Service, Newcastle, New South Wales, Australia), 13 January 1987 to 22 November 2002. Decision rules were derived with a classification-tree method (CART) in 473 admissions after overdose of a single SSRI, rule 5 (for hypertonic, febrile people) was then added by hand, and the rules were tested in all 2,222 admissions in which at least one serotonergic drug had been taken in overdose, a set that includes the 473. Three reference outcomes were used: the admitting toxicologist’s diagnosis (the main one), Sternbach’s criteria, and treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist (chlorpromazine or cyproheptadine). People intubated for serotonin toxicity were reviewed separately (6 intubated solely for worsening toxicity).
can_establish: In people admitted to one Australian toxicology unit after an overdose of a serotonergic drug, how closely a six-step rule built from seven bedside findings reproduces the diagnosis the unit’s toxicologists made, set beside Sternbach’s older criteria applied to the same records, and which single findings (clonus, agitation, sweating, tremor, brisk reflexes) went with that diagnosis.
cannot_establish: Whether the rules are accurate against a diagnosis made independently of them (the reference diagnosis is the same unit’s clinical judgment on the same kind of findings the rules use, and the paper itself says there is no gold standard), in people taking a prescribed dose, in other hospitals, or in people who combined drugs in the way that causes the most severe toxicity; how often any particular combination leads to serotonin toxicity; or whether the temperature and rigidity feature (rule 5) picks out who becomes seriously ill, since it was added from 6 intubated people and the literature and was not tested on its own.

sample.recruitment: Clinic and registry: consecutive overdose presentations and admissions to a regional toxicology unit that serves about 350,000 people and takes tertiary referrals from a further 150,000. Every overdose presentation or admission is entered prospectively into the unit’s clinical database, from a preformatted admission sheet completed by medical staff, by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses being tested (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 637).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Test set: every admission in the period in which at least one serotonergic drug had been taken in overdose, with no exclusions (Methods › Test dataset, p. 638). Derivation set: admissions with a single SSRI taken, identified from the history; excluded were admissions with a tricyclic antidepressant, MAOI, venlafaxine, nefazodone or lithium taken at the same time, admissions with two SSRIs (9), and admissions with any anti-serotonergic drug taken at the same time (a list of 16 drugs is given) (Methods › Derivation dataset, p. 638).
sample.demographics: Not reported. Age is listed as a variable that went with the diagnosis (p = 0.004) but no ages, no sex split, no intent of overdose and no breakdown by drug are given for either set.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (consecutive admissions), but 203 of the 2,222 admissions (9%, editors’ calculation) are absent from Table 1a, whose cells total 2,019, and Table 2 covers the same 2,019 rows. The paper does not say why. Tables 1b and 1c cover all 2,222, so the 203 are all admissions the rules did not flag (2,015 in those tables against 1,812 in Table 1a, editors’ calculation); a missing toxicologist’s diagnosis is one possible reason, but the paper does not say.
sample.selection_effects: People who were admitted to a toxicology unit after an overdose, so selected by presenting and by that unit’s admission practice; a single centre whose toxicologists’ diagnoses are both the standard the rules were built to reproduce and the standard they are scored against; a test set in which 473 of 2,222 admissions (21%, editors’ calculation) are the same single-SSRI admissions the rules were derived from; no people taking a prescribed dose and no emergency department or psychiatric ward patients. The most severe cases came from the full set (6 intubated for worsening toxicity) and were not in the learning set, because the authors say they occur with combinations of serotonergic drugs (Results › Decision rules, p. 639).

exposure.measurement: Overdose of one or more serotonergic drugs, taken from the clinical history in the unit’s database (the single-SSRI admissions were identified from a history that an SSRI alone had been taken). No drug concentrations are reported, and the paper does not tabulate which drugs make up the 2,222.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported: the amounts taken, the time from ingestion to examination and the route. These were overdose admissions, so the findings describe poisoning and do not describe people taking a prescribed dose.
exposure.polysubstance: The test set has no exclusions, so it includes combinations of serotonergic drugs with each other and with other drugs; how many is not given. The derivation set was limited to a single SSRI with nothing else of the listed kinds, to get findings from a purely serotonergic drug (Introduction, last paragraph, p. 637); this left out the combinations in which, by the authors’ account, the life-threatening cases occur (p. 639).

comparison.controls: No control group. The people in the 2,222 not diagnosed with serotonin toxicity are the comparison for each rule (1,847 of the 2,019 in Table 1a). Each admission is classified three ways: by the admitting toxicologist (the main reference), by Sternbach’s criteria, and by whether a 5-HT2A antagonist was given.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: age and sex, the other drugs taken, the time since ingestion, whether the person was already taking a serotonergic medicine, the examiner’s experience in eliciting clonus and reflexes, and the toxicologists’ own diagnostic thresholds.

outcomes.instruments: A preformatted admission sheet completed by medical staff, from which 26 items were extracted (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Score, akathisia, nystagmus, skin colour, oculogyric crisis, mydriasis, confusion, bowel sounds, ataxia, hallucination, clonus, seizures, myoclonus, diarrhoea, delirium, diaphoresis, reflexes, lacrimation, muscle tone, rhabdomyolysis, shivering, agitation, tremor; Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 637), and three definitions of serotonin toxicity: the admitting toxicologist’s assessment, Sternbach’s criteria (Figure 1) and treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist.
outcomes.validity_norms: None for the toxicologist’s diagnosis. The authors say there is no gold standard for clinically significant serotonin toxicity and that the approach was therefore arbitrary (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 640). How many toxicologists made the diagnoses, how they decided, how well they agreed with one another and whether the diagnosis was recorded before the findings used by the rules are not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Serotonin toxicity was (a) a diagnosis by the admitting toxicologist, (b) Sternbach’s criteria met, or (c) a 5-HT2A antagonist given. A life-threatening case was one intubated and ventilated for serotonin toxicity. The rules predict whether the toxicologist would diagnose serotonin toxicity at that admission; they do not predict a later outcome. The temperature in the rules is written as above 38 °C (rule 5, Figure 2), above 38.5 °C (the six intubated people, p. 640) and at or above 38.5 °C (Discussion, p. 641).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The number of variables screened is not stated (26 items listed, several split into types); 22 categorical variables and age were associated with the toxicologist’s diagnosis at the 5% level, a screening step for the tree. Three reference outcomes were each used to score the rules. No confidence intervals are given for any sensitivity or specificity.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Database entry was by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses (p. 637). The toxicologists’ diagnoses were made at the admission, before the rules existed, but by the same unit whose department the authors belong to, and the rules were built to reproduce them. Whether the people who recorded the signs knew the toxicologist’s diagnosis is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Derivation set (473 single-SSRI overdoses, p. 638): 73 (15.4%, 95% CI 12.3 to 19.0) diagnosed by a toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 11.7 to 18.4) met Sternbach’s criteria, 44 (9.3%, 6.8 to 12.3) were given a 5-HT2A antagonist. Test set against the toxicologist’s diagnosis (Table 1a, p. 639): correctly not flagged 1,785, wrongly flagged 62, missed 27, correctly flagged 145; 172 diagnosed, 1,847 not diagnosed, 207 flagged, 2,019 in the table; printed sensitivity 84% and specificity 97%. Editors’ calculation from the cells (Wilson 95% intervals; the paper gives none): sensitivity 145/172 = 84.3% (78.1 to 89.0); specificity 1,785/1,847 = 96.6% (95.7 to 97.4); positive predictive value 145/207 = 70.0% (63.5 to 75.9); negative predictive value 1,785/1,812 = 98.5% (97.8 to 99.0); share diagnosed 172/2,019 = 8.5% (7.4 to 9.8); wrongly flagged 62/1,847 = 3.4% and missed 27/172 = 15.7%. Against Sternbach’s criteria as the reference (Table 1b): 1,951, 67, 64, 140; printed sensitivity 69% and specificity 97%. Against 5-HT2A antagonist treatment (Table 1c): 1,991, 124, 24, 83; printed 78% and 94%. Sternbach’s criteria against the toxicologist’s diagnosis in the same 2,019 (Table 2, p. 640): 1,772, 75, 43, 129; printed sensitivity 75% and specificity 96%; editors’ calculation from the cells: 129/172 = 75.0% (68.0 to 80.9) and 1,772/1,847 = 95.9% (94.9 to 96.7). Sternbach’s positive predictive value from the cells is 129/204 = 63.2% (editors’ calculation), against 129/186 = 69.4% if the printed column total is used. No test is given for whether 84% against 75% differs. Life-threatening cases (p. 640): 42 people intubated for reduced consciousness or decontamination and 6 solely for worsening serotonin toxicity (editors’ sum 48), all 6 with fever above 38.5 °C and several features; 6/2,222 = 0.27% (0.1 to 0.6, editors’ calculation).
analysis.covariates: None. Univariate chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests and a t-test (age) against the toxicologist’s diagnosis; a CART classification tree on the derivation set (minimum subgroup size five, tree chosen by cross-validation) presented as if-then rules; rule 5 added by hand (Methods › Statistical analysis, p. 638).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Retrospective analysis of an existing database; no registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The univariate results for Sternbach’s criteria and for antagonist treatment are described as not shown (Results, p. 639) and the clonus results as data not shown (Discussion, p. 640). No confidence intervals for sensitivity or specificity, and no accuracy for the rules in the derivation set alone, are given. The rule thresholds were fitted to the same admissions they are scored on.
analysis.power: No sample size or precision calculation. With 172 diagnosed and 1,847 not diagnosed, the editors’ 95% interval for sensitivity is about 11 percentage points wide (78 to 89%); the 9-point gap from Sternbach’s 75% is paired within the same people and cannot be read against these intervals.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 2,019 tabulated overdose admissions at one toxicology unit, a six-step rule built from seven findings agreed with the unit’s own toxicologists for 145 of 172 diagnosed people (84%) and left 1,785 of 1,847 undiagnosed people unflagged (97%); on the same records Sternbach’s criteria agreed for 129 of 172 (75%) and 1,772 of 1,847 (96%). The rules flagged 62 people the toxicologists had not diagnosed and missed 27 they had. Serotonin toxicity was diagnosed in 15.4% of 473 single-SSRI overdoses. Six people were intubated solely for worsening toxicity; the fever and rigidity step was added from them and from the literature.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the new criteria were “simpler, more sensitive (84% vs. 75%) and more specific (97% vs. 96%)” than Sternbach’s (p. 635), that hypertonicity and a maximum temperature above 38 °C were “universal” in life-threatening cases (p. 635), and the title calls the rules “simple and accurate”. The Discussion adds that the rules need validating in other settings (p. 641). Gaps: (1) the standard is the same unit’s clinical diagnosis, made on the kind of findings the rules use and reproduced by them, so a rule built to match it will look better against it than Sternbach’s criteria do (incorporation and circularity); (2) the test set contains the derivation set, and no accuracy outside it is given; (3) no intervals or paired test are given for 84 against 75 and 97 against 96; (4) universal in the abstract is prominent in the Results (p. 640) and rests on six people picked out by the same unit; (5) 203 admissions are missing from Table 1a without explanation; (6) accurate rests on a reference the authors themselves call arbitrary (p. 640).

timeline.event: This paper: derivation and same-unit test of the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria from a large consecutive series of overdose admissions (Sternbach’s 1991 criteria had been derived from 38 published cases, p. 636).

Boyer and Shannon restate the rules and the 84 against 75 percent sensitivity and 97 against 96 percent specificity figures in a review, with the added condition of a serotonergic drug in the past five weeks; no new data (as read for this library).
Gillman describes the Hunter rules in a review as decision rules for the diagnosis, without new data (as read for this library).
Buckley and colleagues describe the Hunter criteria as validated and cite only this paper for that statement; the authors are from the same Newcastle group (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: No independent test of these rules against a separate reference diagnosis was found among the three later reviews read for this library (Boyer and Shannon 2005; Gillman 2005; Buckley and colleagues 2014), and each of them rests on this paper for the numbers. The literature outside those three was not searched, so this card does not say that no one has tested the rules; it says that no test is in the sources read.

funding.funder: No funding statement. The Acknowledgments thank named staff for data entry and data extraction only (p. 641).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared; the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are from the University of Newcastle and from the toxicology department of the Newcastle Mater Misericordiae Hospital, which runs the unit whose database supplied the data and whose toxicologists’ diagnoses are the main reference (p. 635). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study in emergency departments, psychiatric units and toxicology units, including people taking prescribed doses and people with drug combinations, in which examiners record the findings at the bedside and an independent panel, blind to the rule result, assigns the final diagnosis after the course is known; reported with confidence intervals, a paired comparison with Sternbach’s criteria, and severe outcomes (intubation, intensive care, death) as separate end points, so the fever and rigidity step can be tested on its own.

domains.note: Consecutive admissions to one unit with no exclusions in the test set; the derivation set’s exclusions affect which people the rules describe, not who was chosen for scoring them.

The rules were built from the same database they are scored on (the test set contains the 473 derivation admissions), the cut points were fitted to the data, rule 5 was added by hand after the analysis, and the findings the rules use come from the same record as the reference diagnosis.

The admitting toxicologist’s diagnosis, made at the bedside on much the same findings the rules use, with no independent panel, no agreement between diagnosers reported, and no gold standard (the authors’ own words); the standard is partly built from the index test.

Index findings and reference diagnosis come from the same admission, so timing is not a concern, but 203 of 2,222 admissions (9%) are missing from Table 1a and Table 2 without explanation, and Tables 1b and 1c cover all 2,222.

Overdose admissions to a toxicology unit, with the rules derived in single-SSRI overdoses; not people taking a prescribed dose, not emergency or psychiatric settings, and not the drug combinations (MAOI plus MDMA, MAOI plus an opioid) behind the most severe cases.
The seven findings are bedside signs any clinician can look for, although clonus and reflexes depend on the examiner’s skill, and here they were read from a record.
The reference defines what this unit calls clinically significant serotonin toxicity; whether other clinicians would draw the line in the same place is not tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Patient selection is sound, but the index test and the reference standard are both high risk: the rules are fitted to and scored on overlapping data, and the reference diagnosis is the same unit’s judgment on much the same findings, so the stated sensitivity and specificity are likely to be higher than an independent test would give. Flow is unclear because 9% of admissions are missing from the main table. The source may be cited for the rules as the authors wrote them, for how often a toxicology unit’s toxicologists diagnosed serotonin toxicity in single-SSRI overdose (15.4%), and for which signs went with that diagnosis in this unit. It may not be cited for the accuracy of the rules outside this unit, for the rules being better than Sternbach’s criteria without that caveat, or for how common or how dangerous any drug combination is.

key_findings.finding: The data come from the Hunter Area Toxicology Service, a regional unit serving about 350,000 people and taking tertiary referrals from a further 150,000. All overdose presentations and admissions are entered prospectively into a clinical database from a preformatted admission sheet, by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses being tested.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 9,960 admissions to the unit between 13 January 1987 and 22 November 2002, 2,222 involved at least one serotonergic drug taken in overdose; this is the test set. It includes the single-SSRI admissions used to derive the rules.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph (p. 637); Methods › Test dataset and Results, 1st paragraph (p. 638)

key_findings.finding: Derivation set: 473 admissions with a single SSRI taken, after excluding 9 with two SSRIs and any with a tricyclic antidepressant, MAOI, venlafaxine, nefazodone, lithium or an anti-serotonergic drug taken at the same time. Of the 473, 73 (15.4%, 95% CI 12.3 to 19.0) were diagnosed with serotonin toxicity by a toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 11.7 to 18.4) met Sternbach’s criteria and 44 (9.3%, 6.8 to 12.3) were given a 5-HT2A antagonist.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Derivation dataset; Results › SSRI-alone overdoses

key_findings.finding: In the derivation set, 22 categorical variables and age went with the toxicologist’s diagnosis at the 5% level, among them spontaneous, inducible and ocular clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, shivering, diarrhoea, delirium, mydriasis and peripheral hypertonicity (most with p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Univariate analysis of SSRI-alone overdoses
key_findings.note: Editors’ count of the 22 from the list in the text; no correction for multiple testing.

key_findings.finding: The classification-tree analysis kept spontaneous, inducible and ocular clonus, agitation, diaphoresis, tremor and hyperreflexia. Rule 5 (hypertonia with a temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus) was added by the authors although the analysis did not select it, because clonus and hyperreflexia are often not demonstrable in severe rigidity; the life-threatening cases were not in the learning set, because the authors say they occur with combinations of serotonergic drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Decision rules, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the presence of a serotonergic agent the rules say yes if: (1) spontaneous clonus; (2) inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (3) ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; (4) tremor with hyperreflexia; or (5) hypertonia with a temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus; otherwise no.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Hunter rules against the toxicologist’s diagnosis: not diagnosed and not flagged 1,785; not diagnosed but flagged 62; diagnosed but not flagged 27; diagnosed and flagged 145 (172 diagnosed, 1,847 not diagnosed, 207 flagged, 2,019 in the table). Printed sensitivity 84% and specificity 97%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1a
key_findings.note: The table covers 2,019 of the 2,222 admissions; the 203 missing are not explained.

key_findings.finding: Editors’ calculation from Table 1a (Wilson 95% intervals): sensitivity 84.3% (78.1 to 89.0); specificity 96.6% (95.7 to 97.4); positive predictive value 145/207 = 70.0% (63.5 to 75.9); negative predictive value 1,785/1,812 = 98.5% (97.8 to 99.0); share diagnosed 172/2,019 = 8.5%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1a (calculated by the editors; the paper gives no intervals)
key_findings.note: Editors’ calculation.

key_findings.finding: Hunter rules against Sternbach’s criteria as the reference: 1,951, 67, 64, 140 (2,018 not meeting and 204 meeting Sternbach’s criteria); printed sensitivity 69% and specificity 97%. Against treatment with a 5-HT2A antagonist: 1,991, 124, 24, 83 (2,115 not treated, 107 treated); printed 78% and 94%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1b and Table 1c
key_findings.note: The printed grand total of Table 1b is 222; the cells and margins sum to 2,222.

key_findings.finding: Sternbach’s criteria against the toxicologist’s diagnosis in the same records: not diagnosed and not flagged 1,772; not diagnosed but flagged 75; diagnosed but not flagged 43; diagnosed and flagged 129. Printed sensitivity 75% and specificity 96%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: The printed column totals (1,833 and 186) do not match the cells (1,815 and 204); the printed sensitivity and specificity match the cells.

key_findings.finding: People intubated and ventilated after an overdose of a serotonergic drug: 42 for reduced consciousness or for decontamination and 6 solely for worsening serotonin toxicity. All 6 had a high fever (above 38.5 °C) and several features of serotonin toxicity; progressive rigidity that compromised breathing was what prompted intervention, preceded by high fever and increasing, particularly truncal, rigidity and peripheral hypertonicity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Life-threatening serotonin toxicity
key_findings.note: Editors’ sum: 48 intubated in all. 6 of 2,222 is 0.27% (editors’ calculation).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the approach was arbitrary because there is no gold standard for clinically significant serotonin toxicity and it is a spectrum, so they used the toxicologist’s diagnosis as the standard and compared it with Sternbach’s criteria and with treatment.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (continues in the right-hand column, from the words The arbitrary approach taken)

key_findings.finding: Clonus (spontaneous, inducible and ocular) is called the most important sign in the criteria; all three types were common and went with all three reference outcomes in the single-SSRI overdoses (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Clonus (spontaneous, inducible and ocular)

key_findings.finding: Rigidity did not occur in any of the 473 single-SSRI admissions. Hypertonicity and rigidity were included because of their frequent occurrence in life-threatening cases in the literature and in the six people in the full dataset, and were made a required part of rule 5.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Rigidity did not occur

key_findings.finding: Mydriasis (31.6% of people) and tachycardia (40%) were common, but both also occur with anticholinergic and other kinds of drug toxicity, so the authors call them poor at telling serotonin excess apart from other poisonings.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Although mydriasis occurred commonly (top of the left-hand column)

key_findings.finding: From their unit’s experience the authors state that a temperature at or above 38.5 °C, or marked hypertonia or rigidity (particularly truncal), indicated severe serotonin toxicity with a high risk of progression to respiratory compromise.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning In our clinical practice

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the rules need validating in other settings, including other toxicology centres, emergency departments and psychiatric units, and studied prospectively in people taking toxic and therapeutic amounts of serotonergic drugs.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, last paragraph (beginning The decision rules will need to be validated)

key_findings.finding: The Introduction treats serotonin excess as a spectrum of toxicity rather than a defined syndrome with a clear prognosis, concentration-dependent and able to develop in anyone rather than an idiosyncratic reaction, and as a triad of autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Serotonin excess is best thought of as a spectrum

key_findings.finding: Sternbach’s criteria (1991) are three or more of ten listed features (mental status changes, agitation, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, shivering, tremor, diarrhoea, incoordination, fever) with a recent addition or increase of a serotonergic agent, other causes excluded and no recent neuroleptic. The authors object that four of the ten are mental-status features, so that someone with an anticholinergic delirium could meet them.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1; Introduction, paragraphs beginning Central nervous system (CNS) serotonin excess and A significant problem with Sternbach’s criteria

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states that the combination of an MAOI with a drug that blocks serotonin reuptake, such as an SSRI, is the most important interaction and can cause life-threatening serotonin toxicity (two references: a paper then in press from the same group on moclobemide poisoning, and a case report of one fatal overdose of moclobemide with clomipramine and fluoxetine), and that serotonin toxicity occurs in 16% of people taking SSRIs in overdose (an earlier abstract from the same unit).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, paragraph beginning Many cases of serotonin toxicity occur
key_findings.note: A statement supported by references, not by data in this paper. The paper’s own count is 15.4% of 473 (p. 638).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1a covers 2,019 admissions, but the test set is 2,222 and Tables 1b and 1c total 2,222 (2,015 predicted no and 207 predicted yes). All 203 admissions missing from Table 1a are among those the rules did not flag; the text does not say why they are absent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline 84% and 97% rest on 2,019 admissions (91%); if the 203 have no toxicologist’s diagnosis recorded they cannot be scored, but the paper does not say, and any of them diagnosed but missed would lower sensitivity.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed grand total of Table 1b is 222, not 2,222.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical error; the cells and the row and column totals sum to 2,222.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the printed column totals are 1,833 and 186, but the cells sum to 1,815 (1,772 + 43) and 204 (75 + 129). The 204 matches the Sternbach-positive row total in Table 1b, and the printed 75% and 96% match the cells.
reporting_issues.consequence: The totals are probably wrong and the cells right; the positive predictive value of Sternbach’s criteria is 63.2% from the cells and 69.4% from the printed total (editors’ calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The test set includes all 473 derivation admissions (stated in the Introduction and in Methods), and the paper gives no accuracy for the rules in the admissions outside the derivation set; cross-validation is mentioned only for choosing the tree, and rule 5 was added by hand after it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sensitivity and specificity are likely to be higher than they would be in admissions the rules had not been fitted to.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference standard is the unit’s own toxicologist’s diagnosis, which the authors call arbitrary and describe as the best available because there is no gold standard; the rules were built to predict it and use findings that the diagnosis itself rests on.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison with Sternbach’s criteria favours the rules, since only the rules were built to match this reference; sensitivity and specificity measure agreement with this unit’s judgment, not accuracy against a proven condition.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says hypertonicity and a maximum temperature above 38 °C were universal in life-threatening cases (p. 635); the Results say they were prominent (p. 640); the temperature is above 38 °C in rule 5, above 38.5 °C for the six intubated people, and at or above 38.5 °C in the Discussion (p. 641). The six people are those intubated solely for worsening toxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: Universal rests on six people picked out by the same unit; the thresholds differ between sections, and later reviews (Boyer and Shannon 2005, Buckley 2014) give yet other forms.

reporting_issues.issue: No confidence intervals are given for any sensitivity or specificity, and no test is given for the difference from Sternbach’s criteria (84% against 75%; 97% against 96%), although intervals are given for the three rates in the derivation set.
reporting_issues.consequence: The editors’ sensitivity intervals for the two sets of criteria (78.1 to 89.0 and 68.0 to 80.9) overlap and the specificity intervals (95.7 to 97.4 and 94.9 to 96.7) overlap almost entirely; because the same people are scored by both, the right comparison is a paired one, which needs the cross-tabulation of the two sets of predictions (not given). Whether the rules are more sensitive or more specific than Sternbach’s criteria is therefore not tested in the paper.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 635–642 (full text: summary, introduction, Methods, Results, Figures 1 and 2, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion, acknowledgments, reference list); the tables and paragraph breaks were checked against page renders. The earlier papers cited (Sternbach 1991; Isbister and colleagues, in press in 2003; Whyte and Dawson 2002) were not read.

design_detail: Review article in the British Journal of Anaesthesia (advance access 28 July 2005; eight pages, 84 references) by a single author at a private hospital in Queensland, Australia (his specialty is not stated in the paper). The aim is to clarify interactions between monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and opioid analgesics using recent data on serotonin toxicity, its clinical features and each drug’s strength as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SRI) in laboratory assays. One sentence describes the search for opioid-related reports (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, about 40 reports, listed on the author’s website). Tables 1 to 3 are reproduced from the author’s own website document (reference 29). The treatment section gives doses, which this card does not record.
can_establish: How one author reads the old and recent literature on pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan, fentanyl and other opioids taken with MAOIs, in light of each drug’s strength as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor in laboratory assays and of which opioids have and have not been reported in cases, and what a 1968 hospital test of pethidine in 15 patients did and did not look for.
cannot_establish: How often any opioid taken with an MAOI causes serotonin toxicity or death (no rate is given, and the author says the basis for an accurate estimate is insufficient); whether the individual reports he counts were serotonin toxicity (he judges many by a subjective reading of old descriptions); whether opioids with no reports are safe, since absence of reports is the main evidence for them; or whether laboratory transporter binding predicts risk in people.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The case evidence is about 40 reports of serotonin toxicity with opioid analgesics found by a search of the listed papers and standard databases and listed on the author’s website, outside the paper; the paper cites a few by reference number. The Hunter Area Toxicology Service’s more than 2,000 overdose cases are cited for the diagnostic rules.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond the one-sentence description of the search (p. 437).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Case reports mostly from the 1950s to the 1970s, written before serotonin toxicity was defined and re-read by the author by a subjective interpretation (p. 437); reports exist because something happened, so the many uneventful uses are unseen (the author says this of fentanyl); the transporter-binding figures come from several sources, species and methods that the author says cannot be compared directly (Table 2 caption).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Exposure is as reported in the cited case reports (not read individually); drug potency is in-vitro binding to the serotonin transporter (Ki in nanomolar; a lower value is a stronger reuptake inhibitor) from the sources cited in Table 2, mostly Codd and colleagues.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the causes. Study conditions only: in the 1968 test the author describes, graded injections of pethidine up to a maximum single dose of 75 mg and morphine up to 7.5 mg were given to 15 patients. Treatment doses are in the paper and are not recorded here.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. The review concerns MAOIs (irreversible, non-selective, or the reversible moclobemide) taken with opioids, serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin releasers; the reports it counts often involved anaesthesia and other drugs, which the paper does not itemise.

comparison.controls: The review compares opioids by their strength as serotonin reuptake inhibitors in laboratory assays and by whether cases have been reported. The only controlled human data are the 1968 test of pethidine, morphine and water in 15 patients (p. 437).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Serotonin toxicity as the author reads it from report descriptions, using the triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity, autonomic hyperactivity and altered mental status and the Hunter decision rules; serotonin transporter binding (Ki).
outcomes.validity_norms: The author states that binding affinities below 1 nM are invariably associated with the ability to precipitate toxicity with MAOIs and that 1 to 10 nM is borderline (p. 436); the phenylpiperidine opioids with values in Table 2 lie above that range (14.1 to 760 nM) and are called weak or borderline (p. 437), and morphine, codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone lie above 100,000 nM.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed. The reports with MAOIs column of Table 2 rates each drug as definite, possible, uncertain or none, with no stated criteria.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new analysis and no rates. Table 2 (p. 436), serotonin transporter binding in nM (lower is stronger) and reports with MAOIs: SSRIs 0.13 to 2.2, definite, frequent fatalities; clomipramine 0.14, definite, frequent fatalities; imipramine 1.3, definite, occasional fatalities; amitriptyline 4.3, none; venlafaxine 8, definite, fatalities; morphine 500,000 and over 100,000, none; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone over 100,000, none; tramadol 760 and 528, definite, possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413, definite, some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain (one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death reported); remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known but unlikely. The 1968 test (p. 437): 15 patients, none had serotonergic symptoms at a maximum single pethidine dose of 75 mg; reflexes and clonus were not examined. The Treatment section (p. 438) repeats that serotonin toxicity needing admission occurred in 15% of SSRI overdoses and that more than 50% of MAOI or reversible-MAOI plus SRI overdoses had severe toxicity (reference 38, not read).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: The case list behind the table (about 40 reports) is on the author’s website and not in the paper, so the basis for each definite or possible cannot be checked from the paper. The abstract, the discussion of the phenylpiperidine opioids (p. 437) and the conclusion (p. 439) place methadone among opioids involved in or able to cause toxicity with MAOIs, while Table 2 says no reports are known for it; the Table 1 caption names fatalities only with pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and possibly fentanyl, while the abstract says pethidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and propoxyphene have all been involved in reactions with MAOIs including some fatalities.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A single author’s reading of the opioid literature: morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine have no reports and are not serotonin reuptake inhibitors; pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan are weak reuptake inhibitors with reports of serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, some fatal; fentanyl is uncertain (one case, one possible death); methadone is a weak reuptake inhibitor with no reports known. He judges the risk with known serotonergic opioids to be probably low but unpredictable, and says there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate for fentanyl.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says pethidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and propoxyphene “have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities)” and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine “do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs” (p. 434); the conclusion says the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low (p. 439).
