Gaps: (1) Table 2 says no reports are known for methadone and the Table 1 caption names fatalities with pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and possibly fentanyl, against the abstract’s all and some fatalities; (2) the statement for the morphine-type drugs rests on absence of reports and on binding assays, not on tests in people taking MAOIs; (3) the case list is on the author’s website, and old reports, written before serotonin toxicity was defined, are judged by a subjective interpretation; (4) the 1968 test, which found no toxicity and did not look for clonus or reflexes, is read as confirming the spectrum concept; (5) probably low has no denominator.

timeline.event: Evans-Prosser: graded injections of pethidine or morphine or water in 15 patients, none with serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus not examined (as described in this review; not read).

Codd and colleagues: serotonin and noradrenaline uptake inhibition by centrally acting analgesics, the only published screen of several opioids by one method (reference 10, as described in this review; not read).
Vuori and colleagues: four deaths with MDMA and moclobemide in Finland, cited in this review as a recent case series (the paper read for this library).
This review.

Buckley and colleagues cite this review among six reviews of case reports for the statement that nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI; they list pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan as opioids associated with toxicity (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: A single-author review whose opioid conclusions are repeated by Buckley and colleagues (2014), who cite it, so the two are not independent evidence. No newer review specific to opioids with MAOIs was read for this library, and the case reports and the 1968 test are known here only as this review describes them.

funding.funder: No funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared; no conflict-of-interest statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author at Pioneer Valley Private Hospital, Mackay, Queensland (p. 434). The acknowledgements thank his wife for maintaining the computers and programs used (p. 439). Tables 1 to 3 and the case list come from the author’s own website document (reference 29). Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic search of case reports and pharmacovigilance reports for each opioid taken with an MAOI, with stated search terms and dates and each report assessed against the Hunter criteria by two readers; prospective data from people taking MAOIs who are given measured opioid exposures and examined for clonus and reflexes; and denominators for how many people took each pair, so that a rate can be stated.

domains.note: One sentence (a search of the listed papers and standard databases, about 40 reports) with no terms, dates or criteria; the case list is on the author’s website, outside the paper.

The 1968 test is appraised (reflexes and clonus not examined) and old reports are read against the modern definition, but individual fatality reports are not appraised, and the references given for fatalities include a rabbit study (reference 31) and a paper whose title concerns malignant hyperthermia with hypocalcaemia (reference 60), judged by their titles.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 12 of 84 references (18 to 29) are the author’s own; Tables 1 to 3 and the case list come from his own website document (reference 29); the spectrum concept and the reading of old reports rest on his 1998 review (reference 20).

Much is hedged (in my opinion, almost certainly, might possibly), but the abstract and conclusion state as known that the morphine-type drugs do not precipitate toxicity, on absence of reports, and that the 1968 test confirms the spectrum concept.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against serious reactions with opioids taken with MAOIs
domains.note: The null 1968 test and the uneventful uses of fentanyl are set against the case reports, and earlier reviews that called fentanyl safe are mentioned; but the argument that risk is probably low rests on reports the reader cannot see and gives no denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. The search is a single sentence, the case list is outside the paper, and a seventh of the references and the source of the tables are the author’s own. It may be cited for how one specialist reads the opioid and MAOI literature in 2005, for which opioids have and have not been reported with MAOIs in his judgment, and for what the 1968 test did and did not examine. It may not be cited for a rate of serious reactions, for any opioid being safe with an MAOI, or for the number or nature of the underlying fatalities.

key_findings.finding: The abstract states that serotonin toxicity is related to the concentration of serotonin at the synapse; that SRI overdoses frequently produce marked serotonergic side-effects and, in 15% of cases, moderate toxicity but not severe toxicity with hyperthermia and risk of death; that only combinations of serotonergic drugs acting by different mechanisms can raise serotonin to a life-threatening level; and that the combination that most commonly does so is an MAOI with any SRI, with lesser-known MAOIs (linezolid, moclobemide) and serotonergic opioids able to contribute.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: The abstract states that the phenylpiperidine opioids pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan, and propoxyphene, appear to be weak serotonin reuptake inhibitors and have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities), and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be SRIs and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (last sentences)
key_findings.note: Table 2 says no reports are known for methadone; see the reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: The Introduction says there have been periodic reviews of opioid analgesics in people taking MAOIs since 1955; that the difficulty has several causes: the reuptake-inhibiting capacity of opioids is only partly documented, there was until recently a lack of systematic data on the features of serotonin toxicity, and the spectrum concept, that it is dose-related and not idiosyncratic, is recent.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, right-hand column, paragraph beginning Ever since the initial report by Oates

key_findings.finding: Serotonin toxicity is described as a spectrum of serotonergic side-effects blending into toxicity, with a dose-effect relationship, and as a triad of neuromuscular hyperactivity (tremor, clonus, myoclonus, hyperreflexia, and in advanced stages pyramidal rigidity), autonomic hyperactivity (diaphoresis, fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea) and altered mental status (agitation, excitement, and in advanced stages confusion).
key_findings.locator: Definition and description (begins at the foot of p. 434, right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: The author summarises the Hunter decision rules from the Hunter Area Toxicology Service’s more than 2,000 prospectively documented overdose cases: in the presence of a serotonergic agent, spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, allows serotonin toxicity to be reliably diagnosed. He says onset of frank toxicity is usually rapid because it follows drug combinations and starts when the second drug reaches effective blood levels, and that rigidity, a decreasing PaCO2 and a fever above 38.5 °C herald life-threatening toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Definition and description, paragraphs beginning The features that usually distinguish it and Clinically, the onset of frank toxicity (left-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, malignant hyperthermia and anticholinergic delirium are said to be distinguishable from serotonin toxicity by onset (hours against days), by the presence of clonus and hyperreflexia and by dry skin and absent hyperreflexia in anticholinergic toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Definition and description, right-hand column (paragraphs beginning A possible differential diagnosis and NMS shares similarities)

key_findings.finding: Implicated drugs: the author states that the only therapeutic drugs implicated in severe reactions capable of precipitating fatalities are MAOIs with SRIs; that illicit stimulants such as MDMA, if combined with MAOIs (including moclobemide), also cause fatalities because they act as serotonin releasers; that serotonin releasers with MAOIs are the only other combination able to cause severe, potentially fatal toxicity; that several unpublished cases of MAOI and releaser combinations are known to him; and that a case series of four deaths has been reported by Vuori.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 435 and ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 436)

key_findings.finding: Theoretically a combination of amphetamine (but not methylphenidate) with an MAOI would precipitate serotonin toxicity, but the author says this is rarely encountered in practice and no fatalities are known.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, 1st paragraph (end), left-hand column

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists drugs with clinically relevant serotonergic potency (SRIs including tramadol, pethidine, fentanyl, methadone, dextromethorphan, dextropropoxyphene and pentazocine; the releasers amphetamine and MDMA; and the MAOIs including moclobemide and linezolid); its caption says fatalities from serotonin toxicity involving analgesics have been with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and its caption

key_findings.finding: Table 2 gives serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; lower is stronger) and reports with MAOIs: tramadol 760 and 528, definite, possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413 (weak, anomalous), definite, some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain, one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death; remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known but unlikely; morphine 500,000 and over 100,000, codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone over 100,000, none.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: The two Ki columns are other references and Codd; the table caption says the figures come from different sources and species and cannot be compared directly.

key_findings.finding: The author states a strong association between SRI potency and the ability to precipitate fatalities with MAOIs: affinities below 1 nM invariably go with the ability to precipitate toxicity and 1 to 10 nM is borderline; venlafaxine and tramadol are called anomalous because their estimated potency suggests they should not be a risk (possibly because they also release serotonin); pethidine is a very weak SRI whose discrepancy might be explained by releasing properties, with no direct evidence.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Overall, there is a strong association

key_findings.finding: The author says the early drugs involved in these interactions (pethidine and imipramine) are weak SRIs and, because there is a dose-effect relationship, usually fail to produce a reaction. He describes a 1968 test (Evans-Prosser) in which 15 patients were given injections of pethidine, morphine or water in graduated doses in hospital, in blind random order, to a maximum single pethidine dose of 75 mg and morphine 7.5 mg; none had serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus were not examined, only pulse and arterial pressure. He reads this as confirming that weak SRIs like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity, but only in susceptible people or with particularly large doses.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved (begins at the foot of the right-hand column of p. 436 and continues on p. 437)

key_findings.finding: In the same paragraph the author says about 40 reports of serotonin toxicity with analgesics, found by a search of the listed papers and standard databases, are listed on his website; that pethidine has undoubtedly caused a number of severe reactions and some fatalities and the other SRI analgesics have also precipitated some fatalities; that a small series at usual therapeutic doses may give a false sense of security because the dose-effect relationship is not appreciated; and that differences in cytochrome P450 enzymes produce 20 to 50-fold variations in serum levels between patients.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, same paragraph (sentences beginning The complete list of the references and Pethidine has undoubtedly caused)

key_findings.finding: The author says the limited clinical and experimental data agree that morphine analogues are not SRIs and none precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine), with no reports; that the phenylpiperidine opioids (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl and congeners, dextromethorphan, propoxyphene) are probably all borderline weak SRIs, and have been implicated in multiple reports almost certainly of serotonin toxicity, as judged by a subjective interpretation of the old case reports.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The limited available clinical and experimental data agree

key_findings.finding: In summary all the opioid analgesics with serotonergic effects have been involved in serotonin toxicity reports, but none of the drugs without SRI capacity have been; drugs with anomalous properties, like tramadol and pethidine, may yet be shown to act as serotonin releasers.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Details of all cases involving analgesics (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl: the author judges that one case report with a fatality (Noble) was probably serotonin toxicity, that another (Roy) may represent unrecognised toxicity, and that there is a question mark over fentanyl, although its potency as an SRI is low and it has been reported used with impunity; he thinks it probable that fentanyl has been used in many unreported cases with MAOIs because there was no problem, and says there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate of the risk, which would seem so low that one could not call its use strongly contra-indicated if there is no alternative. Remifentanil has no SRI data and its safe use with an MAOI has been reported.
key_findings.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning There are a few individual case reports worthy of particular comment (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Treatment section: an overdose of an SSRI alone produces at worst moderate toxicity (in 15% of cases enough for admission and active treatment) with no serious sequelae or fatalities; if an MAOI or a reversible MAOI plus an SRI were co-ingested in overdose, more than 50% of cases had severe toxicity (reference 38, not read); even therapeutic doses of moclobemide have been associated with severe toxicity when combined with SRIs, especially venlafaxine.
key_findings.locator: Treatment, 1st paragraph (beginning Careful consideration of the need for treatment)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are said to be known not to be SRIs and not to precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs; pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and methadone are said definitely to be weak SRIs that may infrequently precipitate dose-dependent toxicity with any type of MAOI, perhaps only in large doses or susceptible people. The author says the ability to estimate risk is compromised by a lack of systematically recorded clinical data and of precise potency data, and that for propoxyphene, pentazocine, fentanyl, remifentanil and congeners there are no SRI affinity data, so interpolation and the presence or absence of reports are used.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author writes that the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low, but its unpredictable and serious nature makes it difficult to form judgments, and that any reaction is dose-dependent.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion, 2nd paragraph (beginning However, the clinical situation and the risks are now more clearly defined)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (p. 434), the discussion of the phenylpiperidine opioids (p. 437) and the conclusion (p. 439) place methadone among opioids that have been involved in, or may precipitate, serotonin toxicity with MAOIs; Table 2 says no reports are known for methadone, but unlikely.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not agree with itself on whether methadone has been reported with MAOIs; the table row, which is the more specific, says it has not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says pethidine, tramadol, methadone, dextromethorphan and propoxyphene have all been involved in reactions with MAOIs including some fatalities; the Table 1 caption names fatalities only with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl; Table 2 lists fatalities only for pethidine (some) and tramadol (possible).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which opioids have been linked to deaths differs between the abstract and the tables; the tables are the more specific, and none of the three gives a number.

reporting_issues.issue: Borderline potency is defined as 1 to 10 nM, but the phenylpiperidine opioids are called probably all borderline although every value in Table 2 for them is above 10 nM (methadone 14.1 and 270, dextromethorphan 23, pethidine 413, tramadol 528 and 760).
reporting_issues.consequence: By the paper’s own bands these opioids are weaker than borderline, so the transporter data do not by themselves support the prediction that they can precipitate toxicity.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1968 test found no serotonergic symptoms in 15 patients at a maximum single pethidine dose of 75 mg, without examining reflexes or clonus, yet is described as confirming the spectrum concept, that weak SRIs like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity in susceptible people or with large doses.
reporting_issues.consequence: A null result that could not have detected the signs in question cannot show that the drug sometimes does precipitate toxicity; it shows only that no toxicity was recorded under those conditions.

reporting_issues.issue: The references given for fatalities with pethidine and the other SRI analgesics include a study in rabbits (reference 31) and a paper whose title concerns malignant hyperthermia associated with hypocalcaemia (reference 60), judged by their titles in the printed reference list; the cases are mostly from 1955 to 1971.
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of human fatalities cannot be checked from the paper; some of the cited items may not be case reports of serotonin toxicity (the cited papers were not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The search is described in one sentence, and the list of about 40 reports, Tables 1 to 3 and the updated review are on the author’s website (reference 29), outside the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence behind each definite, possible or no reports entry is not in the paper and cannot be checked from it.

reporting_issues.issue: The Hunter rules are described as demonstrating clearly that serotonin toxicity may be reliably diagnosed on the stated findings, without the source paper’s caveats that its reference diagnosis was the same unit’s and that the rules need validating elsewhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: Reliably is stronger than the source supports (see the card for Dunkley and colleagues, 2003).

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 434–441 (full text: abstract, introduction, Definition and description, Implicated drugs, Tables 1 and 2 (checked against a page render), Treatment, Conclusion, acknowledgements, reference list). The treatment doses and Table 3 were read for context only and are not recorded. The cited primary sources, the 1968 paper, the author’s website list and reference 38 were not read.

design_detail: Review article in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry (received 4 March 2007, accepted 24 April 2007; seven printed pages, 87 references) by three authors at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales, Sydney. It calls itself a qualitative review. Aim: to bring together what is known about serotonin syndrome when ecstasy (MDMA) is taken with other serotonergic substances, as a hierarchy of risk for psychiatrists and other doctors. Method (p. 650): a search of Embase, CINAHL, Medline and PubMed and of grey literature to 2006, with the search terms listed in part (a minority taken from ecstasy-related websites); substances were placed in a less, intermediate or high risk group by the proportion of agreement between studies; no comment was made on the quality of any study; national medical and pharmacological experts were consulted when appropriate. No inclusion criteria and no count of records found or used are given. Table 1 (p. 651) sets out the hierarchy. The text cites narrative reviews, case reports, animal studies and surveys.
can_establish: How three authors at a drug research centre grouped serotonergic substances by the risk of serotonin syndrome when taken with ecstasy in 2007; which of the grouped substances have reported human cases (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, phenelzine, from 1987, and a handful of deaths with moclobemide) and which rest on mechanism or animal studies; and what an Australian survey of people who use ecstasy found about deliberate combining with moclobemide and antidepressants, as the review reports it.
cannot_establish: How often any mix causes serotonin syndrome or death (no rates, counts or denominators); that the order of the hierarchy is the order of risk in people, because the groups are the authors’ judgment from an unreported tally with no appraisal; that mixes in the less-risk group are safe (the review says only less likely to produce life-threatening serotonin levels); or anything about the amounts, strengths or timing at which a mix becomes dangerous.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Records from four databases and grey literature to 2006; how many were found or used is not stated. The human evidence cited for the high-risk group is one case series of four deaths (reference 17, Vuori and colleagues, 2003), two older case reports (references 22 and 52) and a survey source (references 54 and 55) by two of the review’s authors; one animal study (reference 53) is cited as further evidence.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated. Search terms ‘included, but were not limited to’ those listed; a minority came from ecstasy-related websites (p. 650).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Cases of serotonin syndrome and death with ecstasy are published because of what happened, and the authors say less serious cases are not usually published, so the extent of non-fatal harm is hard to estimate (p. 652); the groups follow the proportion of agreement between studies with no weighting for design; sources include animal studies, narrative reviews and website posts.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Exposure is as reported in the cited sources, of which only the Vuori case series and three reviews were read for this library; the survey figures (about one in 25 people deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide) are self-reports, cited from a technical report by two of the review’s authors.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. The review gives no doses as findings. It says high doses or repeated use of ecstasy and its analogues intensify serotonin release (reference 40, not read) and gives an 80% loss of brain serotonin within four hours of intravenous use (reference 16, species not stated).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable; the review is about combinations. It says people who use ecstasy tend to use other illicit drugs with serotonergic potency on the same occasions, with alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine frequently combined with ecstasy (p. 652, references 77 and 84 to 87).

comparison.controls: No comparison group. The hierarchy ranks groups of substances against each other by the authors’ reading of the literature; two volunteer studies of ecstasy with citalopram (references 32 and 33, effects of ecstasy reduced) are cited in the less-risk section.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Serotonin syndrome as defined in the cited sources. The review cites the Hunter criteria (reference 24) for the description of signs but states no criteria for deciding which reports in the grouped studies were serotonin syndrome; its discussion refers to case reports that fit the diagnostic criteria for the syndrome (p. 652).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Four groups in Table 1: less risk, intermediate risk, high risk and unknown risk. The first three are said to follow the proportion of agreement between studies (p. 650); no thresholds or counts are given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Table 1 (p. 651, checked on a page render): less risk, SSRIs (citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants (clomipramine, imipramine), opioid analgesics (tramadol, dextromethorphan) and antihistamines (chlorpheniramine, brompheniramine), grouped as serotonin reuptake inhibitors; intermediate risk, amphetamine (dexamphetamine, and ‘ethylphenidate’ as printed), amphetamine derivatives (methamphetamine) and cocaine, grouped as serotonin releasers, and 5-HTP and L-tryptophan, grouped as serotonin precursors; high risk, MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, nialamide, isoniazid, clorgyline) and RIMAs (moclobemide), grouped as inhibitors of serotonin metabolism; unknown risk, Saint John’s wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs (dihydroergotamine, bromocriptine) and lithium. Figures in the text: about one in 25 people in a recent Australian study (reference 54) reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide, no denominator given; cases with phenelzine reported from 1987; a handful of documented cases with fatalities for moclobemide (reference 17); susceptibility to an interaction up to 2 weeks after stopping a long-acting MAOI (references 26 and 28).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: The groups depend on the proportion of agreement between studies, which cannot be reconstructed: no table links studies to groups, and the number of records is not given. Some placements rest on mechanism and are worded in theory or is expected (5-HTP, L-tryptophan), and Table 1 does not show which entries rest on cases and which on theory.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative grouping of serotonergic substances by risk of serotonin syndrome when taken with ecstasy, built from reviews, a few case reports, animal studies and surveys. The high-risk group (MAOIs and moclobemide) rests on one case series of four deaths, two older case reports, one animal study and mechanism; the less-risk group on a mechanism argument, animal studies and two volunteer studies in which ecstasy’s effects were reduced by citalopram; the intermediate group mostly on mechanism, with 5-HTP placed there although the review says no human cases have been reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake are less likely to lead to life-threatening elevations in serotonin when taken with ecstasy, that inhibitors of monoamine oxidase are ‘most likely to lead to serious increases’ (p. 649), and that findings highlight the importance of screening for ecstasy and other serotonergic substances when prescribing antidepressants (p. 649). Gaps: (1) the order of the groups is a judgment from an unreported tally; (2) the less-risk statement cites a review that does not address ecstasy with reuptake inhibitors, and the volunteer studies measured ecstasy’s effects, not toxicity; (3) the high-risk group’s human evidence is four deaths in one report and two older case reports; (4) the screening recommendation is not a finding of the review.

timeline.event: Smilkstein and colleagues: a case of an MAOI taken with MDMA (reference 22 of this review, as cited; not read).
Kaskey: a possible interaction between an MAOI and ecstasy (reference 52, as cited; not read).
Vuori and colleagues: four deaths with MDMA and moclobemide in Finland, the review’s source for deaths with moclobemide (reference 17).
Gillman: review of MAOIs and opioids that names MDMA as a serotonin releaser that causes fatalities with MAOIs, including moclobemide (reference 26).
This review.
Buckley and colleagues state that serotonin-releasing agents might even attenuate the toxicity of an SSRI, citing one of the same volunteer studies of citalopram with MDMA (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source. Its statements about MAOIs and moclobemide trace to one case series read for this library (Vuori and colleagues, 2003) and to Gillman (2005), also read; its less-risk statements trace to reviews and volunteer studies not read, and the later review by Buckley and colleagues (2014) rests on one of the same volunteer studies, so the two are not independent. No newer systematic review of ecstasy taken with each class of serotonergic medicine was read for this library.

funding.funder: The paper originated from a study funded by the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing (p. 653).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed in the pages read.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales, Sydney (p. 649). Two of them (Copeland and Dillon) are authors of references 54 and 55, the source of the one-in-25 figure and of the self-reported effects. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with stated criteria, a count of records and two-reader appraisal for each combination of ecstasy with a class of serotonergic medicine, with each case report checked against the Hunter criteria; poison-centre and emergency-department data with the number of exposures, so that a rate can be stated; and controlled human data for the pairs where only mechanism or animal studies exist.

domains.note: Databases, years and part of the search terms are given (a minority of terms from ecstasy-related websites), but there are no inclusion criteria, no number of records found or used, and the grouping rule (proportion of agreement between studies) is not shown.
The Method says comment on the quality of each study was not made, so reviews, case reports, animal studies and surveys are used side by side.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Two of the three authors wrote references 54 and 55, the source of the one-in-25 figure and the self-reported effects (reference 54 is a technical report from their centre); one wrote reference 87. The other references are by other groups.
Hedged wording is common (likely, expected, in theory) and some placements are said to rest on mechanism, but Table 1 does not show which entries rest on reports of people and which on theory.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the grouping
domains.note: Null and limiting evidence is stated (no reported human case of serotonin syndrome with 5-HTP; low fatality incidence against use; non-fatal harm hard to estimate), but disagreements between cited sources are not discussed (methylphenidate; tramadol and venlafaxine).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. The search is partly described, but no group can be traced to a count of studies, no study was appraised, and the strongest statements (the high-risk group) rest on one case series, two older case reports, one animal study and reviews. It may be cited for how three authors grouped serotonergic substances by risk with ecstasy in 2007, and for the cases and surveys it points to. It may not be cited for the order of risk as established, for how often any combination causes harm, or for any combination being safe.

key_findings.finding: The abstract gives the aim as bringing together the risk of serotonin syndrome from taking ecstasy with other serotonergic substances into a hierarchy for doctors, from an extensive online database search. Findings: substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake are less likely to lead to life-threatening elevations in serotonin when taken with ecstasy; high doses or repeated use of stimulants such as methamphetamine and cocaine with ecstasy increase the risk, as does pharmaceutical amphetamine with ecstasy; serotonin precursors also influence the course; and substances that inhibit monoamine oxidase are most likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin with ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: Serotonin syndrome is described as a drug-induced toxic state from excess serotonin in the central nervous system, with autonomic signs, neuromuscular changes and altered mental status (references 23 and 24), most likely to appear with rapid onset, usually within 24 hours of introducing a serotonergic substance (reference 25).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, left-hand column, paragraph beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state

key_findings.finding: The review says people with serotonin syndrome from illicit drugs such as ecstasy usually reach emergency departments with more advanced symptoms, because some early mild signs are generally seen by many people who use ecstasy as part of normal drug effects (reference 20, Parrott 2002).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, same paragraph (beginning Serotonin syndrome is a drug-induced toxic state)
key_findings.note: A statement with no data in the review; the source cited was not read.

key_findings.finding: The typical picture is agitation or hypervigilance with tremor and exaggerated reflexes; muscle spasms start in the lower limbs and become generalised as toxicity increases; fever, sweating, dilated pupils, fast heart rate and fast breathing become more evident as the syndrome progresses; fixed rigidity develops in severe cases and can impair breathing and raise carbon dioxide; confusion, rigidity and a body temperature above 38.5 °C are said to indicate life-threatening toxicity (references 24 and 26).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, left-hand column, paragraph beginning Typically, the serotonin-toxic person
key_findings.note: The text extraction drops the greater-than sign before 38.5; the printed page image shows it.

key_findings.finding: Method: a review of peer-reviewed and grey literature up to 2006, searching Embase, CINAHL, Medline and PubMed with search terms that included, but were not limited to, those listed; a minority of terms came from ecstasy-related websites; substances were placed in a less, intermediate or high risk group according to the proportion of agreement between studies; comment on the methodological quality of each study was not made; national medical and pharmacological experts were consulted when appropriate.
key_findings.locator: Method, single paragraph (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Numerous substances are said to have been implicated in serotonin syndrome, including several illicit drugs, antidepressants, opioid analgesics, migraine medication and herbal products (references 23 and 27 to 30); when taken with ecstasy they are said to have a potential for increased toxicity and are arranged in the hierarchy of Table 1.
key_findings.locator: Results, Hierarchy of risk, paragraph beginning Numerous substances have been implicated

key_findings.finding: Table 1 groups, for use with ecstasy: less risk (SSRIs, venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, the opioid analgesics tramadol and dextromethorphan, and antihistamines, all labelled serotonin reuptake inhibitors); intermediate risk (amphetamine and its derivatives and cocaine, labelled serotonin releasers; 5-HTP and L-tryptophan, labelled serotonin precursors); high risk (MAOIs and the RIMA moclobemide, labelled inhibitors of serotonin metabolism); and unknown risk (Saint John’s wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs and lithium).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Substances that inhibit serotonin reuptake (SSRIs, venlafaxine, tricyclic antidepressants, tramadol and dextromethorphan, and antihistamines) are said not to be likely to raise serotonin to life-threatening levels when taken with ecstasy (references 23, 26 and 31), because they compete with MDMA at the serotonin receptor site and so lessen its effects (references 23 and 31).
key_findings.locator: Results, Less risk, 1st paragraph (beginning Substances that inhibit serotonin re-uptake are not likely)
key_findings.note: Reuptake inhibitors act at the serotonin transporter, not a receptor; the wording is loose. See the reporting issues for what the cited sources address.

key_findings.finding: Controlled studies are said to find that the physiological and subjective effects of ecstasy are substantially reduced in participants given citalopram (references 32 and 33); animal experiments are said to show that some SSRIs block MDMA-induced serotonin release (references 31 and 34 to 36), and some animal evidence that some SSRIs may protect against long-lasting neurotoxic effects of MDMA (references 36 to 38); whether this holds in people is said to be yet to be determined.
key_findings.locator: Results, Less risk, 2nd paragraph (beginning Controlled studies have found)

key_findings.finding: Bupropion is said to be devoid of clinically significant serotonergic effects (reference 39), so that taking it with ecstasy is unlikely to increase the risk of serotonin syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Results, Less risk, 3rd paragraph (beginning Bupropion, initially used; it ends at the top of the left-hand column of p. 651)

key_findings.finding: Intermediate risk: because severity depends on the type and quantity of the substance (reference 23), ecstasy, a potent releaser of serotonin, with other releasers or precursors is said to be likely to carry a greater risk of serious serotonin syndrome; high doses or repeated use of ecstasy and its analogues intensify serotonin release (reference 40); serious serotonergic symptoms are said to have been reported more often when ecstasy is taken with amphetamine and cocaine (reference 41, an emergency-department study by its title; not read).
key_findings.locator: Intermediate risk, 1st paragraph (beginning Because the severity of serotonin syndrome depends), left-hand column

key_findings.finding: Dexamphetamine and methylphenidate (Table 1 prints ethylphenidate) are said to be relatively potent serotonin releasers with some reuptake inhibition (references 29 and 42), as is methamphetamine; amphetamine and MDMA are said to have clinically relevant serotonergic potency, and taking them together is said to be likely to raise the risk (reference 43); cocaine is described as a serotonin releaser that may strongly influence the course of serotonin syndrome, possibly more so with ecstasy (references 25, 28 and 43).
key_findings.locator: Intermediate risk, paragraphs beginning The pharmaceutical stimulants dexamphetamine and The illicit drug cocaine, left-hand column

key_findings.finding: 5-HTP: a review is cited as finding no reported human cases of serotonin syndrome from 5-HTP (reference 49, by its title a review of fibromyalgia and the serotonin pathway; not read), with deaths from overdose in animals (reference 50, dogs by its title); the review says 5-HTP has shown serotonergic potency and that its use with ecstasy is in theory likely to precipitate the syndrome. L-tryptophan is said to have shown serotonergic potency and the risk to be likely to rise if it is combined with ecstasy, especially if taken beforehand (references 23, 28, 30 and 51).
key_findings.locator: Intermediate risk, paragraphs beginning The serotonin precursor 5-hydroxy tryptophan and The serotonin precursor L-tryptophan, right-hand column

key_findings.finding: High risk: taking ecstasy with MAOI antidepressants (phenelzine, tranylcypromine), other MAOIs (nialamide, isoniazid, clorgyline) or the RIMA moclobemide is said to be likely to lead to serious increases in serotonin (references 17 and 26), because these drugs reduce or prevent the enzyme that breaks down serotonin and other neurotransmitters.
key_findings.locator: High risk, 1st paragraph (beginning The use of ecstasy with MAOI antidepressants), right-hand column

key_findings.finding: Cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy with phenelzine are said to have been reported as early as 1987 (references 22 and 52); ecstasy with moclobemide is said to be able to give rise to fatalities, with a handful of cases documented (reference 17, the Vuori case series read for this library: four deaths); further evidence that moclobemide raises the likelihood of severe serotonin syndrome with ecstasy is said to come from animal studies (reference 53).
key_findings.locator: High risk, 2nd paragraph (beginning Cases of serotonin syndrome from ecstasy interactions with phenelezine; it continues at the top of the left-hand column of p. 652)

key_findings.finding: The long half-life of some MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) is said to mean that a person could still be susceptible to interactions with ecstasy up to 2 weeks after stopping the drug class (references 26 and 28).
key_findings.locator: High risk, same paragraph (continuation at the top of the left-hand column)
key_findings.note: A text search of Gillman (2005, reference 26, read for this library) finds no mention of weeks or half-life; Ener and colleagues (reference 28) were not read. Recorded as the review’s statement, not used for a claim.

key_findings.finding: A recent Australian study of people who use ecstasy (reference 54, a technical report by two of the review’s authors) is cited as finding that about one in 25 reported deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide, which participants regarded as a way to strengthen ecstasy’s effects or ease the recovery period; the study (reference 55) also found that deliberately taking antidepressants with ecstasy went with a greater likelihood of reporting potentially serious effects such as muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and profuse sweating.
key_findings.locator: High risk, paragraph beginning In a recent Australian study (left-hand column)
key_findings.note: No sample size, recruitment method or time frame is given in the review.

key_findings.finding: Unknown risk: Saint John’s wort, LSD, anti-migraine drugs (dihydroergotamine, bromocriptine) and lithium are said to have serotonergic properties or to have been implicated in serotonin syndrome, but whether they carry clinically relevant serotonergic potency, or can cause life-threatening symptoms, is said not to be established; the anti-migraine risk is called more a theoretical concern.
key_findings.locator: Unknown risk, four paragraphs (beginning The herbal extract Saint John’s wort, Lysergic acid, Anti-migraine drugs and Relatively little is known about the mechanism of action of lithium)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the authors say only a handful of case reports of ecstasy-induced harm or death that fit the diagnostic criteria for serotonin syndrome have been described since the late 1980s (references 17 and 18); that the incidence of ecstasy-related fatalities seems low compared with the likely frequency of use (references 67 to 70) but the extent of acute non-fatal harm is harder to estimate, because less serious cases are not usually published and people in distress use a range of services; and that fatalities from serotonin syndrome with ecstasy overdose alone are relatively rare, while the potential for serious toxicity is greater when ecstasy is taken with other serotonergic drugs or substances.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (begins at the foot of the left-hand column and ends in the right-hand column, before Based on available evidence)

key_findings.finding: The review says evidence is emerging that serotonergic medicines and supplements are deliberately combined with ecstasy to get a specific effect, in some cases with serious consequences (references 17 and 55); anecdotal information from ecstasy-related websites suggests this is not uncommon (references 82 and 83); the medicines named are SSRIs, MAOIs, 5-HTP, Saint John’s wort and pharmaceutical amphetamine (references 55 and 78); and people who use ecstasy tend to use other serotonergic illicit drugs on the same occasions, with alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine frequently combined with ecstasy (references 77 and 84 to 87).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Emerging evidence that a range of serotonergic pharmaceutical drugs (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Implications: the authors say interactions between ecstasy, other illicit drugs and medicines remain largely under-researched, and that the findings highlight the importance of screening for ecstasy and other serotonergic substances when prescribing antidepressants.
key_findings.locator: Implications for intervention, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A recommendation of the authors, not a finding of the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The groups follow the proportion of agreement between studies (p. 650), but no study counts, thresholds or table linking studies to groups are given, the number of records found or used is not stated, and the text cites narrative reviews and animal studies beside case reports. The Method says the quality of each study was not commented on.
reporting_issues.consequence: The order less, intermediate, high is the authors’ judgment, and a reader cannot check it from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The high-risk group cites, for human evidence, one case series of four deaths (reference 17, read for this library), two older case reports (references 22 and 52, by their titles) and a survey source (references 54 and 55), with an animal study (reference 53) and two reviews (references 26 and 28) for mechanism; the phrase a handful of cases stands for the single cited series.
reporting_issues.consequence: The strongest statement in the review rests on a few reports with no count of how many people took the combination, so it cannot give a rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The less-risk statement cites two reviews by one author (references 23 and 26) and a rat study (reference 31). Gillman (2005, reference 26, read for this library) mentions MDMA only as a releaser taken with MAOIs and in Table 1, and does not discuss it with reuptake inhibitors. The two controlled studies cited (references 32 and 33) are said to show reduced effects of ecstasy, not reduced toxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The placement rests on a mechanism argument, animal data and volunteer studies of effects, not on reports of people who took each pair; the statement says less likely, not safe. The wording competing at the serotonin receptor site also does not name the transporter where reuptake inhibitors act.

reporting_issues.issue: Tramadol and venlafaxine are placed in the less-risk group as reuptake inhibitors that lessen ecstasy’s effects, while Gillman (2005, p. 436), cited for the group, calls both anomalous and says they may also act as serotonin releasers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The placement of these two with SSRIs rests on the reuptake argument alone; no data on either with ecstasy are cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls dexamphetamine and methylphenidate relatively potent serotonin releasers (references 29 and 42), while Table 1 prints ethylphenidate as an example of the amphetamine group and Gillman (2005, p. 436, reference 26) calls methylphenidate a weak releaser, citing the same Feinberg review (reference 42 here).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 1 has a printing error (ethylphenidate is a different drug), and the two papers describe methylphenidate differently, which the review does not mention.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that a person could remain susceptible up to 2 weeks after stopping a long-acting MAOI cites Gillman (2005) and Ener and colleagues (2003); a text search of Gillman (2005) finds no mention of weeks or half-life; Ener and colleagues were not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the 2-week figure could not be traced in the cited paper read for this library, so it is not used for a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-in-25 figure for deliberately combining ecstasy and moclobemide comes from a technical report by two of the review’s authors (reference 54) and is given with no sample size, recruitment method or time frame; the self-reported effects come from a second paper by the same authors (reference 55).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be read as how common the practice is among people who use ecstasy in general.

reporting_issues.issue: The 80% loss of brain serotonin within four hours of intravenous use is given with no species and with a pharmacology review (reference 16, not read) as the source.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader may take it as a human figure; the review does not say where it comes from.

verification.source_read: PDF (cover page plus printed pp. 649 to 655: abstract, introduction, method, results, Table 1 (checked on a page render), discussion, implications, acknowledgements and reference list). Of the 87 cited sources, four (references 17, 24, 26 and 27: Vuori, Dunkley, Gillman and Boyer) were read for this library; the others were not.

design_detail: Four fatal cases identified by the authors in Finland during 2000 and 2001, described from the history that could be obtained, a post-mortem examination and toxicology of blood and urine (with hair and tablet analysis in case 2). Each death was certified by a forensic pathologist as a combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide. The journal labels the paper a case report. How the four were found, and whether other deaths with MDMA or with other drug combinations in the same period were reviewed, is not stated.
can_establish: That MDMA and moclobemide were found together in the blood of four young people who died suddenly in one Finnish region in 2000 and 2001, none of whom had been prescribed moclobemide, with the course that bystanders and hospital staff could describe (confusion, convulsions, collapse, in one a body temperature of 43.2 °C) and with the forensic pathologists’ judgment that the combination caused each death.
cannot_establish: How often the combination causes death or serotonin toxicity (no denominator: the people who took both and lived, or all deaths involving MDMA, are not counted); whether serotonin toxicity rather than the other substances found in all four people (and, in case 2, dextromethorphan at roughly 28 to 110 times the paper’s quoted reference range) caused the deaths; what amounts were taken or why the drugs were combined; or anything about the clinical signs that define serotonin toxicity, which were not recorded.

sample.recruitment: Other: deaths identified by the authors (forensic medicine departments in Helsinki and Turku, an accident and emergency department in London and a provincial state office) as appearing to be a fatal interaction between MDMA and moclobemide; how they were found is not stated (Method, p. 365). All four were from one region (Province of Western Finland) and cases 1 and 2 occurred within a short time of each other (Discussion, p. 367).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Deaths in which MDMA and moclobemide were both found and judged by the authors to be a fatal interaction; no other criteria are stated.
sample.demographics: Case 1, woman aged 18; case 2, man aged 23, who appears to have taken several drugs and had old needle marks, whose hair held MDMA and amphetamine from the previous 1.5 to 2.5 months; case 3, man aged 18 who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years; case 4, man aged 19. For case 1 there was no evidence of mental illness or prescription medicines (p. 366). Moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the four (p. 367).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selected by outcome and by the presence of both drugs: only deaths are described, so the series shows what was found in people who died and says nothing about the many who may have taken both and did not die. The cases come from the authors’ own forensic departments in one region over two years. Almost all the information comes from post-mortem toxicology and a pathologist’s judgment, with only sparse accounts from bystanders and hospital staff.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem blood and urine toxicology (headspace gas chromatography for alcohol; thin-layer chromatographic screening of urine; quantitation of 150 drugs in blood by gas chromatography with nitrogen detection or by mass spectrometry; confirmation by mass spectrometry), hair analysis in case 2 and analysis of the recovered tablets in case 2 (both types held MDMA and no other active substance). Tablets in the other cases were not analysed in the paper: in case 3 they were named ecstasy by a friend at the scene (Method, pp. 365–366; Cases, p. 366).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known for any case; recorded only as case conditions. Case 1: an unknown quantity of street ecstasy; case 2: two kinds of white tablets found (marked 666 or with a star), amounts not stated; case 3: tablets named ecstasy and a pack of moclobemide 300 mg tablets prescribed to a friend, amounts taken not stated; case 4: the paper states ten ecstasy tablets were taken, without giving the source of this history, and the moclobemide amount is not given. Post-mortem blood concentrations in mg/L, MDMA then moclobemide: case 1, 1.6 and 2.3; case 2, 2.0 and 2.1; case 3, 1.7 and 7.9; case 4, 2.1 and 6.5. The paper quotes a reference range of 0.1 to 0.35 mg/L for MDMA and 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L for moclobemide and calls moclobemide a maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and a moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4. Editors’ calculation: the four MDMA concentrations are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the quoted MDMA range.
exposure.polysubstance: Present in all four. Case 1: alcohol (printed as 0.65 g/dL in blood and 0.69 g/dL in urine) and amphetamines in urine. Case 2: dextromethorphan 1.1 mg/L (quoted reference range 0.01 to 0.04), morphine 0.08, amphetamine 0.1, cyclizine 0.3, oxazepam 1, diazepam 1, desmethyldiazepam 0.1 and temazepam 0.2 mg/L, traces of alprazolam; the pathologist considered dextromethorphan a contributor to the death. Case 3: amphetamine 0.15 mg/L, MDA 0.05 mg/L, THC 1.8 µg/L, urine alcohol 0.28 g/dL with none in blood, amphetamines and cannabinoids in urine. Case 4: MDA 0.05 mg/L, THC 3.1 µg/L, lidocaine 1.6 mg/L, no alcohol (Cases, p. 366 and p. 367). The paper does not weigh the other substances in cases 1, 3 and 4.

comparison.controls: None. The paper makes no comparison with deaths from MDMA alone, moclobemide alone or other combinations.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history (stated only for case 1), time between taking the drugs and the collapse (stated only loosely, case 1 the next morning), the setting and activity, fluid intake, and, for cases 1, 2 and 4, body temperature.

outcomes.instruments: Autopsy with histology, toxicology (above) and the history from bystanders and hospital staff; the cause of death was certified by a forensic pathologist in each case (M.J. for cases 1 and 3, T.S. for case 2, P.W. for case 4), and all three are among the authors.
outcomes.validity_norms: No clinical criteria for serotonin toxicity (Sternbach’s or the Hunter rules) are applied. The authors say that the mode of death was consistent with serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it, although the history and clinical observations were limited in most cases (Discussion, p. 367). No post-mortem finding specific to serotonin toxicity is reported: autopsy found no evident cause of death in cases 1 to 3 and, in case 4, oedematous lungs with general visceral congestion.
outcomes.operationalization: Death attributed to a combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide; the authors then describe the mode of death as consistent with serotonin syndrome. The clinical features given: case 1, sudden confusion, convulsions, loss of consciousness and cessation of breathing, no temperature taken; case 2, a confused state before being found dead; case 3, sudden confusion, rolling about on the floor, then collapse, with a body temperature of 43.2 °C (when it was taken is not stated); case 4, found unconscious with breathing difficulties, no temperature available.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. The pathologists who certified the deaths are among the authors, and the cases were identified because both drugs were present.

analysis.effect_sizes: None calculated and none possible: four selected deaths and no denominator. Ages 18 to 23 (one woman, three men). Blood concentrations (mg/L), MDMA then moclobemide: 1.6 and 2.3; 2.0 and 2.1; 1.7 and 7.9; 2.1 and 6.5. Editors’ calculation: MDMA 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end (0.35 mg/L) of the reference range the paper quotes; moclobemide 0.9 and 0.8 times the upper end of its quoted range (2.5 mg/L) in cases 1 and 2 and 3.2 and 2.6 times in cases 3 and 4. The paper states that the risk of death is high when another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAOI, is taken with MDMA (Discussion, last paragraph, p. 367), without a rate or a comparison.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A case report; no protocol or registration applies.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cases were identified because both drugs were present; deaths in the same period with MDMA alone or with other drugs are not described, so the series cannot show how the combination compares. For cases 2 and 4 no body temperature was available and for no case are clonus, reflexes, tone or tremor recorded.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four young people who died suddenly in Western Finland in 2000 and 2001, blood contained MDMA (1.6 to 2.1 mg/L, several times the paper’s quoted reference range) and moclobemide (2.1 to 7.9 mg/L); all had other substances too, moclobemide had been prescribed to none of them, forensic pathologists called each death a combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs, and the sparse histories (confusion, convulsions, collapse; one body temperature of 43.2 °C) are described by the authors as consistent with serotonin syndrome.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the probable cause of death in each case was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs, that each person seems to have taken moclobemide to enhance the effects of MDMA, and that warnings are needed against misinformed attempts to potentiate illicit drugs (p. 365); the Discussion states that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAOI, is taken with MDMA (p. 367). Gaps: (1) the pathologists’ stated cause was combined accidental poisoning with the two drugs; serotonin syndrome is the authors’ reading of limited clinical information, and no examination finding that defines it was recorded; (2) the abstract’s seems to have taken the drug to enhance the effects sits against the Discussion’s statement that it is not known why the victims combined the substances (p. 367); (3) other substances were present in all four and are not excluded as contributors, in case 2 including dextromethorphan; (4) a high risk of death rests on four selected deaths with no denominator; (5) all four MDMA concentrations were well above the paper’s quoted reference range, and the paper does not say whether MDMA alone at those concentrations could have caused the deaths.

timeline.event: This paper: four fatal cases described; by the authors’ knowledge no fatal case of MDMA with moclobemide had been reported before (Discussion, p. 367).
Gillman restates the four deaths in a review and says that he knows of several unpublished cases of MDMA with an MAOI (as read for this library; the unpublished cases are not described).

Silins and colleagues cite these cases among a handful of case reports of deaths with MAOIs and MDMA, and rank MAOIs with MDMA at the highest level of risk in a review that did not appraise study quality (as read for this library).

replication.where_it_stands: The two later reviews read for this library restate this series and add no counted cases (Gillman 2005 mentions unpublished ones without detail); no series with a denominator, and no clinical series with examination findings, was found among the sources read. The literature outside them was not searched, so this card does not say that none exists.

funding.funder: No funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared; the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are from the forensic medicine departments of the Universities of Helsinki and Turku, an academic accident and emergency department in London and the Provincial State Office of Western Finland (p. 365); the pathologists who certified the deaths are among them. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study with a denominator: poison-centre, emergency-department and forensic records from several countries that count every presentation or death involving MDMA, with and without a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (moclobemide and others), noting whether the inhibitor was a prescribed medicine, recording the examination findings that allow the Hunter criteria to be applied, blood concentrations and other substances, and comparing the combination with MDMA alone and with MDMA plus other serotonergic medicines.

domains.note: No comparison group, and every person had other substances in the blood (alcohol, amphetamines, THC; in case 2 dextromethorphan and several sedatives); MDMA alone at 4.6 to 6.0 times the quoted reference range cannot be excluded as the cause.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Post-mortem concentrations, not amounts taken or timing; tablets analysed in one case only; the source of moclobemide is known in one case (a friend’s prescription); concentrations after death may not match concentrations during the illness.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Selected by death and by the presence of both drugs, found by the authors’ departments in one region over two years, with no statement of how.
Resuscitation was attempted in cases 1 to 3 and hospital care is not described for case 4; whether treatment altered the findings is not stated.
The history is limited in every case; no body temperature in cases 1, 2 and 4; no examination finding (clonus, reflexes, tone, tremor) in any; no urine screen in case 4.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Cause of death is a pathologist’s judgment, made by authors who selected the cases for the combination; autopsy found no evident cause in cases 1 to 3; serotonin syndrome is not diagnosed against any criteria.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: A case report with no protocol; all four cases are described in detail, but deaths with other drug combinations in the same period are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: METHODS 5.3 lists no instrument for case series, and the card schema asks for one; ROBINS-E, the tool for non-randomized studies of exposures, was used as the closest fit, with the lack of any comparison group counted under confounding. Two domains are very high and three high: the series has no comparison, no denominator, other substances in every person and a cause of death that is a judgment by authors who picked the cases. The source may be cited as a record that four deaths with MDMA and moclobemide in the blood were reported from Finland, with the pathologists’ conclusion and the sparse clinical details. It may not be cited for how often the combination kills, for serotonin toxicity as the proven mechanism of these deaths, or for the combination being worse than MDMA alone.

key_findings.finding: Four deaths in Finland in 2000 and 2001 that appeared to the authors to be due to an interaction between MDMA and moclobemide. As detailed a history as possible was obtained and a post-mortem examination was carried out in each, with toxicology samples.
key_findings.locator: Method (a single paragraph, pp. 365–366); Abstract (p. 365)

key_findings.finding: Laboratory methods: alcohol by headspace gas chromatography in blood and urine; urine screened for several hundred substances by thin-layer chromatography; blood monitored for 150 drugs by gas chromatography with nitrogen detection; confirmation and quantitation by mass spectrometry. The quoted reference range is 0.1 to 0.35 mg/L for MDMA in blood and 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L for moclobemide; the limit of quantitation for MDMA in blood was 0.04 mg/L.
key_findings.locator: Method (the same paragraph, continued from p. 365)

key_findings.finding: Case 1: woman aged 18 who took an unknown quantity of street ecstasy one night; the next morning she became suddenly confused, convulsed, lost consciousness and stopped breathing; resuscitation failed; no temperature was taken. Autopsy found no evident cause of death. Blood MDMA 1.6 mg/L and moclobemide 2.3 mg/L; blood alcohol printed as 0.65 g/dL and urine alcohol 0.69 g/dL; amphetamines in urine. The pathologist gave the cause of death as combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide.
key_findings.locator: Case 1

key_findings.finding: Case 2: man aged 23 found dead after a confused state, with two kinds of white tablets (both contained MDMA and nothing else active) and old needle marks; no cause of death at autopsy. Blood MDMA 2.0, moclobemide 2.1, dextromethorphan 1.1 (quoted reference range 0.01 to 0.04), morphine 0.08, amphetamine 0.1, cyclizine 0.3, oxazepam 1, diazepam 1, desmethyldiazepam 0.1 and temazepam 0.2 mg/L; hair held MDMA and amphetamine from the previous 1.5 to 2.5 months. The pathologist gave combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide as the cause and considered dextromethorphan a contributor.
key_findings.locator: Case 2

key_findings.finding: Case 3: man aged 18, who had used amphetamine-type drugs for years, who became suddenly confused at a friend’s apartment, rolled about on the floor and collapsed; resuscitation failed; tablets named ecstasy by a friend were found with a pack of moclobemide 300 mg tablets prescribed to the friend; body temperature of the deceased 43.2 °C. Blood MDMA 1.7, amphetamine 0.15, MDA 0.05 and moclobemide 7.9 mg/L, THC 1.8 µg/L; urine alcohol 0.28 g/dL with none in blood. The pathologist gave combined accidental poisoning with moclobemide and MDMA as the cause.
key_findings.locator: Case 3

key_findings.finding: Case 4: man aged 19 who, the paper states, had taken ten ecstasy tablets; he was unconscious with breathing difficulties at a health centre and died in hospital; no further history or temperature. Autopsy: oedematous lungs and general visceral congestion. Blood MDMA 2.1, MDA 0.05, moclobemide 6.5 and lidocaine 1.6 mg/L, THC 3.1 µg/L; no alcohol; no urine drug screen because of small sample volume. The pathologist gave combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide as the cause.
key_findings.locator: Case 4 (begins at the foot of p. 366)

key_findings.finding: Moclobemide had not been prescribed for any of the four people; it was at maximum therapeutic concentration in cases 1 and 2 and in moderate overdose in cases 3 and 4.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning Moclobemide had not been prescribed

key_findings.finding: Editors’ calculation: the four blood MDMA concentrations (1.6, 2.0, 1.7, 2.1 mg/L) are 4.6, 5.7, 4.9 and 6.0 times the upper end of the reference range the paper quotes (0.35 mg/L); the dextromethorphan concentration in case 2 (1.1 mg/L) is roughly 28 to 110 times its quoted range (0.01 to 0.04 mg/L).
key_findings.locator: Method (reference ranges) and Cases 1 to 4 (calculated by the editors)
key_findings.note: Editors’ calculation. What population the quoted reference ranges describe is not stated.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that, to their knowledge, no fatal cases of MDMA with an MAO-A inhibitor such as moclobemide had been reported, and that, although history and clinical observations were limited in most cases, the mode of death in each was consistent with serotonin syndrome as Sternbach described it.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that it is not known why the victims combined the substances; that the only known connection between the cases is the region, with cases 1 and 2 close in time; that case 2 appears to have taken several drugs; and that moclobemide could in case 2 also have slowed the breakdown of dextromethorphan and so added to the serotonergic effect.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning It is not known why the victims combined these substances

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the risk of death is high if another drug affecting serotonin release, especially an MAO inhibitor, is taken together with MDMA, and that many public sources minimize the risk of death from interactions.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, last paragraph
key_findings.note: A statement without a denominator or comparison; the series itself shows four deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the probable cause of death in each case was serotonin syndrome as a result of an interaction between the two drugs. The pathologists’ stated cause in all four is combined accidental poisoning with MDMA and moclobemide, and the Discussion says only that the mode of death was consistent with serotonin syndrome, with limited history and clinical observations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Serotonin syndrome is the authors’ interpretation of sparse bystander accounts, not a finding recorded by an examiner; no feature that defines it (clonus, reflexes, tone, tremor) is reported for any person.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that it seems each person took moclobemide to enhance the effects of MDMA; the Discussion says it is not known why the victims combined the substances.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intent is not known in any case; the one case with a known source (a friend’s prescription, case 3) does not show why it was taken.

reporting_issues.issue: Case 1’s alcohol is printed as 0.65 g/dL in blood and 0.69 g/dL in urine, a blood level that would be many times the legal driving limit and potentially fatal on its own; in case 3 blood held no alcohol while urine held 0.28 g/dL. The paper does not comment on either, or on alcohol as a contributor.
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit in case 1 is probably a misprint (for example g/L), which is the editors’ inference and not stated in the paper; as printed, alcohol would be a competing cause of death in case 1, and either way its role is not weighed.

reporting_issues.issue: All four MDMA concentrations (1.6 to 2.1 mg/L) are 4.6 to 6.0 times the upper end of the reference range quoted in the Method (0.1 to 0.35 mg/L); the paper does not discuss whether MDMA at these concentrations could have caused the deaths without moclobemide. Case 2 also had dextromethorphan at roughly 28 to 110 times its quoted range, which the pathologist considered a contributor.
reporting_issues.consequence: Attributing the deaths to the interaction rests on judgment; the paper gives no comparison with MDMA deaths at similar concentrations without moclobemide.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract describe four deaths after MDMA and moclobemide, but the toxicology shows other drugs in every case (case 2 had at least eight other substances and old needle marks), and lidocaine in case 4 (1.6 mg/L) is unexplained; the explanation given for lidocaine in case 1 is resuscitation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The series is of deaths with MDMA and moclobemide present among other substances, not of deaths from the pair alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the risk of death is high with an MAO inhibitor and MDMA; the paper counts four deaths and gives no number of people who took the combination or of other MDMA deaths in the region and period.
reporting_issues.consequence: No rate or relative risk can be derived; the statement is an opinion supported by four selected cases.

reporting_issues.issue: The clinical information needed to apply the Sternbach or Hunter criteria is missing: body temperature was recorded only for case 3 (43.2 °C, with no statement of when it was taken relative to death), and no case records clonus, reflexes, tone, tremor or sweating.
reporting_issues.consequence: The deaths cannot be classified against either set of criteria; the temperature in case 3 is the only sign that points toward heat-related illness, and it is not tied to a time.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 365–368 (full text: abstract, introduction, Method, the four cases, Discussion, reference list); units of the concentrations (including the THC values in micrograms per litre) were checked against a page render. The earlier case reports and the website pages the paper cites were not read.

design_detail: One-year (calendar 2010) population cohort of all North Carolina residents (9,560,234), built from linked administrative records: the state Controlled Substances Reporting System (prescription monitoring; 54,825,930 dispensing records for 2009-2011, 7,393,375 opioid analgesic records after cleaning) and death certificates with Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) records, linked by name and date of birth. The authors call it a prospective cohort; the records were assembled and analysed afterwards, and for people who died, exposure time was counted back from death (first prescription in the 365 days before death). Exposure: average daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME) from dispensed prescriptions (intent-to-treat); outcome: unintentional or undetermined-intent drug overdose deaths in which a medical examiner judged an opioid analgesic to have a primary or additive role (629 deaths); crude rates by MME stratum from Poisson models (generalized estimating equations); benzodiazepine exposure: any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study. Read in full from the PDF (Pain Med 2016;17:85-98); Table 1 and Figure 5 caption checked on rendered pages 90 and 93; Figures 2 to 4 are images and their values were not read.
can_establish: How overdose death rates involving opioid analgesics in North Carolina in 2010 varied by average prescribed daily dose (crude rates and rate ratios against the lowest-dose group); how many such deaths had a benzodiazepine, alcohol, cocaine or heroin judged involved by the medical examiner; and how many of the people who died had been dispensed an opioid painkiller in the previous year.
cannot_establish: Whether higher doses or co-dispensed benzodiazepines caused the deaths (nothing is adjusted: not age, sex, reason for prescribing, other illness or other drugs, and higher doses go to sicker patients); how much risk a benzodiazepine adds for a person taking both (the rate ratio of about 10 is crude and cannot be reproduced from the numbers printed); when in the year risk falls (assumed constant); deaths involving opioids obtained outside the monitoring programme; anything about illicit opioids.

sample.recruitment: Records: all residents alive in 2010, from the state's mid-year population estimate; prescriptions from the Controlled Substances Reporting System; deaths from the State Center for Health Statistics and the OCME (Methods > Study Design; Data Sources; Statistical Analysis).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Residents who died in 2010 with an underlying cause of unintentional or undetermined drug overdose (ICD-10 X40-X44, Y10-Y14) and an opioid analgesic judged involved in a primary or additive role; deaths with opioids present but judged circumstantial were excluded; suicides excluded. Toxicology records were available for 824 (92%) of the overdose deaths identified from vital statistics. The monitoring programme omits Veterans Administration and Department of Defense pharmacies, Indian Health Service clinics, in-clinic dispensing by physicians and outpatient opioid dependence treatment programmes (Methods > Data Sources, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records-based). About 8% of identified overdose deaths lacked toxicology records and could not be classified (editors' reading of 824 (92%)).
sample.demographics: Decedents: 37.2% female (234), median age 43 years (interquartile range 32-51). Patients: 22.8% of residents were dispensed an opioid analgesic; 2.8% of those patients (61,879) averaged more than 150 mg/day MME; 89.6% of licensed clinicians prescribed an opioid analgesic and 40.0% an extended-release one. No characteristics of patients other than prescribing patterns are given (Results, pp. 89-90).
sample.selection_effects: A whole-state population, so selection is mainly by what the monitoring programme records: opioids from other states or non-medical sources are not seen (p. 94). The 151 deaths (24.0%) with no opioid analgesic dispensed in the previous year are counted in the numerator but cannot belong to any dose group, and unexposed person-years (3,554,850) are under half the unexposed people (7,377,860), unexplained (reporting issue 6).

exposure.measurement: Dispensed prescriptions (strength, quantity, days' supply, formulation) converted to MME with CDC factors (codeine 0.15, fentanyl 25.0, hydrocodone 1.0, hydromorphone 4.0, methadone 3.0, morphine 1.0, oxycodone 1.5, oxymorphone 3.0); average daily MME = total MME divided by days' supply, with overlapping prescriptions taken into account; days' supply was missing or zero for 10% of records and imputed by median for the same quantity and product (Methods > Exposure Definition, pp. 87-88).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: prescribed average daily dose in 16 strata, from more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day MME (reference) up to 500 to 5,000 mg/day; dispensed, not taken: the authors assume each prescription was taken as directed (Limitations, p. 94).
exposure.polysubstance: Benzodiazepine dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study (any, yes or no) was examined as a modifier; medical examiners judged benzodiazepines involved in 61.4% (386) of the 629 deaths, ethanol in 12.2% (77), cocaine in 8.4% (53) and heroin in 1.3% (8). Nothing is adjusted for other drugs (Results, p. 89; Methods, p. 88).
