comparison.controls: Unexposed residents (no opioid analgesic dispensed in 2010): 151 deaths and 3,554,850 person-years in Table 1. Rate ratios use the lowest exposed stratum (more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day; 98 deaths, 1,305,835 person-years) as the reference.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The reasons opioids and benzodiazepines were prescribed (pain, injury, psychiatric disorder, substance use disorder), illness severity, age, sex, prior overdose, duration of therapy and other drugs: the authors say none was controlled for, that patients at higher doses are more likely to have more serious illness, and name exchangeability across doses as the greatest limitation (p. 94).

outcomes.instruments: Death certificates (underlying cause X40-X44, Y10-Y14) with OCME toxicology and investigation records; each drug's role in the death classified by OCME toxicologists as primary (concentration enough to have caused the death alone) or additive (not enough alone but acting with other drugs).
outcomes.validity_norms: The role of each drug is the examiners' judgment, which the authors say 'inherently contains an element of subjective clinical judgment' (p. 94); whether examiners knew the person's prescriptions is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Any overdose death in which at least one of eight named opioid analgesics was judged involved in a primary or additive role; benzodiazepine and ethanol involvement by the same examiners' judgment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; descriptive rates and rate ratios with 95% intervals in 16 dose strata and two benzodiazepine groups.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; examiners classified deaths independently of this study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Crude rates from deaths and person-years: 478 deaths among 2,182,374 patients (0.022%). Printed rate ratios against more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day: 2.6 (95% CI 2.0-3.5) at 40-59.9; 6.2 (4.2-9.2) at 80-99.9; 6.7 (4.3-10.6) at 100-119.9; 14.1 (8.9-22.5) at 120-139.9; 29.5 (17.1-50.7) at 160-179.9; 27.4 (17.5-42.8) at 200-249.9; 90.4 (60.7-134.6) at 500-5,000 mg/day; unexposed 0.57 (0.44-0.73); no distinct threshold at 100 or 120 mg/day. Benzodiazepines: crude rate 7.0 (6.3-7.8) per 10,000 person-years among patients co-dispensed benzodiazepines against 0.7 (0.6-0.9) with opioid analgesics alone, about ten times higher; the rate difference was 2.8 per 10,000 person-years at more than 0 to 74.9 mg/day, rising to 45.8 at 300 to 5,000 mg/day (Figure 5, image). Editors' checks: the printed rates in Table 1 exceed deaths divided by person-years in every exposed stratum (reference stratum 1.3 printed against 0.75 calculated from 98 deaths and 1,305,835 person-years; highest stratum 80.0 against 68.3) while the printed rate ratios match ratios of the calculated rates (500-5,000 mg/day: 91.0 calculated against 90.4 printed); the unexposed rate prints as 0.34 against 0.42 calculated.
analysis.covariates: None.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration; the hypothesis that part of the dose-dependent risk comes from co-prescribed benzodiazepines is stated at the end of the Introduction (p. 86).
analysis.selective_reporting: The benzodiazepine rates are in the text and Figure 5 only; no table gives deaths, person-years or rates by dose and benzodiazepine status, and the 7.0 and 0.7 rates have no counts printed.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the five highest dose strata have 14 to 32 deaths each, and the intervals are wide.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In North Carolina in 2010, 629 overdose deaths involved an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role according to medical examiners: 478 in people dispensed an opioid analgesic in the year (about 2.2 per 10,000 person-years, editors' calculation) and 151 in people with none. Crude death rates rose steadily with average daily dose, without a visible jump at 100 or 120 mg/day, to a rate ratio near 90 at 500 mg/day or more, against the lowest dose group. Medical examiners judged benzodiazepines involved in 61.4% of the 629 deaths and ethanol in 12.2%; 80% of patients had been dispensed a benzodiazepine in the previous year; crude death rates were about ten times higher among patients dispensed both than with opioids alone, with a gap that widened at higher doses.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says half of the 629 deaths had an opioid analgesic prescription active on the day of death; that risk 'increased gradually and did not show evidence of a distinct risk threshold'; and calls for guidance on combined classes of medicines. The discussion says the dose-dependent relationship 'is strongly influenced by' concurrent benzodiazepine exposure; the conclusion says much of the risk at higher doses appears to be associated with co-prescribed benzodiazepines and speaks of dangerous situations created by 'ignoring known drug interactions' at the point of care. Gaps: (1) nothing is adjusted, so 'strongly influenced' and 'much of the risk' rest on crude rate differences that sicker patients taking both drugs would also show; (2) the half is 244 of the 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid (51%), or 39% of all 629; (3) 'ignoring known drug interactions' treats co-prescribing as the cause; (4) the benzodiazepine rates cannot be reproduced from the numbers given (reporting issue 2).

timeline.event: Paulozzi and colleagues (Pain Med), as quoted by this paper (not read): odds ratios of 12.2 for 40 to 120 mg/day and 11.3 for the highest categories, against a combined unexposed and low-dose group, with a similar curve shape

Fulton-Kehoe and colleagues (Med Care), Washington State Medicaid, as quoted by this paper (not read): 44.5% of methadone poisoning decedents and 48% of other opioid decedents had a sedative prescription in the month before death; 26% and 16% had no opioid prescription

Park and colleagues (BMJ), case-cohort of US veterans receiving opioid analgesics: this paper quotes 27% of patients also receiving benzodiazepines and 49% of decedents with both prescriptions; the full paper, read separately in this library, reports an adjusted hazard ratio for overdose death of 3.86 (95% CI 3.49-4.26) during benzodiazepine prescription against none

Sun and colleagues, privately insured adults aged 18 to 64 (read separately in this library): adjusted odds ratio 2.14 (95% CI 2.05-2.24) for a hospital-treated opioid overdose in years with at least one day of overlapping benzodiazepine and opioid prescriptions, against years without

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the finding (more overdose deaths where benzodiazepines are also prescribed, higher with higher opioid doses) agrees with the adjusted cohorts read for this library (Park and colleagues; Sun and colleagues); the size reported here (about tenfold) is crude and cannot be used. The finding that no clear risk threshold appears at 100 or 120 mg/day is from this single analysis, with unadjusted rates.

funding.funder: Dasgupta's time was partly funded by grants from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation Public Health Law Research programme (for analysis) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (U01CE002162, for publication support); the funding organizations had no direct role in the study. The work was done as part of a doctoral dissertation (p. 85; Acknowledgments, p. 95).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dasgupta is employed by Epidemico, Inc., a public health software company with no direct contracts with opioid manufacturers (as of 1 May 2015), and served on a Risk Safety Advisory Board for Covidien, dissolved in August 2012; no other author has disclosures (p. 85).
funding.affiliations_note: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (Epidemiology; Injury Prevention Research Center; Health Behavior); North Carolina Division of Public Health (Injury and Violence Prevention Branch), which also supplied the death data; CDC/CSTE Applied Epidemiology Fellowship.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort with individual-level covariates (age, sex, diagnoses, prior psychiatric and substance use treatment, other medicines) and time-varying exposure to opioid dose and to concurrent benzodiazepine days' supply, a design that starts follow-up when people first begin a medicine, or compares two active treatments, and a self-controlled analysis comparing each person's periods with and without benzodiazepines; with death classification by examiners blind to prescriptions, and counts printed for every rate.

domains.note: No covariate is used. For the benzodiazepine contrast (about ten times higher crude rate; 80% of patients exposed) the exposed and comparison groups differ in reasons for prescribing, illness and substance use; for the dose contrast alone this would be high, since higher doses go to sicker patients (the authors' greatest limitation, p. 94).

Dispensed, not taken; 10% of days' supply imputed; the monitoring programme omits several sources; the Methods define benzodiazepine exposure by person (any dispensing in 365 days) but the printed rates imply a much smaller exposed person-time (reporting issue 2).

Whole-state population, a strength; person-time for decedents starts at the first prescription in the 365 days before death while for survivors it starts at the first prescription in 2010; unexposed and total person-years are unexplained (reporting issue 6).
Intent-to-treat classification and an assumption of constant risk across the year, which the authors say is unlikely to hold at higher doses (risk may be highest shortly after starting).
About 8% of identified overdose deaths lacked toxicology records; 10% of days' supply imputed; no covariate data to be missing.

Medical examiners' judgment of a primary or additive role, with whether they knew the prescriptions unstated; an examiner's finding of benzodiazepine involvement may be likelier when a benzodiazepine prescription is known.
No registration; Table 1 rates do not match its own deaths and person-years; benzodiazepine rates shown without counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The descriptive findings (how many deaths, the share with a benzodiazepine or alcohol judged involved, the share of decedents with an opioid prescription) are not affected by confounding and may be cited as what these medical examiners judged in North Carolina in 2010, with the counts' limits stated. The comparative findings are unadjusted: the dose-specific rate ratios and especially the ten-fold benzodiazepine rate ratio are too confounded to estimate any effect, and the benzodiazepine rates cannot be reproduced from the paper's own numbers. The study may not be cited for how much a benzodiazepine or a higher dose adds to risk, or for the absence of a threshold at 100 mg/day.

key_findings.finding: Design and results in the abstract: a prospective observational cohort with one year of follow-up of the North Carolina residential population (9,560,234; 2,182,374 opioid analgesic patients); 629 overdose deaths, half with an active opioid analgesic prescription on the day of death; 478 deaths among 2,182,374 patients (0.022% per year); rates rose gradually across daily MME; 80.0% of patients also received benzodiazepines; death rates among those co-dispensed benzodiazepines and opioids were ten times higher (7.0 per 10,000 person-years, CI 6.3 to 7.8) than with opioids alone (0.7, CI 0.6 to 0.9).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Subjects, Results)
key_findings.note: 'Half' is 244 of 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid, not of 629.

key_findings.finding: Data: the prescription monitoring programme (since 2007) captures pharmacy dispensing in the state but omits Veterans Administration and Department of Defense pharmacies, Indian Health Service clinics, in-clinic dispensing by physicians, veterinary clinics and outpatient opioid dependence treatment programmes. Deaths come from death certificates supplemented by OCME records; post-mortem toxicology is done as part of autopsy.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Data Sources, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: For each overdose decedent, prescriptions dispensed in the 365 days before death were identified by linking the first five letters of the last name and date of birth, then confirmed with first name, full last name and date of birth.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Data Linkage

key_findings.finding: Exposure: dispensed solid oral or transdermal opioid analgesics (codeine, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl, methadone, morphine, oxycodone, oxymorphone), converted to MME with CDC factors; days' supply imputed for 10% of records; average daily MME from total MME over days' supply with overlaps; benzodiazepine exposure dichotomised as any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Exposure Definition

key_findings.finding: Outcome: underlying cause of unintentional or undetermined drug overdose (X40-X44, Y10-Y14); OCME toxicologists classified each drug as having a primary or additive role from scene investigation, toxicology, records and interviews; deaths with opioids merely present were excluded; records were abstracted for decedents with toxicology available, 824 (92%) of the deaths identified.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Outcome Definition

key_findings.finding: Analysis: person-time accrued in 2010 or in the 365 days before death; intent-to-treat exposure from the first opioid prescription; incidence rates and rate ratios from Poisson regression with person-days as offset, generalized estimating equations; no covariates.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 89); no covariates: Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs (p. 94)

key_findings.finding: 2,182,374 residents (22.8%) were dispensed an opioid analgesic in 2010; hydrocodone to 70% of patients and oxycodone to 39%; 89.6% of licensed clinicians prescribed opioid analgesics and 40.0% an extended-release formulation; 61,879 patients (2.8%) averaged more than 150 mg/day MME.
key_findings.locator: Results > Opioid Analgesic Prescribing Patterns

key_findings.finding: 629 deaths involved an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role; 37.2% were female and median age was 43; ethanol was judged involved in 12.2% (77), cocaine in 8.4% (53) and heroin in 1.3% (8); 478 deaths among 2,182,374 patients (0.022%).
key_findings.locator: Results > Overdose Deaths, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Half of decedents (51%, 244) had a current opioid analgesic prescription on the day of death; among the 629 deaths, 24.0% (151) had no opioid analgesic dispensed in the previous 365 days; of the 478 with an opioid, 43.1% had received at least one extended-release formulation.
key_findings.locator: Results > Overdose Deaths, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The percentage of 51 is of the 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid; of all 629 it is 38.8% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Dose-dependent risk: incidence rates rose gradually and stayed elevated beyond 200 mg/day MME; no distinct threshold at 100 or 120 mg/day. Table 1 gives, against more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day, rate ratios of 6.7 (4.3-10.6) at 100-119.9, 27.4 (17.5-42.8) at 200-249.9 and 90.4 (60.7-134.6) at 500-5,000 mg/day, based on 23, 24 and 32 deaths in those strata and 98 in the reference stratum.
key_findings.locator: Results > Dose-Dependent Overdose Risk, 1st paragraph (p. 90); Table 1 (p. 93)
key_findings.note: Table 1 values checked on a rendered page; the printed rates do not match deaths divided by person-years (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepines were dispensed in the past year to 80.0% (1,747,166) of opioid analgesic patients and judged involved by medical examiners in 61.4% (386) of the 629 deaths; crude death rates were about ten times higher with both (7.0 per 10,000 person-years) than with opioid analgesics alone (0.7); compared with patients at the same MME, the rate difference was 2.8 per 10,000 person-years at more than 0 to 74.9 mg/day, rising to 45.8 at 300 to 5,000 mg/day.
key_findings.locator: Results > Dose-Dependent Overdose Risk, 2nd paragraph; Figure 5 (p. 93, image)

key_findings.finding: The authors call the 80% a surprise, compared with 5% of the US adult population receiving benzodiazepines; they quote Washington State Medicaid (44.5% of methadone poisoning decedents and 48% of other opioid decedents with a sedative prescription in the month before death) and US veterans (27% of patients also received benzodiazepines; 49% of decedents had both prescriptions), and say differences between studies are probably due to the time definitions used.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations named: the model assumes continuous risk during exposed and unexposed time, unlikely at higher doses (risk may be highest soon after starting; duration of therapy not considered); medical examiner determination 'inherently contains an element of subjective clinical judgment'; opioids from other states or non-medical sources are unseen; dispensed doses assumed taken as directed; many high-dose immediate-release opioids contain acetaminophen; the greatest limitation is exchangeability, since patients at higher doses are likely to have more serious illness, with no covariates available to adjust for it.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 9th to 12th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: higher doses were associated with increased overdose risk with smaller incremental increases above 200 mg/day MME; much of the risk at higher doses 'appears to be associated with' co-prescribed benzodiazepines; the authors call for understanding what level of extended-release prescribing balances access and overdose risk and say dangerous situations arise 'by ignoring known drug interactions at the point of care'.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: The rates per 10,000 person-years printed in Table 1 are higher than deaths divided by person-years in every exposed stratum (reference stratum: 1.3 printed against 0.75 from 98 deaths and 1,305,835 person-years; 100-119.9: 8.3 against 5.05; 500-5,000: 80.0 against 68.3), and the unexposed rate is lower (0.34 printed, 0.42 calculated), while the printed rate ratios match the ratio of the calculated rates (for example 90.4 printed against 91.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: The rates and rate ratios in the same table cannot both be right as printed; use counts and person-years, not the rate column.

reporting_issues.issue: The benzodiazepine-stratified rates cannot be reproduced. The Methods classify benzodiazepine exposure by person (any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study) and 80% of patients (1,747,166) were exposed; at 7.0 per 10,000 person-years that implies more than 1,200 deaths (0.8 x 2,181,847 person-years x 7.0 per 10,000, editors' calculation), more than the 478 deaths among patients and the 629 in all. The printed intervals imply a few hundred deaths and a much smaller exposed person-time.
reporting_issues.consequence: How benzodiazepine exposure was timed in the rate calculation is not stated; the ten-fold contrast should not be quoted as a rate ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says there were 629 deaths, half of which had an opioid analgesic prescription active on the day of death, and the text says half of all decedents; the 51% is 244 of the 478 decedents who had been dispensed an opioid, and 244 of 629 is 38.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote the proportion with its denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The 80.0% of patients dispensed a benzodiazepine in a year is about three times the 27% the paper quotes for US veterans, and implies that 18% of all North Carolina residents (0.228 x 0.80) were dispensed one, against the 5% of US adults the paper quotes; the paper calls the 80% 'surprising', puts differences between studies down to time definitions, and does not list which drugs counted as benzodiazepines.
reporting_issues.consequence: The benzodiazepine classification may be wider than expected; treat the 80% and the ten-fold contrast with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion and conclusion say the dose-dependent relationship is 'strongly influenced' by benzodiazepines and that much of the risk at higher doses appears associated with them; no model includes benzodiazepines or tests an interaction, and nothing is adjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are interpretation of crude rate differences, not results.

reporting_issues.issue: Person-years do not match the population: the total of 5,736,696 is 60% of the 9,560,234 residents followed for a year, the 3,554,850 unexposed person-years are under half of the 7,377,860 unexposed residents who the Methods say contributed person-days for all of 2010, and the exposed person-years (2,181,847) almost equal the number of patients (2,182,374), although the Methods count exposure from each patient's first prescription in 2010, which would give most patients less than a full year.
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators, and so every rate, cannot be reconstructed from the Methods.

reporting_issues.issue: The captions of Figures 4 and 5 give the reference group as more than 0 to 19.9 mg/day, whereas Table 1 and the text use more than 0 to 39.9 mg/day; the Discussion gives rate ratios of 'IRR ranging from 16.6 through 90.4' for the highest categories, and 16.6 does not appear in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference group for the figures is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is labelled prospective but the records were assembled and analysed after the deaths, and for decedents exposure time was counted back from death while for survivors it was counted forward from the first prescription in 2010.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treated here as a retrospective cohort; the different time starts for decedents and survivors could bias rates.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 85-98 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Dasgupta_2016_HighDoseOpioidOverdoseMortalityCohort.pdf), full text including abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, Table 1, figure legends, disclosures, acknowledgments and reference list; Table 1 and the Figure 5 caption checked on rendered pages 90 and 93; Figures 2 to 5 are images and no values were read from them. Rates and ratios were recalculated from the printed counts and person-years.

design_detail: Brief research report (a 3-page letter, published online first on 21 August 2018): a population-based nested case-control study of Ontario residents eligible for public drug coverage who were dispensed opioids between 1 August 1997 and 31 December 2016 (aged 15 to 105). Cases: people who died of an opioid-related cause, excluding deaths determined to be suicide or homicide; index date = date of death. Each of 1,417 cases was matched to up to 4 controls (5,097) on age (within 3 years), sex, index year (within 1 year), chronic kidney disease (previous 5 years) and Charlson comorbidity index score (within 0.2 standard deviations). Exposure: a pregabalin prescription dispensed in the 120 days before the index date (primary); pregabalin supply overlapping the index date and a sub-analysis matched on recent benzodiazepine, antidepressant or other CNS depressant prescription (sensitivity); pregabalin dose at or below, or above, 300 mg/day (secondary); NSAIDs as a predefined control exposure. Conditional logistic regression adjusted for characteristics that remained imbalanced after matching and, in every model, for recent gabapentin exposure. The letter says its methods, data sources and statistical analyses are consistent with the same team's 2017 gabapentin study and that any differences are described; it does not itself describe how cases were ascertained or controls sampled. Read in full from the online-first PDF (letter p. 1 text; Table p. 2; Figure and references p. 3); Table and Figure values checked on rendered pages. No supplements exist in the PDF. Locators below are section and paragraph within the letter, counting paragraphs in reading order.
can_establish: Whether, among people in Ontario's public drug programme who were dispensed opioids, those who died of an opioid-related cause were more likely than matched living opioid recipients to have been dispensed pregabalin in the preceding 120 days, after adjustment for recorded medicines, comorbidity and opioid dose.
cannot_establish: Whether pregabalin caused any of the deaths or interacts with opioids (a comparison of pregabalin plus opioid against opioid alone cannot separate an interaction from separate risks or from the reasons pregabalin was prescribed); absolute risk; any dose-response (two dose groups, overlapping intervals, no trend test); anything about people who obtain pregabalin or opioids outside the public drug plan; whether the pregabalin was being taken when death occurred.

sample.recruitment: Records-based: Ontario residents eligible for public drug coverage who received publicly funded opioid prescriptions, 1 August 1997 to 31 December 2016; the data sources are said to be those of the 2017 gabapentin study and are not described in the letter (Methods and Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, p. 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort aged 15 to 105 with publicly funded opioid prescriptions; cases died of an opioid-related cause with suicides and homicides excluded; no other inclusion or exclusion rules, and no definition of 'opioid-related cause', are given in the letter.
sample.attrition: All 1,417 cases were matched in the main analysis; 1,199 cases and 3,935 controls (218 fewer cases, 15.4%) are in the sub-analysis matched on other CNS depressants, with no reason given (presumably cases with no suitable control; not stated).
sample.demographics: Median age 48 years (interquartile range 42 to 54) in cases and 49 (42 to 54) in controls; 43.5% and 44.6% female; 43.0% and 43.1% in the lowest income quintile; 12.1% and 12.8% rural; median duration of opioid use 8 years (4 to 12) in both groups (Table, p. 2).
sample.selection_effects: A public drug-plan population (low income, mostly under 65) dispensed opioids; prescriptions paid privately or obtained illicitly are not seen; the letter does not discuss generalisability. Control sampling method is not stated in the letter.

exposure.measurement: Pregabalin dispensed in the 120 days before the index date (primary); prescription overlapping the index date (sensitivity). Adherence and non-prescribed supply are unknown; the letter does not discuss exposure measurement.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: prescribed pregabalin daily dose grouped as low or moderate (300 mg or less) and high (above 300 mg); median dose among exposed 225 mg/day (interquartile range 150 to 300) in cases and 150 (150 to 300) in controls. Opioid dose in morphine milligram equivalents per day (1 to 19, 20 to 49, 50 to 99, 100 to 199, 200 or more) is a covariate: 200 or more in 27.0% of cases and 16.2% of controls; long-acting opioids dispensed in the exposure window to 51.4% and 36.3% (Table, p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Recent SSRIs, other antidepressants, benzodiazepines (75.7% of cases against 53.7% of controls), other CNS depressants and opioid agonist therapy (methadone or buprenorphine-naloxone; 5.9% against 4.5%) are listed; per the unlabelled footnote to the Figure, the adjustment covers SSRIs, other antidepressants, benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, number of medications, Charlson score, numbers of opioid-prescribing physicians and pharmacies, long-acting opioid receipt and opioid dose, and every model adjusts for recent gabapentin. Alcohol use disorder is listed in the Table (23.9% against 20.4%) but balanced after weighting (24.1%) and not in the adjustment list. Non-prescribed and illicit drug use is not measured.

comparison.controls: Up to 4 living opioid recipients per case (5,097 for 1,417 cases; 3.6 per case on average); the letter does not describe how they were sampled (the 2017 study used incidence density sampling at the case's index date).
comparison.matching: Age (within 3 years), sex, index year (within 1 year), chronic kidney disease in the previous 5 years and Charlson comorbidity index score (within 0.2 standard deviations); the 2017 study matched on a disease risk index and age within 5 years instead of the Charlson score and age within 3 years. A sub-analysis also matched on recent benzodiazepine, antidepressant or other CNS depressant prescription.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The reasons pregabalin was prescribed (neuropathic or other pain, anxiety, epilepsy), pain severity, non-prescribed drug use and opioid use disorder are not measured; only proxies (opioid agonist therapy, numbers of prescribers and pharmacies) appear. The letter has no limitations section.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls also received opioids. After matching, cases had more recent benzodiazepines (standard difference 0.45), other antidepressants (0.22), other CNS depressants (0.22), SSRIs (0.17), long-acting opioids (0.31) and high opioid doses (0.26 for 200 or more MME/day), and received more medications in the year (median 11 against 9); these are adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Opioid-related death as stated in the letter ('died of an opioid-related cause', suicides and homicides excluded); the ascertainment source is not named in the letter (the 2017 study used coroner-confirmed accidental opioid-related deaths).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed in the letter.
outcomes.operationalization: Odds of recent pregabalin dispensing in cases against matched controls, from conditional logistic regression.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; one primary analysis, two sensitivity analyses, one dose analysis (two groups) and one control exposure.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Recent pregabalin: 69 of 1,417 cases (4.9%) against 153 of 5,097 controls (3.0%); unadjusted OR 1.85 (95% CI 1.36-2.53), adjusted OR 1.68 (1.19-2.36). Supply overlapping the index date: 60 (4.2%) against 121 (2.4%); 2.03 (1.45-2.83), adjusted 1.81 (1.26-2.60). Sub-analysis matched on other CNS depressant use (1,199 cases, 3,935 controls): 59 (4.9%) against 116 (3.0%); 2.05 (1.44-2.93), adjusted 2.00 (1.39-2.88). Dose: above 300 mg/day 17 (1.2%) against 25 (0.5%), 3.02 (1.58-5.77), adjusted 2.51 (1.24-5.06); 300 mg/day or less 52 (3.7%) against 128 (2.5%), 1.74 (1.22-2.49), adjusted 1.52 (1.04-2.22). NSAIDs (control exposure): 531 cases against 1,830 controls (35.9%); 1.07 (0.95-1.21), adjusted 1.04 (0.90-1.19); the printed case percentage is 34.5, but 531 of 1,417 is 37.5% (editors' calculation; reporting issue 1). The printed exposed percentages otherwise match the counts. Odds ratios from matched case-control sampling estimate rate ratios; no absolute risks.
analysis.covariates: Per the unlabelled Figure footnote: SSRIs, other antidepressants, benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants; number of medications dispensed in the past 6 months; Charlson comorbidity index score; numbers of physicians and pharmacies prescribing and dispensing opioids in the past 6 months; receipt of a long-acting opioid during the exposure window; opioid dose; and recent gabapentin exposure (Figure title).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. NSAIDs are called a 'predefined' control exposure; the study protocol and statistical code are said to be available from the corresponding author, and the dataset to people who meet access criteria at ICES (Reproducible Research Statement, p. 3). Research Ethics Board approval is from Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre.
analysis.selective_reporting: The sub-analysis matched on other CNS depressants is shown only as exposed counts and odds ratios; no full model, no trend test across dose groups, and no test of interaction with opioid dose or benzodiazepines, although the Discussion advises caution when the dose of either drug class is high.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the high-dose estimate rests on 17 exposed cases and 25 exposed controls and has a wide interval.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among Ontario public-plan opioid recipients, people who died of an opioid-related cause were more often than matched living opioid recipients dispensed pregabalin in the previous 120 days (4.9% against 3.0%; adjusted odds ratio 1.68, 95% CI 1.19-2.36, from 69 exposed cases). Estimates were similar when pregabalin supply overlapped the death date (1.81) and in a sub-analysis matched on other CNS depressants (2.00); higher above 300 mg/day (2.51, from 17 exposed cases) than at or below it (1.52), with overlapping intervals; and null for NSAIDs (1.04).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says the study found 'compelling evidence for a potentially life-threatening drug–drug interaction' between pregabalin and opioids, like the same team's earlier gabapentin finding; recommends caution when coprescribing gabapentinoids with opioids, 'particularly when the dose of either drug class is high'; and says the finding warrants revising the pregabalin product monographs. Gaps: (1) the design compares pregabalin plus opioid with opioid alone, among people already taking opioids, so it can show an association but cannot show an interaction (a combined effect different from the drugs' separate effects) or a cause; (2) 'compelling' is strong for an adjusted odds ratio whose interval starts at 1.19, from 69 exposed cases, with pregabalin prescribed to people with pain or anxiety that the data do not capture; (3) the NSAID result addresses pain severity only in part, not non-prescribed drug use or the indication for pregabalin; (4) 'dose-response' rests on two dose groups with widely overlapping intervals (2.51, 1.24-5.06 against 1.52, 1.04-2.22) and no trend test, while the advice about opioid dose was not tested; (5) the letter has no limitations section.

timeline.event: Gomes and colleagues (PLOS Med), the same team and data source, gabapentin in Ontario opioid recipients: adjusted OR 1.49 (95% CI 1.18-1.88) for recent gabapentin against none; this letter's methods are said to follow it, and cases from 1997 to 2013 are probably shared

Macleod and colleagues (PLOS Med), UK people in methadone or buprenorphine treatment: gabapentinoid prescription not clearly associated with drug-poisoning death (hazard ratio 1.54, 0.60-3.98; 5 deaths) but associated with deaths from other causes (1.83), a different population and too small for drug-poisoning deaths

replication.where_it_stands: The pregabalin estimate (1.68) is close to the same team's gabapentin estimate (1.49) in an overlapping data source and period, so the two are consistent but not independent. The only other study read for the class (the UK treatment cohort) is a different population and too small to confirm or contradict. No independent replication in people prescribed opioid analgesics has been read.

funding.funder: Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care (grant 06673); a note says the funding source had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript; a disclaimer says the results are the authors' and that no endorsement by ICES, the Ministry or the Canadian Institute for Health Information is intended (p. 2).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not stated in the PDF: it gives a web link to the journal's disclosure forms, which was not opened (p. 2).
funding.affiliations_note: Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute of St. Michael's Hospital, ICES and University of Toronto; Academic Medical Center, University of Amsterdam; Sunnybrook Research Institute; McMaster University.

what_would_settle_it: An active-comparator cohort of people on stable opioid therapy who newly start pregabalin against people who newly start a non-sedating adjuvant, with measured substance use disorders, ascertained outcomes, pregabalin dose over time, and an analysis that tests for a combined effect beyond the two drugs' separate effects (for example by including people prescribed pregabalin without opioids); or a self-controlled analysis of each person's periods on and off pregabalin.

domains.note: Matched on five factors and adjusted for recorded sedating medicines, comorbidity, prescribing patterns, long-acting opioids and opioid dose; adjustment moved the estimate little (1.85 to 1.68) and the NSAID control is null (1.04). Remaining: the indication for pregabalin, non-prescribed drug use and misuse (large imbalance on benzodiazepines, standard difference 0.45, adjusted only as recent receipt); matching used the Charlson score, not the 2017 study's disease risk index.
Any dispensing in 120 days from public-plan records; adherence and non-prescribed supply unknown; the overlapping-supply analysis gave a similar estimate (1.81).
Public drug-plan population; how controls were sampled is not stated in the letter; 218 cases are missing from the sub-analysis without explanation.
Not a concern for a 120-day window before death.
Records-based; the only missing variable shown is income (0.7% of cases, 0.6% of controls).

The letter defines cases only as opioid-related deaths excluding suicide and homicide; ascertainment and whether other sedating drugs were found are not described, and attribution could be likelier when a sedating medicine is known.
A short report; protocol available on request; all listed analyses are reported with counts, but there is no trend test, no interaction test and no limitations section.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The letter applies the same design as the 2017 gabapentin study (matching, adjustment for sedating co-medicines and opioid dose, a null negative-control exposure) to pregabalin, with the same unmeasured threats (the indication and non-prescribed drug use), and is too short to judge case ascertainment or control sampling from its own text. It may be cited for the adjusted association between recent pregabalin dispensing and opioid-related death among Ontario public-plan opioid recipients (adjusted OR 1.68, 69 exposed cases), with the dose and sub-analysis estimates described as imprecise and consistent in direction. It may not be cited for a causal interaction, a dose-response relation, absolute risk, or as independent of the gabapentin study.

key_findings.finding: Background and objective: pregabalin is an anticonvulsant increasingly prescribed as an adjunct for chronic pain; it can be sedating and may augment CNS depression in people also receiving opioids (cited to a pharmacology comparison); the same team's earlier study found concomitant opioid and gabapentin use associated with opioid-related death; the objective is to examine the risk of opioid-related death among people coprescribed pregabalin and opioids.
key_findings.locator: Background, and Objective (before the Methods and Findings paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: A population-based nested case-control study of Ontario residents eligible for public drug coverage who received prescription opioids between 1 August 1997 and 31 December 2016; approved by the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre ethics board; methods, data sources and statistical analyses said to be consistent with the 2017 gabapentin study, with differences described.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Findings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cohort aged 15 to 105 with publicly funded opioid prescriptions; cases died of an opioid-related cause excluding suicide or homicide, with the index date the date of death; each case matched to up to 4 controls on age (within 3 years), sex, index year (within 1 year), chronic kidney disease (previous 5 years) and Charlson score (within 0.2 standard deviations); a sensitivity analysis also matched on recent benzodiazepine, antidepressant or other CNS depressant prescription.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Findings, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure and analysis: recent exposure is a pregabalin prescription in the 120 days before the index date; secondary dose analysis at 300 mg/day or less against above 300 mg/day; sensitivity analysis with supply overlapping the index date; NSAIDs as a predefined control exposure; conditional logistic regression adjusting for characteristics that remained imbalanced after matching.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Findings, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 1,417 cases were matched to 5,097 controls; cases were more likely to have recently been prescribed other CNS depressants, to receive more medications and to have more comorbidities. Table: benzodiazepines 75.7% of cases against 53.7% of controls (standard difference 0.45 after weighting), other antidepressants 49.9% against 38.7%, long-acting opioids 51.4% against 36.3%, 200 or more MME/day 27.0% against 16.2%, alcohol use disorder 23.9% against 20.4%; median age 48 and 49; median opioid use 8 years in both.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Findings, 4th paragraph (p. 1); Table (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: After multivariable adjustment, recent pregabalin was associated with increased odds of opioid-related death against opioids alone (adjusted OR 1.68, 95% CI 1.19-2.36); consistent results with overlapping use (1.81, 1.26-2.60) and matching on prior CNS depressant use (2.00, 1.39-2.88); above 300 mg/day 2.51 (1.24-5.06) and at or below 300 mg/day 1.52 (1.04-2.22); NSAIDs 1.04 (0.90-1.19), described as expected.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Findings, 5th paragraph (first paragraph of the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Figure: exposed case patients and exposed control participants, unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios: recent pregabalin 69 (4.9%) and 153 (3.0%), 1.85 and 1.68; overlapping 60 (4.2%) and 121 (2.4%), 2.03 and 1.81; CNS-depressant matched analysis 59 (4.9%) and 116 (3.0%) in 1,199 cases and 3,935 controls, 2.05 and 2.00; above 300 mg/day 17 (1.2%) and 25 (0.5%), 3.02 and 2.51; 300 mg/day or less 52 (3.7%) and 128 (2.5%), 1.74 and 1.52; NSAIDs 531 (34.5%) and 1,830 (35.9%), 1.07 and 1.04. All models adjusted for recent gabapentin exposure.
key_findings.locator: Figure (title, panels and footnotes)
key_findings.note: 531 of 1,417 is 37.5%, not 34.5% (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the authors say they found 'compelling evidence for a potentially life-threatening drug–drug interaction' like the earlier gabapentin finding; note that more than half of Ontario residents who start pregabalin are concurrently prescribed an opioid (cited to another study); recommend caution when coprescribing gabapentinoids with opioids, particularly at a high dose of either class; and say gabapentin product monographs warn about use with opioids while pregabalin's do not, which warrants revision.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Funding from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care (grant 06673), with a statement that the funder had no role; a note that Mr. Greaves had full access to all of the data; disclosures are by web link only.
key_findings.locator: Note; Disclaimer; Grant Support; Disclosures (end of page)

key_findings.finding: Reproducible Research Statement: the protocol and statistical code are available from the corresponding author; the dataset is available to people who meet prespecified criteria for confidential access through ICES.
key_findings.locator: Reproducible Research Statement

reporting_issues.issue: In the Figure, exposed case patients for NSAIDs print as 531 (34.5%), but 531 of 1,417 cases is 37.5%; the printed unadjusted odds ratio 1.07 matches 37.5% against the controls' 35.9% (a 34.5% share would give about 0.94), so the percentage appears to be a typographical error. The other printed percentages match their counts.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the conclusions, but it shows the Figure was not fully proofread; use the count.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says its methods and data sources are consistent with the 2017 gabapentin study and that differences are described, yet it words the case definition differently (an opioid-related cause with suicide and homicide excluded, against coroner-confirmed accidental opioid-related deaths in the 2017 card) and changes the matching (Charlson score and age within 3 years, against a disease risk index and age within 5 years), without saying how cases were ascertained or controls sampled. It reports 1,417 cases over 1997 to 2016, close to the 1,391 eligible (1,256 matched) over 1997 to 2013 in the 2017 study despite three more years, with no explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: How the two studies' cases overlap and how comparable their definitions are cannot be judged from the letter; treat the pregabalin result as not independent of the gabapentin one.

reporting_issues.issue: The text speaks of a dose-response analysis with two dose groups (above and at or below 300 mg/day) whose adjusted intervals overlap widely (2.51, 1.24-5.06 against 1.52, 1.04-2.22), describes the high-dose odds as 'markedly increased', and gives no trend test; the high-dose estimate rests on 17 exposed cases and 25 exposed controls.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose pattern is suggestive and imprecise; it cannot be cited as a dose-response relation.

reporting_issues.issue: The sub-analysis matched on other CNS depressant use contains 1,199 of 1,417 cases and 3,935 of 5,097 controls, which the text does not mention, and the Figure footnote does not say why cases were dropped; the text describes its results as consistent.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 15% of cases excluded may differ from the rest, so that sub-analysis is not a like-for-like check.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter states no limitations. It does not discuss the indication for pregabalin, non-prescribed drug use, the one-sided comparison among people already taking opioids, or generalisability beyond the public drug plan, although a standard difference of 0.45 for benzodiazepines remained after matching.
reporting_issues.consequence: The wording 'compelling evidence for a potentially life-threatening drug–drug interaction' is stronger than the design supports.

verification.source_read: Online-first PDF, 3 pages (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Gomes_2018_PregabalinOpioidDeath.pdf), full text: letter (p. 1), Table (p. 2), Figure, Reproducible Research Statement and references (p. 3); Table and Figure values checked on rendered pages. No supplement is included in the PDF; the disclosure forms linked on p. 2 were not opened.

design_detail: A 'For Debate' article in Addiction (2008;103:1060-1062; three pages, 26 references) by six researchers at the Universities of Bristol and Bath, arguing for a 'translational' approach (animal experiments to test hypotheses raised by epidemiology, then corroboration in clinical and population studies) with one case study: whether alcohol raises the risk of a heroin or opiate overdose through a pharmacological interaction. It is an argument and a short review of selected evidence, not a systematic review: no search, selection criteria or appraisal is described. It quotes figures from other papers (listed in its reference list) that were not read for this card. Read in full from the PDF, including the declaration of interest and reference list.
can_establish: What six researchers argued, in 2007 to 2008, the existing evidence on alcohol and opioid overdose death showed and did not show; which other explanations they thought fit the same evidence; and what kind of study they thought was needed.
cannot_establish: How strongly alcohol raises the risk of opioid overdose in people (no new data, no pooled estimate, no figure for risk); that the figures it quotes (alcohol in about half of heroin-related deaths, about a third of methadone-related deaths; 60% lower blood morphine when blood alcohol was above 100 mg/dl) are complete or accurate, because the underlying studies were not read; or that the evidence it describes is all the evidence there was.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (opinion and review article; no search described). Evidence quoted comes from post-mortem and audit studies of heroin and methadone deaths in the UK, Sweden, the United States and Australia, a hair-analysis study, and reviews.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The studies quoted were chosen by the authors to support a case for further research; the article does not say how many other studies exist or whether any found no relation between alcohol and opioid levels at post mortem. Post-mortem samples include only people who died, so they cannot show how often alcohol was present in people who used opioids and did not die.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Alcohol and opioid exposure is described as measured in the cited post-mortem studies (blood alcohol and blood morphine concentrations).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; a figure quoted from cited studies (blood alcohol above or below 100 mg/dl) is a post-mortem measurement, not a dose.
exposure.polysubstance: The article states that heroin or methadone were detected as sole agents in only a small proportion of deaths, with no figure; alcohol is described as the most common other substance detected.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The post-mortem studies it quotes compared dead people with high and low blood alcohol; no living comparison group is described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The article names the main alternatives itself: alcohol might impair judgement of tolerance and safe use; alcohol use is linked to heroin relapse; people who have stopped or reduced heroin may drink more, so low or falling tolerance could be the underlying problem; and polydrug use may mark people at higher risk for other reasons.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; the article does not mention post-mortem redistribution of drugs or other limits of post-mortem concentrations that the review by White and Irvine (1999) raises.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None of its own. Figures quoted from other papers: alcohol detected in about 50% of heroin-related deaths and about a third of methadone-related deaths (four cited sources); a significant inverse relation between blood alcohol and blood morphine at post mortem in multiple studies of heroin deaths (four cited); morphine blood concentrations 60% lower in heroin-related deaths with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl than below it in studies in the United States and Australia (two cited); opioid levels at autopsy often below the predicted fatal range for highly tolerant people (one hair-analysis study).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative article.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: An argued summary of post-mortem and audit data: opioid overdose deaths rarely involve a single drug; alcohol is the most common other substance; blood morphine tends to be lower when blood alcohol is higher; and morphine levels at autopsy are often below those expected in highly tolerant people. The authors say this pattern is consistent with a pharmacological interaction and is also consistent with lost or low tolerance, relapse, impaired judgement and shared risk factors, and that they cannot be told apart without experimental evidence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that people who drink may need less heroin to overdose, 'all other factors being equal', because of a pharmacological interaction; the text says the interaction 'remains unproven', that the effect of alcohol and heroin on breathing at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated systematically, and that animal experiments should test it. These claims are measured and the article states its own alternatives. One statement goes beyond its source: that overdose risk appears to rise after incarceration or detoxification, which it cites to White and Irvine (1999), who describe only a period of abstinence.

timeline.event: Ruttenber, Kalter and Santinga (J Forensic Sci): the role of ethanol in heroin-related death (as quoted by this article; not read)
Levine, Green and Smialek (J Forensic Sci), with Darke (1999): lower blood morphine with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl in heroin-related deaths (as quoted by this article; not read)
White and Irvine review the pharmacology of breathing depression and of loss of tolerance; the source this article cites for risk after a break in use

Lintzeris and colleagues, diazepam given with methadone or buprenorphine under high-dose conditions: named by this article as an example of a clinical challenge study of breathing (as quoted; not read)
This article

replication.where_it_stands: A position paper and secondary source. Its post-mortem facts trace to four to six earlier studies not read here; its main contribution is to state the evidence limits (an inverse blood alcohol and morphine pattern and frequent co-detection fit several explanations) and to call for experimental tests. It is a source for what was and was not established by 2008, not for the size of any effect.

funding.funder: No grants were involved in the writing (Declaration of interest, p. 1062).
funding.declared_conflicts: Several co-authors receive funding from the pharmaceutical industry for some of their research (Nutt, Lingford-Hughes, Henderson); no other agencies requested the paper (p. 1062).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Social Medicine, Community Psychiatry and Pharmacology at the University of Bristol, and Pharmacology at the University of Bath. One of the 26 references (reference 6, a London audit of overdose deaths) has the first author as first author. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Animal experiments of opioid and alcohol effects on breathing at realistic blood levels, linked human clinical challenge studies of breathing with and without alcohol, and epidemiological studies that test whether drinking tracks with reduced opioid use or relapse; and, as the article says, a controlled trial is unlikely to be feasible.

domains.note: No methods; the quoted studies were chosen by the authors to make a case.

It explains why observational associations can mislead and lists alternative explanations for the post-mortem pattern; it does not appraise the specific post-mortem studies it quotes or mention post-mortem redistribution of drugs.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: One of 26 references (a London audit of overdose deaths) is by the first author; it is cited for toxicology findings alongside other sources.
Consistently worded as 'consistent with', 'may' and 'remains unproven'; hypotheses and evidence are kept apart.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the main conclusions
domains.note: It sets out alternatives to the interaction hypothesis well, but cites only studies that found an inverse relation or frequent co-detection of alcohol, and does not say whether any studies found otherwise.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative article (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The article is careful about what its evidence does not show, but it has no search method, quotes figures from papers not read here, and is an argument for a research approach. It may be cited for what the authors said was and was not established in 2008, for its list of alternative explanations, and for the facts it quotes with their sources, flagged as second-hand. It may not be cited for the size of any alcohol effect on opioid overdose risk, for the safety or danger of any level of drinking, or for a statement about incarceration or detoxification, which it attributes to White and Irvine and they do not make.

key_findings.finding: The abstract argues for a translational approach using one case study. It says the positive epidemiological evidence is that opiate overdose deaths rarely involve a single drug, that alcohol is the most common other drug involved, that blood alcohol and morphine concentrations at post mortem are inversely related, and that post-mortem morphine levels are often below those expected for highly tolerant people. It says this is consistent with the hypothesis of a pharmacological interaction but does not rule out other causal and non-causal pathways, such as alcohol being linked with lower tolerance or being confounded by other factors; experimental evidence is needed, unlikely to come from further epidemiology or randomised trials.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: Overdose is described as the main cause of excess mortality linked with injection opiate use in the UK and many other countries; risk 'appears to be increased' after periods of relative abstinence, for example after incarceration or detoxification, 'probably because tolerance is decreased' (cited to White and Irvine, 1999). Many reviews suggest that concomitant use of other depressant drugs, particularly alcohol, raises the risk of fatal opiate overdose.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: White and Irvine mention a period of abstinence and naltrexone treatment only; they do not mention incarceration or detoxification.

key_findings.finding: Toxicology shows substantial polydrug use, with heroin or methadone detected alone in only a small proportion of deaths. Alcohol is the most commonly detected substance in heroin-related deaths (about 50%) and in approximately a third of methadone-related deaths (cited to four sources); multiple studies of heroin deaths report a significant inverse relation between blood alcohol and blood morphine at post mortem; studies in the United States and Australia found blood morphine 60% lower with blood alcohol above 100 mg/dl than below it; autopsy opioid levels in people with a history of dependent heroin use were often below the predicted fatal range for highly tolerant people; alcohol levels at post mortem were not particularly high.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The prevailing interpretation is that alcohol and opiates have additive or interactive effects on breathing so that less heroin is needed for a fatal overdose. The authors list other routes: alcohol may impair judgement of tolerance and safe levels; alcohol use is associated with heroin relapse; people who have stopped or are reducing heroin may drink more, so low or falling tolerance could be the underlying problem; and polydrug use may mark people at risk for other reasons. They say the issue of causality matters because it changes how to intervene.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 3rd paragraph (p. 1061, left column)

key_findings.finding: Observational epidemiology and case series have a history of producing associations later found misleading, even when repeated across studies and backed by a plausible mechanism (hormone replacement therapy and heart disease given as an example); observational evidence generates hypotheses but is poorly placed to test them; a controlled trial of alcohol and fatal overdose risk would be challenging and raises practical and ethical issues.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Euphoric and breathing-depressant effects of morphine and heroin both come from mu-opioid receptor activation, and tolerance to breathing depression has been seen in animals and humans; studies of whether alcohol in turn affects mu-receptor function are 'extremely limited'; the effect of alcohol with heroin on breathing at realistic levels of drinking 'has not been evaluated systematically' and a pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic interaction 'remains unproven'.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Proposal: animal experiments to test whether alcohol changes opioid effects on breathing, translated to human relevance through linked clinical challenge studies (one example cited is diazepam given with methadone or buprenorphine) and epidemiological studies of whether drinking tracks with reduced heroin use or relapse; animal evidence alone, even if replicated, would be insufficient to direct public health action.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 5th paragraph (end of p. 1061) and 7th paragraph (pp. 1061–1062)

key_findings.finding: A prevention message aimed at drinking around opioid use would differ from one aimed at loss of tolerance and relapse; the authors say which applies matters for how alcohol use is managed in people who use opioids.
key_findings.locator: Main text, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: A further unanswered question named: to what extent and for how long opiate substitution drugs confer tolerance to the breathing depression of heroin, i.e., how long patients are protected if they relapse or take heroin on top of a prescription.
key_findings.locator: Main text, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Declaration of interest: several co-authors receive funding from the pharmaceutical industry for some of their research; no grants were involved in the writing of the paper.
key_findings.locator: Declaration of interest

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that overdose risk appears to rise after incarceration or detoxification is cited to White and Irvine (1999), but that review describes only 'a period of abstinence' and naltrexone treatment; it does not mention prison release or detoxification.
reporting_issues.consequence: The specific settings are the present authors' addition; cite White and Irvine only for the general idea of lost tolerance.

reporting_issues.issue: The figures for alcohol in heroin-related deaths (about 50%), methadone-related deaths (about a third), the inverse relation with blood morphine and the 60% lower morphine level are given without sample sizes or years, as reference numbers only (the 60% figure names only the United States and Australia).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures can be used only as quoted, with the sources listed; the studies were not read here.

reporting_issues.issue: Post-mortem blood concentrations are used as evidence of dose and interaction without mentioning that they may not reflect the situation at the time of death (post-mortem redistribution, time to sampling, site), a limit that White and Irvine (1999) state.
reporting_issues.consequence: The inverse blood alcohol and morphine relation may be partly a post-mortem artefact as well as a tolerance or interaction effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the epidemiological evidence is 'consistent with the hypothesis' of an interaction 'all other factors being equal', while the text says the effect on breathing at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated; the 'all other factors being equal' condition is not one that post-mortem data can show.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read the abstract's sentence as a statement about consistency, not as support for an effect; whether other factors were equal cannot be told from post-mortem data.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1060-1062 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Hickman_2008_AlcoholOverdoseDeathTranslational.pdf), full text including abstract, declaration of interest and reference list. The cited primary studies were not read.

design_detail: Repeated annual national surveillance analysis, 2004 to 2011, of two separate series. (1) Emergency department (ED) visits related to nonmedical use of opioid analgesics, benzodiazepines, or both, from the public use files of the Drug Abuse Warning Network (DAWN ED; weighted national estimates; the authors say the sample was designed and weighted to represent the US population and refer to other reports for details). DAWN defines nonmedical use as taking more than the recommended dose, taking a drug prescribed for another person, drug-facilitated assault, or documented misuse or abuse. (2) Overdose deaths from the National Vital Statistics System multiple cause-of-death file (death certificates): underlying cause drug poisoning (ICD-10 X40-X44, X60-X64, X85, Y10-Y14, so all intents), with opioid analgesics counted from contributing-cause codes T40.2-T40.4 and benzodiazepines from T42.4; 'combined' means both codes appear. Counts were converted to rates per 100,000 population (US Census estimates); trends were fitted by Joinpoint regression and summarised as average annual percentage change (AAPC); DAWN used SPSS Complex Samples. Analyses ran from March to June 2014. Read in full from the PDF (Am J Prev Med 2015;49:493-501); Table 1 (p. 496) and Table 2 (p. 498) checked on rendered pages for minus signs and row values; Figures 1 to 3 are images and no values were read from them.
can_establish: How many US ED visits related to nonmedical use, and how many overdose deaths, named both an opioid analgesic and a benzodiazepine in each year from 2004 to 2011; how those counts and rates changed and how they differed by sex, age group and race/ethnicity; and what share of opioid analgesic overdose deaths named a benzodiazepine.
cannot_establish: Whether taking the two drugs together raises the chance of an ED visit or death, or by how much (there is no count of people taking each drug alone or together, so no rate per person and no comparison group); whether both drugs were taken at the same time, in what amounts, or prescribed to the person; whether the rise reflects more combined use, more testing and recording, or more nonmedical use; anything about people taking prescribed medicines as directed in the ED series (it counts only nonmedical use); the 25% of overdose death certificates that name no drug.

sample.recruitment: No recruitment: DAWN ED public use files for 2004-2011 (the last year DAWN collected data) and the National Vital Statistics System multiple cause-of-death file for 2004-2011 (Methods > Data Sources and Study Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: ED: visits the medical record linked to recent drug use that documented nonmedical use of an opioid analgesic, a benzodiazepine, or both; up to 20 drugs per visit; drugs listed in the record but unrelated to the visit are not recorded; alcohol counts only when combined with a pharmaceutical or illicit drug at age 21 or over, or alone under 21. Deaths: drug poisoning as underlying cause with the named drug codes among contributing causes. Estimates were suppressed when the unweighted ED count was under 30, the estimate under 30 or the relative standard error over 50%, and death counts under 20 (Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: About 25% of overdose death certificates do not specify the drugs involved, so death counts are probably underestimates; about 15% of ED records each year lack race/ethnicity (Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Suppressed cells: Table 1 non-Hispanic black 2006; Table 2 ages 12 to 17 in 2005.
sample.demographics: 2011 ED visit rates per 100,000: males 35.5, females 32.9; ages 25 to 34 years 79.8 and 18 to 24 years 54.5; non-Hispanic white 45.1, non-Hispanic black 21.0, Hispanic 5.1. 2011 death rates per 100,000: overall 1.7; males 1.9, females 1.4; ages 45 to 54 years 3.4 and 35 to 44 years 3.1; non-Hispanic white 2.3, non-Hispanic black and Hispanic 0.5 each (Results; Tables 1 and 2). Other race/ethnicity groups were not analysed.
sample.selection_effects: Neither series is a sample of people taking the drugs. ED visits enter only if staff documented nonmedical use as related to the visit (the authors say this requirement likely led to underestimation); deaths enter only if the certificate names the drugs, which depends on whether toxicology was done and recorded (Limitations).

exposure.measurement: Drug involvement as coded from ED medical records (DAWN; staff judgment of which drugs were related to the visit) and from cause-of-death codes on certificates (T40.2-T40.4 opioid analgesics; T42.4 benzodiazepines). The two classes are 'combined' when both are listed; nothing records timing, amount, route, or whether the drug was prescribed to the person.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Up to 20 drugs per ED visit and several causes per certificate; the paper does not say whether other drugs or alcohol were excluded from the comparison groups 'opioid analgesics without benzodiazepines' and 'benzodiazepines without opioid analgesics'.

comparison.controls: No unexposed or population comparison. The paper compares trends for visits and deaths naming both drug classes with those naming each class without the other; nobody is followed, so there is no rate of harm per person taking each drug.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a descriptive analysis. The Introduction (4th paragraph) states that people receiving both drug classes differ from people receiving opioids alone (longer and higher-dose opioid treatment, more often a history of substance use disorder and depression), and that benzodiazepine use may be both a marker of high risk and a partial explanation of it.

outcomes.instruments: DAWN ED case definition and coding of drug involvement; ICD-10 underlying and contributing cause-of-death codes.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state that medical records vary in accuracy and detail, that ED staff judged which drugs were related to the visit so unrelated drugs may be included, that the nonmedical use definition was deliberately broad and not identical to that of other national surveys, and that about 25% of death certificates name no drug (Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Annual counts and rates per 100,000 population for visits and deaths naming both classes, by sex, seven age groups and three race/ethnicity groups; the share of opioid analgesic events naming a benzodiazepine and of benzodiazepine events naming an opioid analgesic.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. About 34 trend tests are reported (13 groups in each of Tables 1 and 2, four percentage trends in Figure 3 and four trends for single-drug groups); the Joinpoint permutation method applies to choosing joinpoints, not to the number of groups tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Visits naming both drug classes: 11.0 per 100,000 in 2004 to 34.2 in 2011 (AAPC 19.1%, 95% CI 15.5-22.8; p-trend < 0.0001; weighted visits 32,112 to 106,425). Deaths naming both: 0.6 to 1.7 per 100,000 (AAPC 15.0%, 12.3-17.9; 1,816 to 5,188 deaths). Comparison groups: ED visits AAPC 12.6% (9.0-16.3) for opioid analgesics without benzodiazepines and 11.4% (8.4-14.4) for benzodiazepines without opioid analgesics; deaths 5.1% (4.4-5.8) and 8.9% (6.8-11.0). Benzodiazepines were named in 18.4% (2004) to 31% (2011) of opioid analgesic overdose deaths (p-trend < 0.0001) and in 22% to 28% of opioid nonmedical-use ED visits (p = 0.0055); opioid analgesics in 69% to 75% of benzodiazepine overdose deaths (p = 0.0017) and 22% to 30% of benzodiazepine ED visits (p = 0.0017). No intervals are given for annual rates. Editors' checks: the sexes sum to the overall death count in every year of Table 2 and to the overall ED estimate in 2008 and 2011 (other years differ by 4 to 102 visits, up to 0.2%); rates match counts divided by US population (2011 ED: 106,425 at 34.2 per 100,000 implies 311 million).
analysis.covariates: None (descriptive trend analysis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Demographic breakdowns are given only for the combined group, not for the single-drug groups; nothing is analysed by opioid type, by whether the drug was prescribed to the person, or by intent of death.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the 12-to-17 group has small counts (23 to 39 deaths a year) and an unstable ED series (3,227 visits in 2010 and 1,770 in 2011).

interpretation_gap.results_show: From 2004 to 2011 in the US, the annual count and rate of nonmedical-use ED visits, and of overdose deaths, whose records name both an opioid analgesic and a benzodiazepine rose several-fold (ED visits 11.0 to 34.2 per 100,000; deaths 0.6 to 1.7), faster than records naming either class without the other. Benzodiazepines were named in 18.4% of opioid analgesic overdose deaths in 2004 and 31% in 2011. In 2011 rates were highest in ages 25 to 34 (ED visits) and 45 to 54 (deaths) and in non-Hispanic white people; death rates levelled off from 2010 to 2011 in several groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion says the study expands the literature 'by highlighting the increasing harms resulting from combined opioid and benzodiazepine use', that the rise in opioid-related deaths from 2006 to 2011 appears to be driven largely by deaths involving both drugs (a point from another analysis, a 2014 data brief), and that the findings are 'not surprising' given 'synergistic respiratory depressant effects' (citing the White and Irvine review). The conclusions describe an increasing public health burden of co-ingestion and call for prescriber and public awareness, prescription monitoring and drug utilization review. Gaps: (1) counts and population rates do not show a rising risk per person taking the drugs, since there are no denominators of people prescribed or taking each drug and prescribing of both rose over the period (the authors name the denominator limit); (2) 'combined use' means both drugs are named on a record, not that they were taken together; (3) the death series has all intents and cannot separate prescribed from nonmedical use, while the ED series counts only nonmedical use, so the two series are not measuring the same thing; (4) more testing and fuller certificates could raise counts without a change in events, and about 25% of certificates name no drug; (5) the paper's own Introduction says benzodiazepine use may be a marker of high risk, which this design cannot separate from a contribution; (6) the synergy statement rests on a narrative review.

timeline.event: Gomes and colleagues (Arch Intern Med), a Canadian study as quoted by this paper (not read): among people aged 15 to 64 prescribed an opioid for non-cancer pain, 60.4% of those with an opioid-related death also had benzodiazepines detected on toxicology

Peirce and colleagues (Med Care), West Virginia overdose decedents, as quoted by this paper (not read): drug-related death was threefold likelier with a filled opioid prescription in the past 6 months, sevenfold with a benzodiazepine prescription and almost 15-fold with both, against neither

Chen and colleagues (National Center for Health Statistics data brief), as quoted by this paper (not read): from 2006 to 2011 opioid overdose deaths involving benzodiazepines rose 14% a year on average while opioid analgesic overdose deaths not involving benzodiazepines did not change significantly
Park and colleagues (BMJ), US veterans on opioid analgesics: 49% of overdose deaths occurred during a benzodiazepine prescription, a prescription-based measure
Gomes and colleagues (PLOS Med), Ontario public-plan opioid recipients: 77.3% of accidental opioid-related deaths had a benzodiazepine dispensed in the prior 120 days, a prescription-based measure

Tori and colleagues (JAMA Netw Open), the same US death-certificate source for 1999 to 2017 and all opioid types: benzodiazepines named in 8.7% of opioid overdose deaths in 1999, 26.2% in 2010 and 21.0% in 2017

replication.where_it_stands: The rise to 2010 and 2011 in the death series is reproduced by Tori and colleagues, who also show a later fall in the certificate share; but they use the same national certificates, so this is a re-analysis, not an independent replication, and their denominator (all opioid deaths) differs from this paper's (opioid analgesics). Prescription-based studies (Park; Gomes 2017) find benzodiazepines present or prescribed in about half or more of opioid deaths among people prescribed opioids. The ED series has no later replication read. The paper's data end in 2011.

funding.funder: Not stated; both authors are employed by the US Food and Drug Administration (Office of the Commissioner; Center for Drug Evaluation and Research).
funding.declared_conflicts: 'No financial disclosures were reported by the authors of this paper'; the paper states that the conclusions are the authors' and not the official position of the Food and Drug Administration (p. 501).
funding.affiliations_note: US Food and Drug Administration, Silver Spring, Maryland.

what_would_settle_it: Person-level data with denominators: a cohort of people prescribed opioid analgesics, with and without a benzodiazepine prescription, followed for ED visits and deaths, with doses and timing from dispensing records, adjustment for illness and other drugs, and toxicology on every death, so that changes in occurrence can be told from changes in testing and recording.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: A national death-certificate file and a national ED survey are the right frames for counts of visits and deaths naming both drug classes.
Deaths are a census of certificates; DAWN is a weighted sample whose design is described only by reference to other reports.
27,920 deaths and weighted estimates of over half a million visits across eight years; small cells (ages 12 to 17; some race/ethnicity years) were suppressed or unstable.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sex, seven age groups and three race/ethnicity groups are reported; intent of death, opioid type, other drugs and whether the drug was prescribed to the person are not; about 15% of ED records lack race/ethnicity.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: About 25% of overdose certificates name no drug, so deaths are undercounted by an unknown amount that may change over time; suppressed cells.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Nonmedical use depends on documentation in the ED record and was defined broadly; certificate codes show a drug was named, not that it caused the death or was taken with the other; no validation is reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The authors state that medical records vary in accuracy and detail, that ED staff decided which drugs were related to the visit, and that death certificates are incompletely specified; whether this varied across years or places is not examined, so trends may partly reflect recording.

Joinpoint regression with complex-sample methods suits trend description, but there are about 34 trend tests without correction, no intervals on annual rates, no test of the difference between AAPCs (19.1% against 12.6% for ED visits has overlapping intervals), and no person-level denominators.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Hospital participation in DAWN is not reported in the paper.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of how many ED visits and certified deaths named both drug classes, the counts are probably reasonable but are floors, and part of the rise may reflect more testing and recording. The paper may be cited for the counts, the trend and the share of opioid analgesic overdose deaths that named a benzodiazepine (18.4% in 2004, 31% in 2011), with the limits stated.
