It may not be cited for how much risk the combination adds, for harm 'resulting from' combined use, or as independent of the later Tori analysis of the same certificates.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: nonmedical-use ED visits naming both opioid analgesics and benzodiazepines rose from 11.0 to 34.2 per 100,000 population from 2004 to 2011, and overdose deaths naming both from 0.6 to 1.7 per 100,000; increases were significant in males and females, all three race/ethnicity groups and all age groups except 12 to 17; benzodiazepines were named in 18% of opioid analgesic overdose deaths in 2004 and 31% in 2011.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results)

key_findings.finding: Context from other studies, as quoted by the authors: West Virginia decedents who filled opioid prescriptions had a threefold increased risk of a drug-related death, benzodiazepine prescriptions sevenfold and both almost 15-fold, against neither; a Canadian study found 60.4% of opioid-related deaths among people prescribed opioids for non-cancer pain also had benzodiazepines on toxicology.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepines are said to rarely cause clinically significant respiratory depression alone; with opioids they 'can result in synergistic respiratory depression' (citing two reviews; the GABA statement cites the White and Irvine review), but the exact mechanisms are 'not fully understood'.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors note that people prescribed both drug classes differ from people prescribed opioids alone (opioids for longer and at higher doses; more often a history of substance use disorder and depression; 46% of admissions to publicly funded treatment programmes for benzodiazepine and opioid problems with a co-occurring psychiatric disorder, against 28% of other admissions) and write that benzodiazepine use may both act as a marker for people at high risk of opioid overdose and partially explain the risk.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sources and definitions: DAWN ED public use files 2004 to 2011 (nonmedical use defined as higher-than-recommended dose, a drug prescribed for another person, drug-facilitated assault, or documented misuse or abuse; up to 20 drugs per visit); National Vital Statistics System death certificates with underlying cause drug poisoning (X40-X44, X60-X64, X85, Y10-Y14) and contributing-cause codes T40.2-T40.4 (opioid analgesics) and T42.4 (benzodiazepines); combined deaths have both codes.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Data Sources and Study Population, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Counts were converted to rates per 100,000 population with US Census estimates; ED visits and deaths were broken down by sex, seven age groups and three race/ethnicity groups.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Measures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Analysis: SPSS Complex Samples for DAWN; ED estimates suppressed when the unweighted count was under 30, the estimate under 30 or the relative standard error over 50%, and death counts under 20; Joinpoint regression and the average annual percentage change (AAPC) for trends overall and by group.
key_findings.locator: Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Overall, the ED visit rate rose from 11.0 to 34.2 per 100,000 (AAPC 19.1%, 95% CI 15.5-22.8) and the death rate from 0.6 to 1.7 per 100,000 (AAPC 15.0%, 12.3-17.9), both p-trend < 0.0001.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2 (pp. 496, 498)

key_findings.finding: AAPCs for visits and deaths naming both drugs were larger than for either class without the other: ED visits 19.1% against 12.6% (opioid analgesics without benzodiazepines) and 11.4% (benzodiazepines without opioid analgesics); deaths 15.0% against 5.1% and 8.9%. No test of the differences is reported.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Figures 1 and 2 (p. 499, images)

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine involvement in opioid analgesic overdose deaths rose from 18.4% to 31% (p-trend < 0.0001) and in opioid nonmedical-use ED visits from 22% to 28%; opioid involvement in benzodiazepine overdose deaths rose from 69% to 75% and in benzodiazepine ED visits from 22% to 30%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph (begins p. 495); Figure 3 (p. 500, image)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the authors say the rise in opioid-related deaths from 2006 to 2011 appears to be driven largely by deaths involving both drugs, citing a 2014 data brief (not read), and that findings are not surprising given synergistic respiratory depressant effects (citing the White and Irvine review), rising opioid prescribing and widespread co-prescribing, including a survey figure of 12.0% a year growth in opioid and benzodiazepine co-prescription in US primary care (cited to a 2014 J Pain supplement page, S41).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: 2011 ED rates were similar in males and females but the male death rate was 1.4 times the female rate; people aged 25 to 54 had the highest rates; non-Hispanic white people had the highest rates of both outcomes. Encouraging signs named: ages 12 to 17 had the lowest rates and a stable death rate, and death rates levelled between 2010 and 2011 in some groups (male rate 2.0 to 1.9); the authors say more years of data are needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 498)

key_findings.finding: Limitations: about 25% of overdose certificates name no drug, so deaths are likely underestimated; population denominators do not account for differences in drug use across groups or over time; DAWN records vary in accuracy and detail, about 15% lack race/ethnicity, the nonmedical use definition was deliberately broad, and requiring documentation of nonmedical use likely led to underestimation of visits.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the study describes the increasing public health burden of opioid analgesic and benzodiazepine co-ingestion; readily available interventions named are prescription drug monitoring programs, insurer drug utilization review, and provider and patient education.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2, ages 18 to 24: the AAPC prints as 11.1 with 95% CI (12.9, 22.7), an interval that cannot contain its own estimate and is identical to the interval printed for ages 25 to 34 (17.7; 12.9, 22.7). The counts and rates in the row (rate 0.7 in 2004 to 1.5 in 2011) imply an average annual rise of roughly 11%, so the estimate looks right and the interval looks copied.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval for this age group is unreliable; confirmed on a rendered page, so it is not an extraction error.

reporting_issues.issue: The ED series split by sex is irregular while the overall series is smooth: the male rate is 17.3 against 13.5 for females in 2006, and the female rate 29.7 against 22.4 for males in 2008, whereas the sexes are within about 1 to 3 per 100,000 in most other years; the male count rises 30,442 to 33,477 in 2008 and then to 48,254 in 2009, while the female count rises 29,643 to 45,947 in 2008 and then falls to 45,651. The paper does not comment.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex-specific ED trends (AAPC 19.0% and 18.5%) rest on irregular annual values; the sex breakdown of the ED series should be used with caution.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results and Discussion say the AAPC for ED visits naming both drugs (19.1%, 15.5-22.8) was greater than for opioid analgesics without benzodiazepines (12.6%, 9.0-16.3) and the Discussion says it was greater for 'either drug class individually'; the two intervals overlap and no test of the difference is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: For ED visits the faster rise for the combined group against opioid analgesics alone is a difference in point estimates; for deaths the intervals do not overlap.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract speak of deaths 'from combined use', but the deaths counted are those with both drug codes among the causes on the certificate; the paper has no information on timing, amounts, route, whether the drugs were prescribed to the person, or whether the drugs were taken together.
reporting_issues.consequence: Describe the deaths as certificates naming both drug classes, not as deaths from combined use.

reporting_issues.issue: The ED series counts only visits with documented nonmedical use, while the death series counts all intents and all sources of the drugs, but the Discussion presents them as 'parallel increases' of the same kind of harm.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two series cannot be added or compared like with like; the ED series says nothing about people taking prescribed medicines as directed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the 2006 to 2011 rise in opioid-related deaths 'appears to be driven largely' by deaths involving both drugs is taken from another analysis (a 2014 data brief, not read) and is not tested here; this paper reports no opioid-only death series by year except the AAPC of 5.1% for deaths naming opioid analgesics without benzodiazepines.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the data brief for that statement, not this paper.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 493-501 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Jones_2015_OpioidBenzodiazepineEDVisitsDeaths.pdf), full text including abstract, Methods, Results, Discussion, Tables 1 and 2, figure legends, Limitations, Conclusions, disclosure and reference list; Table 1 (p. 496) and Table 2 (p. 498) checked on rendered pages; Figures 1 to 3 are images and no values were read from them.

design_detail: Double-blind, within-person, placebo-controlled laboratory study in 8 adults with DSM-IV cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse who were already using both drugs together, on an inpatient unit in New Haven, Connecticut (Yale Psychiatric Institute or the Connecticut Mental Health Center). Each person attended three 480-minute sessions in random order, at least 2 days apart: four doses of intranasal cocaine with oral alcohol, the same cocaine with a placebo drink, or a placebo powder with the same alcohol. Heart rate, blood pressure, ratings of drug effects and blood levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol were followed for 8 hours. Read in full from the PDF (Biol Psychiatry 1998;44:250-259); Table 1 and the heart-rate figure with its legend were checked on rendered pages. Figures 2 to 4 are images: their values were not used except the areas under the curve printed in the legend of Figure 1.
can_establish: Whether, in these 8 people under these conditions, adding alcohol to repeated intranasal cocaine changed heart rate, blood pressure, ratings of high and well-being, and the blood levels of cocaine and its alcohol-linked metabolite cocaethylene, compared with each drug alone.
cannot_establish: Anything about heart attacks, rhythm disturbances or other harm (none was measured); whether the combination leads people to take more (no self-administration or choice procedure); effects of smoked or injected cocaine, of other doses or sequences of dosing, or of the combination in people with other drinking patterns; whether the combination adds more than the sum of its parts (no test of additivity); blood-pressure effects, which this sample could not detect.

sample.recruitment: Non-treatment-seeking volunteers recruited by word of mouth or newspaper advertisement and paid for taking part (Methods and Materials > Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Actively using cocaine and alcohol together at entry, with cocaine as the preferred drug; DSM-IV cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse; full psychiatric and medical evaluation; one person also met criteria for cannabis abuse and no other substance use or psychiatric disorder was present. Participants were told to abstain from drugs and alcohol for 3 days before admission, had a urine drug screen and breathalyzer on admission, and were watched for alcohol withdrawal for 2 days (Subjects; Procedures).
sample.demographics: Mean age 33 years (SE 4); 4 men and 4 women; 7 African-American and 1 Caucasian. Printed usual intake: cocaine about 5 g a week (SE 7) by the smoked route and alcohol 14 standard drinks a week (SE 50), figures whose spread is implausible as printed (reporting issue 1).
sample.attrition: Not reported; every analysis appears to include all 8 people, but completion of all three sessions is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Eight paid volunteers who already used both drugs together, chosen on purpose so that nobody met a new combination (Discussion, p. 257). They usually smoked cocaine but received it intranasally, so results come from people with tolerance to both drugs and may not carry over to people who use the drugs less often or by other routes; the authors say the intranasal route probably understates effects seen with smoked or injected cocaine.

exposure.measurement: Study-administered drugs, dosed by lean body weight; blood concentrations of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol measured by liquid and gas chromatography with reproducibility below 5%.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: cocaine hydrochloride powder 1 mg/kg intranasally at 0, 30, 60 and 90 minutes; oral alcohol 1 g/kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg/kg at 60 minutes, calculated to hold plasma alcohol near 100 mg/dL during the cocaine doses; the third session used lactose in place of cocaine and the second a placebo drink in place of alcohol (Study Design). Plasma alcohol 30 minutes after the second drink averaged 99 mg/dL (SE 7) with cocaine and 118 (SE 10) without.
exposure.polysubstance: One participant also met cannabis abuse criteria; no urine results on admission are reported beyond the screen having been done; other substances were not tested during sessions.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Told to abstain for 3 days before admission and checked by urine screen and breathalyzer; watched for withdrawal for 2 days.

comparison.controls: Within-person: each participant received all three conditions (cocaine with alcohol; cocaine with placebo alcohol; placebo cocaine with alcohol) in random order, double-blind, sessions at least 2 days apart. There was no session with placebo for both drugs, so each single-drug condition is compared with the combination, not with nothing.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to within-person contrasts, but tolerance, usual dose and craving differ between people and were not analysed as moderators; the authors raise whether people who use both drugs differ from people who use cocaine alone as an open question.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Everyone already used both drugs together; one also met cannabis abuse criteria; no comparison group of people who use cocaine only.

outcomes.instruments: Heart rate and blood pressure by automated monitor (Hewlett-Packard 43200A) with cardiac rhythm monitoring until 3 hours after the last cocaine dose; 100-mm visual analogue scales for any high, rush, sleepy, paranoid, sad or depressed, crash, desire for cocaine and feel good; a five-anchor rating of the quality of the cocaine high; clinician-rated analogue scales; plasma cocaine and cocaethylene by reverse-phase liquid chromatography; plasma alcohol by gas chromatography.
outcomes.validity_norms: Assays cite earlier validation; the analogue scales are standard in laboratory work. Clinician ratings were collected to confirm drug effects but are not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: For each measure, the area under the curve (AUC) over the session, compared between the combination and each single drug by planned comparisons; pharmacokinetic values (peak, half-life, AUC) from a multiple-dose one-compartment model compared by paired t test.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: one set of planned one-tailed comparisons for each of 15 measures (heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure, eight ratings, plasma cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol), justified by directional hypotheses taken from the authors' earlier study (Data Analysis, p. 252).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Described as double-blind; how the alcohol and cocaine placebos were masked, and whether participants could tell the conditions apart, is not described. Participants knew the three possible conditions, and both intranasal cocaine and 1 g/kg of alcohol are noticeable in people who take them regularly.

analysis.effect_sizes: Heart rate (repeated-measures ANOVA on AUC; planned comparisons, one-tailed): combination higher than cocaine alone, p = .002, and than alcohol alone, p = .002. Printed heart-rate AUCs (mean, SEM; beats per minute x minutes, 0 to 480 min): combination 40,289 (940), cocaine 35,658 (647), alcohol 34,778 (933); editors' calculation (AUC / 480): mean 83.9, 74.3 and 72.5 beats per minute, a difference of 9.7 against cocaine alone and 11.5 against alcohol alone. Blood pressure: no significant difference between the combination and cocaine alone; combination higher than alcohol alone for systolic (p = .008) and diastolic (p = .003) pressure. Ratings: feel good higher with the combination than with cocaine alone, p = .04; any high p = .09 (not significant); the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone and was higher than with alcohol alone, p = .002; rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed and desire for cocaine showed no significant differences. Cocaine: peak 893 ng/mL (SEM 114) with alcohol against 754 (114); AUC 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, printed as about 15% greater, p = .035; half-life 85 (3.2) against 83 (2.9) minutes. Cocaethylene (only in the combination): half-life 156 (15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine, p = .001; peak 114 ng/mL (18) at 180 minutes, about 22% of the cocaine level then; AUC 31,050 (4,706), a ratio to cocaine AUC of 0.20 (0.01); concentration ratio about 0.13 at 120 minutes (time of peak heart rate and feel good) and 0.40 at 360 minutes. Alcohol levels were lower with cocaine than without, p = .008 (data not shown).
analysis.covariates: None (within-person contrasts).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration (1998). Directional hypotheses are stated from the authors' earlier single-dose study, with one planned comparison per measure and one-tailed testing at .05 (Data Analysis, p. 252).
analysis.selective_reporting: Six rating measures are reported only as 'no statistically significant findings', the alcohol comparison as 'data not shown', clinician ratings not at all, and heart rate appears as means only in a figure, with AUCs in its legend; effect sizes and intervals are never given.
analysis.power: Not discussed; 8 people, and a one-tailed p of .035 to .09 on the ratings and cocaine AUC.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8 people who already used both drugs, four intranasal cocaine doses taken with oral alcohol produced a higher heart rate over 8 hours than the same cocaine with a placebo drink (mean about 84 against 74 beats per minute, editors' calculation) or the same alcohol with placebo cocaine (about 72), a roughly 13% larger cocaine exposure (p = .035, one-tailed), cocaethylene with a half-life nearly twice that of cocaine, and higher ratings of feeling good than cocaine alone (p = .04, one-tailed), without a significant rise in ratings of any high (p = .09) or in blood pressure over cocaine alone.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract say the combination is more potent and potentially more toxic and produced greater euphoria; the abstract concludes that stronger psychological effects may encourage people to take larger amounts and so run a higher risk of toxicity; the discussion says the findings point to an increased risk of organ ischaemia, infarction and arrhythmia and that combined use is a likely factor in adverse events now attributed to cocaine alone, and credits cocaethylene with a role in the heart-rate effect.

timeline.event: Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat (Life Sciences): single doses of cocaine after alcohol, as described by Pennings et al. (2002; not read): cocaethylene formed, plasma cocaine higher, heart-rate rises additive

Farre et al. (J Pharmacol Exp Ther) and McCance-Katz et al. (Psychopharmacology), single-dose studies as described by Pennings et al. (2002; not read): cocaethylene formed, plasma cocaine up to 30% higher with alcohol, greater-than-additive or additive heart-rate rises

Perez-Reyes (Life Sciences), as described by Pennings et al. (2002; not read): when cocaine was taken 30 minutes before alcohol, plasma cocaine and heart rate did not rise above the single-drug levels
Signs et al. (as described by Pennings et al.; not read): over 1,000 emergency-room toxicology screens showed no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one

Pennings et al. review (Addiction): lists this study among 14 prospective studies and gives its heart-rate result as greater than additive and its dosing as alcohol first, neither of which this paper states

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the heart-rate, blood-cocaine and cocaethylene findings agrees with earlier single-dose laboratory studies as described in the one review read; the heart-rate result is reported there to depend on dosing order, and retrospective emergency-room data do not show a clear excess of cardiovascular problems. This multiple-dose design has no replication among the sources read; the euphoria finding is the weakest part.

funding.funder: Supported in part by US Public Health Service grants K20-DA00216 and R29-DA09573 (McCance-Katz), K02-DA00112 (Kosten), P50-DA04060 and M01-RR00125, and by the Connecticut Department of Mental Health (Acknowledgments, p. 258).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Yale Psychiatric Institute and the General Clinical Research Center; Connecticut Mental Health Center; Departments of Psychiatry and Laboratory Medicine, Yale University School of Medicine, New Haven, Connecticut.

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized, double-blind crossover study with a session of placebo for both drugs, two-tailed tests with intervals, heart rhythm and blood-pressure outcomes, both orders of dosing, smoked as well as intranasal cocaine, measured cocaethylene kinetics, and a self-administration or choice procedure to test whether the combination changes how much is taken.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three sessions)
domains.note: Order was random but how it was generated and concealed is not described, and no order or period effect is reported.
At least 2 days between sessions, longer than the half-lives measured; heart rate had not returned to baseline by 8 hours after the combination, and no check for carryover is reported.

Double-blind in form, but 1 g/kg of alcohol and intranasal cocaine are noticeable in people who take them regularly, participants knew the three possible conditions and the masking of the placebos is not described; the ratings that carry the euphoria finding are self-rated.
All 8 people appear in every analysis; completion is not stated explicitly.
Heart rate, blood pressure and drug concentrations are instrument-measured; the euphoria and well-being ratings are self-rated, and the clinician ratings are not reported.
No registration; 15 measures tested one-tailed without correction; several results given only as 'not significant' or 'data not shown'; no intervals or effect sizes.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A within-person, randomized-order, double-blind comparison with objective drug levels is a sound way to study this pair, and the heart-rate and drug-level findings are large relative to their printed spread. The overall judgment is set by the unmaskable alcohol condition, by 8 participants, by one-tailed uncorrected tests and by reporting that gives p values but few numbers. The source may be cited for what happened in these sessions: a higher heart rate and a somewhat higher cocaine exposure with the combination, cocaethylene formed only with the combination and cleared more slowly than cocaine, and no detectable blood-pressure difference from cocaine alone. It may not be cited for greater euphoria beyond the single feel-good rating, for toxicity, for additivity, for risk of heart events, or for smoked or injected cocaine.

key_findings.finding: Eight volunteers (4 men and 4 women, mean age 33 years, SE 4; 7 African-American and 1 Caucasian), non-treatment-seeking, recruited by word of mouth or newspaper advertisement and paid; actively using cocaine and alcohol together at entry with cocaine as the preferred drug; DSM-IV cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse; one also met cannabis abuse criteria. Printed usual intake: cocaine about 5 g a week (SE 7) by smoking; alcohol 14 standard drinks a week (SE 50).
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Subjects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Inpatient stay for the whole study; told to abstain from drugs and alcohol for 3 days before admission; urine drug screen and breathalyzer on admission; watched for alcohol withdrawal for the first 2 days.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Procedures, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Double-blind, within-person, three 480-minute sessions in random order, no more often than every 2 days: four doses of intranasal cocaine hydrochloride (1 mg/kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol (1 g/kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg/kg at 60 minutes, calculated to hold plasma alcohol near 100 mg/dL); the same cocaine with placebo alcohol; lactose in place of cocaine with the same alcohol. Participants knew the three possible conditions. Doses were calculated from lean body weight.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Study Design, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blood sampling and monitoring at 16 time points between -15 and 480 minutes; heart rate and blood pressure by automated monitor; cardiac rhythm monitoring for 3 hours after the last cocaine dose; analogue scales for any high, rush, sleepy, paranoid, sad or depressed, crash, desire for cocaine and feel good; a five-anchor quality-of-high scale; clinician-rated scales.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Cocaine Study Drug Administration Sessions, 1st paragraph (starts p. 251)

key_findings.finding: Analysis: AUC of each measure over the session in a repeated-measures ANOVA, then planned comparisons of the combination with each drug alone; only one set of comparisons per measure because the authors had directional hypotheses from earlier work; every test with p below .05 one-tailed counted as significant; pharmacokinetic parameters (one-compartment model) compared by paired t test.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Pharmacokinetics Analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Heart rate was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .002) or alcohol alone (p = .002) after each dose of study drug. Printed AUCs in the Figure 1 legend: combination 40,289 (SEM 940), cocaine 35,658 (647), alcohol 34,778 (933); editors' calculation (AUC / 480 minutes): mean 83.9, 74.3 and 72.5 beats per minute.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 252); Figure 1 and its legend (p. 253)
key_findings.note: Means over time appear only in the figure, an image; no heart-rate values are given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure: both cocaine conditions raised systolic and diastolic pressure; no significant difference between the combination and cocaine alone; the combination was higher than alcohol alone for systolic (p = .008) and diastolic (p = .003) pressure.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Any high was greater with the combination than with cocaine alone, approaching significance (p = .09); the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone and was higher than with alcohol alone (p = .002); feel good was higher than with cocaine alone (p = .04), peaking at 120 minutes. Cocaine alone gave no rise in feel good over the session.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 254-255, images)

key_findings.finding: Rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed, and desire for cocaine: no statistically significant findings (no values given).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Peak cocaine concentration 893 ng/mL (SEM 114) at 113 minutes with alcohol and 754 (114) at 116 minutes without; AUC 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, described as about 15% greater with alcohol (p = .035); cocaine half-life 85 (3.2) and 83 (2.9) minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starts p. 252); Table 1 (p. 255)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed means: AUC ratio 1.134 and peak ratio 1.184; the peak difference is not tested.

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene appeared only with the combination; half-life 156 (SEM 15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine (p = .001); peak 114 ng/mL (18) at 180 minutes, about 22% of the cocaine concentration then; concentration ratio to cocaine about 0.13 at 120 minutes, rising to 0.40 at 360 minutes; AUC 31,050 (4,706) ng x min/mL, a ratio of 0.20 (0.01) to the cocaine AUC.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (continued, p. 253); Table 1 (p. 255); Discussion, 4th paragraph (pp. 256-257)

key_findings.finding: Plasma alcohol was higher with alcohol alone than with the combination (p = .008; data not shown); 30 minutes after the second alcohol dose it averaged 99 mg/dL (SE 7) with cocaine and 118 (10) without. The authors suggest swallowed cocaine reduces alcohol absorption through gastric vasoconstriction.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (continued, p. 253); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 255-256)

key_findings.finding: Heart rate remained above baseline at 8 hours after the combination; the authors suggest cocaethylene, whose ratio to cocaine reached 0.40 late in the session, may matter more for heart effects than for the early high, and that it 'probably contributes minimally' to the initial high; no test separates cocaethylene from the rise in cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (pp. 256-257) and 5th paragraph (p. 257)

key_findings.finding: Stated limits: intranasal route (smoked or injected cocaine may give larger effects); participants were chosen because they already used both drugs; whether people who use both drugs differ in vulnerability, or the combination is more toxic to the brain, is unknown.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th, 7th and 9th paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Usual intake is printed as 14 standard drinks a week with a standard error of 50, and cocaine as 5 g a week with a standard error of 7: for 8 people these spreads are far larger than the means (a standard error of 50 implies a standard deviation near 140 drinks a week), so a symbol or figure is misprinted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Participants' tolerance to each drug cannot be judged from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and title say the combination produced greater euphoria and is more potent, but any high rose only to p = .09 and the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone; only feel good differed (p = .04, one-tailed, which is about .08 two-tailed by the editors' calculation of doubling).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the study for a higher feel-good rating, not for a general increase in euphoria.

reporting_issues.issue: All tests are one-tailed at .05, justified by hypotheses taken from the authors' earlier study, with no correction across 15 measures; the cocaine AUC (p = .035) and feel-good (p = .04) results would not be significant at .05 two-tailed (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The heart-rate result (p = .002) survives; the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results are fragile.

reporting_issues.issue: Cocaine AUC is described as about 15% greater with alcohol, but the printed means give 13.4% (153,562 against 135,371); the peak values have the same printed standard error (114) and the peak difference is untested; heart-rate means are shown only in a figure, with no table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote exposure as roughly 13% to 15% higher; do not quote a heart-rate difference in beats per minute except as the editors' calculation from the AUCs.

reporting_issues.issue: Clinician-rated analogue scales were collected as a method of 'observing and confirming drug effects' but their results are absent; six rating items and the alcohol-level comparison are reported without values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unreported measures cannot be weighed; negative findings are known only as 'not significant' in 8 people.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusions that stronger psychological effects will lead people to take more and that toxicity will follow, and the discussion's statement that the findings point to an increased risk of ischaemia, infarction and arrhythmia, go beyond what was measured: there was no self-administration procedure and no heart events or rhythm findings are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the study for heart rate and drug levels, not for clinical harm or for a change in how much is taken.

reporting_issues.issue: Doses were fixed by body weight and given intranasally on a fixed schedule to people who usually smoked cocaine, and the second alcohol dose was timed to hold a target blood level; the paper presents this as closer to street practice than single-dose studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the doses and timing as study conditions, not as what happens outside the laboratory.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 250-259 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/McCanceKatz_1998_CocaineAlcoholMultipleDose.pdf), full text including the reference list; Table 1 and Figure 1 (with its legend) checked on rendered pages 253 and 255; Figures 2 to 4 are images and no values were read from them.

design_detail: Literature review (Addiction 2002;97:773-783; eleven pages, about 80 references) by three toxicologists at the Toxicology Laboratory, Leiden University Medical Center. It describes a search of Medline (from 1963), the Science Citation Index/Web of Science (from 1988) and Toxline (from 1980) in May to June 1999, repeated in October 2001, with English-language, human-only inclusion rules, but gives no count of records found, screened or excluded, no appraisal tool and no method of synthesis, so it is treated here as a narrative review. Results are split into prospective (laboratory) studies, summarised in Table 1 (14 studies), and retrospective studies (surveys, hospital, death and treatment samples); Tables 2 to 4 condense them. Read in full from the PDF, including the reference list; Tables 1 to 4 were checked on rendered pages 775 and 776. None of the cited studies was read for this card except McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998), which this library has read and which is used below to check how the review describes it.
can_establish: How three toxicologists, searching to 2001, summarised what small placebo-controlled laboratory studies and mostly uncontrolled retrospective studies had found about alcohol and cocaine taken together: blood levels, cocaethylene, heart rate, ratings of high and drunkenness, performance, and links to violence and other outcomes; and where they thought the evidence was thin.
cannot_establish: How large or how certain any effect is (no pooled estimate, no intervals, no counts of studies found or excluded); whether the combination adds more than the sum of its parts (the review itself says most studies do not test this); anything about smoked cocaine or about repeated high doses, which the laboratory studies did not use; whether cocaethylene or the higher cocaine level explains any heart-rate rise; whether the combination causes heart attacks or deaths (no controlled study of these is described); or what the primary studies found beyond what the review says about them.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (literature review). The 14 prospective studies in Table 1 had from 6 to 34 people each (13 had 12 or fewer; 147 participations in all by the editors' sum, with possible overlap between studies); the review does not describe who the volunteers were. Retrospective studies range from a national household survey of more than 25,000 people (1997) to a single case report; their number is not stated.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Retrospective studies were included if they identified people who had used both alcohol and cocaine. Prospective studies were included if they used placebos, blind evaluation, a crossover design and appropriate presentation of data and statistics (Table 1); two between-subjects studies were kept despite design flaws. Excluded: studies comparing only alcohol with cocaine, studies not in humans, studies of 'polydrug' use and studies not in English (p. 774).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Prospective studies all gave cocaine intranasally or by injection and never smoked (p. 774), mostly as single doses of 48 to 100 mg or 1.25 to 2 mg/kg, to volunteers whose drug history the review does not describe; the review itself says repeated high doses were not studied for ethical reasons, so toxicity of heavy binge use may be underestimated (p. 781). Retrospective studies sample people in emergency rooms, treatment programmes, crime and death records, who differ from people who combine the drugs and are never seen in these settings.

exposure.measurement: As described in the cited studies; not independently reported by the review. Blood levels of cocaine, cocaethylene and alcohol were measured in the laboratory studies; the retrospective studies rely on self-report, urine and blood tests in emergency rooms, and post-mortem findings.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, from Table 1: alcohol 0.5 to 1 g/kg (or 19.4 to 58.1 g) in most studies; cocaine intranasal, 48 to 100 mg or 1.25 to 2 mg/kg in most, 0.6 mg/kg intravenous in one and a radioactive tracer dose in one; one study gave four intranasal doses of 1 mg/kg (McCance-Katz and colleagues, 1998). In most studies the placebo was itself a 4 mg or 5 mg dose of cocaine (Table 1, footnote a).
exposure.polysubstance: 'Polydrug' studies were excluded from the review, yet several retrospective studies include people who also used other drugs (for example, the review's case report of a death involved cocaine, alcohol and cannabis); other-drug use is not controlled in the summaries.

comparison.controls: Prospective: placebo-controlled within-person crossover in 12 of 14 studies; two between-subjects studies (Pirwitz and colleagues, 1995, with 34 people having heart catheterisation for a medical reason; Volkow and Fowler, 1994, 7 people, no placebo and no blinding). Retrospective: many studies compare people who used both drugs with people who used cocaine alone and have no alcohol-only comparison group, which the review points out several times (pp. 778-779).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: In retrospective studies the people who combine the drugs differ in how much alcohol and cocaine they take, how they take cocaine (for example, smoked or not) and other features; the review notes this for some studies (Castaneda and colleagues, 1995; Easton and Bauer, 1997) but offers no adjusted analysis.

outcomes.instruments: Outcomes are those of the cited studies: heart rate, blood pressure, rate-pressure product, coronary artery diameter, rating scales for high and drunkenness, performance tests, EEG, blood levels, hospital and death records, interviews.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Effects are judged as additive, 'greater-than-additive' (called potentiation by the review), subtractive or inhibitive, after Berenbaum (1977, 1989); the review says only a few studies met Berenbaum's criterion of at least two active doses of each drug, and uses 'potentiation' loosely for that reason (p. 774).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable; no statistical synthesis.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the review.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled analysis. Figures the review gives from other studies: blood cocaine up to 30% higher when cocaine was given with or after alcohol (five studies; Table 1 gives 30% for a 6-person study and 15% for McCance-Katz and colleagues, 1998); blood alcohol unchanged or about 10% lower (non-significant) when cocaine followed alcohol; 57 of 451 cocaine-positive hospital urine samples (12.6%) contained cocaethylene (Bailey, 1995); 88% of people positive for both alcohol and cocaine in more than 1,000 emergency-room screens had cocaethylene (Signs and colleagues, 1996); 21 of 600 and 12 of 285 fatally injured drivers positive for both drugs (Los Angeles County; Spain); 40% against 26% severely beating someone and 39% against 24% threatening with a weapon among 320 male veterans in cocaine treatment who used the combination against cocaine alone (Denison and colleagues, 1997); three times and five times as likely to have homicidal ideas or plans as people who used alcohol only or cocaine only (Salloum and colleagues, 1996).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol; search dates are given (May to June 1999, repeated October 2001).
analysis.selective_reporting: No counts of records identified, screened or excluded; no list of the retrospective studies considered; no appraisal of the prospective studies beyond the inclusion filter; the two included studies with a between-subjects design, one of which had no placebo and no blinding, do not meet the review's own stated inclusion rules.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the review does not comment that most laboratory studies had 12 or fewer people.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Fourteen small laboratory studies, with caveats the review lists, found that alcohol taken with or before cocaine was followed by higher blood cocaine (up to 30%) and by cocaethylene, that heart-rate rises were at least additive, with a trend towards greater than additive in most studies (the review says only a few had the two active doses of each drug needed to test this), that ratings of cocaine high tended to rise and ratings of drunkenness tended to fall a little (Table 1 labels two of the three reported falls non-significant), and that cocaine lessened some alcohol-impaired test performance; one 6-person study that gave alcohol after cocaine did not find the heart-rate or blood-cocaine excess. Retrospective studies show frequent co-use, no clear cardiovascular excess in emergency-room data but without alcohol-only comparison groups, and mostly alcohol-attributable violence with one study of homicidal ideas pointing to more than alcohol or cocaine alone.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says there is generally no evidence that the combination does more than add up the effects of each drug, with exceptions: cocaine works against alcohol's deficits; heart-rate effects 'tend' to be greater than additive; cocaethylene 'may potentiate' cardiotoxic effects; and, 'more importantly', retrospective data suggest the combination can potentiate violent thoughts and threats. Table 3 gives a 'greater-than-additive increase' in high, and Table 4 gives a 'more-than-additive risk' of birth defects. The conclusions say the combination does not cause more cardiovascular problems than expected from additive effects.

timeline.event: Foltin and Fischman (Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior; as described by this review, not read): greater-than-additive heart-rate effects with smaller doses and additive effects with higher doses of alcohol and cocaine
Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat (Life Sciences; as described by this review, not read): alcohol before cocaine; additive heart-rate rise, higher blood cocaine and cocaethylene
Farre and colleagues and McCance-Katz and colleagues (as described by this review, not read): cocaethylene formed and blood cocaine higher with alcohol
Perez-Reyes (Life Sciences; as described by this review, not read): 6 people; alcohol 30 minutes after cocaine; no excess in blood cocaine or heart rate; cocaethylene still formed
McCance-Katz, Kosten and Jatlow: four doses of intranasal cocaine in 8 people; heart rate and blood cocaine higher with alcohol, cocaethylene formed
This review; no later laboratory studies are included

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source. The laboratory findings it summarises (higher blood cocaine, cocaethylene, a heart-rate rise at least as large as the sum, a modest fall in drunkenness ratings) come from about a dozen studies of 6 to 12 people each, several of which share first authors (Farre, Foltin, Higgins, McCance-Katz, Perez-Reyes) and so may not be independent; the review does not discuss this. The only primary study of the 14 that this library has read (McCance-Katz and colleagues, 1998) agrees in direction, but the review describes it in ways the primary paper does not support (see reporting issues).

funding.funder: The Nationaal Instituut voor Gezondheidsbevordering en Ziektepreventie (NIGZ), the Brijderstichting and the Jellinek (Acknowledgements, p. 781); the paper does not say what these bodies are or what they funded beyond 'this study'.
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Toxicology Laboratory, Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden, the Netherlands. None of the three authors appears in the reference list.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a registered protocol, counts at each step, a risk-of-bias judgment for each primary study and effect sizes with intervals; new placebo-controlled studies with at least two doses of each drug, both orders of dosing, smoked cocaine, heart rhythm and blood-pressure outcomes and a test of additivity; and cohort or case-crossover studies of heart events and injury that include alcohol-only and cocaine-only comparison groups.

domains.note: Databases, years, search terms, language and design rules are stated, and the search was repeated before revision; but no counts of records found or excluded, no screening method and no list of retrospective studies are given.

Prospective studies were filtered on placebo, blinding, crossover and data presentation; the review repeatedly points out missing alcohol-only comparison groups, between-subjects designs and untested tracer doses; but it does not comment on sample sizes of 6 to 12 people, one-tailed testing, or the 4 to 5 mg cocaine placebo.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the three authors appears in the reference list.

Mechanisms are hedged in the text ('may be due to', 'one possible explanation'), and the text says the cocaethylene discussion 'may be premature'; but the abstract says cocaethylene 'may potentiate' cardiotoxic effects, Table 3 states a greater-than-additive rise in high, and Table 4 states a more-than-additive risk of birth defects from one case report.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the main conclusions
domains.note: The text reports contrary findings (no cardiovascular excess in emergency-room data; people using both drugs doing better on some tests; one laboratory study with no excess when alcohol followed cocaine), but the abstract gives violence the weight of 'more importantly' although the two violent-behaviour studies lack alcohol-only comparison groups and the one controlled study, which concerns thoughts, needs replication, as the review says.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is more transparent than most narrative reviews about how studies were found, and it points out many weaknesses in its sources; but it cannot show that its set of studies is complete, it summarises effect sizes only as a 'trend towards greater-than-additive' and as 'up to' figures, and it describes at least one primary study in ways that study does not support. It may be cited for what a 2002 review reported about blood cocaine, cocaethylene, heart rate and ratings of drunkenness in small laboratory studies, for the rates of co-use it quotes, and for its own list of what the retrospective evidence lacks. It may not be cited for the size of any effect, for an order-of-dosing rule, for toxicity of the combination, for violence, or for birth defects.

key_findings.finding: The abstract concludes there is generally no evidence that alcohol and cocaine together do more than add up the effects of each drug, with exceptions: cocaine consistently works against alcohol-induced deficits in learning, psychomotor performance and driving; heart-rate effects tend to be greater than additive, with up to 30% higher blood cocaine; cocaethylene may potentiate cardiotoxic effects; and retrospective data suggest the combination can potentiate violent thoughts and threats.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: Search: Medline (from 1963), Science Citation Index/Web of Science (from 1988) and Toxline (from 1980); done May to June 1999 and repeated October 2001. Excluded: studies comparing only alcohol with cocaine, studies not in humans, studies of 'polydrug' use and studies not in English. No count of records identified, screened or excluded is given.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (continues onto p. 774) and 2nd paragraph (p. 774); Inclusion and exclusion, 1st paragraph (p. 774)

key_findings.finding: Prospective studies were included if they used placebos, blind evaluation, a crossover design and appropriate data presentation; two between-subjects studies were kept despite design flaws (Pirwitz and colleagues, 1995, with heart catheterisation for a medical reason; Volkow and Fowler, 1994, with radiolabelled tracer). Prospective studies gave cocaine only intranasally or intravenously, never smoked. Only a few studies had at least two active doses of each drug, so the review uses 'potentiation' in place of 'synergism'.
key_findings.locator: Inclusion and exclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists 14 prospective studies with 6 to 34 people each (13 had 12 or fewer). Alcohol 0.5 to 1 g/kg in most; cocaine intranasal, mostly 48 to 100 mg or 1.25 to 2 mg/kg; in most studies the placebo was a 4 mg or 5 mg dose of cocaine. Pirwitz and colleagues are listed as 'within' although the text calls that study between-subjects.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and footnote a
key_findings.note: Study conditions only.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol-induced deficits in the laboratory were consistently lessened by cocaine: digit-symbol substitution (Foltin and colleagues, 1993; Higgins and colleagues, 1993), sedation (Foltin and colleagues, 1993), and learning and psychomotor performance (Higgins and colleagues, 1992).
key_findings.locator: Results > Prospective research > Behavioural

key_findings.finding: Heart rate: when cocaine was given at the same time as or after alcohol, most studies showed a trend towards greater-than-additive effects but did not support the idea that the effects are synergistic; studies with at least two active doses of each drug are needed. Table 1 gives greater-than-additive rises in four studies (Farre 1993, Farre 1997, Higgins 1993, McCance-Katz 1998), additive rises in two (McCance-Katz 1993; Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat, 1992), and greater-than-additive rises at smaller doses with additive rises at higher doses in one (Foltin and Fischman, 1988).
key_findings.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 1st paragraph (p. 774); Table 1 (p. 775)

key_findings.finding: One study of 34 people (Pirwitz and colleagues, 1995) found that the combination raised the rate-pressure product (a measure of the heart's oxygen demand) with a concomitant rise in the width of the coronary artery; the review says the limits of its between-subjects design apply.
key_findings.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Order of dosing: in a 6-person study with alcohol given 30 minutes after cocaine (35 in Table 1), heart-rate increases were additive in the text and 'no effect' in Table 1, blood cocaine was not higher than with cocaine alone, and 'high' did not change, whereas with alcohol first the earlier studies found greater-than-additive heart-rate rises; cocaethylene formed in both. The review calls alcohol before cocaine the more common order, without a source.
key_findings.locator: Heart rate, 2nd paragraph (pp. 774, 776); Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 776); Effect on perceived inebriation, 2nd paragraph (p. 777); Table 1 (p. 775)
key_findings.note: One small study; cited here as a limit on how far the heart-rate and blood-level results generalise, not as a finding about what people do.

key_findings.finding: Blood levels: cocaine given at the same time as or after alcohol raised blood cocaine by up to 30% (five studies). Blood alcohol was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, non-significantly, in four; the review offers competitive inhibition of cocaine-metabolising esterases and cocaine-related vasoconstriction slowing alcohol absorption as possible explanations, and says cocaethylene is too small to account for the lower alcohol levels.
key_findings.locator: Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Alcohol had no effect on the uptake or clearance of radiolabelled tracer cocaine from the brain or heart in 7 people; the review notes that study had no placebo, no blinding and a tracer dose that may not generalise to active doses.
key_findings.locator: Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Perceived drunkenness: several studies found cocaine produced a slight decrease (Farre 1993, Higgins 1993, Farre 1997), one found no effect (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat, 1992); Table 1 labels the Farre falls 'non-significantly reduced drunk'. Ratings of cocaine 'high' or global intoxication were greater when alcohol was given before or with cocaine in six studies; EEG indices of intoxication matched in one (Mannelli and colleagues, 1993); alcohol pretreatment raised preference for cocaine over cash in one study (Higgins and colleagues, 1996).
key_findings.locator: Effect on perceived inebriation, 1st paragraph (pp. 776–777); Table 1 (p. 775)

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene was made only when both drugs were given, never with either alone (six studies), and was also made when alcohol came 30 minutes after cocaine. The review says it has similar behavioural and toxicological effects to cocaine, slightly less potent, and that people could not tell it from cocaine when given intranasally or by injection.
key_findings.locator: Cocaethylene production

key_findings.finding: Co-use in surveys and clinical samples: a 1990 US survey estimated about 4 million people used alcohol and cocaine at the same time in the previous month and 9 million in the previous year; in the 1997 National Household Survey (over 25,000 people) people who drank in the past month were six times as likely, and those who drank heavily eight times as likely, to have used cocaine in the past month; 43% of 3,762 emergency-room patients in 1983–1993 had used cocaine, about a third of them with alcohol; 57% and 61% of people in cocaine treatment were also alcohol-dependent; about 60% of cocaine- or crack-using patients in a methadone programme reported using alcohol to come down.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Extent of use, 1st paragraph (p. 777) and 2nd paragraph (p. 778)

key_findings.finding: Driving: retrospective research points to a major role for alcohol alone; the combination gave no definitive protection, since 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain were positive for both.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Operating motor vehicles, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cocaethylene in hospital samples: 57 of 451 cocaine-positive urine samples (12.6%) contained it, 53 from emergency or trauma patients, with higher mean blood alcohol in the positive samples (1.3 against 0.6 g/l); in 18 emergency patients positive for alcohol and cocaine, 11 had cocaethylene; in more than 1,000 emergency screens, 88% of those positive for both had it, and its level correlated with cocaine; a second laboratory found no correlation.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review says whether cocaethylene or a higher cocaine level explains the heart-rate rise is controversial and that the talk of greater cardiotoxicity may be premature: no retrospective study shows unequivocally that the combination causes more; one study of more than 1,000 emergency screens found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one; another found less chest pain but more back and limb pain with the combination, without an alcohol-only group.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 2nd paragraph (pp. 778–779)

key_findings.finding: A single case report of an 18-year-old who died suddenly of cardiotoxicity after cocaine, alcohol and cannabis (unknown dose and schedule) is set against the 1,000-patient study that found a predominant role for cocaine alone.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 3rd (last) paragraph

key_findings.finding: Violence: many studies found a predominant role for alcohol; two studies suggest more violent behaviour with the combination but have no alcohol-only comparison group (emergency-room trauma: 50% combination against 22% cocaine only; 320 male veterans in treatment: 40% against 26% severely beat someone); one 'well-designed' study found the combination three times as likely as alcohol only and five times as likely as cocaine only to go with homicidal ideas or plans, which the review says must be replicated.
key_findings.locator: Retrospective studies > Violence, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Neuropsychology: mixed; four studies found people using the combination in some ways better off than those using one drug; the review suggests that opposing effects or differences in dose and route (for example, less smoked crack) may explain this.
key_findings.locator: Neuropsychology and psychiatry, paragraph beginning 'There are four studies' (p. 780)

key_findings.finding: Birth defects: a single case report of one child exposed to both drugs in pregnancy; Table 4 records this as 'more-than-additive risk (one report found)'.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 776); Liver function, HIV risk and teratology, last paragraph (p. 780)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: prospective studies show greater feeling of intoxication from the combination (high), no or opposing effect on alcohol drunkenness and lessened alcohol deficits; heart-rate increases 'statistically additive' with a trend towards greater than additive; retrospective studies suggest no more cardiovascular problems than additive expectations and show flawed emergency-room data lacking alcohol-only controls; high repeated cocaine doses have not been studied, so the behavioural toxicity of heavy binge use with alcohol may be underestimated.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes the participants of McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998) as showing the usual 'alcohol first' pattern of effects, with greater-than-additive increases in heart rate, plasma cocaine and 'high'; the primary paper gave the first cocaine dose first with alcohol immediately after (as the review's own Table 1 footnote b says), compared the combination only with each drug alone (never against the sum), and found 'any high' not significant (p = .09).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's table and text overstate this study; cite the primary paper for what it found. The same slip may affect other rows, which could not be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Table 3 say the combination gives a 'greater-than-additive' rise in high, but the text and Table 1 show additive effects (Mannelli 1993; McCance-Katz 1993), no or variable effects (Higgins 1993; Perez-Reyes 1994) and non-significant increases (Farre 1993, 1997).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the text, not Table 3, for how consistent the 'high' findings are.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says retrospective data suggest the combination potentiates violent thoughts and threats and calls this 'more importantly' a finding, but in the text the two violent-behaviour studies lack alcohol-only comparison groups and the one controlled study concerns homicidal ideas, not threats, and 'must be replicated'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The weight the abstract gives to violence is not supported by the studies as the review describes them.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 states 'more-than-additive risk (one report found)' for birth defects, and the text shows that report is a single case of one child.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single case cannot show risk of any size; the table treats a case report as a risk statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says cocaethylene 'may potentiate' cardiotoxic effects, while the text says that part of the discussion may be premature, that no retrospective study shows greater cardiotoxicity, and that the best-sized study (over 1,000 emergency screens) found no excess with the combination.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text, not the abstract, represents the evidence on heart harm.

reporting_issues.issue: The 1990 US survey figures on simultaneous use of alcohol and cocaine are cited to a paper whose title (Grant and Harford, 1990) concerns alcohol with sedatives and tranquilizers; the source was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: The attribution cannot be checked here; use the survey figures only as quoted by the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's summary of blood alcohol (no effect or about a 10% non-significant fall) omits McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998), whose own paper reports significantly lower blood alcohol with cocaine (p = .008; 99 against 118 mg/dL, 30 minutes after the second drink).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review understates the fall in blood alcohol seen in the one multiple-dose study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says cocaine consistently works against alcohol-induced learning, psychomotor and driving deficits, but the text describes no prospective test of driving (the laboratory findings concern digit-symbol substitution, sedation, learning and psychomotor tasks), and the retrospective section and the conclusions say alcohol alone has the major role in driving deficits, with no evidence that cocaine adds to them and no definitive protection from them (21 of 600 and 12 of 285 fatally injured drivers positive for both).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the laboratory findings for test performance only; the review gives no basis for saying that cocaine lessens the effect of alcohol on driving.

reporting_issues.issue: Small details do not match between the table and the text: Pirwitz and colleagues are 'within' in Table 1 but between-subjects in the text; Perez-Reyes (1994) has 'no effect on heart rate' and alcohol 35 minutes after cocaine in Table 1 but additive heart-rate rises and 30 minutes in the text; two studies by Foltin give different middle alcohol doses (38.7 and 38.1 g) in Table 1; the Volkow and Fowler study fails the review's own inclusion rules (no placebo, no blinding) but is included.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary tables cannot be relied on for detail without the primary papers.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 773-783 (PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Pennings_2002_AlcoholCocaineConcurrent.pdf), full text including Tables 1 to 4 and the reference list; Tables 1 to 4 checked against rendered pages 775 and 776. The cited primary studies were not read except McCance-Katz and colleagues (1998).

design_detail: Review article in the 'New Horizons' series of Addiction (1999;94(7):961-972; twelve pages, about 60 references) by two pharmacologists at the University of Adelaide, based on a paper given at the International Opioid Overdose Symposium, Sydney, August 1997. It has no methods section: no search, selection criteria or appraisal is described. It covers the anatomy and chemistry of breathing control, opioid receptors, metabolism of heroin and methadone, tolerance, partial agonists, antagonists, and interactions with sedatives (alcohol and benzodiazepines) and stimulants, then lists research gaps. Much of the mechanism rests on animal and laboratory work, as the review says (p. 962). Read in full from the PDF, including the reference list; Figures 1 and 2 are diagrams and carry no data.
can_establish: How two pharmacologists described, in 1998, the receptor and brain-stem basis of opioid-induced breathing depression, why alcohol and benzodiazepines would be expected to add to it, and why loss or incompleteness of tolerance might raise the risk of fatal overdose; it points to primary sources and names open questions.
cannot_establish: How often or how strongly alcohol or benzodiazepines raise the risk of a fatal opioid overdose in people (no human interaction study is described; the section on interactions cites no study of its own); how quickly tolerance is lost after a break in use, or for how long (the review says information on this is sparse); whether the review's list of studies is complete (no search was done); anything about opioid-involved deaths that is not breathing depression.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review; no search described). Human evidence is drawn from a few small studies of methadone maintenance patients (tolerance), post-mortem concentration studies (Darke and colleagues, 1997), one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro and colleagues, 1998), a study of volunteers given naltrexone, and clinical data on buprenorphine; most mechanisms rest on animal work.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated: no criteria for choosing the references.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The studies cited were chosen by the authors; the review says that much of the understanding of breathing control arises from animal models (p. 962) and that post-mortem drug measurements may not reflect the situation at the time of death (p. 965).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Exposure is described as in the cited literature: opioids (heroin, morphine, methadone, fentanyl, buprenorphine), alcohol, benzodiazepines, antagonists (naloxone, naltrexone), stimulants (caffeine).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the review's conclusions; doses quoted from the cited studies (for example, a caffeine quantity 'in a few cups of strong coffee') are not recorded in this library.
exposure.polysubstance: A section on 'Opioid-drug interactions' covers sedatives (alcohol, benzodiazepines) and stimulants; the review says many overdoses involve combined effects of opioids with other drugs, but cites no source at that point.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Respiratory rate, tidal volume, chemoreceptor sensitivity, post-mortem drug concentrations and hair concentrations, as measured in the cited studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: The review cautions that post-mortem drug levels vary with time after death, tissue sampled and body site, and that post-mortem metabolism or breakdown is possible; it treats heroin concentration data with 'some caution' (p. 965).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None given for interactions. Figures quoted from other work: methadone half-life estimates from 15 to 55 hours across studies (Wolff and colleagues, 1997); fewer than 10% of Caucasians are poor metabolizers of CYP 2D6; in a naltrexone study (Cornish and colleagues) a dose of morphine that caused mild to moderate breathing depression was equally effective before and after two weeks of naltrexone; buprenorphine's effect on breathing rate reaches a plateau with rising dose (Walsh and colleagues, 1995). No effect sizes or intervals are given for tolerance or interaction effects.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged; the review does not state how many human studies of interactions or tolerance exist.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative synthesis, to 1998, of the neuropharmacology of breathing depression by opioids: mu (and delta) receptor actions in brain-stem breathing centres and chemoreceptors; GABA-A as the main inhibitory transmitter, on which benzodiazepines and alcohol act (alcohol also reduces excitation at the NMDA receptor); incomplete and possibly slower tolerance to breathing depression than to other effects, shown in two small studies of methadone maintenance patients; and a hair study in which people who died of overdose had lower morphine content than people who were currently using, read as a possible loss of tolerance. No study of an opioid with alcohol or a benzodiazepine in people is described in the interactions section.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the pharmacology 'explains the potential for interaction of opioids with benzodiazepines and alcohol'; the text says there is 'considerable evidence' that many overdoses are due to combined effects, that the interaction effects 'should be at least additive', that tolerance 'could also account for' the relatively high risk after a period of abstinence, and that a relatively high risk among people with long experience of opioids 'may' follow incomplete tolerance. Most of these are hedged as possibilities. Gaps: (1) the 'considerable evidence' sentence has no citation and the section cites no human interaction study; (2) the additive prediction comes from receptor reasoning, not from measurement in people; (3) the loss-of-tolerance statement rests on one hair-analysis study, with the review itself saying that information on the rate of loss is sparse.

timeline.event: Marks and Goldring: tolerance to the breathing-depressant effect of methadone shown to be incomplete in maintenance patients (as described by this review; not read)
Santiago, Pugliese and Edelman: incomplete tolerance to the hypoxia-sensitive part of the breathing response in methadone patients (as described by this review; not read)
Siegel: more overdoses than expected happened in a setting where the person had not used heroin before, read as lessened tolerance in an unfamiliar setting (as described by this review; not read)
Tagliaro and colleagues (Lancet), hair analysis: morphine content lower in people who died of heroin overdose than in people who were currently using (as described by this review; not read)
This review
Hickman and colleagues cite this review for the statement that overdose risk rises after incarceration or detoxification, which this review does not state

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary mechanistic source. Its account of how alcohol and benzodiazepines depress breathing, and of why tolerance to breathing depression may be incomplete, was later cited by the observational papers in this library as support for an interaction; the review itself offers a mechanism and a prediction, not a measured interaction in people. Its statements about loss of tolerance rest on one published hair study and two small methadone studies, none read here.
